UnadjustedLangevin/StrongConvexity.lean.title: Supporting planes and strong monotonicity
UnadjustedLangevin/StrongConvexity.lean.summary:
Throughout this section \(H\) is a real inner-product space with inner product \(\langle\cdot,\cdot angle\) and norm \(\|v\|=\langle v,v angle^{1/2}\); from the second step on, \(H\) is in addition complete, that is, a real Hilbert space. A function \(f:H o\mathbb R\) is convex if \(f(au+bv)\le af(u)+bf(v)\) for all \(u,v\in H\) and all \(a,b\ge0\) with \(a+b=1\). For a real number \(m\) (of any sign), \(f\) is \(m\)-strongly convex if

\[f(au+bv)\le af(u)+bf(v)- rac m2\,ab\,\|u-v\|^2\qquad ext{for all }u,v\in H ext{ and }a,b\ge0 ext{ with }a+b=1.\]

The function \(f\) is differentiable at \(x\) if there is a continuous linear functional \(Df(x):H o\mathbb R\), the derivative, with \(f(x+u)=f(x)+Df(x)[u]+o(\|u\|)\) as \(u o0\). When \(H\) is a Hilbert space, the Riesz representation theorem provides a unique vector \( abla f(x)\in H\), the gradient, such that \(Df(x)[u]=\langle abla f(x),u angle\) for every \(u\in H\).

For a function \(f\) that is differentiable at every point we prove three first-order inequalities: the supporting-plane inequality \(f(x)+Df(x)[y-x]\le f(y)\) when \(f\) is convex; the quadratic lower bound \(f(x)+\langle abla f(x),y-x angle+ rac m2\|y-x\|^2\le f(y)\) when \(f\) is \(m\)-strongly convex; and the strong monotonicity of the gradient, \(m\|x-y\|^2\le\langle abla f(x)- abla f(y),x-y angle\), under the same hypothesis. Only first derivatives occur. The quadratic lower bound is used in the sharp contraction estimate for the gradient step and in the tail bounds for the Gibbs measure; strong monotonicity is used in the first one-step estimate for the unadjusted Langevin algorithm.

steps.title: The supporting-plane inequality
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(H\) be a real inner-product space and let \(f:H\to\mathbb R\) be convex on \(H\) and differentiable at every point of \(H\). Then for all \(x,y\in H\),

\[f(x)+Df(x)[y-x]\le f(y).\]

Proof. Fix \(x,y\in H\). Define the affine map \(\ell:\mathbb R\to H\), \(\ell(t)=x+t(y-x)\), and the real function \(\varphi=f\circ\ell\), so that \(\varphi(0)=f(x)\) and \(\varphi(1)=f(y)\).

(a) \(\varphi\) is convex. Let \(s,t\in\mathbb R\) and \(a,b\ge0\) with \(a+b=1\). Because \(\ell\) is affine and \(a+b=1\), \(\ell(as+bt)=x+(as+bt)(y-x)=a\,\ell(s)+b\,\ell(t)\). Convexity of \(f\) gives

\[\varphi(as+bt)=f\bigl(a\,\ell(s)+b\,\ell(t)\bigr)\le af(\ell(s))+bf(\ell(t))=a\varphi(s)+b\varphi(t).\]

(b) \(\varphi\) is differentiable at \(0\) with \(\varphi'(0)=Df(x)[y-x]\). For \(s\ne0\) the difference quotient of \(\ell\) is \((\ell(t+s)-\ell(t))/s=y-x\), so \(\ell\) is differentiable with \(\ell'(t)=y-x\) for every \(t\); moreover \(\ell(0)=x\). By the chain rule for the composition of the differentiable curve \(\ell\) with the function \(f\), which is differentiable at \(\ell(0)=x\),

\[\varphi'(0)=Df(x)[\ell'(0)]=Df(x)[y-x].\]

(c) The derivative at \(0\) is at most the slope of the secant over \([0,1]\). Let \(0<t\le1\). Writing \(t=(1-t)\cdot0+t\cdot1\) and applying (a) with \(a=1-t\), \(b=t\),

\[\varphi(t)\le(1-t)\varphi(0)+t\varphi(1).\]

Subtracting \(\varphi(0)\) and dividing by \(t>0\) gives

\[\frac{\varphi(t)-\varphi(0)}{t}\le\varphi(1)-\varphi(0)\qquad(0<t\le1).\qquad(1)\]

As \(t\downarrow0\), the left-hand side of (1) converges to \(\varphi'(0)\) by (b), while the right-hand side does not depend on \(t\). Passing to the limit in (1) yields \(\varphi'(0)\le\varphi(1)-\varphi(0)\).

(d) Conclusion. Substituting \(\varphi'(0)=Df(x)[y-x]\), \(\varphi(0)=f(x)\) and \(\varphi(1)=f(y)\) gives \(Df(x)[y-x]\le f(y)-f(x)\), which is the claim after adding \(f(x)\) to both sides. \(\square\)

Only the differentiability of \(f\) at the base point \(x\) and the values of \(f\) on the segment from \(x\) to \(y\) were used. Completeness of \(H\) is not needed, since no gradient appears.

steps.title: The quadratic lower bound
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(m\in\mathbb R\), and let \(f:H\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable at every point and \(m\)-strongly convex on \(H\). Then for all \(x,y\in H\),

\[f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac m2\|y-x\|^2\le f(y).\]

Proof. Define the shifted function \(g(v)=f(v)-\frac m2\|v\|^2\) on \(H\).

(a) \(g\) is convex. We first verify the identity

\[a\|u\|^2+b\|v\|^2-\|au+bv\|^2=ab\|u-v\|^2\qquad(u,v\in H,\ a+b=1).\qquad(1)\]

Indeed, \(\|au+bv\|^2=a^2\|u\|^2+2ab\langle u,v\rangle+b^2\|v\|^2\), and \(a-a^2=a(1-a)=ab\), \(b-b^2=b(1-b)=ab\); hence the left-hand side of (1) equals \(ab(\|u\|^2-2\langle u,v\rangle+\|v\|^2)=ab\|u-v\|^2\). Now let \(a,b\ge0\) with \(a+b=1\). By strong convexity and then by (1),

\[\begin{aligned}g(au+bv)&=f(au+bv)-\tfrac m2\|au+bv\|^2\\&\le af(u)+bf(v)-\tfrac m2\bigl(ab\|u-v\|^2+\|au+bv\|^2\bigr)\\&=af(u)+bf(v)-\tfrac m2\bigl(a\|u\|^2+b\|v\|^2\bigr)=ag(u)+bg(v).\end{aligned}\]

(Read backwards, the same computation shows that convexity of \(g\) is equivalent to \(m\)-strong convexity of \(f\).)

(b) \(g\) is differentiable, with \(Dg(v)[u]=\langle\nabla f(v),u\rangle-m\langle v,u\rangle\). Expanding the square, \(\|v+u\|^2=\|v\|^2+2\langle v,u\rangle+\|u\|^2\), and \(\|u\|^2=o(\|u\|)\) as \(u\to0\). Hence \(v\mapsto\|v\|^2\) is differentiable at every \(v\) with derivative \(u\mapsto2\langle v,u\rangle\). Differentiability is preserved by scalar multiples and differences, so \(g\) is differentiable and \(Dg(v)[u]=Df(v)[u]-\frac m2\cdot2\langle v,u\rangle\). The definition of the gradient gives \(Df(v)[u]=\langle\nabla f(v),u\rangle\).

(c) The supporting plane of \(g\). By (a), (b) and the supporting-plane inequality of the previous step, applied to \(g\) at the points \(x,y\),

\[f(x)-\frac m2\|x\|^2+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle-m\langle x,y-x\rangle\le f(y)-\frac m2\|y\|^2.\qquad(2)\]

(d) Rearrangement. Expanding \(\langle x,y-x\rangle=\langle x,y\rangle-\|x\|^2\),

\[\|y\|^2-\|x\|^2-2\langle x,y-x\rangle=\|y\|^2-2\langle x,y\rangle+\|x\|^2=\|y-x\|^2.\qquad(3)\]

Adding \(\frac m2\|y\|^2\) to both sides of (2) and using (3) gives \(f(x)+\langle\nabla f(x),y-x\rangle+\frac m2\|y-x\|^2\le f(y)\). \(\square\)

No sign condition on \(m\) is needed. Completeness of \(H\) is used only to define the gradient through the Riesz representation theorem. If \(\nabla f(x)=0\), the claim reads \(f(y)\ge f(x)+\frac m2\|y-x\|^2\): a minimiser of an \(m\)-strongly convex function with \(m>0\) is surpassed quadratically by every other value.

steps.title: Strong monotonicity of the gradient
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, \(m\in\mathbb R\), and let \(f:H o\mathbb R\) be differentiable at every point and \(m\)-strongly convex on \(H\). Then for all \(x,y\in H\),

\[m\|x-y\|^2\le\langle abla f(x)- abla f(y),x-y angle.\]

Proof. Let \(g(v)=f(v)- rac m2\|v\|^2\). By parts (a) and (b) of the previous proof, \(g\) is convex and differentiable with \(Dg(v)[u]=\langle abla f(v),u angle-m\langle v,u angle\). Apply the supporting-plane inequality of the first step to \(g\) twice, at the pair \((x,y)\) and at the pair \((y,x)\):

\[ egin{aligned}g(x)+\langle abla f(x),y-x angle-m\langle x,y-x angle&\le g(y),\ g(y)+\langle abla f(y),x-y angle-m\langle y,x-y angle&\le g(x).\end{aligned}\]

Adding the two inequalities, the values \(g(x)+g(y)\) cancel and

\[\langle abla f(x),y-x angle+\langle abla f(y),x-y angle-m igl(\langle x,y-x angle+\langle y,x-y angle igr)\le0.\qquad(1)\]

Since \(y-x=-(x-y)\), linearity of the inner product gives

\[ egin{aligned}\langle abla f(x),y-x angle+\langle abla f(y),x-y angle&=-\langle abla f(x)- abla f(y),x-y angle,\\langle x,y-x angle+\langle y,x-y angle&=-\langle x-y,x-y angle\&=-\|x-y\|^2.\end{aligned}\]

Substituting both identities into (1) gives \(-\langle abla f(x)- abla f(y),x-y angle+m\|x-y\|^2\le0\), which is the claim. \(\square\)

Equivalently, the claim is the sum of the quadratic lower bounds of the previous step at \((x,y)\) and at \((y,x)\). For \(m=0\) it is the monotonicity \(\langle abla f(x)- abla f(y),x-y angle\ge0\) of the gradient of a differentiable convex function.

The rewrites with (hg x).fderiv and (hg y).fderiv insert the derivative formula, and the simp only call with ← inner_gradient_left expresses all derivatives through gradients.

UnadjustedLangevin/Analysis/Smooth.lean.title: The quadratic upper bound
UnadjustedLangevin/Analysis/Smooth.lean.summary:
Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, let \(L\ge0\), and let \(f:H o\mathbb R\) be differentiable at every point, with gradient \( abla f\) (the vector representing the derivative, \(Df(x)[u]=\langle abla f(x),u angle\)). The gradient is \(L\)-Lipschitz if \(\| abla f(u)- abla f(v)\|\le L\|u-v\|\) for all \(u,v\in H\). This section proves the quadratic upper bound

\[f(y)\le f(x)+\langle abla f(x),y-x angle+ rac L2\|y-x\|^2\qquad(x,y\in H),\]

often called the descent lemma. Together with the quadratic lower bound of strong convexity it yields the interpolation inequality behind the sharp contraction of the gradient step, and it is also used for the moment bounds of the Gibbs measure. The proof restricts \(f\) to the segment from \(x\) to \(y\), subtracts the linear part and the quadratic correction, and shows that the resulting function of one variable is nonincreasing; no second derivative of \(f\) is used.

steps.title: The quadratic upper bound for a Lipschitz gradient
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space and \(L\ge0\). Let \(f:H o\mathbb R\) be differentiable at every point and assume \(\| abla f(u)- abla f(v)\|\le L\|u-v\|\) for all \(u,v\in H\). Then for all \(x,y\in H\),

\[f(y)\le f(x)+\langle abla f(x),y-x angle+ rac L2\|y-x\|^2.\]

Proof. Fix \(x,y\) and put \(d=y-x\), \(a=\langle abla f(x),d angle\), \(b=\|d\|^2\). Define \(q:\mathbb R o\mathbb R\) by

\[q(t)=f(x+td)-f(x)-ta- rac L2t^2b.\]

Then \(q(0)=0\) and, since \(x+d=y\), \(q(1)=f(y)-f(x)-\langle abla f(x),y-x angle- rac L2\|y-x\|^2\). The claim is therefore the inequality \(q(1)\le q(0)\).

(a) Derivative of \(q\). The curve \(t\mapsto x+td\) has derivative \(d\) at every \(t\). By the chain rule and the definition of the gradient,

\[ rac{\mathrm d}{\mathrm dt}f(x+td)=Df(x+td)[d]=\langle abla f(x+td),d angle\qquad(t\in\mathbb R).\]

The remaining terms of \(q\) are polynomials in \(t\), with derivatives \(a\) and \( rac L2\cdot2t\,b=Ltb\). Hence \(q\) is differentiable on \(\mathbb R\) and

\[q'(t)=\langle abla f(x+td),d angle-a-Ltb.\]

(b) \(q'(t)\le0\) for \(0<t<1\). Let \(0<t<1\); in particular \(t\ge0\), so \(\|td\|=t\|d\|\). The Lipschitz hypothesis at the points \(x+td\) and \(x\) gives

\[\| abla f(x+td)- abla f(x)\|\le L\|td\|=Lt\|d\|.\qquad(1)\]

By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality \(\langle u,v angle\le\|u\|\|v\|\), and then by (1) multiplied by \(\|d\|\ge0\),

\[\langle abla f(x+td),d angle-a=\langle abla f(x+td)- abla f(x),d angle\le\| abla f(x+td)- abla f(x)\|\,\|d\|\le Lt\|d\|^2=Ltb.\]

By (a) this says exactly \(q'(t)\le0\).

(c) \(q\) is nonincreasing on \([0,1]\). Being differentiable on \(\mathbb R\), \(q\) is continuous on \([0,1]\) and differentiable on \((0,1)\). Let \(0\le s<t\le1\). By the mean value theorem there is \(\xi\in(s,t)\subseteq(0,1)\) with \(q(t)-q(s)=q'(\xi)(t-s)\), and this is \(\le0\) by (b). Hence \(q(t)\le q(s)\).

(d) Conclusion. By (c) with \(s=0\), \(t=1\), we get \(q(1)\le q(0)=0\), that is,

\[f(x+d)-f(x)-a- rac L2b\le0.\]

Substituting \(x+d=y\), \(a=\langle abla f(x),y-x angle\) and \(b=\|y-x\|^2\) and rearranging gives the claim. \(\square\)

Equivalently, \(f(y)-f(x)-\langle abla f(x),d angle=\int_0^1\langle abla f(x+td)- abla f(x),d angle\,dt\le\int_0^1Lt\|d\|^2\,dt= rac L2\|d\|^2\); the monotonicity argument above avoids the fundamental theorem of calculus for the derivative \(t\mapsto\langle abla f(x+td),d angle\), whose integrability would otherwise have to be checked.

UnadjustedLangevin/GradientStep.lean.title: A first estimate for the Euler step
UnadjustedLangevin/GradientStep.lean.summary:
Let \(H\) be a real inner-product space. This section compares two explicit Euler steps \(x\mapsto x-hg_x\) and \(y\mapsto y-hg_y\) with a common step size \(h\ge0\), where \(g_x,g_y\in H\) are given vectors. Write \(d=x-y\) and \(v=g_x-g_y\). If

\[m\|d\|^2\le\langle v,d\rangle\qquad\text{and}\qquad\|v\|\le L\|d\|\]

for some \(m\in\mathbb R\) and \(L\ge0\), then expanding \(\|d-hv\|^2\) gives

\[\|(x-hg_x)-(y-hg_y)\|^2\le(1-2hm+h^2L^2)\|x-y\|^2,\]

and taking square roots gives \(\|(x-hg_x)-(y-hg_y)\|\le\sqrt{1-2hm+h^2L^2}\,\|x-y\|\). Throughout, \(\sqrt s\) denotes the nonnegative square root of \(s\) when \(s\ge0\), and \(\sqrt s=0\) when \(s<0\); with this convention no sign assumption on \(1-2hm+h^2L^2\) is needed. The vectors \(g_x,g_y\) are arbitrary; in the next section they are the gradients \(\nabla U(x),\nabla U(y)\) of a strongly convex potential with Lipschitz gradient, for which the two hypotheses are strong monotonicity and the Lipschitz bound.

steps.title: The squared Euler-step bound
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(H\) be a real inner-product space, \(x,y,g_x,g_y\in H\), \(m,h\in\mathbb R\) and \(L\ge0\). Assume \(h\ge0\) and

\[m\|x-y\|^2\le\langle g_x-g_y,x-y\rangle,\qquad\|g_x-g_y\|\le L\|x-y\|.\]

Then

\[\|(x-hg_x)-(y-hg_y)\|^2\le(1-2hm+h^2L^2)\,\|x-y\|^2.\]

Proof. Write \(d=x-y\) and \(v=g_x-g_y\).

(a) Squared Lipschitz bound. Since \(0\le\|v\|\le L\|d\|\) and both sides are nonnegative (here \(L\ge0\) is used), squaring preserves the inequality:

\[\|v\|^2\le L^2\|d\|^2.\qquad(1)\]

(b) Scaled hypotheses. Multiplying the monotonicity hypothesis by \(2h\ge0\) and inequality (1) by \(h^2\ge0\),

\[2hm\|d\|^2\le2h\langle v,d\rangle,\qquad h^2\|v\|^2\le h^2L^2\|d\|^2.\qquad(2)\]

(c) Expansion. By linearity, \((x-hg_x)-(y-hg_y)=d-hv\). Expanding the square of the norm, and using \(\|hv\|=|h|\,\|v\|=h\|v\|\) because \(h\ge0\),

\[\|d-hv\|^2=\|d\|^2-2h\langle v,d\rangle+h^2\|v\|^2.\]

(d) Conclusion. Bounding \(-2h\langle v,d\rangle\) by \(-2hm\|d\|^2\) and \(h^2\|v\|^2\) by \(h^2L^2\|d\|^2\), both by (2),

\[\|d-hv\|^2\le\|d\|^2-2hm\|d\|^2+h^2L^2\|d\|^2=(1-2hm+h^2L^2)\|d\|^2.\qquad\square\]

The cross term is bounded with the signed lower bound \(\langle v,d\rangle\ge m\|d\|^2\). Bounding it instead by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality would only give the factor \((1+hL)^2\), which exceeds one for every \(h>0\) with \(L>0\).

steps.title: The square-root Euler-step bound
steps.body:
Claim. Under the hypotheses of the previous step (\(H\) a real inner-product space, \(m\in\mathbb R\), \(L\ge0\), \(h\ge0\), \(m\|x-y\|^2\le\langle g_x-g_y,x-y\rangle\) and \(\|g_x-g_y\|\le L\|x-y\|\)),

\[\|(x-hg_x)-(y-hg_y)\|\le\sqrt{1-2hm+h^2L^2}\;\|x-y\|,\]

where \(\sqrt s=0\) for \(s<0\).

Proof. Put \(A=\|(x-hg_x)-(y-hg_y)\|\ge0\), \(r=\|x-y\|\ge0\) and \(c=1-2hm+h^2L^2\). The previous step gives \(A^2\le cr^2\). We use three elementary facts about the square root with the stated convention.

  1. If \(A^2\le s\) for a real number \(s\), then \(A\le\sqrt s\). If \(s<0\), the hypothesis \(0\le A^2\le s\) is impossible. If \(s\ge0\), monotonicity of the square root on \([0,\infty)\) gives \(|A|=\sqrt{A^2}\le\sqrt s\), and \(A\le|A|\).
  2. \(\sqrt{cr^2}=\sqrt c\,\sqrt{r^2}\) for every real \(c\). If \(c\ge0\) this is the product rule for square roots of nonnegative numbers. If \(c<0\) and \(r\ne0\), then \(cr^2<0\) and both sides are \(0\). If \(r=0\), both sides are \(0\).
  3. \(\sqrt{r^2}=r\), because \(r\ge0\).

By the first fact with \(s=cr^2\), then the second and the third, \(A\le\sqrt{cr^2}=\sqrt c\,\sqrt{r^2}=\sqrt c\,r\). \(\square\)

The convention \(\sqrt s=0\) for \(s<0\) only matters when \(r=0\): if \(r>0\), then \(0\le A^2\le cr^2\) forces \(c\ge0\). If \(r=0\), the Lipschitz hypothesis forces \(g_x=g_y\), and both sides of the claim vanish.

  2. hbound := Real.le_sqrt_of_sq_le hsq is the first fact: from \(A^2\le cr^2\) it yields \(A\le\sqrt{cr^2}\).
  3. rwa [Real.sqrt_mul' _ (sq_nonneg _), Real.sqrt_sq (norm_nonneg _)] at hbound applies the second fact (Real.sqrt_mul' splits \(\sqrt{c\,r^2}\) for any \(c\) provided \(r^2\ge0\)) and the third fact (Real.sqrt_sq with \(r\ge0\)); the rewritten hbound is the goal.

UnadjustedLangevin/ULAStep.lean.title: The Langevin update and cancellation under shared noise
UnadjustedLangevin/ULAStep.lean.summary:
For a natural number \(d\), let \(E_d=\mathbb R^d\) with the Euclidean inner product \(\langle x,y angle=\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}x_iy_i\) and norm \(\|x\|=\langle x,x angle^{1/2}\); it is a real Hilbert space, and for \(d=0\) it is the zero space. For a potential \(U:E_d o\mathbb R\) with gradient \( abla U\), a step size \(h\in\mathbb R\) and a noise vector \(z\in E_d\), one step of the unadjusted Langevin algorithm (ULA) maps \(x\in E_d\) to

\[T_h^z(x)=x-h abla U(x)+\sqrt{2h}\,z,\]

with the convention \(\sqrt{2h}=0\) for \(h<0\). If \(h>0\) and \(z\) is a standard Gaussian vector, \(T_h^z(x)\) has the Gaussian law with mean \(x-h abla U(x)\) and covariance \(2hI_d\); this is the Euler–Maruyama step for the Langevin equation \(dX_t=- abla U(X_t)\,dt+\sqrt2\,dB_t\).

When the same noise vector is used at two states, it cancels from the difference of the two updates, which then equals the difference of two deterministic gradient steps. Combined with the previous section, this gives the shared-noise estimate \(\|T_h^z(x)-T_h^z(y)\|\le\sqrt{1-2hm+h^2L^2}\,\|x-y\|\) for a differentiable \(m\)-strongly convex potential with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. The estimate holds for every vector \(z\); no probabilistic assumption on the noise is involved.

steps.title: The Euclidean state space
steps.body:
Definition. For \(d\in\mathbb N\), \(E_d\) is the space \(\mathbb R^d\) of vectors \(x=(x_0,\dots,x_{d-1})\), with the operations defined coordinatewise, the inner product \(\langle x,y\rangle=\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}x_iy_i\) and the norm \(\|x\|=\bigl(\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}x_i^2\bigr)^{1/2}\).

Being finite-dimensional, \(E_d\) is complete, hence a real Hilbert space; all statements of the previous sections that require a Hilbert space apply to it. For \(d=0\) the index set is empty and \(E_0=\{0\}\).

Here Fin d is the set \(\{0,\dots,d-1\}\) and EuclideanSpace ℝ ι is Mathlib's space of real vectors indexed by a finite set \(\iota\) with the Euclidean (\(\ell^2\)) inner product and norm. Declaring E as an abbrev makes it reducible, so that the inner-product, completeness and measurability structures of EuclideanSpace are used for E d without further declarations.

steps.title: One unadjusted Langevin step
steps.body:
Definition. For \(U:E_d\to\mathbb R\), \(h\in\mathbb R\) and \(x,z\in E_d\), the ULA update is

\[T_h^z(x)=x-h\nabla U(x)+\sqrt{2h}\,z,\]

where \(\sqrt{2h}=0\) if \(h<0\).

The update consists of the gradient step \(x-h\nabla U(x)\) and the noise increment \(\sqrt{2h}\,z\). The definition is a deterministic function of \((x,z)\); probabilistic statements arise only when \(x\) and \(z\) are replaced by random vectors. No sign condition on \(h\) is imposed here; the estimates below assume \(h\ge0\).
steps.lean: ulaUpdate U h x z is defined as x - h • gradient U x + Real.sqrt (2 * h) • z; • is scalar multiplication and Real.sqrt is \(0\) on negative arguments. gradient U x is the Riesz representative of the derivative of \(U\) at \(x\); Mathlib sets it to \(0\) at points where \(U\) is not differentiable, but every theorem below assumes that \(U\) is differentiable, so this convention never intervenes. The definition is outside the namespace ULA.

steps.title: Shared noise cancels
steps.body:
Claim. For every \(U:E_d o\mathbb R\), \(h\in\mathbb R\) and \(x,y,z\in E_d\),

\[T_h^z(x)-T_h^z(y)= igl(x-h abla U(x) igr)- igl(y-h abla U(y) igr).\]

Proof. With \(a=x-h abla U(x)\), \(b=y-h abla U(y)\) and \(c=\sqrt{2h}\,z\), the two updates are \(a+c\) and \(b+c\), and \((a+c)-(b+c)=a-b\) in any vector space. \(\square\)

The cancellation requires the same vector \(z\) in both updates. With two different noise vectors \(z,z'\), the additional term \(\sqrt{2h}(z-z')\) would remain.
steps.lean: ulaUpdate_sub is proved by unfolding ulaUpdate and applying the group identity add_sub_add_right_eq_sub, \((a+c)-(b+c)=a-b\).

steps.title: The shared-noise estimate from strong monotonicity
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(U:E_d o\mathbb R\) be differentiable at every point and \(m\)-strongly convex, where \(m\in\mathbb R\), and let \( abla U\) be \(L\)-Lipschitz with \(L\ge0\). Let \(h\ge0\). Then for all \(x,y,z\in E_d\),

\[\|T_h^z(x)-T_h^z(y)\|\le\sqrt{1-2hm+h^2L^2}\;\|x-y\|.\]

Proof. By the previous step, the left-hand side equals \(\|(x-h abla U(x))-(y-h abla U(y))\|\). Apply the square-root Euler-step bound of the previous section with \(g_x= abla U(x)\) and \(g_y= abla U(y)\). Its two hypotheses hold: \(m\|x-y\|^2\le\langle abla U(x)- abla U(y),x-y angle\) is the strong monotonicity of the gradient, proved for differentiable \(m\)-strongly convex functions on the Hilbert space \(E_d\); and \(\| abla U(x)- abla U(y)\|\le L\|x-y\|\) is the Lipschitz assumption. \(\square\)

The factor is less than one exactly when \(h(hL^2-2m)<0\), that is, when \(h>0\) and \(hL^2<2m\). The sharp contraction of the next section improves it: if \(0<m\le L\), then \((1-mh)^2\le1-2hm+h^2L^2\) and \((1-Lh)^2\le1-2hm+h^2L^2\), because \(m^2\le L^2\) and \(-2hL\le-2hm\), so the sharp factor \(\max\{|1-mh|,|1-Lh|\}\) is never larger.

After rw [ulaUpdate_sub] (the noise cancellation of the previous step), the goal is closed by ULA.gradient_step_contract applied to gradient U x and gradient U y. Its monotonicity hypothesis is ULA.strong_gradient_monotone hdiff hsc x y; its Lipschitz hypothesis is hsm.dist_le_mul x y, with distances rewritten as norms of differences by dist_eq_norm.

UnadjustedLangevin/SharpContraction.lean.title: The sharp deterministic contraction
UnadjustedLangevin/SharpContraction.lean.summary:
Let \(H\) be a real inner-product space, and let \(f:H o\mathbb R\) be differentiable, \(m\)-strongly convex, with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, where \(L\ge0\) and \(m\le L\) (from Step 2 on \(H\) is a Hilbert space, so that \( abla f\) is defined). For \(x,y\in H\) write \(u=x-y\) and \(v= abla f(x)- abla f(y)\). The quadratic lower bound of strong convexity and the quadratic upper bound of the Lipschitz gradient together imply the interpolation inequality

\[mL\|u\|^2+\|v\|^2\le(m+L)\langle v,u angle,\]

which is stronger than strong monotonicity. Completing the square, it says that \(v\) lies in the closed ball with centre \( rac{m+L}2u\) and radius \( rac{L-m}2\|u\|\). Decomposing the difference of two gradient steps as \(u-hv=(1-h rac{m+L}2)u-h(v- rac{m+L}2u)\) then gives, for \(h\ge0\),

\[\|(x-h abla f(x))-(y-h abla f(y))\|\le\Bigl(\Bigl|1-h rac{m+L}2\Bigr|+h rac{L-m}2\Bigr)\|x-y\|.\]

If \(m+L>0\), the factor equals \(1-mh\) for \(0\le h\le2/(m+L)\) and \(Lh-1\) for \(h\ge2/(m+L)\); in both cases it is at most \(\max\{|1-mh|,|1-Lh|\}\). These are the contraction factors of Dalalyan's analysis of the unadjusted Langevin algorithm. Since a common noise vector cancels from the difference of two ULA updates, the same factors bound one step of the algorithm under shared noise. The boundary case \(m=L\) is included throughout; no division by \(L-m\) occurs.

The interpolation inequality is derived from an abstract statement (Step 1): if a function \(F\) and a vector field \(G\) satisfy a linear lower model and a quadratic upper model with constant \(K\ge0\), then \(\|G(x)-G(y)\|^2\le K\langle G(x)-G(y),x-y angle\) (cocoercivity). It is applied to \(F=f- rac m2\|\cdot\|^2\), \(G= abla f-m\,\mathrm{id}\) and \(K=L-m\).

steps.title: Cocoercivity from two quadratic models
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(H\) be a real inner-product space, \(f:H\to\mathbb R\), \(g:H\to H\) and \(K\ge0\). Assume that for all \(a,b\in H\)

\[f(a)+\langle g(a),b-a\rangle\le f(b)\qquad\text{and}\qquad f(b)\le f(a)+\langle g(a),b-a\rangle+\frac K2\|b-a\|^2.\]

Then for all \(x,y\in H\),

\[\|g(x)-g(y)\|^2\le K\,\langle g(x)-g(y),x-y\rangle.\]

Proof. (a) A one-sided estimate. Fix \(a,b\in H\) and \(t\ge0\); put \(v=g(a)-g(b)\) and \(z=a-tv\). The lower model with base point \(b\) and the upper model with base point \(a\), both evaluated at \(z\), give

\[f(b)+\langle g(b),z-b\rangle\le f(z)\le f(a)+\langle g(a),z-a\rangle+\frac K2\|z-a\|^2.\]

Here \(z-a=-tv\), \(z-b=(a-b)-tv\) and \(\|z-a\|^2=t^2\|v\|^2\). Substituting, and dropping the middle term,

\[f(b)+\langle g(b),a-b\rangle-t\langle g(b),v\rangle\le f(a)-t\langle g(a),v\rangle+\frac K2t^2\|v\|^2.\]

Since \(\langle g(a),v\rangle-\langle g(b),v\rangle=\langle v,v\rangle=\|v\|^2\), rearranging gives

\[\Bigl(t-\frac K2t^2\Bigr)\|g(a)-g(b)\|^2\le f(a)-f(b)-\langle g(b),a-b\rangle.\qquad(1)\]

(b) Symmetrisation. Put \(A=\|g(x)-g(y)\|^2\) and \(B=\langle g(x)-g(y),x-y\rangle\). Apply (1) to \((a,b)=(x,y)\) and to \((a,b)=(y,x)\) with the same \(t\ge0\). In the second inequality \(\|g(y)-g(x)\|^2=A\) and \(\langle g(x),y-x\rangle=-\langle g(x),x-y\rangle\). Adding the two inequalities, the function values cancel, and

\[(2t-Kt^2)A\le\langle g(x),x-y\rangle-\langle g(y),x-y\rangle=B\qquad\text{for every }t\ge0.\qquad(2)\]

(c) The case \(K>0\). Take \(t=1/K\) in (2): \((2/K-1/K)A=A/K\le B\). Multiplying by \(K>0\) gives \(A\le KB\).

(d) The case \(K=0\). Now (2) reads \(2tA\le B\) for all \(t\ge0\), and the claim is \(A\le0\). Taking \(t=1\) gives \(B\ge2A\ge0\). Suppose \(A>0\). Then \(t=(B+1)/(2A)\) is nonnegative, and (2) with this \(t\) gives \(B+1=2tA\le B\), a contradiction. Hence \(A\le0=K B\). \(\square\)

The choice \(t=1/K\) maximises \(2t-Kt^2\) over \(t\ge0\). When \(K=0\) the conclusion is \(g(x)=g(y)\) for all \(x,y\). The field \(g\) is not assumed to be a gradient: the two model inequalities are the only hypotheses.

steps.title: The interpolation inequality
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, \(m\in\mathbb R\) and \(L\ge0\) with \(m\le L\). Let \(f:H\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable at every point and \(m\)-strongly convex, and let \(\nabla f\) be \(L\)-Lipschitz. Then for all \(x,y\in H\),

\[mL\|x-y\|^2+\|\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\|^2\le(m+L)\,\langle\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y),x-y\rangle.\]

Proof. Define \(F(w)=f(w)-\frac m2\|w\|^2\) and \(G(w)=\nabla f(w)-mw\). We use the identity

\[\|b\|^2-\|a\|^2-2\langle a,b-a\rangle=\|b-a\|^2\qquad(a,b\in H),\qquad(1)\]

which follows by expanding \(\|b-a\|^2=\|b\|^2-2\langle a,b\rangle+\|a\|^2\). By (1),

\[F(a)+\langle G(a),b-a\rangle=f(a)+\langle\nabla f(a),b-a\rangle+\frac m2\|b-a\|^2-\frac m2\|b\|^2.\qquad(2)\]

(a) Lower model. The quadratic lower bound of strong convexity states \(f(a)+\langle\nabla f(a),b-a\rangle+\frac m2\|b-a\|^2\le f(b)\). Subtracting \(\frac m2\|b\|^2\) and using (2) gives \(F(a)+\langle G(a),b-a\rangle\le F(b)\).

(b) Upper model with constant \(L-m\). The quadratic upper bound for the \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient states \(f(b)\le f(a)+\langle\nabla f(a),b-a\rangle+\frac L2\|b-a\|^2\). Subtracting \(\frac m2\|b\|^2\) and using (2),

\[F(b)\le F(a)+\langle G(a),b-a\rangle+\frac{L-m}2\|b-a\|^2.\]

(c) Cocoercivity. Since \(m\le L\), the constant \(K=L-m\) is nonnegative, and (a), (b) are the hypotheses of Step 1 for \((F,G,K)\). Hence

\[\|G(x)-G(y)\|^2\le(L-m)\,\langle G(x)-G(y),x-y\rangle.\qquad(3)\]

(d) Expansion. With \(u=x-y\) and \(v=\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)\) we have \(G(x)-G(y)=v-mu\), so \(\|G(x)-G(y)\|^2=\|v\|^2-2m\langle v,u\rangle+m^2\|u\|^2\) and \(\langle G(x)-G(y),u\rangle=\langle v,u\rangle-m\|u\|^2\). Inequality (3) becomes

\[\|v\|^2-2m\langle v,u\rangle+m^2\|u\|^2\le(L-m)\langle v,u\rangle-(L-m)m\|u\|^2.\]

Collecting terms, \(m^2+(L-m)m=mL\) and \((L-m)+2m=m+L\), so \(\|v\|^2+mL\|u\|^2\le(m+L)\langle v,u\rangle\). \(\square\)

For \(m=L\), (3) holds with constant \(0\) and Step 1 gives \(G(x)=G(y)\), i.e. \(\nabla f(x)-\nabla f(y)=m(x-y)\); the claim then holds with equality. The hypothesis \(m\le L\) is needed for \(K\ge0\); it holds automatically for every potential on a nonzero space satisfying both assumptions, since \(m\|u\|^2\le\langle v,u\rangle\le L\|u\|^2\).

steps.title: The gradient difference lies in a ball
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(H\) be a real inner-product space, \(x,y,g_x,g_y\in H\) and \(m,L\in\mathbb R\) with \(m\le L\). Assume

\[mL\|x-y\|^2+\|g_x-g_y\|^2\le(m+L)\,\langle g_x-g_y,x-y\rangle.\]

Then

\[\Bigl\|(g_x-g_y)-\frac{m+L}2(x-y)\Bigr\|\le\frac{L-m}2\,\|x-y\|.\]

Proof. Put \(u=x-y\), \(v=g_x-g_y\), \(c=(m+L)/2\) and \(r=(L-m)/2\); then \(r\ge0\) because \(m\le L\). Both sides of the claim are nonnegative, and for nonnegative numbers \(\alpha,\beta\) the inequality \(\alpha^2\le\beta^2\) implies \(\alpha\le\beta\); it therefore suffices to prove \(\|v-cu\|^2\le r^2\|u\|^2\). Expanding and using the hypothesis in the form \(\|v\|^2-(m+L)\langle v,u\rangle\le-mL\|u\|^2\),

\[\|v-cu\|^2=\|v\|^2-2c\langle v,u\rangle+c^2\|u\|^2=\|v\|^2-(m+L)\langle v,u\rangle+c^2\|u\|^2\le(c^2-mL)\|u\|^2.\]

Finally \(c^2-mL=\frac{(m+L)^2-4mL}4=\frac{(L-m)^2}4=r^2\). \(\square\)

Conversely, expanding \(\|v-cu\|^2\le r^2\|u\|^2\) returns the hypothesis, so the two statements are equivalent. When \(m=L\) the radius is zero and \(v=mu\).

The rewrites expand \(\|v-cu\|^2\) (norm_sub_sq_real, real_inner_smul_right, norm_smul, sq_abs, mul_pow), and nlinarith completes the computation above.

steps.title: The centred Euler-step bound
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(H\) be a real inner-product space, \(x,y,g_x,g_y\in H\) and \(m,L,h\in\mathbb R\) with \(m\le L\) and \(h\ge0\). If \(mL\|x-y\|^2+\|g_x-g_y\|^2\le(m+L)\langle g_x-g_y,x-y\rangle\), then

\[\|(x-hg_x)-(y-hg_y)\|\le\Bigl(\Bigl|1-h\frac{m+L}2\Bigr|+h\frac{L-m}2\Bigr)\|x-y\|.\]

Proof. With \(u,v,c,r\) as in the previous step, that step gives \(\|v-cu\|\le r\|u\|\). Since \((1-hc)u-h(v-cu)=u-hv\), the difference of the two Euler steps decomposes as

\[(x-hg_x)-(y-hg_y)=u-hv=(1-hc)\,u+(-h)\,(v-cu).\]

By the triangle inequality and the homogeneity \(\|\lambda w\|=|\lambda|\,\|w\|\), with \(|-h|=h\) because \(h\ge0\),

\[\|u-hv\|\le|1-hc|\,\|u\|+h\,\|v-cu\|.\]

Multiplying \(\|v-cu\|\le r\|u\|\) by \(h\ge0\) and substituting gives \(\|u-hv\|\le(|1-hc|+hr)\|u\|\). \(\square\)

The absolute value is kept on the coefficient \(1-hc\) so that one formula covers both sides of the threshold \(hc=1\), i.e. \(h=2/(m+L)\); the next two steps remove it on each side.

steps.title: The small-step factor
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(H\) be a real inner-product space, \(x,y,g_x,g_y\in H\) and \(m,L,h\in\mathbb R\). Assume \(m\le L\), \(m+L>0\), \(0\le h\le2/(m+L)\), and \(mL\|x-y\|^2+\|g_x-g_y\|^2\le(m+L)\langle g_x-g_y,x-y\rangle\). Then

\[\|(x-hg_x)-(y-hg_y)\|\le(1-mh)\,\|x-y\|.\]

Proof. Because \(m+L>0\), the inequality \(h\le2/(m+L)\) is equivalent to \(h(m+L)\le2\). Hence \(1-h\frac{m+L}2\ge0\), and the absolute value in the previous step may be removed:

\[\Bigl|1-h\frac{m+L}2\Bigr|+h\frac{L-m}2=1-h\frac{m+L}2+h\frac{L-m}2=1-mh.\qquad\square\]

In this regime \(1-mh\ge0\): indeed \(2mh=h(m+L)-h(L-m)\le h(m+L)\le2\), since \(h(L-m)\ge0\). For \(m>0\) and \(h>0\) the factor is strictly less than one.

steps.title: The large-step factor
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(H\) be a real inner-product space, \(x,y,g_x,g_y\in H\) and \(m,L,h\in\mathbb R\). Assume \(m\le L\), \(m+L>0\), \(h\ge0\), \(2/(m+L)\le h\), and \(mL\|x-y\|^2+\|g_x-g_y\|^2\le(m+L)\langle g_x-g_y,x-y\rangle\). Then

\[\|(x-hg_x)-(y-hg_y)\|\le(Lh-1)\,\|x-y\|.\]

Proof. Because \(m+L>0\), the inequality \(2/(m+L)\le h\) is equivalent to \(2\le h(m+L)\). Hence \(1-h\frac{m+L}2\le0\), so its absolute value is its negative, and

\[\Bigl|1-h\frac{m+L}2\Bigr|+h\frac{L-m}2=h\frac{m+L}2-1+h\frac{L-m}2=Lh-1.\qquad\square\]

In this regime \(Lh-1\ge0\), because \(2\le h(m+L)\le2hL\). The factor is less than one exactly when \(Lh<2\); that condition is not needed for the inequality and is imposed only when the bound is iterated.

UnadjustedLangevin/LocalError.lean.title: The local Euler defect
UnadjustedLangevin/LocalError.lean.summary:
Let \(H\) be a real Banach space, let \(g:H\to H\) be a map (the drift), and let \(Y,B:\mathbb R\to H\) be curves. Integrals of \(H\)-valued functions of time are Bochner integrals with respect to Lebesgue measure, written as oriented integrals \(\int_a^b\) (for \(b<a\), \(\int_a^b=-\int_b^a\)); the integrands below are assumed integrable on the intervals in question, which holds in the application because they are continuous. We use linearity, the formula \(\int_a^bc\,dt=(b-a)c\) for a constant vector \(c\), and the norm estimate \(\|\int_a^b\phi(t)\,dt\|\le\int_a^b\psi(t)\,dt\) for \(a\le b\) whenever \(\|\phi(t)\|\le\psi(t)\) on \((a,b]\) and \(\psi\) is integrable.

The local defect of one Euler step of length \(h\) is

\[D_h(g,Y)=\int_0^h\bigl(g(Y_t)-g(Y_0)\bigr)\,dt.\]

If \(Y\) solves the integral equation \(Y_t-Y_0=-\int_0^tg(Y_s)\,ds+B_t\) on \([0,h]\), then \(Y_h=Y_0-hg(Y_0)+B_h-D_h(g,Y)\): the exact value after time \(h\) is one Euler step with the same additive input \(B_h\), minus the defect. If moreover \(g\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, \(\|g(Y_t)\|\le G\) and \(\|B_t\|\le N\sqrt t\) for \(0\le t\le h\), then

\[\|D_h(g,Y)\|\le L\Bigl(\frac{h^2G}2+\frac23h\sqrt h\,N\Bigr),\]

and with \(G=\sqrt{Ld}\), \(N=\sqrt{2d}\) and \(Lh\le2\) this becomes \(\|D_h(g,Y)\|\le\frac{33}{20}Lh\sqrt{hd}\), where \(\frac{33}{20}\) is a rational upper bound for \(\frac76\sqrt2\). In the application, \(H\) is the space of square-integrable random vectors in \(\mathbb R^d\), so all norms are root-mean-square norms; \(Y\) is the stationary Langevin process, \(B_t\) is \(\sqrt2\) times a Brownian motion, and the two moment bounds come from the score moment of the Gibbs measure and from Gaussian moments. Those facts are hypotheses in this section and are proved elsewhere.

steps.title: Definition of the local defect
steps.body:
Definition. For \(g:H\to H\), \(Y:\mathbb R\to H\) and \(h\in\mathbb R\),

\[D_h(g,Y)=\int_0^h\bigl(g(Y_t)-g(Y_0)\bigr)\,dt\in H.\]

The integrand vanishes at \(t=0\); the defect measures how much the drift along the curve differs from its value at the initial point, which is the value used by one Euler step.
steps.lean: localDefect g Y h is defined as ∫ t in 0..h, g (Y t) - g (Y 0). The notation ∫ t in a..b, f t is Mathlib's oriented interval integral with respect to Lebesgue measure: the Bochner integral over \((a,b]\) if \(a\le b\), and minus the integral over \((b,a]\) otherwise. The variable declaration makes \(H\) a real Banach space ([NormedAddCommGroup H] [NormedSpace ℝ H] [CompleteSpace H]). Mathlib assigns the value \(0\) to the integral of a function that is not integrable; the hypotheses of the following results make the relevant integrands integrable whenever this matters.

steps.title: The defect as exact minus frozen drift
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(g:H\to H\), \(Y:\mathbb R\to H\) and \(h\in\mathbb R\), and assume that \(t\mapsto g(Y_t)\) is integrable on the interval between \(0\) and \(h\). Then

\[D_h(g,Y)=\int_0^hg(Y_t)\,dt-h\,g(Y_0).\]

Proof. A constant function is integrable on every bounded interval. By linearity of the integral of the two integrable functions \(t\mapsto g(Y_t)\) and \(t\mapsto g(Y_0)\),

\[\int_0^h\bigl(g(Y_t)-g(Y_0)\bigr)\,dt=\int_0^hg(Y_t)\,dt-\int_0^hg(Y_0)\,dt,\]

and \(\int_0^hg(Y_0)\,dt=(h-0)\,g(Y_0)=h\,g(Y_0)\), for either sign of \(h\). \(\square\)

steps.title: An exact step is an Euler step minus its defect
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(g:H\to H\), \(Y,B:\mathbb R\to H\) and \(h\in\mathbb R\). Assume that \(t\mapsto g(Y_t)\) is integrable on the interval between \(0\) and \(h\) and that

\[Y_h-Y_0=-\int_0^hg(Y_t)\,dt+B_h.\]

Then

\[Y_h=Y_0-h\,g(Y_0)+B_h-D_h(g,Y).\]

Proof. The hypothesis gives \(Y_h=-\int_0^hg(Y_t)\,dt+B_h+Y_0\). By the previous step, \(\int_0^hg(Y_t)\,dt=D_h(g,Y)+h\,g(Y_0)\). Substituting,

\[Y_h=-D_h(g,Y)-h\,g(Y_0)+B_h+Y_0=Y_0-h\,g(Y_0)+B_h-D_h(g,Y).\qquad\square\]

If a numerical step \(X'=X-hg(X)+B_h\) uses the same input \(B_h\), the input cancels from the difference: \(X'-Y_h=(X-hg(X))-(Y_0-hg(Y_0))+D_h(g,Y)\). This is how the defect enters the coupling argument.

steps.title: Continuity gives integrability of the drift
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(H\) be a normed space, \(L\ge0\), let \(g:H\to H\) be \(L\)-Lipschitz, i.e. \(\|g(a)-g(b)\|\le L\|a-b\|\), and let \(Y:\mathbb R\to H\) be continuous. Then for every \(h\in\mathbb R\) the function \(t\mapsto g(Y_t)\) is integrable on the interval between \(0\) and \(h\).

Proof. A Lipschitz map is continuous, so \(t\mapsto g(Y_t)\) is continuous. On the compact interval \(I\) with endpoints \(0\) and \(h\) it is therefore bounded, and it is strongly measurable: its image of \(I\) is compact, hence separable, and the function is a uniform limit on \(I\) of step functions by uniform continuity. A bounded strongly measurable function on a set of finite measure is Bochner integrable. \(\square\)

In the application \(H\) is a space of square-integrable random vectors and continuity of \(Y\) is continuity in the root-mean-square norm.

The line omit [NormedSpace ℝ H] [CompleteSpace H] in removes the scalar structure and completeness, which this statement does not need.

steps.title: The square-root integral
steps.body:
Claim. For every \(h\ge0\),

\[\int_0^h\sqrt t\,dt=\frac23\,h\sqrt h.\]

Proof. For \(t\ge0\), \(\sqrt t=t^{1/2}\). For \(r>-1\) and \(h\ge0\) the power rule gives \(\int_0^ht^r\,dt=\frac{h^{r+1}-0^{r+1}}{r+1}\); it follows from the fundamental theorem of calculus, since \(t\mapsto t^{r+1}/(r+1)\) is continuous on \([0,h]\) with derivative \(t^r\) on \((0,h)\), and \(t^r\) is integrable near \(0\) because \(r>-1\). With \(r=\frac12\), \(0^{3/2}=0\), and \(h^{3/2}=h^{1/2}\,h=h\sqrt h\) (valid because \(h\ge0\)),

\[\int_0^h\sqrt t\,dt=\frac{h^{3/2}}{3/2}=\frac23\,h\sqrt h.\qquad\square\]

Real.zero_rpow evaluates \(0^{3/2}=0\), Real.rpow_add_one' hh rewrites \(h^{1/2+1}=h^{1/2}\cdot h\) (using \(h\ge0\)), and ring collects the constants.

steps.title: The increment of a solution of the integral equation
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(g:H\to H\), \(Y,B:\mathbb R\to H\) and \(h,G,N\in\mathbb R\). Assume that for every \(s\in[0,h]\)

\[\|g(Y_s)\|\le G,\qquad\|B_s\|\le N\sqrt s,\qquad Y_s-Y_0=-\int_0^sg(Y_r)\,dr+B_s.\]

Then for every \(t\in[0,h]\),

\[\|Y_t-Y_0\|\le tG+N\sqrt t.\]

Proof. Fix \(t\in[0,h]\), so \(t\ge0\). Every \(s\in(0,t]\) lies in \([0,h]\), hence \(\|g(Y_s)\|\le G\) there. The norm of an integral over \((0,t]\) is at most the bound of the integrand times the length of the interval:

\[\Bigl\|\int_0^tg(Y_s)\,ds\Bigr\|\le G\,|t-0|=Gt.\qquad(1)\]

By the integral equation at \(t\), the triangle inequality and \(\|-w\|=\|w\|\),

\[\|Y_t-Y_0\|=\Bigl\|-\int_0^tg(Y_s)\,ds+B_t\Bigr\|\le\Bigl\|\int_0^tg(Y_s)\,ds\Bigr\|+\|B_t\|\le Gt+N\sqrt t,\]

using (1) and the bound on \(B_t\). \(\square\)

This is a deterministic norm inequality; no independence between the drift and the input \(B\) is used.

steps.title: The two-term defect bound
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(L\ge0\) and let \(g:H\to H\) be \(L\)-Lipschitz. Let \(Y,B:\mathbb R\to H\) and \(h,G,N\in\mathbb R\) with \(h\ge0\), and assume that for every \(t\in[0,h]\)

\[\|g(Y_t)\|\le G,\qquad\|B_t\|\le N\sqrt t,\qquad Y_t-Y_0=-\int_0^tg(Y_s)\,ds+B_t.\]

Then

\[\|D_h(g,Y)\|\le L\Bigl(\frac{h^2G}2+\frac23h\sqrt h\,N\Bigr).\]

Proof. (a) Pointwise bound. For \(t\in(0,h]\), the Lipschitz property and the previous step (multiplied by \(L\ge0\)) give

\[\|g(Y_t)-g(Y_0)\|\le L\|Y_t-Y_0\|\le L\bigl(tG+N\sqrt t\bigr)=:\psi(t).\]

(b) The majorant is integrable. The function \(\psi\) is continuous on \(\mathbb R\) (the square root is continuous on \([0,\infty)\) and equal to \(0\) on \((-\infty,0)\)), hence integrable on \([0,h]\).

(c) Norm estimate. Since \(h\ge0\), the norm estimate for integrals with an integrable majorant on \((0,h]\) gives

\[\|D_h(g,Y)\|=\Bigl\|\int_0^h\bigl(g(Y_t)-g(Y_0)\bigr)\,dt\Bigr\|\le\int_0^h\psi(t)\,dt.\]

(d) Evaluation. By linearity, \(\int_0^ht\,dt=\frac{h^2}2\) and the square-root integral of Step 5,

\[\int_0^h\psi(t)\,dt=L\Bigl(G\int_0^ht\,dt+N\int_0^h\sqrt t\,dt\Bigr)=L\Bigl(\frac{h^2G}2+\frac23h\sqrt h\,N\Bigr).\qquad\square\]

The first term comes from the drift accumulated over the step and is of order \(h^2\); the second comes from the square-root growth of the input and is of order \(h^{3/2}\).

steps.title: The rational constant
steps.body:
Claim.

\[\frac76\sqrt2\le\frac{33}{20}.\]

Proof. Suppose instead that \(\frac76\sqrt2>\frac{33}{20}\). Both numbers are positive, so squaring preserves the strict inequality: \(\frac{49}{36}\cdot2>\frac{1089}{400}\), i.e. \(\frac{49}{18}>\frac{1089}{400}\). Multiplying by \(7200\) gives \(19600>19602\), which is false. \(\square\)

The bound is close to optimal: \(\frac{1089}{400}-\frac{49}{18}=\frac1{3600}\), and \(\frac{33}{20}-\frac76\sqrt2<10^{-4}\). The constant \(\frac76\sqrt2\) arises in the next step as \(\sqrt2\,(\frac12+\frac23)\).

Claim. Let \(L\ge0\), let \(g:H\to H\) be \(L\)-Lipschitz, let \(Y,B:\mathbb R\to H\), and let \(h,d\in\mathbb R\) with \(h\ge0\), \(d\ge0\) and \(Lh\le2\). Assume that for every \(t\in[0,h]\)

\[Y_t-Y_0=-\int_0^tg(Y_s)\,ds+B_t,\qquad\|g(Y_t)\|\le\sqrt{Ld},\qquad\|B_t\|\le\sqrt{2d}\,\sqrt t.\]

Then

\[\|D_h(g,Y)\|\le\frac{33}{20}\,Lh\sqrt{hd}.\]

Proof. (a) We show \(h\sqrt{Ld}\le\sqrt2\sqrt{hd}\). Both sides are nonnegative, so it suffices to compare squares. Since \(Ld\ge0\) and \(hd\ge0\), \((h\sqrt{Ld})^2=h^2Ld\) and \((\sqrt2\sqrt{hd})^2=2hd\). Multiplying \(Lh\le2\) by \(hd\ge0\) gives \(h^2Ld=(Lh)(hd)\le2hd\).

\[\|D_h(g,Y)\|\le L\cdot\frac76\sqrt2\;h\sqrt{hd}.\]

(e) Multiplying \(\frac76\sqrt2\le\frac{33}{20}\) (Step 8) by \(Lh\sqrt{hd}\ge0\) gives the claim. \(\square\)

The step-size condition \(Lh\le2\) is used only in (a), where it brings the drift term, of order \(h^2\sqrt{Ld}\), to the order \(h^{3/2}\sqrt d\) of the noise term.

UnadjustedLangevin/GaussianMoments.lean.title: Gaussian and Brownian noise moments
UnadjustedLangevin/GaussianMoments.lean.summary:
Let \(P\) be a measure on a measurable space \(\Omega\), let \(d\in\mathbb N\) and \(E_d=\mathbb R^d\). For \(v\ge0\), \(\mathcal N(0,v)\) denotes the centred Gaussian law on \(\mathbb R\) with variance \(v\): the measure with density \((2\pi v)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/(2v)}\) if \(v>0\), and the point mass at \(0\) if \(v=0\). A function \(X:\Omega\to\mathbb R\) has law \(\mu\) under \(P\) if it is \(P\)-almost everywhere measurable and its image measure \(X_\#P\), \(A\mapsto P(X^{-1}(A))\), equals \(\mu\). We write \(L^2(P;E_d)\) for the Hilbert space of equivalence classes, modulo equality \(P\)-almost everywhere, of almost everywhere measurable \(X:\Omega\to E_d\) with \(\int\|X\|^2\,dP<\infty\); its inner product is \(\langle X,Y\rangle=\int\langle X(\omega),Y(\omega)\rangle\,dP(\omega)\), so \(\|X\|_{L^2}=(\int\|X\|^2dP)^{1/2}\). The class of \(X\) is written \([X]\).

If every coordinate \(X_i\) of \(X:\Omega\to E_d\) has law \(\mathcal N(0,v)\), then \(\int\|X\|^2\,dP=dv\), because \(\|X\|^2=\sum_iX_i^2\) has no cross terms; independence of the coordinates is not needed. Consequently \([X]\in L^2(P;E_d)\), \(\|[X]\|_{L^2}=\sqrt{dv}\) and \(\|\sqrt2[X]\|_{L^2}=\sqrt{2d}\sqrt v\).

A real process \((W_t)_{t\ge0}\) is a pre-Brownian motion under \(P\) if its finite-dimensional laws are those of Brownian motion: for all times \(t_1,\dots,t_k\ge0\), the vector \((W_{t_1},\dots,W_{t_k})\) is centred Gaussian with covariances \(\mathbb E[W_{t_i}W_{t_j}]=\min(t_i,t_j)\). Continuity of paths is not required. Then \(W_t\sim\mathcal N(0,t)\) and \(W_s-W_r\sim\mathcal N(0,|s-r|)\). Assembling \(d\) such processes as coordinates gives vectors \(W_t\) and increments \(W_{a+t}-W_a\) with \(\|\sqrt2[W_{a+t}-W_a]\|_{L^2}=\sqrt{2d}\sqrt t\). This is the noise bound \(\|B_t\|\le\sqrt{2d}\sqrt t\) required by the local-defect estimate, for the input \(B_t=\sqrt2(W_{a+t}-W_a)\) of a step starting at time \(a\).

steps.title: Second moment of a centred Gaussian
steps.body:
Claim. For every \(v\ge0\),

\[\int_{\mathbb R}x^2\,\mathcal N(0,v)(dx)=v.\]

Proof. If \(v=0\), \(\mathcal N(0,0)\) is the point mass at \(0\) and the integral is \(0^2=0\). Let \(v>0\) and \(c=(2\pi v)^{-1/2}\), so that \(c\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-x^2/(2v)}dx=1\). Integration by parts with \(u=x\) and \(dw=xe^{-x^2/(2v)}dx\), \(w=-ve^{-x^2/(2v)}\), gives on \([-R,R]\)

\[\int_{-R}^Rx^2e^{-x^2/(2v)}\,dx=\Bigl[-vxe^{-x^2/(2v)}\Bigr]_{-R}^R+v\int_{-R}^Re^{-x^2/(2v)}\,dx.\]

The boundary term equals \(-2vRe^{-R^2/(2v)}\to0\) as \(R\to\infty\), and the integrands are nonnegative, so by monotone convergence \(c\int_{\mathbb R}x^2e^{-x^2/(2v)}dx=v\,c\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-x^2/(2v)}dx=v\). \(\square\)

Equivalently: the mean of \(\mathcal N(0,v)\) is \(0\) and its variance \(\int(x-0)^2\,\mathcal N(0,v)(dx)\) is \(v\).

The proof uses the form "variance minus mean": hv is Mathlib's variance_fun_id_gaussianReal, \(\operatorname{Var}=v\); rewriting with variance_eq_integral expresses the variance as \(\int(x-\text{mean})^2\), and integral_id_gaussianReal gives mean \(0\); sub_zero finishes.

steps.title: Gaussian coordinates give a square-integrable vector
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(v\ge0\) and \(X:\Omega\to E_d\), and assume that every coordinate \(X_i\) (\(0\le i\le d-1\)) has law \(\mathcal N(0,v)\) under \(P\). Then \(X\) is square integrable: it is almost everywhere measurable and \(\int\|X\|^2\,dP<\infty\).

Proof. Each \(X_i\) is almost everywhere measurable, and by the change-of-variables formula for image measures and the previous step,

\[\int_\Omega X_i^2\,dP=\int_{\mathbb R}x^2\,(X_i)_\#P(dx)=\int_{\mathbb R}x^2\,\mathcal N(0,v)(dx)=v<\infty.\]

Hence each coordinate is square integrable. A function with values in \(E_d\) is almost everywhere measurable if and only if its coordinates are, and \(\|X\|^2=\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}X_i^2\); so \(\int\|X\|^2\,dP=\sum_i\int X_i^2\,dP<\infty\). \(\square\)

The conclusion MemLp X 2 P is square integrability. The proof applies memLp_piLp_iff (a vector-valued function on EuclideanSpace is in \(L^p\) if and only if all coordinates are) and, for each coordinate, (hlaw i).memLp (memLp_id_gaussianReal (2 : ℝ≥0)): Mathlib's HasLaw.memLp transfers \(L^p\) membership of the identity under the law (here memLp_id_gaussianReal, finiteness of Gaussian moments) to the random variable.

steps.title: Summing the coordinate moments
steps.body:
Claim. Under the hypotheses of the previous step,

\[\int_\Omega\|X(\omega)\|^2\,P(d\omega)=dv.\]

Proof. By the previous proof each \(X_i^2\) is integrable with \(\int X_i^2\,dP=v\). Since \(\|X(\omega)\|^2=\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}X_i(\omega)^2\), linearity of the integral over this finite sum of integrable functions gives

\[\int_\Omega\|X\|^2\,dP=\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}\int_\Omega X_i^2\,dP=\sum_{i=0}^{d-1}v=dv.\qquad\square\]

Only the laws of the individual coordinates enter; correlations between different coordinates would change neither side.

EuclideanSpace.real_norm_sq_eq writes \(\|X\|^2=\sum_iX_i^2\), integral_finsetSum exchanges the finite sum and the integral (each summand integrable by (hmem i).integrable_sq), and the final simp only sums \(d\) copies of \(v\) (Finset.sum_const, Fintype.card_fin, nsmul_eq_mul).

steps.title: The squared norm of the class in \(L^2\)
steps.body:
Claim. Under the same hypotheses, the class \([X]\in L^2(P;E_d)\) satisfies

\[\|[X]\|_{L^2}^2=dv.\]

Proof. By definition of the inner product on \(L^2\), \(\|[X]\|_{L^2}^2=\langle[X],[X]\rangle=\int\langle\tilde X(\omega),\tilde X(\omega)\rangle\,dP(\omega)\), where \(\tilde X\) is any representative of \([X]\). Since \(\tilde X=X\) almost everywhere, the integrand equals \(\|X(\omega)\|^2\) almost everywhere, and integrals of almost everywhere equal functions coincide. The previous step gives the value \(dv\). \(\square\)

The proof rewrites \(\|[X]\|^2\) as the inner product (real_inner_self_eq_norm_sq) and the inner product as an integral (L2.inner_def). hid identifies the two integrals by integral_congr_ae; the almost-everywhere equality of representative and function is coeFn_toLp, applied inside filter_upwards. The value comes from gaussian_vector_second_moment.

steps.title: The norm of the class in \(L^2\)
steps.body:
Claim. Under the same hypotheses,

\[\|[X]\|_{L^2}=\sqrt{dv}.\]

Proof. By the previous step \(dv=\|[X]\|_{L^2}^2\), and \(\sqrt{a^2}=a\) for \(a=\|[X]\|_{L^2}\ge0\). \(\square\)

The cases \(d=0\) and \(v=0\) are included; then both sides vanish.

steps.title: The Langevin factor \(\sqrt2\)
steps.body:
Claim. Under the same hypotheses,

\[\|\sqrt2\,[X]\|_{L^2}=\sqrt{2d}\,\sqrt v.\]

Proof. By homogeneity of the norm and \(\sqrt2\ge0\), \(\|\sqrt2[X]\|_{L^2}=\sqrt2\,\|[X]\|_{L^2}=\sqrt2\sqrt{dv}\). Since \(d,v\ge0\), \(\sqrt{dv}=\sqrt d\sqrt v\), and since \(2\ge0\), \(\sqrt2\sqrt d=\sqrt{2d}\). \(\square\)

The factor \(\sqrt2\) is the diffusion coefficient of the Langevin equation \(dY_t=-\nabla U(Y_t)\,dt+\sqrt2\,dW_t\).

steps.title: Assembling scalar processes into a vector
steps.body:
Definition. Let \(W_0,\dots,W_{d-1}\) be real processes indexed by time \(t\ge0\), i.e. maps \(W_i:[0,\infty)\times\Omega\to\mathbb R\). The associated vector process is

\[W_t(\omega)=\bigl(W_0(t,\omega),\dots,W_{d-1}(t,\omega)\bigr)\in E_d\qquad(t\ge0,\ \omega\in\Omega).\]

Its \(i\)-th coordinate at time \(t\) is the scalar variable \(W_i(t,\cdot)\).

WithLp.toLp 2 regards the coordinate function \(i\mapsto W_i(t,\omega)\) as an element of EuclideanSpace ℝ (Fin d), so that the Euclidean norm, not the supremum norm of functions, is used.

steps.title: Brownian marginals are Gaussian
steps.body:
Claim. Assume that each \(W_i\) is a pre-Brownian motion under \(P\). Then for every \(t\ge0\) and every coordinate \(i\), the \(i\)-th coordinate of \(W_t\) has law \(\mathcal N(0,t)\).

Proof. The \(i\)-th coordinate of \(W_t\) is \(W_i(t,\cdot)\). The finite-dimensional law of \(W_i\) for the single time \(t\) is the centred Gaussian law with variance \(\min(t,t)=t\). \(\square\)

steps.title: Brownian vectors are square integrable
steps.body:
Claim. If each \(W_i\) is a pre-Brownian motion under \(P\), then \(W_t\) is square integrable for every \(t\ge0\).

Proof. By the previous step all coordinates of \(W_t\) have law \(\mathcal N(0,t)\); apply the square-integrability statement for Gaussian coordinates with \(v=t\). \(\square\)

steps.title: The Brownian noise norm
steps.body:
Claim. If each \(W_i\) is a pre-Brownian motion under \(P\), then for every \(t\ge0\)

\[\|\sqrt2\,[W_t]\|_{L^2}=\sqrt{2d}\,\sqrt t.\]

Proof. Apply the scaled Gaussian norm identity with \(v=t\), using the coordinate laws of Step 8. \(\square\)

steps.title: Increments over an interval
steps.body:
Definition. For \(a,t\ge0\), the increment of the vector process over \([a,a+t]\) is

\[\Delta_aW_t(\omega)=W_{a+t}(\omega)-W_a(\omega)\in E_d.\]

Its \(i\)-th coordinate is \(W_i(a+t,\omega)-W_i(a,\omega)\). The starting time \(a\) and the length \(t\) are kept separate, so that each step of length \(h\) of the algorithm, starting at time \(a=kh\), is described on the local time interval \([0,h]\).

steps.title: The law of an increment
steps.body:
Claim. If each \(W_i\) is a pre-Brownian motion under \(P\), then for all \(a,t\ge0\) and every coordinate \(i\),

\[W_i(a+t)-W_i(a)\ \text{has law}\ \mathcal N(0,t).\]

Proof. For times \(s,r\ge0\), the pair \((W_i(s),W_i(r))\) is centred Gaussian with variances \(s,r\) and covariance \(\min(s,r)\). A linear image of a centred Gaussian vector is centred Gaussian, so \(W_i(s)-W_i(r)\) is centred Gaussian with variance \(s+r-2\min(s,r)=|s-r|\). With \(s=a+t\) and \(r=a\), the variance is \(|(a+t)-a|=|t|=t\), because \(t\ge0\). \(\square\)

The law depends only on the length \(t\) of the interval, not on its starting time \(a\).

steps.body:
Claim. If each \(W_i\) is a pre-Brownian motion under \(P\), then for all \(a,t\ge0\)

\[\|\sqrt2\,[W_{a+t}-W_a]\|_{L^2}=\sqrt{2d}\,\sqrt t.\]

UnadjustedLangevin/LpDrift.lean.title: The gradient map on square-integrable random vectors
UnadjustedLangevin/LpDrift.lean.summary:
Let \(P\) be a finite measure on a measurable space \(\Omega\) and \(H\) a normed space (from Step 6 on, a real Hilbert space). We write \(L^2(P;H)\) for the space of equivalence classes, modulo equality \(P\)-almost everywhere, of almost everywhere strongly measurable functions \(X:\Omega\to H\) with \(\int\|X\|^2\,dP<\infty\), normed by \(\|X\|_{L^2}=(\int\|X\|^2\,dP)^{1/2}\). For a class \(X\) we write \(X(\omega)\) for the values of a fixed representative; every identity between such values holds for \(P\)-almost every \(\omega\) and does not depend on the representative. When \(H\) is a Hilbert space, so is \(L^2(P;H)\), with inner product \(\langle X,Y\rangle=\int\langle X(\omega),Y(\omega)\rangle\,dP(\omega)\).

For an \(L\)-Lipschitz map \(g:H\to H\) we construct the map \(\mathcal G:L^2(P;H)\to L^2(P;H)\) with \(\mathcal G(X)(\omega)=g(X(\omega))\) almost everywhere (the lifted drift) and prove that it is again \(L\)-Lipschitz and that \(\|\mathcal G(X)\|_{L^2}^2=\int\|g(X)\|^2\,dP\). Finiteness of \(P\) is needed because \(g(0)\) need not vanish and constant functions must be square integrable. For \(g=\nabla U\), with \(U\) strongly convex with Lipschitz gradient, the sharp contraction factors \(1-mh\) and \(Lh-1\) of the gradient step carry over to \(L^2\), and the local-defect bound applies in the Banach space \(L^2(P;H)\), where time integrals are Bochner integrals of \(L^2\)-valued curves. Finally the ULA update \(X-h\mathcal G(X)+\sqrt{2h}\,Z\) and the resulting chain are defined on \(L^2(P;E_d)\), and every iterate is shown to agree almost everywhere with the pointwise ULA recursion driven by the representatives of the initial state and the noise. In this way the coupling argument for random vectors becomes an argument in a Hilbert space whose norm is the root-mean-square distance.

steps.title: Centring a Lipschitz map
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(H\) be a normed additive group, \(L\ge0\), and \(g:H\to H\) be \(L\)-Lipschitz. Then \(\tilde g(x)=g(x)-g(0)\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz.

Proof. For \(x,y\in H\), \(\tilde g(x)-\tilde g(y)=(g(x)-g(0))-(g(y)-g(0))=g(x)-g(y)\), so \(\|\tilde g(x)-\tilde g(y)\|=\|g(x)-g(y)\|\le L\|x-y\|\). \(\square\)

Moreover \(\tilde g(0)=0\), so \(\|\tilde g(x)\|=\|\tilde g(x)-\tilde g(0)\|\le L\|x\|\) for every \(x\).

steps.title: The lifted drift
steps.body:
Definition. Let \(P\) be a finite measure, \(L\ge0\) and \(g:H\to H\) be \(L\)-Lipschitz. For \(X\in L^2(P;H)\) put

\[\mathcal G(X)=[\tilde g\circ X]+[g(0)],\]

where \(\tilde g=g-g(0)\) and \([g(0)]\) is the class of the constant function.

Both terms lie in \(L^2(P;H)\). The function \(\tilde g\) is continuous, so \(\tilde g\circ X\) is almost everywhere strongly measurable, and by the previous step \(\|\tilde g(X(\omega))\|^2\le L^2\|X(\omega)\|^2\), hence \(\int\|\tilde g\circ X\|^2\,dP\le L^2\|X\|_{L^2}^2<\infty\). If two representatives of \(X\) agree almost everywhere, so do their compositions with \(\tilde g\); thus \([\tilde g\circ X]\) depends only on the class. The constant function has \(\int\|g(0)\|^2\,dP=\|g(0)\|^2P(\Omega)<\infty\) because \(P\) is finite.

Mathlib's LipschitzWith.compLp composes an element of Lp with a Lipschitz map vanishing at \(0\); its side condition \(\tilde g(0)=0\) is proved by simp. Lp.const 2 P (g 0) is the class of the constant function, available because of the instance [IsFiniteMeasure P].

steps.title: The lift acts pointwise
steps.body:
Claim. For a finite measure \(P\), an \(L\)-Lipschitz \(g\) and \(X\in L^2(P;H)\),

\[\mathcal G(X)(\omega)=g(X(\omega))\qquad\text{for }P\text{-almost every }\omega.\]

Proof. Each of the following holds outside a \(P\)-null set: the representative of the sum \(\mathcal G(X)\) is the sum of the representatives of the two terms; the representative of \([\tilde g\circ X]\) equals \(\tilde g(X(\omega))\); the representative of \([g(0)]\) equals \(g(0)\). A union of three null sets is null, and outside it

\[\mathcal G(X)(\omega)=\bigl(g(X(\omega))-g(0)\bigr)+g(0)=g(X(\omega)).\qquad\square\]

steps.title: Square integrability of the drift
steps.body:
Claim. For a finite measure \(P\), an \(L\)-Lipschitz \(g\) and \(X\in L^2(P;H)\), the function \(\omega\mapsto g(X(\omega))\) is square integrable.

Proof. The class \(\mathcal G(X)\) lies in \(L^2(P;H)\), so its representative is square integrable. By the previous step it agrees almost everywhere with \(g\circ X\), and square integrability is preserved under almost-everywhere equality. \(\square\)

steps.title: The lifted drift is Lipschitz
steps.body:
Claim. For a finite measure \(P\) and an \(L\)-Lipschitz \(g\), the map \(\mathcal G\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz on \(L^2(P;H)\):

\[\|\mathcal G(X)-\mathcal G(Y)\|_{L^2}\le L\,\|X-Y\|_{L^2}\qquad(X,Y\in L^2(P;H)).\]

Proof. The constant terms cancel: \(\mathcal G(X)-\mathcal G(Y)=[\tilde g\circ X]-[\tilde g\circ Y]\). For almost every \(\omega\), the representative of this difference is \(\tilde g(X(\omega))-\tilde g(Y(\omega))\) and that of \(X-Y\) is \(X(\omega)-Y(\omega)\), and by Step 1

\[\|\tilde g(X(\omega))-\tilde g(Y(\omega))\|^2\le L^2\|X(\omega)-Y(\omega)\|^2.\]

Integrating over \(\Omega\) and taking square roots gives the claim. \(\square\)

The constant \(g(0)\) does not contribute to the difference, so no term proportional to \(\|g(0)\|\) appears.

steps.title: The small-step contraction in \(L^2\)
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, \(P\) a finite measure, \(m,h\in\mathbb R\), \(L\ge0\), and \(U:H\to\mathbb R\) differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. Assume \(m\le L\), \(m+L>0\) and \(0\le h\le2/(m+L)\). Let \(\mathcal G\) be the lift of \(g=\nabla U\). Then for all \(X,Y\in L^2(P;H)\),

\[\bigl\|(X-h\mathcal G(X))-(Y-h\mathcal G(Y))\bigr\|_{L^2}\le(1-mh)\,\|X-Y\|_{L^2}.\]

Proof. (a) Pointwise bounds integrate. Let \(F,G\in L^2(P;H)\) and \(c\in\mathbb R\) with \(\|F(\omega)\|\le c\,\|G(\omega)\|\) for almost every \(\omega\). If \(c\ge0\), squaring and integrating gives \(\int\|F\|^2\le c^2\int\|G\|^2\), hence \(\|F\|_{L^2}\le c\|G\|_{L^2}\). If \(c<0\), the inequality forces \(F(\omega)=0\) and \(G(\omega)=0\) almost everywhere, and both sides vanish.

(b) The pointwise bound. Apply (a) with \(F=(X-h\mathcal G(X))-(Y-h\mathcal G(Y))\), \(G=X-Y\) and \(c=1-mh\). Outside a null set (the union of finitely many null sets on which the representatives of differences and scalar multiples, and the formula of Step 3 for \(\mathcal G(X)\) and \(\mathcal G(Y)\), may fail),

\[F(\omega)=\bigl(X(\omega)-h\nabla U(X(\omega))\bigr)-\bigl(Y(\omega)-h\nabla U(Y(\omega))\bigr),\qquad G(\omega)=X(\omega)-Y(\omega).\]

The sharp small-step contraction of the gradient step at \(x=X(\omega)\), \(y=Y(\omega)\) gives \(\|F(\omega)\|\le(1-mh)\|G(\omega)\|\). \(\square\)

The contraction acts on random states through their representatives; no assumption on the joint law of \(X\) and \(Y\) is involved.

steps.title: The large-step bound in \(L^2\)
steps.body:
Claim. With \(H\), \(P\), \(U\), \(m\), \(L\) and \(\mathcal G\) as in the previous step, assume \(m\le L\), \(m+L>0\), \(h\ge0\) and \(2/(m+L)\le h\). Then for all \(X,Y\in L^2(P;H)\),

\[\bigl\|(X-h\mathcal G(X))-(Y-h\mathcal G(Y))\bigr\|_{L^2}\le(Lh-1)\,\|X-Y\|_{L^2}.\]

Proof. As in the previous step, with the constant \(c=Lh-1\) and the sharp large-step bound of the gradient step in place of the small-step bound. \(\square\)

steps.title: The local defect in \(L^2\)
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, \(P\) a finite measure, \(L\ge0\), \(U:H\to\mathbb R\) with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, and \(\mathcal G\) the lift of \(\nabla U\). Let \(Y,B:\mathbb R\to L^2(P;H)\) and \(h,d\in\mathbb R\) with \(h\ge0\), \(d\ge0\) and \(Lh\le2\). Assume that for every \(t\in[0,h]\)

\[\|\mathcal G(Y_t)\|_{L^2}\le\sqrt{Ld},\qquad\|B_t\|_{L^2}\le\sqrt{2d}\,\sqrt t,\qquad Y_t-Y_0=-\int_0^t\mathcal G(Y_s)\,ds+B_t,\]

the integral being the Bochner integral of an \(L^2(P;H)\)-valued function. Then

\[\|D_h(\mathcal G,Y)\|_{L^2}\le\frac{33}{20}\,Lh\sqrt{hd},\qquad D_h(\mathcal G,Y)=\int_0^h\bigl(\mathcal G(Y_t)-\mathcal G(Y_0)\bigr)\,dt.\]

Proof. The space \(L^2(P;H)\) is a real Banach space, and by Step 5 the map \(\mathcal G\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz on it. The hypotheses are those of the local-defect bound with the stationary moment scales, applied in the Banach space \(L^2(P;H)\) to the drift \(\mathcal G\); that bound gives the claim. \(\square\)

Differentiability and convexity of \(U\) are not needed here; only the Lipschitz constant of the gradient enters. The norms are root-mean-square norms: \(\|\mathcal G(Y_t)\|_{L^2}^2=\int\|\nabla U(Y_t)\|^2dP\) by the next step.

The integral ∫ s in 0..t, ... in heq is a Bochner integral in Lp H 2 P, which is complete.

steps.title: The drift norm as a second moment
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(H\) be a real inner-product space, \(P\) a finite measure, \(g:H\to H\) \(L\)-Lipschitz and \(X\in L^2(P;H)\). Then

\[\|\mathcal G(X)\|_{L^2}^2=\int_\Omega\|g(X(\omega))\|^2\,P(d\omega).\]

Proof. By definition of the inner product of \(L^2\),

\[\begin{aligned}\|\mathcal G(X)\|_{L^2}^2&=\langle\mathcal G(X),\mathcal G(X)\rangle\\&=\int\langle\mathcal G(X)(\omega),\mathcal G(X)(\omega)\rangle\,dP.\end{aligned}\]

By Step 3 the integrand equals \(\langle g(X(\omega)),g(X(\omega))\rangle=\|g(X(\omega))\|^2\) almost everywhere, and integrals of almost-everywhere equal functions coincide. \(\square\)

If \(X\) has law \(\pi\) under \(P\), the right-hand side equals \(\int\|g(x)\|^2\,\pi(dx)\); for \(g=\nabla U\) and \(\pi\) the Gibbs measure this is the score moment.

Completeness of \(H\) is omitted from the hypotheses (omit [CompleteSpace H] in).

steps.title: A second-moment bound gives a drift bound
steps.body:
Claim. Under the hypotheses of the previous step, if \(C\in\mathbb R\) and \(\int\|g(X(\omega))\|^2\,P(d\omega)\le C\), then

\[\|\mathcal G(X)\|_{L^2}\le\sqrt C.\]

Proof. By the previous step \(\|\mathcal G(X)\|_{L^2}^2\le C\). For a real number \(a\) and any real \(s\), \(a^2\le s\) implies \(a\le\sqrt s\) (if \(s<0\) the hypothesis is impossible; otherwise \(a\le|a|=\sqrt{a^2}\le\sqrt s\)). \(\square\)

With \(g=\nabla U\) and \(C=Ld\), this converts the score moment bound into the hypothesis \(\|\mathcal G(Y_t)\|_{L^2}\le\sqrt{Ld}\) of the local-defect estimate.

steps.title: The ULA update in \(L^2\)
steps.body:
Definition. Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space, \(P\) a finite measure, \(U:H\to\mathbb R\) with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, \(\mathcal G\) the lift of \(\nabla U\), and \(h\in\mathbb R\). For \(X,Z\in L^2(P;H)\),

\[\mathsf T_h(X,Z)=X-h\,\mathcal G(X)+\sqrt{2h}\,Z\in L^2(P;H),\]

with \(\sqrt{2h}=0\) if \(h<0\). All three terms lie in \(L^2(P;H)\), which is a vector space.

steps.title: The update acts pointwise
steps.body:
Claim. In the setting of the previous definition, for all \(X,Z\in L^2(P;H)\),

\[\mathsf T_h(X,Z)(\omega)=X(\omega)-h\nabla U(X(\omega))+\sqrt{2h}\,Z(\omega)\qquad\text{for }P\text{-almost every }\omega.\]

Proof. Outside the union of five null sets, the representatives of the sum, of the difference, of the two scalar multiples and of \(\mathcal G(X)\) (Step 3) are given by the corresponding pointwise formulas; substituting them gives the claim. \(\square\)

No assumption on the law of \(Z\) is involved.

steps.title: The ULA chain in \(L^2\)
steps.body:
Definition. Let \(P\) be a finite measure, \(U:E_d\to\mathbb R\) with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, \(h\in\mathbb R\), \(X_0\in L^2(P;E_d)\), and \(Z_0,Z_1,\ldots\in L^2(P;E_d)\). The ULA chain in \(L^2\) is defined recursively by

\[X_0\ \text{given},\qquad X_{n+1}=\mathsf T_h(X_n,Z_n)\quad(n\ge0).\]

Each \(X_n\) belongs to \(L^2(P;E_d)\), because \(\mathsf T_h\) maps \(L^2\times L^2\) into \(L^2\).

Proof. This is the second clause of the recursive definition. \(\square\)

The noise used in the step from \(n\) to \(n+1\) is \(Z_n\).

steps.title: The chain in \(L^2\) is the pointwise algorithm
steps.body:
Claim. In the setting of Step 13, let \(x_n(\omega)\) denote the pointwise ULA recursion driven by the representatives,

\[x_0(\omega)=X_0(\omega),\qquad x_{n+1}(\omega)=x_n(\omega)-h\nabla U(x_n(\omega))+\sqrt{2h}\,Z_n(\omega).\]

Then for every \(n\ge0\), \(X_n(\omega)=x_n(\omega)\) for \(P\)-almost every \(\omega\).

Proof. Induction on \(n\). For \(n=0\), both sides are the representative of the initial class, for every \(\omega\). Assume the claim for \(n\). By Step 12 applied to \(X_n\) and \(Z_n\), for almost every \(\omega\),

\[X_{n+1}(\omega)=X_n(\omega)-h\nabla U(X_n(\omega))+\sqrt{2h}\,Z_n(\omega).\]

Outside the union of this null set and the null set of the induction hypothesis, we may replace \(X_n(\omega)\) by \(x_n(\omega)\), and the right-hand side becomes \(x_{n+1}(\omega)\). \(\square\)

Hence the chain in \(L^2\) is the ordinary ULA algorithm applied to random inputs; in particular \(X_n\) has the same law as \(x_n\).

UnadjustedLangevin/Dynamics.lean.title: The noise-driven iterates
UnadjustedLangevin/Dynamics.lean.summary:
Let \(U:E_d o\mathbb R\) be a potential with gradient \( abla U\), let \(h\in\mathbb R\), and let \(T_h^z(x)=x-h abla U(x)+\sqrt{2h}\,z\) be the ULA update. Given an initial vector \(x_0\in E_d\) and a sequence of noise vectors \(\xi_0,\xi_1,\ldots\in E_d\), the ULA iterates are

\[X_0=x_0,\qquad X_{k+1}=T_h^{\xi_k}(X_k)=X_k-h abla U(X_k)+\sqrt{2h}\,\xi_k\qquad(k\ge0).\]

The iterate \(X_n\) depends only on \(x_0\) and \(\xi_0,\dots,\xi_{n-1}\). When \(x_0\) and the \(\xi_k\) are random vectors, with the \(\xi_k\) independent standard Gaussian vectors independent of \(x_0\), this is the unadjusted Langevin algorithm. The recursion itself is deterministic and is defined for every input sequence; the coupling estimates of the later sections hold for every common noise sequence. This section records the defining identities and proves that every iterate is a measurable function of the randomness when the gradient is Lipschitz and the inputs are measurable, so that the law of each iterate is defined.

steps.title: Measurability of every iterate
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(\Omega\) be a measurable space, \(L\ge0\), and \(U:E_d o\mathbb R\) with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. Let \(x_0:\Omega o E_d\) and \(\xi_k:\Omega o E_d\) (\(k\ge0\)) be measurable, where \(E_d\) carries its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra. Then for every \(n\), the map \(\omega\mapsto X_n(\omega)\), the \(n\)-th iterate with initial vector \(x_0(\omega)\) and noise \((\xi_k(\omega))_k\), is measurable.

Proof. A Lipschitz map is continuous, and continuous maps between metric spaces are Borel measurable; so \( abla U\) is measurable. We argue by induction on \(n\). For \(n=0\), \(X_0=x_0\) is measurable by hypothesis. Assume \(X_n\) is measurable. Then \( abla U\circ X_n\) is measurable as a composition of measurable maps. Scalar multiples, differences and sums of measurable \(E_d\)-valued maps are measurable (the vector operations are continuous and \(E_d\) is separable, so the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra of \(E_d imes E_d\) is the product \(\sigma\)-algebra). Hence \(X_{n+1}=X_n-h\, abla U\circ X_n+\sqrt{2h}\,\xi_n\) is measurable. \(\square\)

Consequently the law \((X_n)_\#P\) of every iterate is defined for every measure \(P\) on \(\Omega\).

UnadjustedLangevin/Coupling.lean.title: Couplings and the quadratic transport distance
UnadjustedLangevin/Coupling.lean.summary:
Let \(H\) be a normed additive group (for instance a normed space) whose topology is second countable, equipped with its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra; then the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra of \(H imes H\) is the product \(\sigma\)-algebra and \((x,y)\mapsto x-y\) is measurable. For a measure \(\mu\) and a measurable map \(f\), the image measure is \(f_\#\mu(A)=\mu(f^{-1}(A))\). A coupling of two measures \(\mu, u\) on \(H\) is a measure \(\gamma\) on \(H imes H\) whose marginals \((\mathrm{pr}_1)_\#\gamma\) and \((\mathrm{pr}_2)_\#\gamma\) are \(\mu\) and \( u\); the set of couplings is \(\Gamma(\mu, u)\).

For a measure \(P\) on \(\Omega\) and a function \(f:\Omega o H\) we use the extended \(L^2\)-norm \(\|f\|_{2,P}=(\int\|f\|^2\,dP)^{1/2}\in[0,\infty]\) when \(f\) is \(P\)-almost everywhere strongly measurable (equal almost everywhere to a pointwise limit of measurable functions with finitely many values), and \(\|f\|_{2,P}=\infty\) otherwise. With this convention, Minkowski's inequality \(\|f-g\|_{2,P}\le\|f\|_{2,P}+\|g\|_{2,P}\) holds for all \(f,g\), and \(\|f\|_{2,P}\) does not change if \(f\) is modified on a null set. In \([0,\infty]\) we use \(a+\infty=\infty\), \(a\cdot\infty=\infty\) for \(a>0\) and \(0\cdot\infty=0\).

The quadratic cost of \(\gamma\) is \(c(\gamma)=\|(x,y)\mapsto x-y\|_{2,\gamma}=(\int\|x-y\|^2\,\gamma(dx,dy))^{1/2}\), and the quadratic Wasserstein distance is

\[W_2(\mu, u)=\inf_{\gamma\in\Gamma(\mu, u)}c(\gamma)\in[0,\infty],\]

with \(\inf\varnothing=\infty\). We also use the real number \(W_2^{\mathbb R}(\mu, u)\), equal to \(W_2(\mu, u)\) if this is finite and to \(0\) otherwise; every bound below on \(W_2^{\mathbb R}\) is accompanied by a proof or a hypothesis of finiteness. No optimal coupling and no metric property of \(W_2\) is used.

The main facts are: every coupling bounds \(W_2\) from above; the joint law \((X,Y)_\#P\) of two random vectors is a coupling of their laws, with cost \(\|X-Y\|_{2,P}\), so \(W_2(X_\#P,Y_\#P)\le\|X-Y\|_{2,P}\); and if \(X'-Y'=A-V\) with \(\|A\|\le q\|X-Y\|\) pointwise, then Minkowski's inequality gives \(\|X'-Y'\|_{2,P}\le q\|X-Y\|_{2,P}+\|V\|_{2,P}\). Combined, these turn a pointwise contraction plus a defect into a bound on the transport distance between the laws of the next pair. No independence between the compared random vectors is required.

steps.title: Couplings
steps.body:
Definition. Let \(\mu, u\) be measures on \(H\). A coupling of \(\mu\) and \( u\) is a measure \(\gamma\) on \(H imes H\) such that

\[(\mathrm{pr}_1)_\#\gamma=\mu\quad ext{and}\quad(\mathrm{pr}_2)_\#\gamma= u,\qquad ext{i.e.}\quad\gamma(A imes H)=\mu(A),\ \gamma(H imes B)= u(B)\]

for all Borel sets \(A,B\subseteq H\).

The dependence between the two coordinates is arbitrary. For probability measures the product \(\mu\otimes u\) is a coupling, so \(\Gamma(\mu, u)\) is nonempty.
steps.lean: structure Coupling (μ ν : Measure H) has three fields: joint : Measure (H × H) is \(\gamma\); fst : joint.map Prod.fst = μ and snd : joint.map Prod.snd = ν are the two marginal conditions, where γ.map f is the image measure \(f_\#\gamma\) and Prod.fst, Prod.snd are the projections. An element of the structure is a coupling together with the proofs of its marginal conditions.

steps.title: The quadratic cost of a coupling
steps.body:
Definition. For a measure \(\gamma\) on \(H\times H\),

\[c(\gamma)=\|(x,y)\mapsto x-y\|_{2,\gamma}=\Bigl(\int_{H\times H}\|x-y\|^2\,\gamma(dx,dy)\Bigr)^{1/2}\in[0,\infty].\]

The displacement \((x,y)\mapsto x-y\) is continuous, hence measurable, so the integral formula applies. The value \(\infty\) is allowed; it occurs exactly when the second moment of the displacement is infinite.
steps.lean: couplingCost γ is eLpNorm (fun p : H × H ↦ p.1 - p.2) 2 γ. Mathlib's eLpNorm f p μ is the extended \(L^p\)-seminorm with values in ℝ≥0∞, the extended nonnegative reals \([0,\infty]\): for \(p=2\) and an almost everywhere strongly measurable \(f\) it equals \((\int\|f\|^2\,d\mu)^{1/2}\), and it is \(\infty\) for other functions. Keeping the value in ℝ≥0∞ prevents an infinite cost from being silently replaced by a real number.

steps.title: The quadratic Wasserstein distance
steps.body:
Definition. For measures \(\mu, u\) on \(H\),

\[W_2(\mu, u)=\inf_{\gamma\in\Gamma(\mu, u)}c(\gamma)\in[0,\infty],\]

the infimum being taken in \([0,\infty]\), so that \(W_2(\mu, u)=\infty\) if \(\Gamma(\mu, u)=\varnothing\) or every coupling has infinite cost.

steps.title: The real-valued distance
steps.body:
Definition. For measures \(\mu, u\) on \(H\), let \(W_2^{\mathbb R}(\mu, u)=W_2(\mu, u)\) if \(W_2(\mu, u)<\infty\), and \(W_2^{\mathbb R}(\mu, u)=0\) if \(W_2(\mu, u)=\infty\).

This real number coincides with the transport distance whenever the latter is finite. The theorems below that bound \(W_2^{\mathbb R}\) either assume finiteness or prove it from a coupling of finite cost, so the value \(0\) assigned to an infinite distance never enters a conclusion.

steps.title: Every coupling gives an upper bound
steps.body:
Claim. For measures \(\mu, u\) on \(H\) and every \(\gamma\in\Gamma(\mu, u)\), \(W_2(\mu, u)\le c(\gamma)\).

Proof. An infimum is a lower bound of the family over which it is taken. \(\square\)

steps.title: The joint law of two random vectors
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(P\) be a measure on \(\Omega\) and \(X,Y:\Omega\to H\) measurable. Then the joint law \(\gamma=(X,Y)_\#P\), the image of \(P\) under \(\omega\mapsto(X(\omega),Y(\omega))\), is a coupling of \(X_\#P\) and \(Y_\#P\).

Proof. The map \((X,Y):\Omega\to H\times H\) is measurable for the product \(\sigma\)-algebra because both coordinates are measurable, and the projections are measurable. For measurable maps the image of an image measure is the image under the composition: \((\mathrm{pr}_1)_\#(X,Y)_\#P=(\mathrm{pr}_1\circ(X,Y))_\#P=X_\#P\), since \(\mathrm{pr}_1\circ(X,Y)=X\). Likewise \((\mathrm{pr}_2)_\#\gamma=Y_\#P\). \(\square\)

No relation between \(X\) and \(Y\) (such as independence) is required.

steps.title: Joint laws of almost everywhere measurable vectors
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(P\) be a measure on \(\Omega\) and \(X,Y:\Omega\to H\) be \(P\)-almost everywhere measurable. Then \((X,Y)_\#P\) is a coupling of \(X_\#P\) and \(Y_\#P\).

Proof. For an almost everywhere measurable map, the image measure is computed with any measurable map equal to it almost everywhere, and does not depend on that choice. The pair \((X,Y)\) is almost everywhere measurable, the projections are measurable, and the composition rule \((\mathrm{pr}_i)_\#(X,Y)_\#P=(\mathrm{pr}_i\circ(X,Y))_\#P\) holds in this setting; the proof is then that of the previous step. \(\square\)

This form applies to representatives of classes in \(L^2\), which are in general only almost everywhere measurable.

steps.title: The cost of a joint law
steps.body:
Claim. For measurable \(X,Y:\Omega\to H\),

\[c\bigl((X,Y)_\#P\bigr)=\|X-Y\|_{2,P}.\]

Proof. Let \(\varphi(x,y)=x-y\), a continuous map on \(H\times H\). By the change-of-variables formula for image measures, \(\int\|\varphi\|^2\,d\bigl((X,Y)_\#P\bigr)=\int\|\varphi\circ(X,Y)\|^2\,dP\), and \(\varphi\circ(X,Y)=X-Y\). Taking square roots gives the claim; both sides are infinite simultaneously. \(\square\)

steps.title: A coupled pair bounds the transport distance
steps.body:
Claim. For measurable \(X,Y:\Omega\to H\),

\[W_2(X_\#P,Y_\#P)\le\|X-Y\|_{2,P}.\]

Proof. By Step 6, \((X,Y)_\#P\in\Gamma(X_\#P,Y_\#P)\). By Step 5, \(W_2(X_\#P,Y_\#P)\le c((X,Y)_\#P)\), and by Step 8 this cost equals \(\|X-Y\|_{2,P}\). \(\square\)

Thus any two random vectors defined on a common probability space, for instance two copies of an algorithm driven by the same noise, give an upper bound for the transport distance between their laws.

steps.body:
Claim. Let \(X,Y:\Omega\to H\) be measurable with \(X-Y\) square integrable, i.e. \(\|X-Y\|_{2,P}<\infty\). Then \(W_2(X_\#P,Y_\#P)<\infty\) and

Only the difference \(X-Y\) needs a finite second moment, not \(X\) and \(Y\) separately.

steps.title: The transport bound for classes in \(L^2\)
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(P\) be a measure and \(X,Y\in L^2(P;H)\), with representatives also denoted \(X,Y\). Then

\[W_2(X_\#P,Y_\#P)\le\|X-Y\|_{L^2}<\infty.\]

Proof. Representatives of classes in \(L^2\) are almost everywhere strongly measurable, hence almost everywhere measurable, so Step 10 gives \(W_2(X_\#P,Y_\#P)\le\|\omega\mapsto X(\omega)-Y(\omega)\|_{2,P}\). The function \(\omega\mapsto X(\omega)-Y(\omega)\) agrees almost everywhere with the representative of the class \(X-Y\); hence its extended norm is \(\|X-Y\|_{L^2}\), which is finite. \(\square\)

steps.title: The real transport bound for classes in \(L^2\)
steps.body:
Claim. For \(X,Y\in L^2(P;H)\),

\[W_2^{\mathbb R}(X_\#P,Y_\#P)\le\|X-Y\|_{L^2}.\]

Proof. By the previous step \(W_2(X_\#P,Y_\#P)\) is finite and at most \(\|X-Y\|_{L^2}\); hence \(W_2^{\mathbb R}(X_\#P,Y_\#P)=W_2(X_\#P,Y_\#P)\le\|X-Y\|_{L^2}\). \(\square\)

This is the form used at the end of the convergence proofs: if \(X\) is the output of the algorithm and \(Y\) has the target law \(\pi\), any bound on \(\|X-Y\|_{L^2}\) bounds \(W_2^{\mathbb R}(X_\#P,\pi)\).

steps.title: Pointwise domination passes to the \(L^2\)-norm
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(P\) be a measure on \(\Omega\), \(A,D:\Omega\to H\) and \(q\ge0\). Assume that \(A\) is almost everywhere strongly measurable and that \(\|A(\omega)\|\le q\|D(\omega)\|\) for \(P\)-almost every \(\omega\). Then

\[\|A\|_{2,P}\le q\,\|D\|_{2,P}\qquad\text{in }[0,\infty].\]

Proof. If \(D\) is almost everywhere strongly measurable, squaring the pointwise bound (both sides are nonnegative) and integrating gives \(\int\|A\|^2\,dP\le q^2\int\|D\|^2\,dP\) in \([0,\infty]\); taking square roots gives the claim. Otherwise \(\|D\|_{2,P}=\infty\): if \(q>0\) the right-hand side is \(\infty\); if \(q=0\), then \(A=0\) almost everywhere, so \(\|A\|_{2,P}=0=0\cdot\infty\). \(\square\)

No relation between the laws of \(A\) and \(D\) is needed.

steps.title: One step: contraction plus defect
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(P\) be a measure on \(\Omega\), \(X,Y,X',Y',A,V:\Omega\to H\) and \(q\ge0\). Assume that \(A\) is almost everywhere strongly measurable and that, for \(P\)-almost every \(\omega\),

\[X'(\omega)-Y'(\omega)=A(\omega)-V(\omega),\qquad\|A(\omega)\|\le q\,\|X(\omega)-Y(\omega)\|.\]

Then

\[\|X'-Y'\|_{2,P}\le q\,\|X-Y\|_{2,P}+\|V\|_{2,P}\qquad\text{in }[0,\infty].\]

Proof. Since \(X'-Y'=A-V\) almost everywhere, \(\|X'-Y'\|_{2,P}=\|A-V\|_{2,P}\). By Minkowski's inequality, \(\|A-V\|_{2,P}\le\|A\|_{2,P}+\|V\|_{2,P}\), and by the previous step \(\|A\|_{2,P}\le q\|X-Y\|_{2,P}\). \(\square\)

In the application, \(X,Y\) are the current numerical and reference states, \(X',Y'\) the next ones, \(A\) the difference of the two updates with common noise, and \(V\) the local defect. The defect enters additively through Minkowski's inequality; no orthogonality between \(A\) and \(V\) is needed.

steps.title: The one-step inequality in real numbers
steps.body:
Claim. Under the hypotheses of Step 15, assume in addition that \(X-Y\) and \(V\) are square integrable. Then all quantities below are finite and

\[\|X'-Y'\|_{2,P}\le q\,\|X-Y\|_{2,P}+\|V\|_{2,P}\qquad\text{in }\mathbb R.\]

Proof. Since \(q<\infty\), \(\|X-Y\|_{2,P}<\infty\) and \(\|V\|_{2,P}<\infty\), the right-hand side of Step 15 is finite; hence so is the left-hand side, and the inequality of Step 15 is an inequality between real numbers. For finite values, the real value of a sum or product in \([0,\infty]\) is the sum or product of the real values. \(\square\)

In particular \(X'-Y'\) is square integrable whenever \(X-Y\) and \(V\) are. Iterating this one-step inequality gives the scalar recurrence \(e_{k+1}\le qe_k+b\) for \(e_k=\|X_k-Y_k\|_{2,P}\).
