UnadjustedLangevin/Integrability.lean.title: Propagation of finite error moments
UnadjustedLangevin/Integrability.lean.summary:
Suppose \(E=A-V\) almost everywhere, \(A\) is almost everywhere strongly measurable, and \(\|A\|\le q\|D\|\). Finite \(L^p\) membership of \(D\) transfers to \(A\) by domination, and finite \(L^p\) membership of \(V\) then gives that of \(E\). Applied to successive coupled Euler updates, this proves finite second moments of every error from the finite initial error and finite defects.

The common noise cancels in the difference of the updates. Hence the moment induction uses only the preceding error and the defect. A contraction factor strictly below one is not needed for this finiteness result; that restriction is imposed when summing the convergence recurrence.

steps.title: Finite moments under domination and addition
steps.body:
Let \(p\in[0,+\infty]\), \(q\in\mathbb R\), and \(D,A,V,E:\Omega\to H\). Assume \(A\) is almost everywhere strongly measurable, \(E=A-V\) almost everywhere, and \(\|A\|\le q\|D\|\) almost everywhere. If \(D,V\in L^p(P;H)\), then \(E\in L^p(P;H)\).

The domination transfers the finite \(L^p\) moment of \(D\) to \(A\).

The difference \(A-V\) belongs to \(L^p\). Almost everywhere equality then transfers this property to \(E\).

The comparison of norms supplies finite \(p\)-moment size, while almost-everywhere strong measurability supplies the measurability part of membership. Combining both is necessary: a numerical upper bound alone would not define a valid Bochner-integrable random variable. The equality \(E=A-V\) then transfers membership through the algebra of \(L^p\).

steps.title: All coupling errors have finite second moment
steps.body:
Assume \(\nabla U\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, \(q\ge0\), and the initial vector, every noise vector, and every \(Y_k\) are measurable. Suppose

\[Y_{k+1}=T_h(U,h,Y_k,\xi_k)+V_k\quad\text{almost everywhere},\]

and common-noise updates satisfy \(\|T_h(U,h,x,z)-T_h(U,h,y,z)\|\le q\|x-y\|\). If \(X_0-Y_0\in L^2\) and every \(V_k\in L^2\), then \(X_n-Y_n\in L^2\) for all \(n\). This assertion does not require stationarity or \(q<1\).

Let the iterates be \(X_k\), whose measurability follows from the chain lemma. We must prove \(X_n-Y_n\in L^2\).

Induct on \(n\). The initial case is the assumed finite initial error; for the successor, assume \(X_n-Y_n\in L^2\).

Set \(A=T_h(U,h,X_n,\xi_n)-T_h(U,h,Y_n,\xi_n)\), the update difference before adding the reference defect.

The gradient and both update inputs are measurable, so the update difference \(A\) is measurable and hence almost everywhere strongly measurable.

Subtract the recursive updates on the full-measure set where the reference equation holds. This gives \(X_{n+1}-Y_{n+1}=A-V_n\).

The common-noise contraction gives \(\|A\|\le q\|X_n-Y_n\|\) pointwise, hence almost everywhere.

Apply the finite-moment lemma to the induction hypothesis and \(V_n\in L^2\), proving \(X_{n+1}-Y_{n+1}\in L^2\).

At step \(n\), the shared-noise update difference is dominated by \(q\|X_n-Y_n\|\). The assumed defect has a finite second moment, so their difference does as well. Induction repeats this argument for every finite index. The proof establishes moments even in regimes with \(q\ge1\); the strict upper bound on \(q\) is used only later for decay.

UnadjustedLangevin/Recurrence.lean.title: Iteration of the scalar error estimate
UnadjustedLangevin/Recurrence.lean.summary:
This section studies real sequences \((e_n)_{n\ge0}\) satisfying a one-step inequality \(e_{n+1}\le q\,e_n+b\), where \(q\ge0\) and \(b\) are fixed real numbers. Every convergence proof in this report ends with an inequality of this kind: \(e_n\) is an error after \(n\) iterations of an algorithm, \(q\) is the factor by which one iteration contracts the error, and \(b\) is the error newly introduced by each iteration. We prove, in increasing order of simplification, the three bounds

\[e_n\le q^ne_0+b\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}q^j,\qquad e_n\le q^ne_0+\frac{b(1-q^n)}{1-q},\qquad e_n\le q^ne_0+\frac{b}{1-q},\]

the second for \(0\le q<1\) and the third when in addition \(b\ge0\). We then show that the right-hand side of the third bound converges to \(b/(1-q)\) as \(n\to\infty\), and deduce that every tolerance \(\varepsilon>b/(1-q)\) is eventually met by the sequence. No probability enters this section: the one-step inequality for the random algorithm is proved elsewhere, and only the scalar calculation is carried out here.

steps.title: Iteration gives a geometric sum
steps.body:
Claim. Let \((e_n)_{n\ge0}\) be a sequence of real numbers and let \(q,b\in\mathbb R\) with \(q\ge0\). Suppose that

\[e_{k+1}\le q\,e_k+b\qquad\text{for every }k\in\mathbb N.\]

Then for every \(n\in\mathbb N\),

\[e_n\le q^ne_0+b\,S_n,\qquad\text{where}\quad S_n=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}q^j,\]

with the convention that the empty sum \(S_0\) equals \(0\).

Proof. We argue by induction on \(n\).

Base case \(n=0\). Since \(q^0=1\) and \(S_0=0\), the right-hand side equals \(e_0\), and \(e_0\le e_0\).

Inductive step. Fix \(n\) and assume the induction hypothesis \(e_n\le q^ne_0+bS_n\). Because \(q\ge0\), multiplying both sides of this inequality by \(q\) preserves its direction:

\[q\,e_n\le q^{n+1}e_0+b\,qS_n.\qquad(1)\]

Next we compute \(qS_n\). Multiplying the finite sum term by term and shifting the index,

\[qS_n=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}q^{j+1}=\sum_{j=1}^{n}q^{j}=S_n-1+q^n,\]

because the last sum contains every term of \(S_n\) except \(q^0=1\), together with the additional term \(q^n\). Hence \(qS_n+1=S_n+q^n=S_{n+1}\). Multiplying this identity by \(b\) gives

\[b\,qS_n+b=b\,S_{n+1}.\qquad(2)\]

Now apply the hypothesis with \(k=n\), then (1), then (2):

\[e_{n+1}\le q\,e_n+b\le q^{n+1}e_0+b\,qS_n+b=q^{n+1}e_0+b\,S_{n+1}.\]

This is the claim for \(n+1\), which completes the induction. \(\square\)

Written out, the bound reads \(e_n\le q^ne_0+b(1+q+\dots+q^{n-1})\): the initial error is multiplied by \(q\) once per iteration, and the defect \(b\) introduced at iteration \(j\) has been multiplied by \(q\) once for each of the \(n-1-j\) later iterations.

steps.title: The finite geometric-sum bound
steps.body:
Claim. In the setting of the previous step, assume in addition that \(q<1\), so that \(0\le q<1\). Then for every \(n\in\mathbb N\),

\[e_n\le q^ne_0+\frac{b\,(1-q^n)}{1-q}.\]

Proof. By the previous step, \(e_n\le q^ne_0+bS_n\) with \(S_n=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}q^j\). It remains to evaluate \(S_n\). The sum telescopes after multiplication by \(q-1\):

\[(q-1)S_n=\sum_{j=0}^{n-1}\bigl(q^{j+1}-q^{j}\bigr)=q^n-1.\]

Since \(q<1\), we have \(q-1\neq0\), and dividing gives the finite geometric series formula \(S_n=(q^n-1)/(q-1)\). Multiplying numerator and denominator by \(-1\),

\[S_n=\frac{1-q^n}{1-q},\]

a quotient whose denominator \(1-q\) is positive. Substituting this expression into the bound of the previous step and writing \(b\cdot\frac{1-q^n}{1-q}=\frac{b(1-q^n)}{1-q}\) proves the claim. \(\square\)

Since \(0\le q^n\le1\), the factor \(1-q^n\) lies in \([0,1]\). It records that only \(n\) defects have been introduced by iteration \(n\); for \(n=0\) the bound reduces to \(e_0\le e_0\).

steps.title: A uniform additive error bound
steps.body:
Claim. If \(0\le q<1\), \(b\ge0\) and \(e_{k+1}\le qe_k+b\) for all \(k\), then for every \(n\in\mathbb N\),

\[e_n\le q^ne_0+\frac{b}{1-q}.\]

Proof. Start from the bound of the previous step. Since \(q\ge0\), we have \(q^n\ge0\) and hence \(1-q^n\le1\). Multiplying this inequality by \(b\ge0\) gives \(b(1-q^n)\le b\). Dividing both sides by the positive number \(1-q\) preserves the inequality:

\[\frac{b(1-q^n)}{1-q}\le\frac{b}{1-q}.\]

Adding \(q^ne_0\) to both sides and combining with the previous step by transitivity of \(\le\) gives the claim. \(\square\)

The bound consists of the term \(q^ne_0\), which tends to zero as \(n\to\infty\), and the constant \(b/(1-q)\), which does not depend on \(n\). The hypothesis \(b\ge0\) cannot be omitted: if \(b<0\), then \(b(1-q^n)\ge b\), and the comparison of the two fractions is reversed.

steps.title: Limit of the upper-bound sequence
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(0\le q<1\) and let \(b,c\in\mathbb R\). Then

\[\lim_{n\to\infty}\Bigl(q^nc+\frac{b}{1-q}\Bigr)=\frac{b}{1-q}.\]

Proof. First, \(q^n\to0\). If \(q=0\), then \(q^n=0\) for every \(n\ge1\). If \(0<q<1\), write \(q=1/(1+t)\) with \(t=1/q-1>0\). Bernoulli's inequality \((1+t)^n\ge1+nt\), which follows by induction on \(n\), gives

\[0\le q^n=\frac{1}{(1+t)^n}\le\frac{1}{1+nt}\longrightarrow0\qquad(n\to\infty).\]

Limits are compatible with multiplication by a fixed number and with addition of a fixed number. Therefore \(q^nc\to0\cdot c=0\) and \(q^nc+b/(1-q)\to b/(1-q)\). \(\square\)

With \(c=e_0\), this is the limit of the upper bound of the previous step. The statement concerns the bound only: the sequence \((e_n)\) need not converge.

steps.title: Eventual error below any larger tolerance
steps.body:
Claim. Assume \(0\le q<1\), \(b\ge0\) and \(e_{k+1}\le qe_k+b\) for every \(k\). Then for every \(\varepsilon>b/(1-q)\) there exists \(n_0\in\mathbb N\) such that \(e_n<\varepsilon\) for all \(n\ge n_0\).

Proof. Put \(u_n=q^ne_0+b/(1-q)\). By the previous step with \(c=e_0\), \(u_n\to b/(1-q)\). Since \(\varepsilon>b/(1-q)\), the number \(\delta=\varepsilon-b/(1-q)\) is positive. By the definition of the limit there is \(n_0\) such that \(|u_n-b/(1-q)|<\delta\) for all \(n\ge n_0\); for these \(n\),

\[u_n<\frac{b}{1-q}+\delta=\varepsilon.\]

For the same \(n\), the uniform bound proved two steps earlier gives \(e_n\le u_n\), hence \(e_n<\varepsilon\). \(\square\)

Every accuracy level strictly above \(b/(1-q)\) is therefore reached after finitely many iterations. Accuracy below \(b/(1-q)\) is not asserted.

UnadjustedLangevin/InitialCoupling.lean.title: Passing from a chosen initial coupling to an infimum
UnadjustedLangevin/InitialCoupling.lean.summary:
Let the output measures be fixed and assume that every initial coupling gives an affine bound in its cost with the same constants. Taking the infimum over couplings gives the corresponding bound in \(W_2(\mu,\nu)\). This uses the infimum property and does not assume an optimal coupling.

If the initial transport distance is finite, a finite-cost coupling exists. Approximate minimizing couplings then suffice even if the assumed estimate is stated only for finite-cost couplings. When the affine coefficient is zero, one such coupling already proves the constant bound. When it is positive, couplings with cost approaching the infimum give the result by taking a limit.

steps.title: A uniform affine estimate passes to the infimum
steps.body:
Let \(a\ge0\) be finite, \(b\in[0,+\infty]\), and \(\Gamma(\mu, u) e\varnothing\). If the fixed output measures satisfy

\[W_2(\mu', u')\le ac(\gamma)+b\quad ext{for every }\gamma\in\Gamma(\mu, u),\]

then \(W_2(\mu', u')\le aW_2(\mu, u)+b\).

Use the nonempty coupling family and expand transport distances as infima.

Multiplication by finite \(a\ge0\) and addition of \(b\) commute with the nonempty extended-real infimum, including \(a=0\). Thus \(aW_2(\mu, u)+b=\inf_\gamma(ac(\gamma)+b)\).

The output distance lies below every member of this last family, hence below its infimum.

For \(a>0\), choose couplings whose costs approach the infimum and apply the estimate to each one. Multiplication by \(a\) and addition of \(b\) commute with this monotone affine approximation. At \(a=0\), the conclusion is simply the common constant bound \(b\), so no optimizer or limiting transport cost is required.

steps.body:
If \(W_2(\mu,\nu)<+\infty\), then some \(\gamma\in\Gamma(\mu,\nu)\) has \(c(\gamma)<+\infty\). Attainment of the infimum is not asserted.

The coupling-cost infimum is strictly below \(+\infty\) by the finiteness hypothesis.

An infimum strictly below a threshold has a member strictly below that threshold. Apply this with threshold \(+\infty\).

If every admissible coupling had infinite cost, the infimum of their costs would also be infinite. Thus a finite infimum provides at least one finite-cost plan. More quantitatively, an approximate minimizer with cost below the finite infimum plus one is sufficient to establish the required finiteness.

steps.title: Finite-cost initial couplings suffice
steps.body:
Let \(a,b\ge0\) be finite and assume \(W_2(\mu, u)<\infty\) and \(W_2(\mu', u')<\infty\). Suppose every finite-cost initial coupling satisfies

\[W_2(\mu', u')\le a c(\gamma)+b\qquad (\gamma\in\Gamma(\mu, u),\ c(\gamma)<\infty).\]

For every \(\varepsilon>0\), finiteness of the initial infimum supplies a coupling \(\gamma_\varepsilon\) with

\[c(\gamma_\varepsilon)<W_2(\mu, u)+\varepsilon<\infty.\]

Insert this coupling into the uniform estimate. For \(a>0\), let \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) to obtain

\[W_2(\mu', u')\le aW_2(\mu, u)+b.\]

If \(a=0\), any one of these finite-cost couplings already gives the conclusion \(W_2(\mu', u')\le b\). Thus no expression involving zero times infinite cost is needed. Infinite-cost couplings cannot improve a finite infimum, and no minimizing coupling is assumed to exist.

Let \(X_k\) be the numerical iterates and \(Y_k\) a supplied reference on the same probability space, with \(\mathcal L(Y_k)=\pi\). Subtracting the updates gives \(e_{k+1}\le qe_k+b\), where \(e_k=\|X_k-Y_k\|_2\). Moment propagation ensures these norms are finite.

Replacing that cost by an initial Wasserstein distance requires the same construction and constants for every finite-cost initial coupling.

steps.title: Transport bound from a supplied discrete reference
steps.body:
Let \(\nabla U\) be \(L\)-Lipschitz, \(0\le q<1\), and \(b\ge0\). Assume the initial vector, all noise vectors, and all reference vectors \(Y_k\) are measurable; \((Y_k)_\#P=\pi\); and

\[Y_{k+1}=T_h(U,h,Y_k,\xi_k)+V_k\quad\text{almost everywhere}.\]

Suppose the common-noise update is \(q\)-contractive, \(X_0-Y_0\in L^2\), every \(V_k\in L^2\), and \(\|V_k\|_2\le b\). Then

\[W_2((X_n)_\#P,\pi)\le q^n\|X_0-Y_0\|_2+\frac b{1-q}.\]

The initial term is the cost of the chosen coupled pair.

Let the iterates be \(X_k\) and let \(e_k=\|X_k-Y_k\|_2\).

Finite moments propagate from the initial error and the defects, so each \(e_k\) is a finite \(L^2\) norm. Every numerical iterate is measurable.

To derive the recurrence, fix \(k\) and set \(A=T_h(U,h,X_k,\xi_k)-T_h(U,h,Y_k,\xi_k)\).

Measurability of the gradient and the inputs makes \(A\) measurable, hence almost everywhere strongly measurable.

Subtract the two updates on the full-measure set where the reference identity holds. This yields \(X_{k+1}-Y_{k+1}=A-V_k\).

The common-noise contraction gives \(\|A\|\le q\|X_k-Y_k\|\).

The finite-moment synchronous bound and \(\|V_k\|_2\le b\) give the recurrence \(e_{k+1}\le qe_k+b\).

The joint law of the coupled pair bounds transport by \(e_n\). Its reference marginal is \(\pi\) by the supplied stationary law.

Iterate the derived recurrence to get \(e_n\le q^ne_0+b/(1-q)\), and compose with the transport comparison.

For the chosen reference, let \(e_k=(\mathbb E\|X_k-Y_k\|^2)^{1/2}\). The shared-noise decomposition gives \(e_{k+1}\le qe_k+b\), with all norms finite by the preceding induction. Therefore \(e_n\le q^ne_0+b(1-q^n)/(1-q)\). The coupling inequality and stationarity of \(Y_n\) yield the displayed result after replacing the finite geometric factor by its uniform upper bound.

steps.title: The continuous reference assumptions
steps.body:
For an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, step \(h\), noise vectors \(\xi_k\in\mathcal H\), and a measure \(\pi\), a reference consists of segments \(Y_{k,t}\in\mathcal H\) and increments \(B_{k,t}\in\mathcal H\) satisfying the following conditions.

Supply the two families \((Y_{k,t})\) and \((B_{k,t})\) in the Hilbert space \(\mathcal H\).

Require continuity of \(t\mapsto Y_{k,t}\) in the \(L^2\) norm for every \(k\).

Require compatible endpoints, common endpoint noise, and stationary grid laws:

\[Y_{k,h}=Y_{k+1,0},\qquad B_{k,h}=\sqrt{2h}\,\xi_k,\qquad(Y_{k,0})_\#P=\pi.\]

For \(0\le t\le h\), require

\[Y_{k,t}-Y_{k,0}=-\int_0^t g(Y_{k,s})\,ds+B_{k,t}.\]

Require the score moment bound \(\|g(Y_{k,t})\|_2\le\sqrt{Ld}\) throughout each closed step interval.

Require the increment moment bound \(\|B_{k,t}\|_2\le\sqrt{2d}\sqrt t\) on the same interval.

The segment-joining condition makes the local initial point of segment \(k+1\) equal to the endpoint of segment \(k\). The stationary grid-law condition identifies each comparison marginal with \(\pi\), while the endpoint-noise condition identifies the reference's final increment with the algorithm innovation. \[W_2((X_n)_\#P,\pi)\le q^n\|X_0-Y_{0,0}\|_2+\frac{(33/20)Lh\sqrt{hd}}{1-q}.\]

\[b=\frac{33}{20}Lh\sqrt{hd},\qquad D_k=\int_0^h\bigl(g(Y_{k,t})-g(Y_{k,0})\bigr)\,dt.\]

The bound \(b\) is nonnegative. Apply the local-defect theorem to the gradient map on square-integrable classes and the supplied equation and moment bounds, deriving \(\|D_k\|_2\le b\).

We claim the reference endpoints obey

\[Y_{k+1,0}=Y_{k,0}-hg(Y_{k,0})+\sqrt{2h}\,\xi_k-D_k.\]

The lifted gradient is Lipschitz and the reference segment is continuous, so their composition is continuous and Bochner integrable on \([0,h]\).

\[X_{k+1}-Y_{k+1,0}=\bigl(X_k-hg(X_k)\bigr)-\bigl(Y_{k,0}-hg(Y_{k,0})\bigr)+D_k.\]

Apply the triangle inequality, Euler contraction, and the defect bound. Setting \(e_k=\|X_k-Y_{k,0}\|_2\) gives \(e_{k+1}\le qe_k+b\).

The joint law of the pair supplies a finite-cost coupling, so its transport distance is at most \(e_n\). The second marginal is \(\pi\) by the stationary grid-law assumption.

The defect has size \(b=(33/20)Lh\sqrt{hd}\), and this size is uniform in \(k\) because the supplied moment bounds hold on every segment. The recurrence is consequently homogeneous in its constants. steps.body:

\[\frac{(33/20)Lh\sqrt{hd}}{1-(1-mh)}=\frac{(33/20)Lh\sqrt{hd}}{mh}=\frac{33}{20}\frac Lm\sqrt{hd}.\]

This is a finite real number whenever \(\| abla U\|^2\) is integrable with respect to \( ho_k\); every result that uses \(G_k\) below assumes this integrability for all \(k\). steps.title: Finiteness of the entropy of each iterate
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(U:E o\mathbb R\) be any function, let \(h\ge0\), let \(\mu\) and \( u\) be measures on \(E\), and let \( ho_k=P_h^k\mu\). Let \((r_{k,t})_{k\in\mathbb N,\,t\in\mathbb R}\) be real functions on \(E\) such that for every \(k\in\mathbb N\) and every \(t\in[0,h]\)

  1. \(r_{k,t} u=P_t ho_k\), where \(r u\) denotes the measure \(A\mapsto\int_A\max\{r,0\}\,d u\);
  2. \(H_ u(r_{k,t} u)<\infty\).

Then \(H_ u( ho_k)<\infty\) for every \(k\in\mathbb N\).

Proof. Fix \(k\). Since \(h\ge0\), the time \(t=0\) belongs to \([0,h]\), so hypothesis 2 gives \(H_ u(r_{k,0} u)<\infty\) and hypothesis 1 gives \(r_{k,0} u=P_0 ho_k\). At time zero the update map is \(T_0(x,z)=x-0\cdot abla U(x)+\sqrt0\,z=x\), the projection onto the first coordinate. The image of a product measure \( ho\otimes\gamma_n\) under this projection is \(\gamma_n(E)\, ho= ho\), because \(\gamma_n\) is a probability measure. Hence \(P_0 ho_k= ho_k\), and therefore

\[H_ u( ho_k)=H_ u(P_0 ho_k)=H_ u(r_{k,0} u)<\infty.\]

Since \(k\) was arbitrary, the claim follows. \(\square\)

Only the time \(t=0\) is used, and no property of \(U\), \(\mu\) or \( u\) enters: the relative entropy is a function of the pair of measures, and the two measures \( ho_k\) and \(r_{k,0} u\) are equal. The statement is needed because the recurrence below is an inequality between real numbers, and the extended value \(H_ u( ho_k)=\infty\) must be excluded before the entropies are treated as such.

The measure tiltedMeasure ν (r k t) is \(r_{k,t}\nu\), and interpolationLaw U (ulaLaws U h μ k) t is \(P_t\rho_k\). The relative entropy is Mathlib's InformationTheory.klDiv, which takes values in the extended nonnegative reals ℝ≥0∞ \(=[0,\infty]\); the conclusion klDiv (ulaLaws U h μ k) ν ≠ ⊤ says that \(H_\nu(\rho_k)\) is not \(+\infty\) (⊤ is the top element \(\infty\)).

steps.title: The one-step entropy inequality
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(L>0\), \(\alpha>0\) and \(h>0\) satisfy

\[\alpha\le L,\qquad h\le\frac{\alpha}{4L^2}.\]

Let \(U:E\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, \(\|\nabla U(x)-\nabla U(y)\|\le L\|x-y\|\), and assume that the Gibbs measure \(\nu\) of \(U\) satisfies the log-Sobolev inequality with constant \(\alpha\) (in particular \(\nu\) is a probability measure). Let \(\mu\) be a probability measure on \(E\), let \(\rho_k=P_h^k\mu\), and assume that \(\|\nabla U\|^2\) is \(\rho_k\)-integrable for every \(k\); let \(G_k\) be as in the first step. Let \(r_{k,t}:E\to\mathbb R\) and \(H'_k(t)\in\mathbb R\) (\(k\in\mathbb N\), \(t\in\mathbb R\)) be given, and write

\[H_k(t)=H_\nu(r_{k,t}\nu),\qquad J_k(t)=J_\nu(r_{k,t})=\int\|\nabla\log r_{k,t}\|^2\,d(r_{k,t}\nu).\]

Assume that for every \(k\in\mathbb N\):

  1. (law) \(r_{k,t}\nu=P_t\rho_k\) for every \(t\in[0,h]\);
  2. (test class) for every \(t\in[0,h]\), \(r_{k,t}(x)>0\) for all \(x\in E\) and \(r_{k,t}\) is continuously differentiable;
  3. (finiteness) \(H_k(t)<\infty\) and \(J_k(t)<\infty\) for every \(t\in[0,h]\);
  4. (continuity) \(t\mapsto H_k(t)\) is continuous on \([0,h]\);
  5. (right derivative) for every \(t\in[0,h)\), \(H_k\) has right derivative \(H'_k(t)\) at \(t\): \(\bigl(H_k(s)-H_k(t)\bigr)/(s-t)\to H'_k(t)\) as \(s\downarrow t\);
  6. (entropy production) for every \(t\in[0,h)\), \(H'_k(t)\le-\frac34J_k(t)+t^2L^2G_k+2tnL^2\);
  7. (gradient moment) \(G_k\le\frac{4L^2}{\alpha}H_k(0)+2nL\).

Then for every \(k\in\mathbb N\),

\[H_\nu(\rho_{k+1})\le e^{-\alpha h}H_\nu(\rho_k)+6h^2nL^2.\]

By the previous step (with hypotheses 1 and 3), all the divergences \(H_\nu(\rho_j)\) are finite, so this is an inequality between real numbers.

Proof. Fix \(k\). By hypothesis 3 the functions \(H_k\) and \(J_k\) are real-valued on \([0,h]\).

Endpoints. By hypothesis 1 at \(t=0\) and the identity \(P_0\rho=\rho\) (previous step), \(r_{k,0}\nu=\rho_k\), so \(H_k(0)=H_\nu(\rho_k)\). By hypothesis 1 at \(t=h\) and the definition of the iterates, \(r_{k,h}\nu=P_h\rho_k=P_h(P_h^k\mu)=\rho_{k+1}\), so \(H_k(h)=H_\nu(\rho_{k+1})\).

Normalization. Each \(r_{k,t}\nu\) with \(t\in[0,h]\) is a probability measure. Indeed, \(\nabla U\) is Lipschitz, hence continuous, so \(T_t\) is a continuous and therefore Borel measurable map \(E\times E\to E\). The image of a measure under a measurable map has the same total mass, so \(P_t\rho\) is a probability measure whenever \(\rho\) is one. By induction on \(j\), starting from the probability measure \(\rho_0=\mu\) and using \(\rho_{j+1}=P_h\rho_j\), every \(\rho_j\) is a probability measure; hence so is \(P_t\rho_k=r_{k,t}\nu\).

The log-Sobolev inequality along the path. Let \(t\in[0,h)\). By hypothesis 2 and the normalization just proved, \(r_{k,t}\) belongs to the test class of the log-Sobolev inequality, which therefore gives \(2\alpha H_k(t)\le J_k(t)\) in \([0,\infty]\). Both sides are finite by hypothesis 3, so this is the real inequality

\[2\alpha H_k(t)\le J_k(t)\qquad(0\le t<h).\qquad(1)\]

The scalar argument. The relative entropy is nonnegative, so \(H_k(0)\ge0\). The scalar one-step lemma states: if \(\alpha,L,h>0\), \(\alpha\le L\), \(n\ge0\), \(h\le\alpha/(4L^2)\), \(H(0)\ge0\), \(H\) is continuous on \([0,h]\) with right derivatives \(H'(t)\) on \([0,h)\), and on \([0,h)\)

\[2\alpha H(t)\le I(t),\qquad H'(t)\le-\tfrac34I(t)+t^2L^2G+2tnL^2,\qquad G\le\tfrac{4L^2}{\alpha}H(0)+2nL,\]

then \(H(h)\le e^{-\alpha h}H(0)+6h^2nL^2\). (Its proof combines the three inequalities into \(H'\le-\frac32\alpha H+\frac\alpha4H(0)+\frac52hnL^2\), integrates this linear differential inequality and compares exponentials.) We apply it with \(H=H_k\), \(H'=H'_k\), \(I=J_k\), \(G=G_k\) and \(n=\dim E\ge0\): the continuity, right-derivative, production and gradient hypotheses are hypotheses 4–7, and the log-Sobolev hypothesis is (1). It gives \(H_k(h)\le e^{-\alpha h}H_k(0)+6h^2nL^2\). Substituting the endpoint identities \(H_k(0)=H_\nu(\rho_k)\) and \(H_k(h)=H_\nu(\rho_{k+1})\) proves the claim. \(\square\)

The Lipschitz hypothesis is used here only for measurability of the update map, that is, for the normalization of the interpolating laws; quantitatively, \(L\) enters through hypotheses 6 and 7 and the step restriction. Differentiability of \(U\) and integrability of \(\|\nabla U\|^2\) are part of the hypotheses because they make \(G_k\) the integral of an integrable function; the argument does not use them otherwise.

steps.title: Iteration of the one-step inequality
steps.body:
Claim. Under the hypotheses of the previous step, for every \(k\in\mathbb N\),

\[H_\nu(\rho_k)\le e^{-\alpha hk}H_\nu(\mu)+\frac{8hnL^2}{\alpha}.\]

All the divergences are finite (by the second step, applied with hypotheses 1 and 3), so this is an inequality between real numbers.

Proof. Write \(H_j=H_\nu(\rho_j)\). By the previous step,

\[H_{j+1}\le e^{-\alpha h}H_j+6h^2nL^2\qquad\text{for every }j\in\mathbb N.\qquad(1)\]

The product \(\alpha h\) is at most \(1/4\). Since \(4L^2>0\), the step restriction \(h\le\alpha/(4L^2)\) is equivalent to \(4hL^2\le\alpha\). Together with \(\alpha\le L\) this gives \(4hL\cdot L\le L\), and dividing by \(L>0\) gives \(4hL\le1\), that is \(hL\le\frac14\). Since \(h>0\) and \(\alpha\le L\), we get \(\alpha h\le Lh\le\frac14\).

Iteration. Put \(q=e^{-\alpha h}\) and \(c=6h^2nL^2\ge0\). Since \(\alpha h>0\), \(0<q<1\). The discrete recurrence lemma applies to (1) because \(\alpha>0\), \(h>0\), \(n\ge0\) and \(\alpha h\le\frac14\). Its argument is as follows. Iterating (1) gives \(H_k\le q^kH_0+c\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}q^j\le q^kH_0+c/(1-q)\), where the second inequality uses \(c\ge0\) and \(\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}q^j=(1-q^k)/(1-q)\le1/(1-q)\). For \(0\le x\le\frac14\) one has \(1-e^{-x}\ge\frac34x\); with \(x=\alpha h\),

\[\frac{c}{1-q}\le\frac{6h^2nL^2}{\frac34\alpha h}=\frac{8hnL^2}{\alpha}.\]

Finally \(q^k=e^{-\alpha hk}\) and \(H_0=H_\nu(\rho_0)=H_\nu(\mu)\), because \(\rho_0=P_h^0\mu=\mu\). \(\square\)

The local error \(6h^2nL^2\) of one step is of order \(h^2\), while the contraction gap \(1-e^{-\alpha h}\) is of order \(h\); this is why the accumulated error \(8hnL^2/\alpha\) is of order \(h\). The constants \(6\) and \(8\) are those of Vempala and Wibisono (2019).

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/FunctionalInequal.title: Relative entropy, Fisher information and the log-Sobolev inequality
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/FunctionalInequal.summary:
Let \(E\) be a real inner product space with a \(\sigma\)-algebra (Borel where the log-Sobolev inequality is concerned), and let \( u\) be a measure on \(E\). This section fixes the three objects in which the entropy analysis of the unadjusted Langevin algorithm is written: the measure \(r u\) with a prescribed density \(r\) with respect to \( u\), the relative Fisher information \(J_ u(r)\) of a prescribed density, and the log-Sobolev inequality with constant \(\alpha\). The relative entropy is the Kullback–Leibler divergence: for probability measures \( ho, u\),

\[H_ u( ho)= egin{cases}\displaystyle\int_E\log rac{d ho}{d u}\,d ho, & ext{if } ho\ll u ext{ and }\log rac{d ho}{d u}\in L^1( ho),\ +\infty, & ext{otherwise},\end{cases}\]

where \(d ho/d u\) is the Radon–Nikodym derivative. It takes values in \([0,\infty]\) (nonnegativity is Gibbs' inequality). With these definitions, \( u\) satisfies the log-Sobolev inequality with constant \(\alpha\) if \( u\) is a probability measure and

\[2\alpha\,H_ u(r u)\le J_ u(r)=\int_E\| abla\log r\|^2\,r\,d u\]

for every strictly positive continuously differentiable \(r\) such that \(r u\) is a probability measure; this is the normalization of Vempala and Wibisono (2019), where it reads \(H_ u( ho)\le rac1{2\alpha}J_ u( ho)\). Both sides may be infinite. The last result of the section converts the inequality into an inequality between real numbers when both quantities are known to be finite; every later use of the log-Sobolev inequality goes through it.

steps.title: The measure defined by a density
steps.body:
Definition. For a measure \( u\) on \(E\) and a function \(r:E o\mathbb R\), let \(r u\) be the measure

\[(r u)(A)=\int_A r^+\,d u,\qquad r^+=\max\{r,0\},\]

for measurable \(A\subseteq E\). If \(r\ge0\) this is the usual measure with density \(r\) with respect to \( u\), and \(\int f\,d(r u)=\int fr\,d u\) for measurable \(f\ge0\). If moreover \(r\) is measurable and \(\int r\,d u=1\), then \(r u\) is a probability measure.

The definition is made for every real function, and normalization is not part of it: whether \(r u\) is a probability measure is a separate condition, imposed where it is needed (for instance in the test class of the log-Sobolev inequality). In all applications \(r\) is strictly positive and continuous; positivity is needed later to differentiate \(\log r\), and continuity makes \(r\) measurable.
steps.lean: tiltedMeasure ν r is defined as ν.withDensity (fun x ↦ ENNReal.ofReal (r x)). Mathlib's withDensity takes a density with values in ℝ≥0∞ \(=[0,\infty]\) and returns the measure \(A\mapsto\int_A f\,d\nu\), where the integral of a \([0,\infty]\)-valued function is the Lebesgue integral ∫⁻. ENNReal.ofReal converts a real number \(a\) into the extended nonnegative number \(\max\{a,0\}\); composing with it gives the density \(r^+\) of the definition. No measurability or normalization hypothesis is attached to r.

steps.title: Relative Fisher information
steps.body:
Definition. For a measure \( u\) and a function \(r:E o\mathbb R\), the relative Fisher information of \(r\) is

\[J_ u(r)=\int_E\| abla\log r(x)\|^2\,(r u)(dx)\in[0,\infty].\]

It is the integral of a nonnegative function with respect to the measure \(r u\) of the previous step, so it is always defined and may equal \(+\infty\). When \(r\) is strictly positive and differentiable, \( abla\log r= abla r/r\) and \(J_ u(r)=\int\| abla r\|^2/r\,d u\).

The functional depends on the function \(r\), not only on the measure \(r u\): it is the given function that is differentiated, rather than an unspecified version of the Radon–Nikodym derivative \(d(r u)/d u\), which is determined only \( u\)-almost everywhere and need not be differentiable. If \( u(dx)=Z^{-1}e^{-U(x)}\,dx\) and \( ho=r u\) has a positive differentiable Lebesgue density \(p\), then \(r=Zpe^{U}\), \(\log r=\log p+U+\log Z\), and

\[ abla\log r= abla\log p+ abla U,\qquad J_ u(r)=\int\| abla\log p+ abla U\|^2\,d ho.\]

In particular \(J_ u(r)=0\) for \(r\equiv1\), that is for \( ho= u\).

The integrand is nonnegative, so ENNReal.ofReal only changes its type. Mathlib's Real.log is defined on all of \(\mathbb R\) (with \(\log0=0\) and \(\log x=\log|x|\)), and gradient is defined for every function (it is \(0\) at points of non-differentiability); for the strictly positive \(C^1\) densities to which the definition is applied, both agree with the classical notions. The value is extended, so finiteness must be proved separately before it is used as a real number.

steps.title: The log-Sobolev inequality
steps.body:
Definition. Let \(E\) carry its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra, let \( u\) be a measure on \(E\) and \(\alpha\in\mathbb R\). We say that \( u\) satisfies the log-Sobolev inequality with constant \(\alpha\) if

  1. \( u\) is a probability measure, and
  2. for every function \(r:E o\mathbb R\) such that \(r(x)>0\) for all \(x\), \(r\) is continuously differentiable, and \(r u\) is a probability measure,
\[\max\{2\alpha,0\}\cdot H_ u(r u)\le J_ u(r)\qquad ext{in }[0,\infty],\]

with the convention \(0\cdot\infty=0\).

For \(\alpha>0\), the case used throughout, the factor is \(2\alpha\), and the inequality reads \(H_ u( ho)\le rac1{2\alpha}J_ u(r)\) for \( ho=r u\), which is the form in Vempala and Wibisono (2019). If \(H_ u(r u)=\infty\), it forces \(J_ u(r)=\infty\). For \(\alpha\le0\) the left side is \(0\) and the condition reduces to normalization of \( u\).

The test class consists of strictly positive \(C^1\) probability densities. The definition makes no claim about measures outside this class, so to apply it to a law \( ho\) one must first exhibit a strictly positive \(C^1\) function \(r\) with \( ho=r u\). For the unadjusted Langevin algorithm this is done for the interpolating laws at positive times, whose Gaussian smoothing produces such densities. Strict positivity makes \(\log r\) finite and differentiable everywhere, and continuous differentiability makes \( abla\log r= abla r/r\) continuous.

The three assumptions on a test function are ∀ x, 0 < r x, ContDiff ℝ 1 r (continuously differentiable, the order of differentiability being \(1\)) and IsProbabilityMeasure (tiltedMeasure ν r). The inequality ENNReal.ofReal (2 * α) * InformationTheory.klDiv (tiltedMeasure ν r) ν ≤ relativeFisher ν r is stated in ℝ≥0∞: ENNReal.ofReal (2 * α) is \(\max\{2\alpha,0\}\), multiplication in ℝ≥0∞ follows the convention \(0\cdot\infty=0\), and InformationTheory.klDiv is Mathlib's Kullback–Leibler divergence. For probability measures klDiv equals the formula in the summary: Mathlib defines it as \(\infty\) unless \( ho\ll u\) and the log-likelihood ratio is \( ho\)-integrable, and otherwise as the nonnegative part of \(\int\log rac{d ho}{d u}\,d ho+ u(E)- ho(E)\), whose correction term vanishes for probability measures. The Borel assumption [BorelSpace E] is an argument of the definition.

steps.title: The log-Sobolev inequality for finite quantities
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(E\) carry its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra and let \( u\) satisfy the log-Sobolev inequality with constant \(\alpha\ge0\). Let \(r:E o\mathbb R\) be strictly positive and continuously differentiable, with \(r u\) a probability measure, and assume

\[H_ u(r u)<\infty\qquad ext{and}\qquad J_ u(r)<\infty.\]

Then the real numbers \(H_ u(r u)\) and \(J_ u(r)\) satisfy

\[2\alpha\,H_ u(r u)\le J_ u(r).\]

Proof. By the definition applied to the admissible density \(r\),

\[a:=\max\{2\alpha,0\}\cdot H_ u(r u)\le b:=J_ u(r)\qquad ext{in }[0,\infty].\qquad(1)\]

The number \(\max\{2\alpha,0\}\) is finite and \(H_ u(r u)\) is finite by assumption, so their product \(a\) is finite; \(b\) is finite by assumption. On the finite elements of \([0,\infty]\) the order is the order of \(\mathbb R\), so (1) is an inequality between real numbers. The real value of a product of finite elements is the product of the real values, and since \(\alpha\ge0\) we have \(\max\{2\alpha,0\}=2\alpha\). Hence \(a=2\alpha H_ u(r u)\), and (1) is the claim. \(\square\)

Without them one of the two extended values could be \(+\infty\); since an infinite value has no real counterpart, the comparison (1) would then not determine any inequality between real numbers. In the later sections both quantities are first proved finite, and only then is this real inequality combined with differential inequalities.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/EntropyFlow.lean.title: Entropy decay from a dissipation identity
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/EntropyFlow.lean.summary:
Let \(E\) be a real inner product space with its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra, let \( u\) be a measure on \(E\), and let \((r_t)_{t\in\mathbb R}\) be a family of real functions on \(E\), so that \(r_t u\) is the measure with density \(\max\{r_t,0\}\) with respect to \( u\). Write \(H(t)=H_ u(r_t u)\) for the relative entropy and \(J(t)=J_ u(r_t)=\int\| abla\log r_t\|^2\,d(r_t u)\) for the relative Fisher information. This section proves the continuous-time form of exponential entropy decay under a log-Sobolev inequality: if \( u\) satisfies the inequality with constant \(\alpha>0\), if each \(r_t\) with \(0\le t\le T\) is an admissible test density with finite entropy and finite Fisher information, and if \(H\) is continuous on \([0,T]\) with right derivative \(-J(t)\) on \([0,T)\), then

\[H(t)\le e^{-2\alpha t}H(0)\qquad(0\le t\le T).\]

For the Langevin diffusion the identity \( rac{d}{dt}H_ u( ho_t)=-J_ u( ho_t)\) is the de Bruijn-type dissipation identity; here it is a hypothesis, and no stochastic process enters. For the unadjusted Langevin algorithm the derivative of the entropy along the interpolation contains an additional discretization term, and the corresponding statement is the one-step estimate of another section; the present result is the model case without that term. The section also introduces the real-valued entropy of a prescribed density, which is used throughout the later sections.

steps.title: The real entropy of a prescribed density
steps.body:
Definition. For a measure \( u\) on \(E\) and a function \(r:E o\mathbb R\), the real entropy of \(r\) is

\[\mathcal H_ u(r)= egin{cases}H_ u(r u), & ext{if }H_ u(r u)<\infty,\ 0, & ext{if }H_ u(r u)=\infty.\end{cases}\]

The value \(0\) in the second case is a convention without mathematical meaning; every statement in which \(\mathcal H_ u(r)\) appears is accompanied by a hypothesis or a proof that \(H_ u(r u)<\infty\), and then \(\mathcal H_ u(r)\) is the relative entropy itself. In particular \(\mathcal H_ u(r)\ge0\) always. With this function, a path of densities \(t\mapsto r_t\) gives a real function \(t\mapsto\mathcal H_ u(r_t)\), to which continuity, derivatives and differential inequalities apply.

When \(r\ge0\) is measurable, \(r u\) and \( u\) are probability measures and \(r\log r\in L^1( u)\), the divergence is finite and \(\mathcal H_ u(r)=\int r\log r\,d u\), because \(d(r u)/d u=r\) holds \( u\)-almost everywhere when \(r\) is measurable. This representation of the entropy as an integral of the density is proved in the section on the divergence of densities; it is not part of the definition, and it is what is needed before an entropy can be differentiated under the integral sign.

steps.title: Exponential decay of the entropy
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(\nu\) be a measure on \(E\) that satisfies the log-Sobolev inequality with constant \(\alpha>0\), let \(T\in\mathbb R\), and let \((r_t)_{t\in\mathbb R}\) be real functions on \(E\). Write \(H(t)=\mathcal H_\nu(r_t)\) and \(J(t)=J_\nu(r_t)\). Assume:

  1. for every \(t\in[0,T]\), \(r_t(x)>0\) for all \(x\in E\), and \(r_t\) is continuously differentiable;
  2. for every \(t\in[0,T]\), \(r_t\nu\) is a probability measure;
  3. for every \(t\in[0,T]\), \(H_\nu(r_t\nu)<\infty\) and \(J_\nu(r_t)<\infty\), so that \(H(t)=H_\nu(r_t\nu)\) and \(J(t)\) are real numbers;
  4. \(H\) is continuous on \([0,T]\);
  5. for every \(t\in[0,T)\), \(H\) has right derivative \(-J(t)\) at \(t\): \(\bigl(H(s)-H(t)\bigr)/(s-t)\to-J(t)\) as \(s\downarrow t\).

Then

\[H(t)\le e^{-2\alpha t}H(0)\qquad\text{for every }t\in[0,T].\]

Proof. Let \(t\in[0,T)\). Then \(t\in[0,T]\), so by hypotheses 1 and 2 the function \(r_t\) belongs to the test class of the log-Sobolev inequality, and by hypothesis 3 both its entropy and its Fisher information are finite. The finite form of the log-Sobolev inequality (applicable since \(\alpha\ge0\)) gives

\[2\alpha H(t)\le J(t)\qquad(0\le t<T).\qquad(1)\]

By hypothesis 5 and (1), the right derivative of \(H\) satisfies \(-J(t)\le-2\alpha H(t)\) on \([0,T)\). We now apply the scalar comparison lemma : if \(\alpha>0\), \(H\) is continuous on \([0,T]\), \(H\) has right derivative \(-I(t)\) at every \(t\in[0,T)\) and \(2\alpha H(t)\le I(t)\) there, then \(H(t)\le e^{-2\alpha t}H(0)\) on \([0,T]\). Its hypotheses are hypothesis 4, hypothesis 5 with \(I=J\), and (1). (The lemma is proved by comparing \(H\) with the solution \(e^{-2\alpha t}H(0)\) of \(y'=-2\alpha y\): the function \(e^{2\alpha t}H(t)\) is continuous with nonpositive right derivatives, hence nonincreasing.) This proves the claim. \(\square\)

The hypotheses on the densities (positivity, continuous differentiability, normalization, finiteness) are used only to apply the log-Sobolev inequality at each time; continuity and the right derivatives are used only in the scalar comparison. If \(T<0\), the interval \([0,T]\) is empty and the claim is vacuous.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/ULALaw.lean.title: The Gaussian ULA transition and its interpolation
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/ULALaw.lean.summary:
Let \(E\) be a real inner product space of finite dimension \(n\), let \(U:E o\mathbb R\) be a potential, and let \(\gamma_n\) be the standard Gaussian measure on \(E\), the law of \(\sum_{i=1}^n\xi_ie_i\) for an orthonormal basis \((e_i)\) and independent real standard normal variables \(\xi_1,\dots,\xi_n\). For \(t\ge0\) define the update map and the transition on measures

\[T_t(x,z)=x-t abla U(x)+\sqrt{2t}\,z,\qquad P_t ho=(T_t)_\#( ho\otimes\gamma_n),\]

so that, for a probability measure \( ho\), \(P_t ho\) is the law of \(X-t abla U(X)+\sqrt{2t}\,Z\) with \(X\sim ho\) and \(Z\sim\gamma_n\) independent. With step \(h\) and initial law \(\mu\), the unadjusted Langevin algorithm (ULA) has laws \( ho_k=P_h^k\mu\), and the interpolating laws of its \(k\)-th step are \( ho_{k,t}=P_t ho_k\). In Vempala and Wibisono (2019) these are the laws of \(x_{k,t}=x_k-t abla U(x_k)+\sqrt2\,(W_{kh+t}-W_{kh})\), \(0\le t\le h\), along the time-\(t\) Euler step from \(x_k\sim ho_k\).

The section proves the identities that connect the interpolation with the algorithm, namely \(P_0 ho= ho\), \( ho_0=\mu\), \( ho_{k+1}=P_h ho_k\) and hence \( ho_{k,0}= ho_k\), \( ho_{k,h}= ho_{k+1}\); and it proves that, when \(\mu\) is a probability measure and \( abla U\) is Lipschitz, all these laws are probability measures. It also defines the sequence of entropies \(H_ u( ho_k)\) as real numbers. No convexity or log-Sobolev assumption enters, and nothing is asserted here about densities, differentiability in \(t\) or entropy production; those are the subject of later sections, which use the identities proved here to turn an estimate along the interpolation into an estimate between consecutive iterates.

steps.title: The frozen-drift interpolating law
steps.body:
Definition. For \(t\in\mathbb R\) and a measure \( ho\) on \(E\), the frozen-drift interpolation of \( ho\) at time \(t\) is the measure

\[P_t ho=(T_t)_\#( ho\otimes\gamma_n),\qquad T_t(x,z)=x-t abla U(x)+\sqrt{2t}\,z,\]

that is, \((P_t ho)(A)=( ho\otimes\gamma_n) igl(\{(x,z):T_t(x,z)\in A\} igr)\) for Borel sets \(A\subseteq E\), whenever \(T_t\) is measurable. The square root is taken with the convention \(\sqrt s=0\) for \(s<0\); only \(t\ge0\) is used.

The product measure \( ho\otimes\gamma_n\) encodes the independence of the Gaussian innovation from the current state: if \(X\sim ho\) and \(Z\sim\gamma_n\) are independent, then \((X,Z)\) has law \( ho\otimes\gamma_n\) and \(P_t ho\) is the law of \(Y_t=X-t abla U(X)+\sqrt{2t}\,Z\). Conditionally on \(X=x\), \(Y_t\) is Gaussian with mean \(x-t abla U(x)\) and covariance \(2t\,I\). The drift \( abla U\) is evaluated at the initial state \(X\) for every \(t\) (it is frozen), and \(t\) plays the role of the step size: \(P_h\) is one step of the algorithm with step \(h\), and \(t\mapsto P_t ho\) interpolates between \( ho\) and \(P_h ho\).

That transition is (μ.prod (stdGaussian H)).map (fun p ↦ malaProposal U h p.1 p.2), where Measure.prod is the product measure, stdGaussian is Mathlib's standard Gaussian measure on a finite-dimensional inner product space (the image of the product of \(n\) one-dimensional standard normal laws under \(x\mapsto\sum_ix_ie_i\) for an orthonormal basis), μ.map f is the image measure \(f_\#\mu\), and ULA.malaProposal U h x ξ is x - h • gradient U x + Real.sqrt (2 * h) • ξ, the map \(T_h\). Mathlib's Real.sqrt returns \(0\) on negative numbers, which is the convention of the definition. Mathlib's Measure.map f μ is the zero measure when \(f\) is not almost-everywhere measurable, so properties such as total mass require a measurability proof; this is where Lipschitz continuity of the gradient enters below.

steps.title: The laws of the algorithm
steps.body:
Definition. For a step \(h\in\mathbb R\), an initial measure \(\mu\) and \(k\in\mathbb N\), the \(k\)-th ULA law is

\[\rho_k=P_h^k\mu=\underbrace{P_h(P_h(\cdots P_h}_{k\text{ times}}(\mu)\cdots)),\]

the \(k\)-fold composition of the transition \(P_h\) applied to \(\mu\), with \(P_h^0\mu=\mu\).

If \(x_0\sim\mu\) and \(x_{k+1}=x_k-h\nabla U(x_k)+\sqrt{2h}\,Z_k\), where \(Z_0,Z_1,\dots\) are independent standard Gaussian vectors that are independent of \(x_0\), then \(\rho_k\) is the law of \(x_k\): since \(Z_k\) is independent of \(x_k\), which is a function of \(x_0,Z_0,\dots,Z_{k-1}\), the pair \((x_k,Z_k)\) has law \(\operatorname{Law}(x_k)\otimes\gamma_n\), so \(\operatorname{Law}(x_{k+1})=P_h\operatorname{Law}(x_k)\), and induction on \(k\) gives \(\operatorname{Law}(x_k)=\rho_k\). The definition by measures does not refer to any particular probability space realizing the recursion.

steps.title: The interpolating law at time zero
steps.body:
Claim. For every function \(U:E\to\mathbb R\) and every measure \(\rho\) on \(E\), \(P_0\rho=\rho\).

Proof. At \(t=0\), \(T_0(x,z)=x-0\cdot\nabla U(x)+\sqrt0\,z=x\), so \(T_0\) is the projection \(\pi_1(x,z)=x\), which is measurable. For a Borel set \(A\subseteq E\),

\[(P_0\rho)(A)=(\rho\otimes\gamma_n)\bigl(\pi_1^{-1}(A)\bigr)=(\rho\otimes\gamma_n)(A\times E)=\rho(A)\,\gamma_n(E)=\rho(A),\]

where the third equality is the defining property of the product measure on rectangles (valid because \(\gamma_n\) is a finite measure) and the last one uses \(\gamma_n(E)=1\). \(\square\)

No regularity of \(U\) is needed, because the gradient is multiplied by \(0\). The identity is an equality of measures and involves no limit \(t\downarrow0\); continuity of the interpolation at \(t=0\) is a different matter, treated elsewhere.

steps.body:

Proof. The zeroth iterate of any map is the identity, so \(\rho_0=P_h^0\mu=\mu\). \(\square\)

No transition is applied at index \(0\); the initial law of the algorithm and the starting point of the entropy recurrence are the same measure.

steps.title: The recursion for successive laws
steps.body:
Claim. For every \(k\in\mathbb N\), \(\rho_{k+1}=P_h\rho_k\).

Proof. For any map \(f\) and any \(k\), \(f^{k+1}(x)=f(f^k(x))\); this follows by induction on \(k\) from \(f^{k+1}=f^k\circ f\) (both sides equal \(f(x)\) for \(k=0\), and \(f^{k+2}(x)=f^{k+1}(f(x))=f(f^k(f(x)))=f(f^{k+1}(x))\) by the induction hypothesis applied at \(f(x)\)). With \(f=P_h\) and \(x=\mu\) this is \(\rho_{k+1}=P_h\rho_k\). \(\square\)

The order matters: the new transition is applied to the law at index \(k\), which corresponds to updating the current state with a fresh Gaussian innovation.

steps.title: The interpolating law at the end of a step
steps.body:
Claim. For every \(k\in\mathbb N\), \(\rho_{k,h}=P_h\rho_k=\rho_{k+1}\); that is, the interpolation started from the \(k\)-th law reaches the next law at time \(h\).

Proof. By definition \(\rho_{k,h}=P_h\rho_k\), and \(P_h\rho_k=\rho_{k+1}\) is the previous claim read from right to left. \(\square\)

Together with \(\rho_{k,0}=P_0\rho_k=\rho_k\), this shows that the two endpoints of the \(k\)-th interpolation are exactly two consecutive laws of the algorithm. An inequality between the entropies at \(t=0\) and \(t=h\) of the interpolation is therefore an inequality between \(H_\nu(\rho_k)\) and \(H_\nu(\rho_{k+1})\); no comparison with a continuous-time diffusion is involved.

steps.title: The interpolating law is a probability measure
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(E\) carry its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra, let \(\mu\) be a probability measure on \(E\), and let \( abla U\) be \(L\)-Lipschitz for some \(L\ge0\). Then \(P_t\mu\) is a probability measure for every \(t\in\mathbb R\).

Proof. A Lipschitz map is continuous, and a continuous map between metric spaces is Borel measurable; hence \( abla U\) is measurable. The coordinate maps \((x,z)\mapsto x\) and \((x,z)\mapsto z\) are measurable on \(E imes E\), and so are the compositions \((x,z)\mapsto t abla U(x)\) and \((x,z)\mapsto\sqrt{2t}\,z\). Sums and differences of measurable maps into the finite-dimensional space \(E\) are measurable (addition is continuous and \(E\) is separable). Hence \(T_t\) is measurable. Therefore

\[(P_t\mu)(E)=(\mu\otimes\gamma_n) igl(T_t^{-1}(E) igr)=(\mu\otimes\gamma_n)(E imes E)=\mu(E)\,\gamma_n(E)=1. \qquad\square\]

The Lipschitz hypothesis is used only through the measurability of \( abla U\). Its role is to make the image measure well defined; without measurability of the update map the image of \(\mu\otimes\gamma_n\) is not defined.

If \(\rho_k\) is a probability measure, then \(\rho_{k+1}=P_h\rho_k\) by the recursion, and the previous step applied to the probability measure \(\rho_k\) shows that \(P_h\rho_k\) is a probability measure. \(\square\)

Consequently every interpolating law \(\rho_{k,t}=P_t\rho_k\) is also a probability measure, by the previous step applied to \(\rho_k\). This is the normalization required of the densities to which the log-Sobolev inequality is applied.

\[H_k= egin{cases}H_ u( ho_k), & ext{if }H_ u( ho_k)<\infty,\ 0, & ext{otherwise},\end{cases}\]

Claim. For every \(U\), \(h\), \(\mu\) and \( u\), \(H_0\) is the real value of \(H_ u(\mu)\), that is \(H_0=H_ u(\mu)\) if \(H_ u(\mu)<\infty\) and \(H_0=0\) otherwise.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/GaussianDrift.lea.title: Gaussian displacement moments and the drift error
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/GaussianDrift.lea.summary:
Let \(E\) be a real inner product space of finite dimension \(n\) (possibly \(n=0\)) with its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra, let \(\gamma_n\) be the standard Gaussian measure on \(E\), let \(\mu\) be a probability measure on \(E\) and let \(U:E o\mathbb R\). On the product space \(E imes E\) with the product probability measure \(\mu\otimes\gamma_n\) the coordinates \(X(x,z)=x\) and \(Z(x,z)=z\) are independent with laws \(\mu\) and \(\gamma_n\), and the frozen-drift interpolation at time \(t\ge0\) is \(Y_t=T_t(X,Z)=X-t abla U(X)+\sqrt{2t}\,Z\). With \(G=\int\| abla U\|^2\,d\mu\), this section proves the exact identity and the bound

\[\mathbb E\|Y_t-X\|^2=t^2G+2tn,\qquad \mathbb E\| abla U(Y_t)- abla U(X)\|^2\le L^2 igl(t^2G+2tn igr),\]

the second when \( abla U\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, together with the integrability statements that make both sides finite. Only \(G<\infty\) is assumed: the initial position \(X\) cancels from the displacement \(Y_t-X\), so no moment of \(\mu\) itself is needed. The mixed term \(\mathbb E\langle abla U(X),Z angle\) vanishes exactly by independence and \(\mathbb EZ=0\). These are the moment computations of Vempala and Wibisono (2019) behind the term \(t^2L^2G+2tnL^2\) in the derivative of the entropy along the interpolation.

steps.title: The second moment of the standard Gaussian measure
steps.body:
Claim. If \(Z\sim\gamma_n\), then \(\mathbb E\|Z\|^2=\int_E\|z\|^2\,\gamma_n(dz)=n\). This includes \(n=0\), where both sides are \(0\).

Proof. Let \((e_i)_{i=1}^n\) be an orthonormal basis of \(E\). By Parseval's identity,

\[\|z\|^2=\sum_{i=1}^n\langle e_i,z\rangle^2\qquad(z\in E).\qquad(1)\]

A Gaussian measure has finite moments of all orders, so \(z\mapsto z\) is square integrable under \(\gamma_n\), and each \(\langle e_i,z\rangle^2\le\|z\|^2\) is integrable. Applied to \(\ell(z)=\langle e_i,z\rangle\), whose norm is \(\|e_i\|=1\), this gives

\[\int\langle e_i,z\rangle^2\,\gamma_n(dz)=\operatorname{Var}_{\gamma_n}(\ell)+\Bigl(\int\ell\,d\gamma_n\Bigr)^2=1+0=1.\]

Integrating (1) term by term, which is allowed for a finite sum of integrable functions, gives \(\int\|z\|^2\,d\gamma_n=\sum_{i=1}^n1=n\). For \(n=0\) the sum is empty and \(E=\{0\}\). \(\square\)

steps.title: The second moment of an affine Gaussian expression
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(\mu\) be a probability measure on \(E\), let \(g:E\to E\) be square integrable with respect to \(\mu\) (measurable with \(\int\|g\|^2\,d\mu<\infty\)), and let \(a,b\in\mathbb R\). Then

\[\int_{E\times E}\|a\,g(x)+b\,z\|^2\,(\mu\otimes\gamma_n)(dx,dz)=a^2\int_E\|g\|^2\,d\mu+b^2n.\]

In probabilistic notation, for independent \(X\sim\mu\) and \(Z\sim\gamma_n\), \(\mathbb E\|a\,g(X)+bZ\|^2=a^2\,\mathbb E\|g(X)\|^2+b^2n\).

Proof. For every \((x,z)\), expanding the square of the norm of a sum in a real inner product space gives

\[\|a\,g(x)+b\,z\|^2=a^2\|g(x)\|^2+2ab\,\langle g(x),z\rangle+b^2\|z\|^2.\qquad(1)\]

We check that each of the three functions on the right is integrable with respect to \(\mu\otimes\gamma_n\) and compute its integral.

  1. \((x,z)\mapsto\|g(x)\|^2\) depends only on \(x\). By Fubini's theorem and \(\gamma_n(E)=1\), it is integrable and \(\int\|g(x)\|^2\,d(\mu\otimes\gamma_n)=\int\|g\|^2\,d\mu\).
  2. \((x,z)\mapsto\|z\|^2\) depends only on \(z\). In the same way, using \(\mu(E)=1\) and the previous step, its integral is \(\int\|z\|^2\,d\gamma_n=n\).
  3. For the mixed term, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality gives \(|\langle g(x),z\rangle|\le\|g(x)\|\,\|z\|\). Since \(\mu\) and \(\gamma_n\) are probability measures, square integrability implies integrability, so \(\int\|g\|\,d\mu<\infty\) and \(\int\|z\|\,d\gamma_n<\infty\); by Tonelli's theorem \(\int\|g(x)\|\|z\|\,d(\mu\otimes\gamma_n)=\int\|g\|\,d\mu\cdot\int\|z\|\,d\gamma_n<\infty\), so the mixed term is integrable. By Fubini's theorem and linearity of the inner product in each argument, \(\int\langle g(x),z\rangle\,(\mu\otimes\gamma_n)(dx,dz)=\bigl\langle\int g\,d\mu,\int z\,\gamma_n(dz)\bigr\rangle=0\), because the standard Gaussian measure has mean \(0\).

Integrating (1) and using linearity of the integral for the three integrable terms gives \(a^2\int\|g\|^2\,d\mu+2ab\cdot0+b^2n\). \(\square\)

The mixed term is not estimated; it is exactly zero. This uses independence (the product form of the measure) and the zero mean of \(Z\), and it is why the result is an identity.

steps.title: The displacement of the update
steps.body:
Claim. For every \(U:E o\mathbb R\), \(t\in\mathbb R\) and \(x,z\in E\),

\[T_t(x,z)-x=-t\, abla U(x)+\sqrt{2t}\,z.\]

Proof. By definition \(T_t(x,z)=x-t abla U(x)+\sqrt{2t}\,z\); subtracting \(x\) cancels the first term, and \(-t abla U(x)=(-t) abla U(x)\). \(\square\)

The displacement depends on the initial point only through \( abla U(x)\). Consequently its moments involve the gradient moment \(\int\| abla U\|^2\,d\mu\) and Gaussian moments, and no moment of the position \(x\) itself. The identity is algebraic and holds for every \(t\), with the convention \(\sqrt{s}=0\) for \(s<0\).

steps.title: The second moment of the gradient error
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(\mu\) be a probability measure on \(E\), let \( abla U\) be \(L\)-Lipschitz for some \(L\ge0\), assume \(\int\| abla U\|^2\,d\mu<\infty\), and let \(t\ge0\). Then the function \((x,z)\mapsto\| abla U(T_t(x,z))- abla U(x)\|^2\) is integrable with respect to \(\mu\otimes\gamma_n\), and

\[\int\| abla U(T_t(x,z))- abla U(x)\|^2\,(\mu\otimes\gamma_n)(dx,dz)\le L^2\Bigl(t^2\int\| abla U\|^2\,d\mu+2tn\Bigr).\]

That is, \(\mathbb E\| abla U(Y_t)- abla U(X)\|^2\le L^2(t^2G+2tn)\).

Proof. Square integrability of the gradient. \( abla U\) is Lipschitz, hence continuous and measurable, and \(\| abla U\|^2\) is \(\mu\)-integrable by hypothesis; hence \( abla U\in L^2(\mu)\). By the fourth step the displacement \(T_t(x,z)-x\) is in \(L^2(\mu\otimes\gamma_n)\), so \(\|T_t(x,z)-x\|^2\) is integrable.

Measurability. \(T_t\) is continuous on \(E imes E\), as a combination of the coordinate projections, the continuous map \( abla U\), scalar multiplication and addition. Hence \((x,z)\mapsto abla U(T_t(x,z))- abla U(x)\) is continuous, and so is the square of its norm; in particular it is measurable.

Pointwise bound. By the Lipschitz property, for every \((x,z)\),

\[\| abla U(T_t(x,z))- abla U(x)\|\le L\,\|T_t(x,z)-x\|.\]

Both sides are nonnegative, and squaring preserves inequalities between nonnegative numbers; hence

\[\| abla U(T_t(x,z))- abla U(x)\|^2\le L^2\,\|T_t(x,z)-x\|^2.\qquad(1)\]

Integrability and the bound. The right side of (1) is integrable, and the left side is measurable and nonnegative; a measurable function dominated by an integrable function is integrable. Integrating (1) (monotonicity of the integral) and evaluating the right side by the previous step gives

\[ egin{aligned}\int\| abla U(T_t)- abla U(x)\|^2\,d(\mu\otimes\gamma_n)&\le L^2\int\|T_t(x,z)-x\|^2\,d(\mu\otimes\gamma_n)\&=L^2\Bigl(t^2\int\| abla U\|^2\,d\mu+2tn\Bigr).\end{aligned}\]

\(\square\)

This is the bound \(\mathbb E\| abla U(Y_t)- abla U(X)\|^2\le L^2(t^2G+2tn)\) of Vempala and Wibisono (2019) for the drift error of the interpolation. It is a statement about the joint law of the initial state and the Gaussian vector; conditioning on the final state \(Y_t\) is done in another section.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/KLOfDensity.lean.title: Integral formulas for relative entropy and Fisher information
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/KLOfDensity.lean.summary:
Let \((E,\mathcal E)\) be a measurable space, \( u\) a measure on it, and \(r:E o\mathbb R\) a measurable function with \(r\ge0\); \(r u\) is the measure \(A\mapsto\int_Ar\,d u\). The relative entropy \(H_ u(r u)\) is defined through the Radon–Nikodym derivative \(d(r u)/d u\) and its logarithm, the log-likelihood ratio, while the computations in the entropy analysis are carried out with the function \(r\) itself. This section connects the two descriptions. It proves the change-of-measure formula \(\int g\,d(r u)=\int rg\,d u\); the equivalence \(\log r\in L^1(r u)\iff r\log r\in L^1( u)\); the identity of the log-likelihood ratio with \(\log r\) almost everywhere; and, as consequences, that \(r\log r\in L^1( u)\) implies \(H_ u(r u)<\infty\) and, for probability measures,

\[H_ u(r u)=\int_Er\log r\,d u.\]

When \(E\) is a real inner product space, it also proves that square integrability of \(\| abla\log r\|\) under \(r u\) gives finite Fisher information with \(J_ u(r)=\int r\| abla\log r\|^2\,d u\). Only measurability and nonnegativity of \(r\) are needed for the measure-change facts; positivity and smoothness enter only through the Fisher information.

In this section integrals of real or vector-valued functions are Lebesgue (Bochner) integrals, with the convention that the integral of a function that is not integrable is \(0\); every statement below is either an identity valid under this convention or carries an integrability hypothesis. For a finite measure \( ho\ll u\) with log-likelihood ratio \(\ell=\log rac{d ho}{d u}\in L^1( ho)\), the relative entropy is \(H_ u( ho)=\int\ell\,d ho+ u(E)- ho(E)\), a nonnegative real number; otherwise \(H_ u( ho)=\infty\). For probability measures the correction \( u(E)- ho(E)\) vanishes.

steps.title: Integration against a measure with density
steps.body:
Claim. Let \( u\) be a measure on \(E\), let \(r:E o\mathbb R\) be measurable with \(r(x)\ge0\) for all \(x\), and let \(g:E o\mathbb R\) be any function. Then

\[\int_Eg\,d(r u)=\int_Er\,g\,d u,\]

with the convention that the integral of a non-integrable function is \(0\).

Proof. Nonnegative measurable functions. For a measurable set \(A\), \((r u)(A)=\int_Ar\,d u=\int r\mathbf 1_A\,d u\), so the formula \(\int f\,d(r u)=\int rf\,d u\) holds for indicator functions, by linearity for nonnegative simple functions, and by the monotone convergence theorem (applied on both sides to an increasing sequence of simple functions converging to \(f\)) for every measurable \(f:E o[0,\infty]\).

Integrability. Applying this to \(f=|g|\) for measurable \(g\) gives \(\int|g|\,d(r u)=\int r|g|\,d u=\int|rg|\,d u\), so \(g\in L^1(r u)\) if and only if \(rg\in L^1( u)\). Measurability up to null sets transfers as well: if \(g\) agrees \(r u\)-almost everywhere with a measurable \( ilde g\), then \(rg=r ilde g\) \( u\)-almost everywhere, because the two can differ only on a \( u\)-null subset of \(\{r>0\}\) or on \(\{r=0\}\), where both vanish; conversely, if \(rg=h\) \( u\)-almost everywhere with \(h\) measurable, then \(g=\mathbf 1_{\{r>0\}}h/r\) holds \(r u\)-almost everywhere, since \((r u)(\{r=0\})=0\).

Thus \(g\) is integrable with respect to \(r u\) if and only if \(rg\) is integrable with respect to \( u\).

The identity. If \(g\in L^1(r u)\), write \(g=g^+-g^-\); both parts are integrable, the nonnegative case applies to each, and subtracting gives \(\int g\,d(r u)=\int rg^+\,d u-\int rg^-\,d u=\int rg\,d u\). If \(g otin L^1(r u)\), then \(rg otin L^1( u)\) and both sides are \(0\) by the convention. \(\square\)

The density is finite at every point, so the product \(rg\) is an ordinary product of real numbers. This formula is used for \(g=\log r\) and \(g=\| abla\log r\|^2\) below.

steps.title: The log-likelihood ratio of a measure with density
steps.body:
Claim. Let \( u\) be a \(\sigma\)-finite measure on \(E\) and \(r:E o\mathbb R\) measurable with \(r\ge0\). Then the log-likelihood ratio of \(r u\) with respect to \( u\) satisfies

\[\log rac{d(r u)}{d u}(x)=\log r(x)\qquad ext{for }(r u) ext{-almost every }x.\]

Proof. If \( u(A)=0\) then \((r u)(A)=\int_Ar\,d u=0\), so \(r u\ll u\). Since \( u\) is \(\sigma\)-finite, the Radon–Nikodym derivative of the measure \(r u\) with respect to \( u\) exists and is \( u\)-almost everywhere unique; as \(r\) is a measurable density of \(r u\), we get \( rac{d(r u)}{d u}=r\) \( u\)-almost everywhere. The exceptional set is \( u\)-null, hence \((r u)\)-null by absolute continuity, so the equality also holds \((r u)\)-almost everywhere. Taking logarithms of the two equal nonnegative real numbers gives the claim. \(\square\)

The log-likelihood ratio is defined only up to null sets, through an arbitrary version of the Radon–Nikodym derivative; this claim allows it to be replaced by the explicit function \(\log r\) inside integrals with respect to \(r u\).

steps.title: The entropy as an integral of the density
steps.body:
Claim. Let \( u\) be a probability measure, let \(r:E o\mathbb R\) be measurable with \(r\ge0\), assume that \(r u\) is a probability measure and that \(r\log r\in L^1( u)\). Then \(H_ u(r u)\) is finite and

\[H_ u(r u)=\int_Er\log r\,d u.\]

Proof. Finiteness is the previous step. Let \(\ell\) be the log-likelihood ratio; as in the previous step, \(r u\ll u\) and \(\ell\in L^1(r u)\), so by definition

\[H_ u(r u)=\int\ell\,d(r u)+ u(E)-(r u)(E)=\int\ell\,d(r u)+1-1=\int\ell\,d(r u).\]

Since \(\ell=\log r\) \((r u)\)-almost everywhere (third step), \(\int\ell\,d(r u)=\int\log r\,d(r u)\), and by the change-of-measure formula of the first step with \(g=\log r\), \(\int\log r\,d(r u)=\int r\log r\,d u\). \(\square\)

Both probability assumptions are used to cancel the correction term \( u(E)-(r u)(E)\) in the definition of the divergence for finite measures. The resulting signed integral is what is differentiated in time in the entropy calculation; its use requires the integrability hypothesis, which also guarantees that the extended divergence is finite.

steps.title: Finite Fisher information from integrability
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(E\) be a real inner product space with a \(\sigma\)-algebra, \( u\) a measure on \(E\) and \(r:E o\mathbb R\) a function such that \(\| abla\log r\|^2\) is integrable with respect to \(r u\). Then \(J_ u(r)<\infty\).

Proof. By definition \(J_ u(r)\) is the integral, in \([0,\infty]\), of the nonnegative function \(\| abla\log r\|^2\) with respect to \(r u\). A real function \(f\ge0\) is integrable exactly when it is almost-everywhere measurable and its integral in \([0,\infty]\) is finite. The hypothesis therefore gives \(J_ u(r)<\infty\). \(\square\)

This is the finiteness condition under which the log-Sobolev inequality becomes an inequality between real numbers.

steps.title: The Fisher information as an integral against the reference measure
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(E\) be a real inner product space with a \(\sigma\)-algebra, \( u\) a measure on \(E\), \(r:E o\mathbb R\) measurable with \(r\ge0\), and assume that \(\| abla\log r\|^2\) is integrable with respect to \(r u\). Then the finite number \(J_ u(r)\) satisfies

\[J_ u(r)=\int_E\| abla\log r\|^2\,d(r u)=\int_Er\,\| abla\log r\|^2\,d u.\]

Proof. For an integrable nonnegative function, the integral in \([0,\infty]\) is finite and equals the Lebesgue integral as a real number; this gives the first equality, with \(J_ u(r)\) finite by the previous step. The second is the change-of-measure formula of the first step with \(g=\| abla\log r\|^2\). \(\square\)

For a strictly positive differentiable \(r\) the integrand is \(r\| abla\log r\|^2=\| abla r\|^2/r\). This representation, as an integral with respect to the reference measure \( u\), is the form in which the Fisher information appears after integration by parts in the entropy calculation.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/EntropyDerivative.title: Differentiation of the entropy integral
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/EntropyDerivative.summary:
By the formula \(H_ u(r_t u)=\int r_t\log r_t\,d u\) for normalized relative densities, the time derivative of the relative entropy along a path of densities \((r_t)\) is the derivative of a parameter-dependent integral. This section computes it under the hypotheses of the theorem on differentiation under the integral sign. The pointwise derivative is \( rac{d}{dt} igl(r_t\log r_t igr)=\dot r_t(\log r_t+1)\) where \(r_t>0\), and if these derivatives are bounded, uniformly for \(t\) in a neighbourhood of \(t_0\), by a \( u\)-integrable function, then

\[ rac{d}{dt}\Big|_{t=t_0}\int r_t\log r_t\,d u=\int\dot r_{t_0} igl(\log r_{t_0}+1 igr)\,d u.\]

This is the first step of the entropy computation in Vempala and Wibisono (2019), Lemma 3, written in relative-density form. No evolution equation for \(r_t\) and no integration by parts are used here; they enter later, when \(\int\dot r_t(\log r_t+1)\,d u\) is expressed through the Fisher information.

steps.title: The derivative of a positive function times its logarithm
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(r:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable at \(t\) with derivative \(\dot r=r'(t)\), and assume \(r(t)>0\). Then \(s\mapsto r(s)\log r(s)\) is differentiable at \(t\) with derivative

\[\frac{d}{ds}\Big|_{s=t}\bigl(r(s)\log r(s)\bigr)=\dot r\,\bigl(\log r(t)+1\bigr).\]

Proof. Since \(r(t)>0\), the logarithm is differentiable at \(r(t)\) with derivative \(1/r(t)\), so by the chain rule \(s\mapsto\log r(s)\) is differentiable at \(t\) with derivative \(\dot r/r(t)\). The product rule then gives the derivative

\[\dot r\,\log r(t)+r(t)\cdot\frac{\dot r}{r(t)}=\dot r\log r(t)+\dot r=\dot r\bigl(\log r(t)+1\bigr),\]

where the cancellation \(r(t)\cdot\dot r/r(t)=\dot r\) uses \(r(t)\neq0\). \(\square\)

The constant \(+1\) is kept. In the entropy calculation its contribution is \(\int\dot r_t\,d\nu\), the derivative of the total mass \(\int r_t\,d\nu=1\), and it may be dropped only after that derivative has been shown to vanish.

The term hr.mul (hr.log hpos.ne') combines the product rule (HasDerivAt.mul) with the chain rule for the logarithm (HasDerivAt.log, which needs \(r(t)\neq0\), supplied by hpos.ne'); it gives the derivative rdot * Real.log (r t) + r t * (rdot / r t). hcancel is the cancellation \(r(t)\cdot(\dot r/r(t))=\dot r\), proved with div_mul_cancel₀, and simpa only [hcancel, mul_add, mul_one] using! hr.mul (hr.log hpos.ne') rewrites the derivative into the form \(\dot r(\log r(t)+1)\).

steps.title: Differentiation under the integral sign
steps.body:
Claim. Let \((X,\mathcal X)\) be a measurable space with a measure \( u\), let \(r,\dot r:\mathbb R imes X o\mathbb R\), \((u,x)\mapsto r_u(x),\dot r_u(x)\), let \(t\in\mathbb R\), let \(S\subseteq\mathbb R\) be a neighbourhood of \(t\), and let \(M:X o\mathbb R\). Assume:

  1. for all \(u\) in some neighbourhood of \(t\), the function \(x\mapsto r_u(x)\log r_u(x)\) is \( u\)-almost-everywhere measurable, and \(r_t\log r_t\in L^1( u)\);
  2. \(x\mapsto\dot r_t(x) igl(\log r_t(x)+1 igr)\) is \( u\)-almost-everywhere measurable;
  3. (domination) for \( u\)-almost every \(x\), \( igl|\dot r_u(x) igl(\log r_u(x)+1 igr) igr|\le M(x)\) for all \(u\in S\), and \(M\in L^1( u)\);
  4. (positivity) for \( u\)-almost every \(x\), \(r_u(x)>0\) for all \(u\in S\);
  5. (pointwise differentiability) for \( u\)-almost every \(x\) and every \(u\in S\), the function \(v\mapsto r_v(x)\) is differentiable at \(u\) with derivative \(\dot r_u(x)\).

Then \(\dot r_t(\log r_t+1)\in L^1( u)\), and the function \(u\mapsto\int r_u\log r_u\,d u\) is differentiable at \(t\) with

\[ rac{d}{du}\Big|_{u=t}\int_Xr_u\log r_u\,d u=\int_X\dot r_t igl(\log r_t+1 igr)\,d u.\]

Proof. Write \(F(u,x)=r_u(x)\log r_u(x)\) and \(F'(u,x)=\dot r_u(x)(\log r_u(x)+1)\). Let \(N\) be the \( u\)-null set outside of which hypotheses 3–5 hold.

Pointwise derivative. For \(x otin N\) and \(u\in S\), the previous step, applied to \(v\mapsto r_v(x)\), which is differentiable at \(u\) with derivative \(\dot r_u(x)\) and positive at \(u\), shows that \(v\mapsto F(v,x)\) has derivative \(F'(u,x)\) at \(u\).

Lipschitz bound. Choose \(\varepsilon>0\) with \((t-\varepsilon,t+\varepsilon)\subseteq S\). For \(x otin N\), the function \(v\mapsto F(v,x)\) is differentiable on this interval with derivative bounded in absolute value by \(M(x)\), so by the mean value theorem

\[|F(u,x)-F(t,x)|\le M(x)\,|u-t|\qquad(|u-t|<\varepsilon).\qquad(1)\]

Integrability. By hypothesis 3 at \(u=t\in S\), \(|F'(t,x)|\le M(x)\) for \(x otin N\), so \(F'(t,\cdot)\) is measurable by hypothesis 2 and dominated by an integrable function, hence integrable. For \(|u-t|<\varepsilon\) close enough to \(t\) that hypothesis 1 applies, (1) gives \(|F(u,x)|\le|F(t,x)|+\varepsilon M(x)\), so \(F(u,\cdot)\in L^1( u)\).

Difference quotients. Let \(u_k o t\) with \(u_k eq t\). For \(x otin N\), the quotients \(q_k(x)= igl(F(u_k,x)-F(t,x) igr)/(u_k-t)\) converge to \(F'(t,x)\), and by (1) \(|q_k(x)|\le M(x)\) once \(|u_k-t|<\varepsilon\). By the dominated convergence theorem with dominating function \(M\),

\[ rac{\int F(u_k,x)\, u(dx)-\int F(t,x)\, u(dx)}{u_k-t}=\int q_k\,d u\longrightarrow\int F'(t,x)\, u(dx).\]

Since the sequence \((u_k)\) was arbitrary, \(u\mapsto\int F(u,x)\, u(dx)\) is differentiable at \(t\) with the stated derivative. \(\square\)

The bound must hold for all \(u\) in a fixed neighbourhood \(S\), with an \(x\)-dependent but \(u\)-independent integrable majorant; a bound at the single time \(t\) does not suffice, since the mean value inequality (1) uses the derivative at intermediate times. No hypothesis on the derivative of the integral itself is made.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/Regularity.lean.title: Local hypotheses for differentiating the relative entropy
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/Regularity.lean.summary:
Let \( u\) be a measure and let \((r_u)_{u\in\mathbb R}\) be a family of real functions with pointwise time derivatives \(\dot r_u\), so that \(r_u u\) is a path of measures with densities with respect to \( u\). This section packages, at a fixed time \(t\), the hypotheses of the theorem on differentiation under the integral sign for \(u\mapsto\int r_u\log r_u\,d u\) (a time neighbourhood on which the densities are positive and pointwise differentiable, and an integrable majorant of \(|\dot r_u(\log r_u+1)|\) valid on that whole neighbourhood), and draws the consequences for the relative entropy. When \( u\) and every \(r_u u\) are probability measures and \(r_u\) is a strictly positive \(C^1\) function on a real inner product space \(E\), these local hypotheses at every time of \([0,T]\) imply that \(H(u)=H_ u(r_u u)\) is finite, continuous on \([0,T]\), and right-differentiable on \([0,T)\) with

\[H'(t)=\int\dot r_t\,(\log r_t+1)\,d u.\]

If moreover \(r_t\) satisfies at time \(t\) the forced weak equation

\[\int\dot r_t\,\psi\,d u=-\int\langle abla r_t, abla\psi angle\,d u+\int r_t\,\langle e_t, abla\psi angle\,d u\]

for all admissible \(C^1\) test functions \(\psi\), with a drift error \(e_t:E o E\) of finite energy \(\int r_t\|e_t\|^2\,d u\), then testing with \(\psi=\log r_t+1\) gives the entropy production inequality

\[H'(t)\le- rac34J_ u(r_t)+\int r_t\|e_t\|^2\,d u.\]

This is the inequality \( rac{d}{dt}H_ u( ho_t)\le- rac34J_ u( ho_t)+\mathbb E\| abla U(x_t)- abla U(x_0)\|^2\) of Vempala and Wibisono (2019), Lemma 3, stated for a general regular density path. When \( u\) has a differentiable Lebesgue density, also denoted \( u\), the weak equation is the weak form of \(\partial_t(r_t u)= abla\cdot( u abla r_t)- abla\cdot(r_t u\,e_t)\). The section does not construct such a path; the hypotheses are verified for the Gaussian interpolation elsewhere.

steps.title: Local entropy regularity data
steps.body:
Definition. Let \((X,\mathcal X)\) be a measurable space with a measure \(\nu\), let \(r,\dot r:\mathbb R\times X\to\mathbb R\), and let \(t\in\mathbb R\). Local entropy regularity data for \((\nu,r,\dot r)\) at \(t\) consist of a set \(S\subseteq\mathbb R\) and a function \(M:X\to\mathbb R\) such that:

  1. \(S\) is a neighbourhood of \(t\);
  2. for all \(u\) in some neighbourhood of \(t\), \(x\mapsto r_u(x)\log r_u(x)\) is \(\nu\)-almost-everywhere measurable;
  3. \(r_t\log r_t\in L^1(\nu)\);
  4. \(x\mapsto\dot r_t(x)\bigl(\log r_t(x)+1\bigr)\) is \(\nu\)-almost-everywhere measurable;
  5. for \(\nu\)-almost every \(x\), \(\bigl|\dot r_u(x)\bigl(\log r_u(x)+1\bigr)\bigr|\le M(x)\) for all \(u\in S\);
  6. \(M\in L^1(\nu)\);
  7. for \(\nu\)-almost every \(x\), \(r_u(x)>0\) for all \(u\in S\);
  8. for \(\nu\)-almost every \(x\) and every \(u\in S\), \(v\mapsto r_v(x)\) is differentiable at \(u\) with derivative \(\dot r_u(x)\).

These are exactly the hypotheses of the theorem on differentiation of the entropy integral . The neighbourhood \(S\) and the majorant \(M\) may depend on \(t\). The data contain no statement about the derivative of the entropy or about its sign: the derivative is a consequence, proved in the next step.

steps.title: The derivative of the entropy integral
steps.body:
Claim. If local entropy regularity data exist at \(t\), then \(\dot r_t(\log r_t+1)\in L^1( u)\) and \(u\mapsto\int r_u\log r_u\,d u\) is differentiable at \(t\) with

\[ rac{d}{du}\Big|_{u=t}\int r_u\log r_u\,d u=\int\dot r_t\,(\log r_t+1)\,d u.\]

Proof. The eight conditions of the definition are the hypotheses of the theorem on differentiation of the entropy integral, whose conclusion is the claim. That theorem combines the pointwise derivative \( rac{d}{du}(r_u\log r_u)=\dot r_u(\log r_u+1)\), valid where \(r_u>0\), with the mean value inequality and dominated convergence (majorant \(M\)). \(\square\)

steps.title: The entropy production bound from the forced weak equation
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(E\) be a complete real inner product space with a \(\sigma\)-algebra and \( u\) a measure on \(E\). Let \(r,\dot r:\mathbb R imes E o\mathbb R\), \(t\in\mathbb R\) and \(e:E o E\). Assume:

  1. local entropy regularity data exist at \(t\);
  2. \(r_t(x)>0\) for every \(x\), and \(r_t\) is continuously differentiable;
  3. \(r_t\| abla\log r_t\|^2\in L^1( u)\) and \(r_t\|e\|^2\in L^1( u)\);
  4. \(x\mapsto r_t(x)\langle e(x), abla\log r_t(x) angle\) is \( u\)-almost-everywhere measurable;
  5. (forced weak equation) for every continuously differentiable \(\psi:E o\mathbb R\) such that \(\dot r_t\psi\), \(\langle abla r_t, abla\psi angle\) and \(r_t\langle e, abla\psi angle\) are \( u\)-integrable, \[\int\dot r_t\,\psi\,d u=-\int\langle abla r_t, abla\psi angle\,d u+\int r_t\,\langle e, abla\psi angle\,d u.\]

Then \(u\mapsto\int r_u\log r_u\,d u\) is differentiable at \(t\) with derivative \(D=\int\dot r_t(\log r_t+1)\,d u\), and

\[D\le- rac34\int r_t\| abla\log r_t\|^2\,d u+\int r_t\|e\|^2\,d u.\]

Proof. By the previous step, hypothesis 1 gives the derivative \(D\) and the integrability of \(\dot r_t(\log r_t+1)\). Write \(s= abla\log r_t\). We test the weak equation with \(\psi=\log r_t+1\).

The test is admissible. Since \(r_t>0\) and \(r_t\in C^1\), \(\log r_t\) is \(C^1\), and so is \(\psi\). Its gradient is \( abla\psi= abla\log r_t= abla r_t/r_t=s\) (the constant has zero gradient, and the chain rule applies because \(r_t>0\)). Hence \( abla r_t=r_ts\) and

\[\langle abla r_t, abla\psi angle=r_t\|s\|^2,\qquad r_t\langle e, abla\psi angle=r_t\langle e,s angle.\qquad(1)\]

The integrability of \(\dot r_t\psi\) was obtained above, and that of \(r_t\|s\|^2\) is hypothesis 3. For the mixed term, the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and \(ab\le a^2+b^2/4\) (which is \((a-b/2)^2\ge0\)) give \(|\langle e,s angle|\le\|e\|\|s\|\le\|e\|^2+ rac14\|s\|^2\), so

\[ igl|r_t\langle e,s angle igr|\le rac14r_t\|s\|^2+r_t\|e\|^2,\qquad(2)\]

an integrable majorant by hypothesis 3; with the measurability hypothesis 4, \(r_t\langle e,s angle\in L^1( u)\).

The identity and the bound. By the weak equation and (1),

\[D=\int\dot r_t(\log r_t+1)\,d u=-\int r_t\|s\|^2\,d u+\int r_t\langle e,s angle\,d u.\]

Integrating the signed version of (2), \(r_t\langle e,s angle\le rac14r_t\|s\|^2+r_t\|e\|^2\) (valid because \(r_t\ge0\)), gives \(\int r_t\langle e,s angle\,d u\le rac14\int r_t\|s\|^2\,d u+\int r_t\|e\|^2\,d u\). Substituting, \(D\le- rac34\int r_t\|s\|^2\,d u+\int r_t\|e\|^2\,d u\). \(\square\)

The weak equation is required for all \(C^1\) tests with integrable pairings, not only for compactly supported ones: the entropy test \(\log r_t+1\) is in general neither bounded nor compactly supported. The Young coefficient \( rac14\) costs one quarter of the Fisher information, which leaves the factor \( rac34\).

steps.title: Finite relative entropy
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(E\) be a real inner product space with its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra, \( u\) a probability measure on \(E\), and suppose that local entropy regularity data exist at \(t\), that \(r_t(x)>0\) for every \(x\) and that \(r_t\) is continuously differentiable. Then \(H_ u(r_t u)<\infty\).

Proof. \(r_t\) is continuous, hence Borel measurable, and nonnegative. Condition 3 of the data gives \(r_t\log r_t\in L^1( u)\). A probability measure is \(\sigma\)-finite. By the finiteness criterion (a \(\sigma\)-finite reference measure, a measurable nonnegative density and an integrable entropy integrand), \(H_ u(r_t u)<\infty\). \(\square\)

Finiteness is established before the real entropy is used, so that the subsequent real-valued statements concern the actual divergence. Normalization of \(r_t u\) is not needed for this step.

[IsProbabilityMeasure ν] provides the \(\sigma\)-finiteness instance required by the criterion; omit [CompleteSpace E] in removes completeness, which is not used.

steps.title: Continuity of the entropy on the interval
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(E\) carry its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra, let \( u\) be a probability measure and \(T\in\mathbb R\). Assume that for every \(t\in[0,T]\): local entropy regularity data exist at \(t\), \(r_t>0\) everywhere, \(r_t\in C^1\), and \(r_t u\) is a probability measure. Then \(t\mapsto H_ u(r_t u)\) (finite by the previous step) is continuous on \([0,T]\).

Proof. Let \(F(u)=\int r_u\log r_u\,d u\). For \(t\in[0,T]\), the second step shows that \(F\) is differentiable at \(t\), hence continuous at \(t\), hence continuous at \(t\) relative to \([0,T]\). For every \(t\in[0,T]\) the entropy formula applies (\( u\) and \(r_t u\) are probability measures, \(r_t\) is measurable and nonnegative, and \(r_t\log r_t\in L^1( u)\) by condition 3), so \(H_ u(r_t u)=F(t)\). A function that coincides on \([0,T]\) with a function continuous on \([0,T]\) is continuous on \([0,T]\). \(\square\)

Continuity relative to the interval includes one-sided continuity at the endpoints \(0\) and \(T\). The data at each \(t\) provide differentiability on a two-sided neighbourhood of \(t\), but the identification with the entropy is used only at points of \([0,T]\), where normalization is assumed.

steps.body:
Claim. Under the hypotheses of the previous step, let \(t\in[0,T)\). Then \(u\mapsto H_ u(r_u u)\) has right derivative \(\int\dot r_t(\log r_t+1)\,d u\) at \(t\):
