By the second step \(F\) is differentiable at \(t\) with derivative \(\int\dot r_t(\log r_t+1)\,d u\); in particular this number is the right derivative of \(F\) at \(t\). steps.title: The entropy production bound with the Fisher information
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(E\) be a real inner product space with its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra, \( u\) a probability measure, \(T\in\mathbb R\), \(t\in[0,T)\), and \(e:E o E\). Assume that for every \(u\in[0,T]\) local entropy regularity data exist at \(u\), \(r_u>0\) everywhere, \(r_u\in C^1\) and \(r_u u\) is a probability measure. Assume moreover that \(\| abla\log r_t\|^2\in L^1(r_t u)\), that \(r_t\|e\|^2\in L^1( u)\), that \(r_t\langle e, abla\log r_t angle\) is \( u\)-almost-everywhere measurable, and that the forced weak equation (hypothesis 5 of the third step) holds at time \(t\). Then the entropy \(u\mapsto H_ u(r_u u)\) has right derivative \(D=\int\dot r_t(\log r_t+1)\,d u\) at \(t\), and

\[D\le- rac34J_ u(r_t)+\int r_t\|e\|^2\,d u,\]

by . All hypotheses of the third step therefore hold at \(t\in[0,T]\), and its bound, rewritten with this identity, is the claim. \(\square\)

The Fisher integrability is assumed in the form natural for the log-Sobolev inequality, under the measure \(r_t u\), and converted to the weighted form used in the weak equation. UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/ScoreCalculus.lea.title: Relative scores and the entropy test
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/ScoreCalculus.lea.summary:
Let \(E\) be a complete real inner product space and \(r:E o\mathbb R\) a strictly positive differentiable function, a density with respect to a reference measure \( u\). Its relative score is \( abla\log r\). This section proves the pointwise identities

\[ abla\log r= rac{ abla r}{r},\qquad abla(\log r+1)= abla\log r,\qquad igl\langle abla r, abla(\log r+1) igr angle=r\,\| abla\log r\|^2,\]

and uses them to evaluate a weak equation at the entropy test function \(\psi=\log r+1\). If \(\dot r\) satisfies

\[\int\dot r\,\psi\,d u=-\int\langle abla r, abla\psi angle\,d u+\int r\langle e, abla\psi angle\,d u\]

for every admissible \(C^1\) test \(\psi\), then

\[\int\dot r\,(\log r+1)\,d u=-\int r\| abla\log r\|^2\,d u+\int r\langle e, abla\log r angle\,d u,\]

and without the drift error \(e\) the second term is absent. Since \( rac{d}{dt}\int r_t\log r_t\,d u=\int\dot r_t(\log r_t+1)\,d u\), this expresses the entropy derivative through the relative Fisher information \(J_ u(r)=\int r\| abla\log r\|^2\,d u\) and the drift-score pairing; it is the integration-by-parts step in the proof of Vempala and Wibisono (2019), Lemma 3. The test \(\log r+1\) is in general unbounded and not compactly supported, so the weak equation is assumed for all \(C^1\) tests whose three pairings are integrable, and these integrabilities are verified for the entropy test.

steps.title: The gradient of the logarithm of a positive function
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(r:E o\mathbb R\) be differentiable at \(x\) with \(r(x)>0\). Then

\[ abla\log r(x)=r(x)^{-1}\, abla r(x).\]

Proof. The logarithm is differentiable at \(r(x)>0\) with derivative \(1/r(x)\). By the chain rule, the Fréchet derivative of \(\log r\) at \(x\) is the linear functional \(D(\log r)(x)=r(x)^{-1}Dr(x)\). The gradient is the vector representing the derivative through the inner product, \(\langle abla f(x),v angle=Df(x)v\) for all \(v\), and this representation (the Riesz isomorphism between \(E\) and its dual) is linear. Hence \( abla\log r(x)=r(x)^{-1} abla r(x)\). \(\square\)

Positivity is used twice: to differentiate the logarithm at \(r(x)\), and to make \(r(x)^{-1}\) defined.

steps.title: The gradient of the entropy test
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(r:E\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable at \(x\) with \(r(x)>0\). Then

\[\nabla(\log r+1)(x)=\nabla\log r(x).\]

Proof. A function and its sum with a constant have the same increments, \((f+1)(x+v)-(f+1)(x)=f(x+v)-f(x)\); hence one is differentiable at \(x\) exactly when the other is, with the same derivative, and the gradients coincide. Apply this to \(f=\log r\). \(\square\)

The two hypotheses are not needed for this identity; they are stated because it is used only for positive differentiable densities. The constant \(1\) appears in the time derivative \(\frac{d}{dt}(r_t\log r_t)=\dot r_t(\log r_t+1)\), but it does not change spatial gradients, so only the relative score enters the pairing in the weak equation.

steps.title: The Dirichlet integrand of the entropy test
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(r:E o\mathbb R\) be differentiable at \(x\) with \(r(x)>0\). Then

\[ igl\langle abla r(x), abla(\log r+1)(x) igr angle=r(x)\,\| abla\log r(x)\|^2.\]

Proof. By the first step, \( abla\log r(x)=r(x)^{-1} abla r(x)\); multiplying by \(r(x)\) and using \(r(x)\cdot r(x)^{-1}=1\) gives \( abla r(x)=r(x)\, abla\log r(x)\). By the second step, \( abla(\log r+1)(x)= abla\log r(x)\). Therefore, by linearity of the inner product in its first argument,

\[ igl\langle abla r(x), abla(\log r+1)(x) igr angle= igl\langle r(x) abla\log r(x), abla\log r(x) igr angle=r(x)\,\| abla\log r(x)\|^2.\qquad\square\]

The left side is the integrand of the Dirichlet pairing \(\int\langle abla r, abla\psi angle\,d u\) for the entropy test \(\psi=\log r+1\); the right side is the integrand of the relative Fisher information written as \(\int r\| abla\log r\|^2\,d u\). The identity is pointwise; integrating it requires integrability, which is assumed in the next steps.

steps.title: Entropy production for the forced weak identity
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(E\) carry a \(\sigma\)-algebra and let \( u\) be a measure on \(E\). Let \(r,\dot r:E o\mathbb R\) and \(e:E o E\), with \(r(x)>0\) for every \(x\) and \(r\) continuously differentiable. Assume that

  1. \(\dot r\,(\log r+1)\), \(r\| abla\log r\|^2\) and \(r\langle e, abla\log r angle\) are \( u\)-integrable;
  2. (forced weak identity) for every continuously differentiable \(\psi:E o\mathbb R\) such that \(\dot r\psi\), \(\langle abla r, abla\psi angle\) and \(r\langle e, abla\psi angle\) are \( u\)-integrable, \[\int\dot r\,\psi\,d u=-\int\langle abla r, abla\psi angle\,d u+\int r\langle e, abla\psi angle\,d u.\]

Then

\[\int\dot r\,(\log r+1)\,d u=-\int r\| abla\log r\|^2\,d u+\int r\langle e, abla\log r angle\,d u.\]

Proof. Let \(\psi=\log r+1\). Since \(r\) is \(C^1\) and never zero, \(\log r\) is \(C^1\) by the chain rule, and adding a constant preserves this; so \(\psi\) is \(C^1\). We check the three integrability conditions of hypothesis 2. First, \(\dot r\psi=\dot r(\log r+1)\) is integrable by hypothesis 1. Second, by the third step, \(\langle abla r, abla\psi angle=r\| abla\log r\|^2\) at every point, which is integrable by hypothesis 1. Third, by the second step, \( abla\psi= abla\log r\), so \(r\langle e, abla\psi angle=r\langle e, abla\log r angle\), integrable by hypothesis 1. Hypothesis 2 therefore applies to \(\psi\), and substituting the two pointwise identities into its three integrals gives the claim. \(\square\)

For a path \(t\mapsto r_t\) with \(\dot r=\partial_tr_t\), the left side is the derivative of the entropy \(\int r_t\log r_t\,d u\), the first term on the right is \(-J_ u(r_t)\), and the second is the contribution of the drift error. All three are ordinary integrals of integrable functions; the integrability of the drift-score pairing is a separate requirement, which the next section derives from finite energies.

\[\int\dot r\,(\log r+1)\,d u=-\int r\| abla\log r\|^2\,d u.\]

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/EntropyDecay.lean.title: Scalar comparison for entropy decay
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/EntropyDecay.lean.summary:
This section contains the comparison principle for scalar differential inequalities used for the entropy along a time interval. For a continuous function \(H\) on \([0,T]\) with right derivatives \(H'(t)\le-aH(t)+b\) on \([0,T)\), where \(a>0\), it proves

\[H(t)\le e^{-at}H(0)+\frac ba\bigl(1-e^{-at}\bigr)\qquad(0\le t\le T),\]

the value at \(t\) of the solution of \(y'=-ay+b\), \(y(0)=H(0)\). With \(b=0\) and \(a=2\alpha\), combined with the inequality \(2\alpha H\le I\) and the dissipation identity \(H'=-I\), it gives exponential decay \(H(t)\le e^{-2\alpha t}H(0)\). Only real functions occur: identifying \(H\) with a relative entropy and \(I\) with a Fisher information, and proving the right-derivative identity, are done elsewhere. Right derivatives are used rather than two-sided derivatives because at the left endpoint \(t=0\) of an interpolation step only a right derivative is available. In the ULA analysis the comparison is applied with \(a=\frac32\alpha\) and a forcing term \(b\) that collects the discretization error.

steps.title: The comparison principle with linear drift
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(H,H':\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) and \(a,b,T\in\mathbb R\) with \(a>0\). Assume that \(H\) is continuous on \([0,T]\), that for every \(t\in[0,T)\) the function \(H\) has right derivative \(H'(t)\) at \(t\), and that

\[H'(t)\le-a\,H(t)+b\qquad\text{for every }t\in[0,T).\]

Then for every \(t\in[0,T]\),

\[H(t)\le e^{-at}H(0)+\frac ba\bigl(1-e^{-at}\bigr).\]

No sign condition on \(H\), \(H'\) or \(b\) is needed.

Proof. Put \(g(t)=e^{at}\bigl(H(t)-b/a\bigr)\). Then \(g\) is continuous on \([0,T]\), and by the product rule for right derivatives, for \(t\in[0,T)\),

\[g'_+(t)=e^{at}\bigl(H'(t)+a\,H(t)-b\bigr)\le0.\qquad(1)\]

We show \(g(t)\le g(0)\) for \(t\in[0,T]\). Fix \(\varepsilon>0\) and let \(g_\varepsilon(t)=g(t)-\varepsilon t\), whose right derivative is at most \(-\varepsilon\) on \([0,T)\) by (1). Let \(s\) be the supremum of the set of \(\tau\in[0,T]\) such that \(g_\varepsilon(u)\le g_\varepsilon(0)\) for all \(u\in[0,\tau]\); the set contains \(0\), and by continuity of \(g_\varepsilon\), \(g_\varepsilon(u)\le g_\varepsilon(0)\) for all \(u\in[0,s]\). If \(s<T\), then, since the right derivative of \(g_\varepsilon\) at \(s\) is negative, \(g_\varepsilon(u)<g_\varepsilon(s)\le g_\varepsilon(0)\) for all \(u>s\) close enough to \(s\), contradicting the definition of \(s\). Hence \(s=T\) and \(g(t)-\varepsilon t\le g(0)\) for all \(t\in[0,T]\). Letting \(\varepsilon\downarrow0\) gives \(g(t)\le g(0)\), that is,

\[e^{at}\Bigl(H(t)-\frac ba\Bigr)\le H(0)-\frac ba.\]

Multiplying by \(e^{-at}>0\) and rearranging, \(H(t)\le e^{-at}H(0)+\frac ba(1-e^{-at})\). \(\square\)

The right side is the solution of \(y'=-ay+b\) with \(y(0)=H(0)\), so the claim is the comparison principle for this linear equation. Continuity on the closed interval is needed: without it, \(H\) could jump upward at points where the right derivative carries no information about values to the left.

steps.body:
Claim. Let \(H,I:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) and \(\alpha>0\), \(T\in\mathbb R\). Assume that \(H\) is continuous on \([0,T]\), that for every \(t\in[0,T)\) the function \(H\) has right derivative \(-I(t)\) at \(t\), and that \(2\alpha H(t)\le I(t)\) for every \(t\in[0,T)\). Then

In the entropy derivative along the ULA interpolation, the relative score \(s= abla\log r\) is paired with a drift error \(e\), and the pairing \(\int r\langle e,s angle\,d u\) must be absorbed into the dissipation \(-\int r\|s\|^2\,d u\). This section proves Young's inequality in the form

\[\langle e,s angle\le|\langle e,s angle|\le rac14\|s\|^2+\|e\|^2,\]

derives from it that the weighted pairing \(r\langle e,s angle\) is integrable whenever it is measurable and both energies \(\int r\|s\|^2\,d u\) and \(\int r\|e\|^2\,d u\) are finite, integrates it, and combines it with the entropy identity for the forced weak equation to obtain

\[\int\dot r\,(\log r+1)\,d u\le- rac34\int r\| abla\log r\|^2\,d u+\int r\|e\|^2\,d u.\]

This is the step \( rac{d}{dt}H_ u( ho_t)\le-J_ u( ho_t)+ rac14J_ u( ho_t)+\mathbb E\| abla U(x_t)- abla U(x_0)\|^2\) of Vempala and Wibisono (2019), Lemma 3. The coefficient \( rac14\) is chosen so that three quarters of the Fisher information remain. Neither a bound on the error energy nor any differential inequality is assumed.

steps.title: A Young inequality for the inner product
steps.body:
Claim. For all \(e,s\in E\),

\[\langle e,s\rangle\le\frac14\|s\|^2+\|e\|^2.\]

Proof. By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality, \(\langle e,s\rangle\le\|e\|\,\|s\|\). Expanding the nonnegative square,

\[0\le\Bigl(\|e\|-\frac{\|s\|}2\Bigr)^2=\|e\|^2-\|e\|\,\|s\|+\frac14\|s\|^2,\]

so \(\|e\|\,\|s\|\le\|e\|^2+\frac14\|s\|^2\). Combining the two inequalities gives the claim. \(\square\)

This is Young's inequality \(ab\le\frac{\varepsilon}{2}a^2+\frac1{2\varepsilon}b^2\) with \(a=\|e\|\), \(b=\|s\|\) and \(\varepsilon=2\). In the entropy derivative it is applied with \(s\) the relative score, so that adding \(\frac14\|s\|^2\) to the dissipation \(-\|s\|^2\) leaves \(-\frac34\|s\|^2\).

Claim. For all \(e,s\in E\),

\[|\langle e,s\rangle|\le\frac14\|s\|^2+\|e\|^2.\]

Proof. The Cauchy–Schwarz inequality in absolute form gives \(|\langle e,s\rangle|\le\|e\|\,\|s\|\), and \(\|e\|\,\|s\|\le\|e\|^2+\frac14\|s\|^2\) as in the previous step. \(\square\)

The absolute version is needed to dominate the integrand \(r\langle e,s\rangle\), whose sign is unknown, by an integrable function.

steps.title: Integrability of the weighted pairing
steps.body:
Claim. Let \((X,\mathcal X)\) be a measurable space with a measure \(\nu\), let \(r:X\to\mathbb R\) with \(r(x)\ge0\) for all \(x\), and let \(e,s:X\to E\). Assume that \(x\mapsto r(x)\langle e(x),s(x)\rangle\) is \(\nu\)-almost-everywhere measurable and that \(r\|s\|^2\) and \(r\|e\|^2\) are \(\nu\)-integrable. Then \(r\langle e,s\rangle\) is \(\nu\)-integrable.

Proof. For every \(x\), since \(r(x)\ge0\), the previous step gives

\[\begin{aligned}\bigl|r(x)\langle e(x),s(x)\rangle\bigr|&=r(x)\,\bigl|\langle e(x),s(x)\rangle\bigr|\\&\le r(x)\Bigl(\frac14\|s(x)\|^2+\|e(x)\|^2\Bigr)\\&=\frac14r(x)\|s(x)\|^2+r(x)\|e(x)\|^2.\end{aligned}\]

The right side is integrable, as a linear combination of two integrable functions. A measurable function whose absolute value is bounded by an integrable function is integrable. \(\square\)

Integrability of the pairing is therefore not an additional assumption once the Fisher information and the error energy are finite; only its measurability must be checked.

steps.title: The integrated Young inequality
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(\nu\), \(r\ge0\), \(e\) and \(s\) be as in the previous step, and assume that \(r\langle e,s\rangle\), \(r\|s\|^2\) and \(r\|e\|^2\) are \(\nu\)-integrable. Then

\[\int r\langle e,s\rangle\,d\nu\le\frac14\int r\|s\|^2\,d\nu+\int r\|e\|^2\,d\nu.\]

Proof. Multiplying the first step by \(r(x)\ge0\) gives, for every \(x\),

\[r(x)\langle e(x),s(x)\rangle\le\frac14r(x)\|s(x)\|^2+r(x)\|e(x)\|^2.\]

Both sides are integrable, so monotonicity of the integral and linearity of the integral on the right give the claim. \(\square\)

Nonnegativity of \(r\) is needed for the multiplication to preserve the inequality; normalization of \(r\) is not needed.

steps.title: The entropy production bound
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(E\) be complete with a \(\sigma\)-algebra and \( u\) a measure on \(E\). Let \(r,\dot r:E o\mathbb R\) and \(e:E o E\), with \(r(x)>0\) for all \(x\) and \(r\) continuously differentiable. Assume:

  1. \(\dot r(\log r+1)\), \(r\| abla\log r\|^2\) and \(r\|e\|^2\) are \( u\)-integrable;
  2. \(r\langle e, abla\log r angle\) is \( u\)-almost-everywhere measurable;
  3. the forced weak identity \(\int\dot r\psi\,d u=-\int\langle abla r, abla\psi angle\,d u+\int r\langle e, abla\psi angle\,d u\) holds for every \(C^1\) function \(\psi\) for which the three integrands are \( u\)-integrable.

Then

\[\int\dot r\,(\log r+1)\,d u\le- rac34\int r\| abla\log r\|^2\,d u+\int r\|e\|^2\,d u.\]

Proof. Let \(s= abla\log r\) and write \(J=\int r\|s\|^2\,d u\), \(\mathcal E=\int r\|e\|^2\,d u\). By the third step (with \(r\ge0\), hypothesis 2 and the two energies of hypothesis 1), \(r\langle e,s angle\) is integrable. The entropy identity for the forced weak equation , whose hypotheses are now all satisfied, gives

\[\int\dot r\,(\log r+1)\,d u=-J+\int r\langle e,s angle\,d u.\]

By the fourth step, \(\int r\langle e,s angle\,d u\le rac14J+\mathcal E\). Hence \(\int\dot r(\log r+1)\,d u\le-J+ rac14J+\mathcal E=- rac34J+\mathcal E\). \(\square\)

For the ULA interpolation, \(r=r_t\) is the relative density at time \(t\), \(e\) is the drift error \( abla U(y)-\mathbb E[ abla U(X)\mid Y_t=y]\), and the right side becomes \(- rac34J_ u(r_t)+\int r_t\|e\|^2\,d u\), where the error energy is subsequently bounded by \(L^2(t^2G+2tn)\).

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/OneStep.lean.title: The scalar one-step entropy estimate
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/OneStep.lean.summary:
This section proves the scalar part of Vempala and Wibisono (2019), Lemma 3: over one step of length \(h\), a real function \(H\) (the relative entropy along the interpolation) with

\[H'(t)\le-\frac34I(t)+t^2L^2G_0+2tnL^2,\qquad 2\alpha H(t)\le I(t),\qquad G_0\le\frac{4L^2}{\alpha}H(0)+2nL\]

for \(0\le t<h\) satisfies \(H(h)\le e^{-\alpha h}H(0)+6h^2nL^2\), provided \(0<\alpha\le L\), \(0<h\le\alpha/(4L^2)\), \(n\ge0\) and \(H(0)\ge0\). Here \(I(t)\) plays the role of the Fisher information, \(G_0\) of the gradient second moment at the start of the step, and \(n\) of the dimension. The three inequalities combine into \(H'\le-\frac32\alpha H+b\) with \(b=\frac\alpha4H(0)+\frac52hnL^2\); the comparison principle for linear differential inequalities gives \(H(h)\le e^{-3\alpha h/2}H(0)+bh\); and the elementary inequality \(e^{-3x/2}+\frac x4\le e^{-x}\) for \(0\le x\le\frac14\) absorbs the term \(\frac{\alpha h}4H(0)\) into the contraction factor \(e^{-\alpha h}\). No measure theory is involved: the identification of \(H\), \(I\), \(G_0\) with the entropy, Fisher information and gradient moment of the ULA interpolation is made elsewhere.

steps.title: An exponential comparison for small arguments
steps.body:
Claim. For every real \(x\) with \(0\le x\le\frac14\),

\[e^{-\frac32x}+\frac x4\le e^{-x}.\]

Proof. We use the tangent-line inequality \(e^y\ge1+y\) for all real \(y\) (convexity of the exponential function). With \(y=-\frac32x\) and \(x\le\frac14\),

\[e^{-\frac32x}\ge1-\frac32x\ge1-\frac38=\frac58\ge\frac12.\qquad(1)\]

With \(y=\frac x2\), \(e^{x/2}\ge1+\frac x2\). Multiplying by the positive number \(e^{-\frac32x}\) and using \(e^{-\frac32x}e^{\frac x2}=e^{-x}\),

\[e^{-x}\ge e^{-\frac32x}\Bigl(1+\frac x2\Bigr)=e^{-\frac32x}+\frac x2\,e^{-\frac32x}.\qquad(2)\]

Since \(x\ge0\), (1) gives \(\frac x2e^{-\frac32x}\ge\frac x2\cdot\frac12=\frac x4\), and (2) gives the claim. \(\square\)

The inequality is applied with \(x=\alpha h\): a forcing term \(\frac{\alpha h}4H(0)\) proportional to the initial entropy is absorbed by the gap between the contraction factors \(e^{-3\alpha h/2}\) and \(e^{-\alpha h}\).

steps.title: Integration of the entropy differential inequality over one step
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(H,H',I:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) and \(G_0,\alpha,L,h,n\in\mathbb R\) satisfy

  1. \(\alpha>0\), \(L>0\), \(h>0\), \(\alpha\le L\), \(n\ge0\), \(h\le\alpha/(4L^2)\), and \(H(0)\ge0\);
  2. \(H\) is continuous on \([0,h]\) and has right derivative \(H'(t)\) at every \(t\in[0,h)\);
  3. \(2\alpha H(t)\le I(t)\) for every \(t\in[0,h)\);
  4. \(H'(t)\le-\frac34I(t)+t^2L^2G_0+2tnL^2\) for every \(t\in[0,h)\);
  5. \(G_0\le\frac{4L^2}{\alpha}H(0)+2nL\).

Then

\[H(h)\le e^{-\alpha h}H(0)+6h^2nL^2.\]

Proof. Consequences of the step restriction. Since \(4L^2>0\), \(h\le\alpha/(4L^2)\) is equivalent to \(4hL^2\le\alpha\). With \(\alpha\le L\) this gives \(4hL\cdot L\le L\), and dividing by \(L>0\), \(hL\le\frac14\). Since \(h>0\) and \(\alpha\le L\), \(\alpha h\le Lh\le\frac14\). Moreover \(hL^2\le\frac\alpha4\), and squaring this inequality between nonnegative numbers gives \((hL^2)^2\le\alpha^2/16\), hence

\[h^2L^2\cdot\frac{4L^2}{\alpha}=\frac{4(hL^2)^2}{\alpha}\le\frac{4}{\alpha}\cdot\frac{\alpha^2}{16}=\frac\alpha4.\qquad(1)\]

Also \(h^2L^2\cdot2nL=2hnL^2\cdot hL\le2hnL^2\cdot\frac14=\frac12hnL^2\), because \(2hnL^2\ge0\). With \(A=\frac{4L^2}{\alpha}H(0)+2nL\ge0\), multiplying (1) by \(H(0)\ge0\) and adding gives

\[h^2L^2A\le\frac\alpha4H(0)+\frac12hnL^2.\qquad(2)\]

A linear differential inequality. Let \(t\in[0,h)\). Then \(0\le t<h\), so \(t^2\le h^2\). By hypothesis 5, \(t^2L^2G_0\le t^2L^2A\le h^2L^2A\) (the factors \(t^2L^2\) and \(L^2A\) are nonnegative); also \(2tnL^2\le2hnL^2\), and hypothesis 3 multiplied by \(\frac34\) gives \(-\frac34I(t)\le-\frac32\alpha H(t)\). Inserting these bounds into hypothesis 4 and using (2),

\[H'(t)\le-\frac32\alpha H(t)+h^2L^2A+2hnL^2\le-\frac32\alpha H(t)+b,\qquad b=\frac\alpha4H(0)+\frac52hnL^2\ge0.\]

Integration. By the comparison principle with \(a=\frac32\alpha>0\), using hypothesis 2,

\[H(h)\le e^{-\frac32\alpha h}H(0)+\frac{b}{\frac32\alpha}\Bigl(1-e^{-\frac32\alpha h}\Bigr).\]

From \(e^{-y}\ge1-y\) with \(y=\frac32\alpha h\) we get \(1-e^{-\frac32\alpha h}\le\frac32\alpha h\), and since \(b\ge0\) the last term is at most \(bh\). Therefore

\[H(h)\le e^{-\frac32\alpha h}H(0)+\frac{\alpha h}4H(0)+\frac52h^2nL^2.\]

Absorption. By the previous step with \(x=\alpha h\in[0,\frac14]\), multiplied by \(H(0)\ge0\), \(e^{-\frac32\alpha h}H(0)+\frac{\alpha h}4H(0)\le e^{-\alpha h}H(0)\). Finally \(\frac52h^2nL^2\le6h^2nL^2\) because \(h^2nL^2\ge0\). \(\square\)

The hypotheses \(\alpha\le L\) and \(h\le\alpha/(4L^2)\) are used only through \(hL\le\frac14\), \(\alpha h\le\frac14\) and (1); nonnegativity of \(H(0)\) is used in (2) and in the absorption. The constant \(6\) is that of Vempala and Wibisono; the proof gives \(\frac52\).

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/DiscreteEntropy.l.title: Iteration of the entropy recurrence
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/DiscreteEntropy.l.summary:
This section iterates the one-step entropy recurrence of Vempala and Wibisono (2019), Lemma 3,

\[H_{k+1}\le e^{-\alpha h}H_k+6h^2nL^2\qquad(k\in\mathbb N),\]

for a real sequence \((H_k)\), to the bound of their Theorem 2,

\[H_k\le e^{-\alpha hk}H_0+\frac{8hnL^2}{\alpha},\]

valid when \(\alpha,h>0\), \(n\ge0\) and \(\alpha h\le\frac14\). With \(q=e^{-\alpha h}\in(0,1)\) and \(c=6h^2nL^2\), iteration gives the finite geometric sum \(H_k\le q^kH_0+c\frac{1-q^k}{1-q}\) (proved in the section on the scalar recurrence, ); the elementary bound \(1-e^{-x}\ge\frac34x\) for \(0\le x\le\frac14\) then bounds \(c/(1-q)\) by \(\frac{6h^2nL^2}{\frac34\alpha h}=\frac{8hnL^2}{\alpha}\). The local error of order \(h^2\) divided by a contraction gap of order \(h\) produces the asymptotic bias of order \(h\). The recurrence is a hypothesis here: no relative entropy appears, and the recurrence is established for the ULA laws in other sections.

steps.title: The finite geometric sum
steps.body:
Claim. Let \((H_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}\) be real numbers and \(\alpha,h,n,L\in\mathbb R\) with \(\alpha>0\) and \(h>0\). If \(H_{k+1}\le e^{-\alpha h}H_k+6h^2nL^2\) for every \(k\), then for every \(k\in\mathbb N\)

\[H_k\le e^{-\alpha hk}H_0+6h^2nL^2\,\frac{1-e^{-\alpha hk}}{1-e^{-\alpha h}}.\]

Proof. Put \(q=e^{-\alpha h}\) and \(c=6h^2nL^2\). Since \(\alpha h>0\), the exponent \(-\alpha h\) is negative, so \(0\le q<1\). The recurrence is \(H_{k+1}\le qH_k+c\). By the finite geometric-sum bound for such recurrences (proved by induction on \(k\), using \(q\ge0\), together with \(\sum_{j=0}^{k-1}q^j=(1-q^k)/(1-q)\) for \(q\neq1\)), \(H_k\le q^kH_0+c(1-q^k)/(1-q)\). Finally \(q^k=(e^{-\alpha h})^k=e^{-\alpha hk}\). \(\square\)

No sign condition on \(H_0\), \(n\) or \(c\) is needed for this exact form, since the geometric sum is not bounded.

steps.title: A lower bound for the contraction gap
steps.body:
Claim. For every real \(x\) with \(0\le x\le\frac14\),

\[\frac34x\le1-e^{-x}.\]

Proof. From \(e^x\ge1+x\) and \(e^{-x}>0\), \((1+x)e^{-x}\le e^xe^{-x}=1\). Since \(x+1>0\),

\[\frac{x}{x+1}\le1-e^{-x},\qquad(1)\]

because, after multiplication by \(x+1\), (1) reads \(x\le x+1-(x+1)e^{-x}\), which is \((x+1)e^{-x}\le1\). Next, \(x\ge0\) and \(\frac14-x\ge0\) give \(x(\frac14-x)\ge0\), that is \(x^2\le\frac x4\). Hence \(\frac34x(x+1)=\frac34x^2+\frac34x\le\frac3{16}x+\frac34x\le x\), and dividing by \(x+1>0\) gives \(\frac34x\le\frac{x}{x+1}\). Combined with (1), this proves the claim. \(\square\)

The bound gives a lower bound, linear in \(x\), for the contraction gap \(1-e^{-\alpha h}\), which is used before dividing by it.

steps.title: The uniform entropy bound
steps.body:
Claim. Let \((H_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}\) be real numbers and \(\alpha,h,n,L\in\mathbb R\) with \(\alpha>0\), \(h>0\), \(n\ge0\) and \(\alpha h\le\frac14\). If \(H_{k+1}\le e^{-\alpha h}H_k+6h^2nL^2\) for every \(k\), then for every \(k\in\mathbb N\)

\[H_k\le e^{-\alpha hk}H_0+\frac{8hnL^2}{\alpha}.\]

Proof. Let \(q=e^{-\alpha h}\) and \(c=6h^2nL^2\). As before \(0\le q<1\), so \(1-q>0\), and \(c\ge0\) because \(n\ge0\). By the uniform form of the geometric bound for recurrences (iteration as in the first step followed by \(1-q^k\le1\) and \(c\ge0\)),

\[H_k\le q^kH_0+\frac{c}{1-q}.\]

By the previous step with \(x=\alpha h\in(0,\frac14]\), \(1-q\ge\frac34\alpha h\). The number \(\frac{8hnL^2}{\alpha}\) is nonnegative, so

\[\frac{8hnL^2}{\alpha}\,(1-q)\ge\frac{8hnL^2}{\alpha}\cdot\frac34\alpha h=6h^2nL^2=c,\]

and dividing by \(1-q>0\) gives \(c/(1-q)\le8hnL^2/\alpha\). With \(q^k=e^{-\alpha hk}\) this proves the claim. \(\square\)

The hypothesis \(\alpha h\le\frac14\) is used only in the lower bound for \(1-q\); in the ULA theorem it follows from \(h\le\alpha/(4L^2)\) and \(\alpha\le L\). The bound holds for every \(k\), and the term \(e^{-\alpha hk}H_0\) decreases to \(0\) as \(k\to\infty\).

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/RegularizedTheore.title: Entropy convergence from regular density interpolations
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/RegularizedTheore.summary: Suppose a positive regular density path represents each Gaussian ULA interpolation. Assume its weak equation admits the entropy test, its score and error energies are finite, and the stated numerical error and gradient-moment estimates hold. These assumptions imply the entropy derivative estimate, the one-step recurrence, and the iterated KL bound. The construction of the density path and the analytic estimates remain hypotheses of this conditional theorem.

steps.title: Derivation from the regular interpolation assumptions
steps.body:
The equality between the density measure and the ULA interpolation proves normalization. Local domination of the differentiated entropy integrand gives finite KL, continuity, and the right derivative

\[H'_k(t)=\int\dot r_{k,t}(\log r_{k,t}+1)\,d\nu.\]

The finite score energy gives finite Fisher information. The admissible weak equation and Young's inequality imply \(H'_k(t)\le-3I(t)/4+E(t)\). Insert the assumed bound \(E(t)\le t^2L^2G_k+2tdL^2\) and the entropy-dependent bound on \(G_k\). The one-step comparison gives the recurrence with coefficient six, and geometric iteration gives the final coefficient eight. This derives the entropy derivative and recurrence from the listed assumptions; it does not derive those assumptions merely from LSI.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/InterpolationData.title: Assumptions for a regular ULA interpolation
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/InterpolationData.summary: The assumptions specify relative densities \(r_{k,t}\) representing the Gaussian ULA interpolation, their time derivatives, and drift discrepancies. They require positivity, spatial regularity, local integrable domination for entropy differentiation, a weak equation valid for the entropy test, finite score and error energies, and the stated moment estimates. Under these assumptions and LSI, the probability, finiteness, one-step and iterated entropy conclusions below follow.

Require positive \(C^1\) densities, local time derivatives and domination of their entropy derivatives, an admissible forced weak equation, integrable score and discrepancy energies, and the numerical bounds on these energies and the starting gradient moment. The equality of measures holds throughout the interpolation, so the density at every time represents the same law used in the algorithm. An entropy derivative, a recurrence, or a convergence bound is not among these assumptions.

steps.body: Define the proposed entropy derivative by integrating \(\dot r_{k,t}(\log r_{k,t}+1)\). The local differentiation assumptions prove that this is the right derivative of relative entropy. The weak equation and finite energies give the Fisher-information derivative bound. LSI and the stated moment estimates then satisfy the hypotheses of the scalar one-step comparison. Identifying the laws at zero and \(h\) yields the recurrence for successive ULA entropies.

steps.title: The iterated consequence
steps.body: Under LSI, gradient Lipschitzness and the positive step restriction, the regular interpolation assumptions imply the one-step bound at every index. All density, weak-equation and moment hypotheses remain in this conditional conclusion.

UnadjustedLangevin/Gibbs.lean.title: Gibbs normalization and second moments
UnadjustedLangevin/Gibbs.lean.summary:
Throughout this section \(H\) is a real inner product space of finite dimension \(d\ge0\), with inner product \(\langle\cdot,\cdot\rangle\) and norm \(\|x\|=\langle x,x\rangle^{1/2}\), equipped with its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra and with Lebesgue measure, written \(dx\) or \(\lambda\). Lebesgue measure on \(H\) is the translation-invariant measure that gives volume one to the cube spanned by an orthonormal basis; in the coordinates of an orthonormal basis it is Lebesgue measure on \(\mathbb R^d\), and for \(d=0\) (when \(H=\{0\}\)) it is the unit mass at \(0\). For a function \(U:H\to\mathbb R\), the potential, we define the Gibbs weight \(e^{-U}\), the partition function \(Z_U=\int_He^{-U(x)}\,dx\in[0,\infty]\) and the Gibbs measure

\[\pi_U(dx)=Z_U^{-1}e^{-U(x)}\,dx.\]

The main results are that \(0<Z_U<\infty\), that \(\pi_U\) is a probability measure, and that \(\int_H\|x\|^2\,\pi_U(dx)<\infty\), under the sole assumptions that \(U\) is differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex for some \(m>0\); no second derivative of \(U\) is used. The key estimate is the quadratic lower bound

\[U(x)\ge U(0)-\frac{\|\nabla U(0)\|^2}{m}+\frac m4\|x\|^2\qquad(x\in H),\]

which bounds \(e^{-U(x)}\) and \(\|x\|^2e^{-U(x)}\) by constant multiples of the integrable functions \(e^{-(m/4)\|x\|^2}\) and \(\|x\|^2e^{-(m/4)\|x\|^2}\). The measure \(\pi_U\) is the target distribution of the Langevin algorithms of this report. Normalization makes it a probability law, and the finite second moment makes the quadratic Wasserstein distance between \(\pi_U\) and any law with finite second moment finite.

steps.title: The unnormalized Gibbs weight
steps.body:
Definition. For a function \(U:H\to\mathbb R\), the unnormalized Gibbs weight is the function \(w_U:H\to[0,\infty]\) given by

\[w_U(x)=e^{-U(x)}\qquad(x\in H).\]

The weight is regarded as a function with values in the extended half-line \([0,\infty]\), the range in which integrals of nonnegative functions are taken; this allows its integral to be formed before it is known to be finite. Because \(U(x)\) is a real number, \(0<e^{-U(x)}<\infty\) for every \(x\in H\): the weight is finite and strictly positive at every point. Positivity is used below to show that the integral of \(w_U\) is strictly positive. If \(U\) is continuous, then \(w_U\) is continuous as a composition of continuous maps, hence Borel measurable.

The variable block of the file fixes the setting of the whole section: [NormedAddCommGroup H] [InnerProductSpace ℝ H] [FiniteDimensional ℝ H] make \(H\) a finite-dimensional real inner product space, and [MeasurableSpace H] [BorelSpace H] equip it with its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra.

steps.title: The partition function
steps.body:
Definition. The partition function of \(U\) is

\[Z_U=\int_Hw_U(x)\,dx=\int_He^{-U(x)}\,dx\in[0,\infty],\]

the Lebesgue integral of the nonnegative function \(w_U\) with respect to Lebesgue measure on \(H\).

The integral of a function \(f:H\to[0,\infty]\) is the supremum of \(\int s\,dx\) over all nonnegative simple Borel functions \(s\le f\). It is defined for every such \(f\) and may equal \(+\infty\); for Borel \(f\) it is the usual Lebesgue integral. No assumption on \(U\) is made at this stage, and \(Z_U=\infty\) is possible: for \(U=0\) and \(d\ge1\), \(Z_U=\lambda(H)=\infty\). Strict positivity of \(Z_U\) (for differentiable \(U\)) and finiteness of \(Z_U\) (for strongly convex \(U\)) are proved below; both are needed to divide by \(Z_U\).

The notation ∫⁻ x, f x ∂μ is Mathlib's lower Lebesgue integral of a function with values in ℝ≥0∞ with respect to the measure μ. It is defined for every such function, as the supremum over measurable simple functions below it, and takes values in ℝ≥0∞, so a divergent integral has the value ⊤ \(=\infty\). The measure volume is the canonical measure on \(H\): on a finite-dimensional inner product space Mathlib defines it as the additive Haar measure that gives measure one to the parallelepiped spanned by a fixed orthonormal basis, which is Lebesgue measure as described in the summary.

steps.title: The normalized Gibbs measure
steps.body:
Definition. Let \( u_U\) be the measure with density \(w_U\) with respect to Lebesgue measure, \( u_U(A)=\int_Aw_U(x)\,dx\) for Borel sets \(A\subseteq H\). The Gibbs measure of \(U\) is \(\pi_U=Z_U^{-1} u_U\), that is,

\[\pi_U(A)=Z_U^{-1}\int_Ae^{-U(x)}\,dx\qquad(A\subseteq H ext{ Borel}),\]

where \(Z_U^{-1}\in[0,\infty]\).

The formula is evaluated with the conventions of measure theory, \(0^{-1}=\infty\), \(\infty^{-1}=0\) and \(0\cdot\infty=\infty\cdot0=0\), so \(\pi_U\) is a measure for every \(U\). Since \( u_U(H)=Z_U\), we have \(\pi_U(H)=Z_U^{-1}Z_U\), and \(\pi_U\) is a probability measure exactly when \(0<Z_U<\infty\). In the degenerate cases \(\pi_U\) is the zero measure: if \(Z_U=\infty\), then \(Z_U^{-1}=0\); if \(Z_U=0\), then \( u_U(A)\le u_U(H)=0\) for every \(A\), so \( u_U=0\) and \(\infty\cdot0=0\). When \(0<Z_U<\infty\) and \(f\ge0\) is Borel, \(\int f\,d\pi_U=Z_U^{-1}\int_Hf(x)e^{-U(x)}\,dx\). The following steps prove \(0<Z_U<\infty\) for differentiable strongly convex \(U\).

The definition is therefore total, with exactly the conventions above; that it is a probability measure is the separate theorem isProbabilityMeasure_gibbsMeasure.

steps.title: Integrability of a radial Gaussian
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(a>0\). Then the function \(x\mapsto e^{-a\|x\|^2}\) is Lebesgue integrable on \(H\): it is Borel measurable and \(\int_He^{-a\|x\|^2}\,dx<\infty\). This holds in every finite dimension \(d\), including \(d=0\).

Proof. The function is continuous, hence Borel measurable, and it is positive, so integrability means finiteness of its integral. Choose an orthonormal basis \(e_1,\dots,e_d\) of \(H\) and let \(T:\mathbb R^d\to H\), \(T(t)=\sum_{i=1}^dt_ie_i\). The map \(T\) is a linear bijection, it satisfies \(\|T(t)\|^2=\sum_{i=1}^dt_i^2\) by orthonormality, and it carries Lebesgue measure on \(\mathbb R^d\) to Lebesgue measure on \(H\), since both are translation invariant and \(T\) maps the unit cube of \(\mathbb R^d\) onto the cube spanned by \(e_1,\dots,e_d\). By the change of variables \(x=T(t)\) and Tonelli's theorem for the nonnegative product function,

\[\int_He^{-a\|x\|^2}\,dx=\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-a\sum_{i=1}^dt_i^2}\,dt=\int_{\mathbb R^d}\prod_{i=1}^de^{-at_i^2}\,dt=\prod_{i=1}^d\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-as^2}\,ds.\]

Each one-dimensional factor is finite. Indeed \((|s|-1)^2\ge0\) gives \(s^2\ge2|s|-1\), hence \(e^{-as^2}\le e^{a}e^{-2a|s|}\) because \(a>0\), and

\[\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-as^2}\,ds\le e^{a}\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-2a|s|}\,ds=2e^a\int_0^\infty e^{-2as}\,ds=\frac{e^a}{a}<\infty.\]

(In fact the factor equals \(\sqrt{\pi/a}\), so the integral equals \((\pi/a)^{d/2}\).) A finite product of finite numbers is finite. For \(d=0\) the space is \(H=\{0\}\), Lebesgue measure is the unit mass at \(0\), the empty product equals \(1\), and the integral equals \(e^{0}=1\). The hypothesis \(a>0\) is necessary: for \(a\le0\) and \(d\ge1\) the integrand is at least \(1\) everywhere and the integral is infinite. \(\square\)

steps.title: A quadratic lower bound on the potential
steps.body:
Definitions. Let \(m\in\mathbb R\). A function \(U:H\to\mathbb R\) is \(m\)-strongly convex if for all \(x,y\in H\) and all \(s,t\ge0\) with \(s+t=1\),

\[U(sx+ty)\le sU(x)+tU(y)-st\,\frac m2\|x-y\|^2.\]

If \(U\) is differentiable, its gradient \(\nabla U(x)\in H\) is the unique vector with \(\langle\nabla U(x),v\rangle=DU(x)v\) for all \(v\in H\), where \(DU(x)\) is the derivative of \(U\) at \(x\).

Claim. Let \(m>0\) and let \(U:H\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex. Then for every \(x\in H\),

\[U(0)-\frac{\|\nabla U(0)\|^2}{m}+\frac m4\|x\|^2\le U(x).\]

Proof. A differentiable \(m\)-strongly convex function satisfies the strong first-order inequality

\[U(y)\ge U(z)+\langle\nabla U(z),y-z\rangle+\frac m2\|y-z\|^2\qquad(y,z\in H),\]

which follows from the first-order inequality for the convex differentiable function \(U-\frac m2\|\cdot\|^2\). Taking \(z=0\) and \(y=x\) gives

\[U(x)\ge U(0)+\langle\nabla U(0),x\rangle+\frac m2\|x\|^2.\qquad(1)\]

Write \(g=\|\nabla U(0)\|\) and \(r=\|x\|\). By the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality \(|\langle\nabla U(0),x\rangle|\le gr\), hence

\[\langle\nabla U(0),x\rangle\ge-gr.\qquad(2)\]

Next, \(gr\le\frac m4r^2+\frac{g^2}m\). Since \(m>0\), this inequality is equivalent to the one obtained by multiplying both sides by \(m\), namely \(mgr\le\frac{m^2}4r^2+g^2\), and the latter holds because

\[\frac{m^2}{4}r^2+g^2-mgr=\frac14\bigl(mr-2g\bigr)^2\ge0.\qquad(3)\]

Combining (1), (2) and (3),

\[U(x)\ge U(0)-gr+\frac m2r^2\ge U(0)-\frac m4r^2-\frac{g^2}m+\frac m2r^2=U(0)-\frac{g^2}m+\frac m4r^2,\]

which is the claim. \(\square\)

Half of the curvature \(m/2\) is used to absorb the linear term, and the remaining quadratic coefficient \(m/4\) is positive because \(m>0\). The origin plays no special role; it need not be a minimizer of \(U\).

steps.title: Integrability of the Gibbs weight
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(m>0\) and let \(U:H\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex. Then \(x\mapsto e^{-U(x)}\) is Lebesgue integrable on \(H\).

Proof. Put \(C=\|\nabla U(0)\|^2/m-U(0)\), a real constant. Rearranging the quadratic lower bound of the previous step gives, for every \(x\in H\),

\[-U(x)\le C-\frac m4\|x\|^2.\]

The exponential function is increasing and \(e^{u+v}=e^ue^v\), so

\[0<e^{-U(x)}\le e^{C-\frac m4\|x\|^2}=e^{C}\,e^{-\frac m4\|x\|^2}\qquad(x\in H).\qquad(1)\]

By the radial Gaussian step with \(a=m/4>0\), the function \(x\mapsto e^{-(m/4)\|x\|^2}\) is integrable, and so is its product with the constant \(e^{C}\). A differentiable function is continuous, so \(x\mapsto e^{-U(x)}\) is continuous and therefore Borel measurable. Finally we use the domination principle: a measurable function \(f\) with \(|f|\le g\) pointwise, where \(g\) is integrable, is integrable, because \(\int|f|\,dx\le\int g\,dx<\infty\) by monotonicity of the integral. By (1) it applies to \(f=e^{-U}\) and \(g=e^Ce^{-(m/4)\|\cdot\|^2}\). \(\square\)

The constant \(e^{C}\) does not depend on \(x\), and the origin need not minimize \(U\).

steps.title: The Gaussian weighted second moment
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(a>0\). Then \(x\mapsto\|x\|^2e^{-a\|x\|^2}\) is Lebesgue integrable on \(H\).

Proof. The function is continuous, hence measurable, and nonnegative. Fix \(x\in H\) and put \(s=\frac a2\|x\|^2\ge0\). The inequality \(1+u\le e^u\) for real \(u\) (the exponential lies above its tangent line at \(0\), by convexity) gives \(s\le s+1\le e^{s}\). Multiplying by \(e^{-a\|x\|^2}>0\),

\[\frac a2\|x\|^2e^{-a\|x\|^2}\le e^{\frac a2\|x\|^2}e^{-a\|x\|^2}=e^{-\frac a2\|x\|^2}.\]

Dividing by \(a/2>0\),

\[0\le\|x\|^2e^{-a\|x\|^2}\le\frac2a\,e^{-\frac a2\|x\|^2}\qquad(x\in H).\qquad(1)\]

The right-hand side of (1) is a constant multiple of the radial Gaussian with parameter \(a/2>0\), which is integrable by the radial Gaussian step. The domination principle (a measurable function bounded in absolute value by an integrable function is integrable) gives the claim. \(\square\)

Half of the Gaussian decay absorbs the polynomial factor \(\|x\|^2\); the other half remains integrable.

steps.title: The weighted Gibbs second moment
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(m>0\) and let \(U:H\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex. Then \(x\mapsto\|x\|^2e^{-U(x)}\) is Lebesgue integrable on \(H\).

Proof. Multiplying by \(\|x\|^2\ge0\) preserves this inequality, so for every \(x\in H\)

\[0\le\|x\|^2e^{-U(x)}\le\|x\|^2e^{C-\frac m4\|x\|^2}=e^C\,\|x\|^2e^{-\frac m4\|x\|^2}.\]

By the previous step with \(a=m/4>0\), the right-hand side is integrable. The left-hand side is continuous, as the product of the continuous functions \(x\mapsto\|x\|^2\) and \(x\mapsto e^{-U(x)}\) (\(U\) is continuous because it is differentiable), hence measurable. The domination principle gives the claim. \(\square\)

steps.title: Strict positivity of the partition
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(U:H o\mathbb R\) be differentiable. Then \(Z_U>0\). No convexity is assumed, and \(Z_U=\infty\) is allowed.

\[\int_Hf\,dx>0\quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad\lambda(\{f e0\})>0.\]

If \(\lambda(\{f e0\})=0\), then \(f=0\) almost everywhere and \(\int f\,dx=0\). Conversely, if \(\int f\,dx=0\), then for every \(n\ge1\) Markov's inequality gives \(\lambda(\{f>1/n\})\le n\int f\,dx=0\); since \(\{f e0\}= igcup_{n\ge1}\{f>1/n\}\), countable subadditivity gives \(\lambda(\{f e0\})=0\).

Lebesgue measure on \(H\) is not the zero measure: it gives volume one to the cube spanned by an orthonormal basis (to \(H=\{0\}\) itself if \(d=0\)), so \(\lambda(H)\ge1>0\). By the fact above, \(Z_U=\int_Hw_U\,dx>0\). \(\square\)

steps.title: Finiteness of the partition
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(m>0\) and let \(U:H\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex. Then \(Z_U<\infty\).

\[Z_U=\int_Hw_U(x)\,dx=\int_H\bigl|e^{-U(x)}\bigr|\,dx<\infty.\qquad\square\]

steps.title: The ordinary integral formula for the partition
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(m>0\) and let \(U:H\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex. Then the partition function equals the ordinary Lebesgue integral of the real-valued integrable function \(e^{-U}\),

\[Z_U=\int_He^{-U(x)}\,dx,\]

where the right-hand side is a nonnegative real number, regarded as an element of \([0,\infty)\).

Proof. The integral of an integrable real function \(f\) is \(\int f^+\,dx-\int f^-\,dx\), with \(f^\pm=\max(\pm f,0)\), both terms being finite. By the integrability step for the Gibbs weight, \(f=e^{-U}\) is integrable, and \(f\ge0\) gives \(f^+=f\) and \(f^-=0\). Hence the real integral \(\int f\,dx\) equals the integral of the nonnegative function \(f\) taken in \([0,\infty]\), which is \(Z_U\). \(\square\)

In particular the extended number \(Z_U\) is identified with a nonnegative real number, which gives a second proof of \(Z_U<\infty\).

steps.title: Positivity of the ordinary normalizer
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(m>0\) and let \(U:H\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex. Then the real number \(\int_He^{-U(x)}\,dx\) is strictly positive.

Proof. The function \(f=e^{-U}\) is integrable, by the integrability step for the Gibbs weight, and nonnegative. For such \(f\), the real integral equals the integral of \(f\) as a nonnegative function (previous step), and the latter is strictly positive if and only if \(\lambda(\{f\ne0\})>0\) (the fact proved in the positivity step for \(Z_U\)). Every value of \(f\) is positive, so \(\{f\ne0\}=H\), and \(\lambda(H)>0\). Hence \(\int_He^{-U(x)}\,dx>0\). \(\square\)

Together with the two preceding steps this gives \(0<\int_He^{-U(x)}\,dx=Z_U<\infty\), so \(Z_U^{-1}e^{-U(x)}\) is a probability density with respect to Lebesgue measure.

It is applied with \(f=-U\) and \(\mu\) equal to volume, and the integrability hypothesis is integrable_exp_neg_of_strongConvex. Mathlib proves integral_exp_pos by the support argument above: the integral of an integrable nonnegative function is positive exactly when its support has positive measure, and the support of an exponential is the whole space.

steps.title: Normalization of the Gibbs probability
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(m>0\) and let \(U:H o\mathbb R\) be differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex. Then \(\pi_U\) is a probability measure: \(\pi_U(H)=1\).

Proof. By the definition of \(\pi_U\) and of the measure \( u_U\) with density \(w_U\), evaluated on the Borel set \(A=H\),

\[\pi_U(H)=Z_U^{-1}\, u_U(H)=Z_U^{-1}\int_Hw_U(x)\,dx=Z_U^{-1}Z_U.\]

In \([0,\infty]\) the identity \(c^{-1}c=1\) holds precisely for \(c otin\{0,\infty\}\): for \(c=0\) the product is \(\infty\cdot0=0\), and for \(c=\infty\) it is \(0\cdot\infty=0\). By the positivity step \(Z_U e0\), and by the finiteness step \(Z_U e\infty\). Hence \(\pi_U(H)=1\). \(\square\)

Positivity uses only the differentiability (through the continuity) of \(U\); finiteness is where strong convexity with \(m>0\) enters.

steps.title: The normalized Gibbs second moment
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(m>0\) and let \(U:H o\mathbb R\) be differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex. Then the function \(x\mapsto\|x\|^2\) is integrable with respect to \(\pi_U\), that is, \(\int_H\|x\|^2\,\pi_U(dx)<\infty\).

Proof. First consider the measure \( u_U\) with density \(w_U\). For a Borel function \( ho:H o[0,\infty)\) and the measure \( u(A)=\int_A ho\,dx\), every Borel \(\phi:H o[0,\infty]\) satisfies

\[\int\phi\,d u=\int\phi\, ho\,dx:\]

for indicator functions this is the definition of \( u\), for simple functions it follows by linearity, and for general \(\phi\) by monotone convergence along an increasing sequence of simple functions converging to \(\phi\). Consequently a measurable \(g\) is \( u\)-integrable if and only if \( ho g\) is Lebesgue integrable, since \(\int|g|\,d u=\int ho|g|\,dx\). We apply this with \( ho=e^{-U}\), which is continuous (hence Borel) and finite everywhere, and \(g(x)=\|x\|^2\). The function \( ho g=\|x\|^2e^{-U(x)}\) is Lebesgue integrable by the weighted Gibbs moment step, so \(\|x\|^2\) is \( u_U\)-integrable.

Next, \(\pi_U=c\, u_U\) with \(c=Z_U^{-1}\). By the positivity step \(Z_U>0\), so \(c<\infty\). For every measurable \(g\), \(\int|g|\,d(c u_U)=c\int|g|\,d u_U\), which is finite when \(c<\infty\) and \(g\) is \( u_U\)-integrable. Therefore \(\|x\|^2\) is \(\pi_U\)-integrable, with

\[\int_H\|x\|^2\,\pi_U(dx)=Z_U^{-1}\int_H\|x\|^2e^{-U(x)}\,dx.\qquad\square\]

The second paragraph uses only the positivity of \(Z_U\); strong convexity enters through the integrability of \(\|x\|^2e^{-U(x)}\).

steps.title: Square-integrability of the Gibbs state
steps.body:
Definition. Let \(\mu\) be a measure on \(H\), \(E\) a finite-dimensional normed space and \(1\le p<\infty\). A function \(f:H\to E\) belongs to \(L^p(\mu;E)\) if it is \(\mu\)-almost everywhere equal to a Borel function and \(\int\|f\|^p\,d\mu<\infty\).

Claim. Let \(m>0\) and let \(U:H\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex. Then the identity map \(x\mapsto x\) of \(H\) belongs to \(L^2(\pi_U;H)\).

Proof. The identity is continuous, hence Borel measurable. By the definition of \(L^2\) it remains to show that \(\int_H\|x\|^2\,\pi_U(dx)<\infty\), which is the previous step. \(\square\)

In probabilistic language, a random vector with law \(\pi_U\) has a finite second moment.

The proof applies memLp_two_iff_integrable_sq_norm, which states that for an almost everywhere strongly measurable \(f\), MemLp f 2 μ holds if and only if \(x\mapsto\|f(x)\|^2\) is \(\mu\)-integrable. Measurability of the identity is proved by fun_prop, and the integrability is integrable_norm_sq_gibbsMeasure.

steps.title: Square-integrability after translation
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(m>0\), let \(U:H\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex, and let \(z\in H\). Then \(x\mapsto x-z\) belongs to \(L^2(\pi_U;H)\); equivalently \(\int_H\|x-z\|^2\,\pi_U(dx)<\infty\).

Proof. By the normalization step, \(\pi_U\) is a probability measure, in particular a finite measure. The constant map \(x\mapsto z\) is measurable and \(\int\|z\|^2\,d\pi_U=\|z\|^2\pi_U(H)=\|z\|^2<\infty\), so it belongs to \(L^2(\pi_U;H)\). The identity belongs to \(L^2(\pi_U;H)\) by the previous step. The set \(L^2(\pi_U;H)\) is closed under subtraction: the difference of measurable maps is measurable, and by Minkowski's inequality \(\|f-g\|_{L^2}\le\|f\|_{L^2}+\|g\|_{L^2}<\infty\). Hence \(x\mapsto x-z\) belongs to \(L^2(\pi_U;H)\). \(\square\)

The centre \(z\) is arbitrary, for example a minimizer of \(U\); no property of \(z\) is used.

The term (memLp_id_gibbsMeasure U m hm hdiff hsc).sub (memLp_const z) is the closure of \(L^2\) under subtraction (Mathlib's MemLp.sub, proved from the triangle inequality for the \(L^p\) seminorm) applied to the identity and the constant \(z\).

UnadjustedLangevin/GibbsConcentration.le.title: Concentration around a minimizer without differentiability
UnadjustedLangevin/GibbsConcentration.le.summary:
This section proves that the Gibbs measure of a continuous strongly convex potential concentrates around the minimizer of the potential at the dimension-sharp scale. Let \(H\) be a real inner product space of finite dimension \(d\), with Lebesgue measure \(dx\), let \(q>0\), let \(F:H\to\mathbb R\) be continuous and \(q\)-strongly convex, and let \(z\in H\) be a global minimizer of \(F\), that is, \(F(z)\le F(x)\) for all \(x\). With the partition function \(Z_F=\int_He^{-F(x)}\,dx\) and the Gibbs measure \(\pi_F(dx)=Z_F^{-1}e^{-F(x)}\,dx\) of the section on Gibbs normalization, the main result is

\[\int_H\|x-z\|^2\,\pi_F(dx)\le\frac{2d}{q}.\]

No derivative of \(F\) is used. The proof has two parts. First, strong convexity at the midpoint of \(z\) and \(x\) together with minimality gives \(F(x)\ge F(z)+\frac q4\|x-z\|^2\), so \(e^{-F}\) and \(\|x-z\|^2e^{-F}\) are dominated by translated Gaussian functions and are integrable. Second, for \(0<r<1\) the dilation \(x\mapsto z+r(x-z)\), whose Jacobian determinant is \(r^d\), is combined with strong convexity to give

\[Z+\frac q2r(1-r)M\le r^{-d}Z,\qquad Z=\int_He^{-F(x)}\,dx,\quad M=\int_H\|x-z\|^2e^{-F(x)}\,dx;\]

both sides are equal at \(r=1\), and comparing their derivatives at \(r=1\) gives \(\frac q2M\le dZ\). Dividing by \(Z\) gives the bound. The estimate is used later for the concentration of parameter marginals of particle targets.

steps.title: The quadratic potential bound at a minimizer
steps.body:
Recall that \(F:H\to\mathbb R\) is \(q\)-strongly convex if \(F(sx+ty)\le sF(x)+tF(y)-st\frac q2\|x-y\|^2\) for all \(x,y\in H\) and \(s,t\ge0\) with \(s+t=1\).

Claim. Let \(H\) be a real inner product space, let \(q\in\mathbb R\), let \(F:H\to\mathbb R\) be \(q\)-strongly convex, and let \(z\in H\) satisfy \(F(z)\le F(x)\) for all \(x\in H\). Then for every \(x\in H\),

\[F(z)+\frac q4\|x-z\|^2\le F(x).\]

Proof. Fix \(x\). Strong convexity with the points \(z,x\) and the weights \(s=t=\frac12\) gives, since \(st\frac q2=\frac q8\) and \(\|z-x\|=\|x-z\|\),

\[F\Bigl(\tfrac12z+\tfrac12x\Bigr)\le\tfrac12F(z)+\tfrac12F(x)-\frac q8\|x-z\|^2.\qquad(1)\]

Minimality of \(z\), applied at the midpoint \(\frac12z+\frac12x\), gives

\[F(z)\le F\Bigl(\tfrac12z+\tfrac12x\Bigr).\qquad(2)\]

Combining (2) with (1) yields \(F(z)\le\frac12F(z)+\frac12F(x)-\frac q8\|x-z\|^2\). Subtracting \(\frac12F(z)\) and multiplying by \(2\) gives \(F(z)\le F(x)-\frac q4\|x-z\|^2\), which is the claim. \(\square\)

The argument uses only values of \(F\): no derivative, no continuity, no finite dimension and no sign of \(q\) are needed. For \(q>0\) it gives quadratic growth of \(F\) away from \(z\) without any loss in the constant term, in contrast with the bound at an arbitrary base point used in the section on Gibbs normalization.

steps.title: Integrability around the minimizer
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(H\) be finite-dimensional, let \(q>0\), let \(F:H\to\mathbb R\) be continuous and \(q\)-strongly convex, and let \(z\) be a global minimizer of \(F\). Then \(x\mapsto e^{-F(x)}\) is Lebesgue integrable on \(H\).

Proof. By the previous step, \(-F(x)\le-F(z)-\frac q4\|x-z\|^2\) for every \(x\). The exponential is increasing and \(e^{u+v}=e^ue^v\), so

\[0<e^{-F(x)}\le e^{-F(z)}\,e^{-\frac q4\|x-z\|^2}\qquad(x\in H).\qquad(1)\]

The function \(g(y)=e^{-\frac q4\|y\|^2}\) is integrable, by the integrability of radial Gaussians with parameter \(a=q/4>0\) . Lebesgue measure is invariant under the translation \(x\mapsto x-z\), so \(\int_H g(x-z)\,dx=\int_Hg(y)\,dy<\infty\) and \(x\mapsto g(x-z)\) is integrable; so is its product with the constant \(e^{-F(z)}\). Since \(F\) is continuous, \(e^{-F}\) is continuous and hence Borel measurable. By (1) and the domination principle (a measurable function bounded in absolute value by an integrable function is integrable), \(e^{-F}\) is integrable. \(\square\)

Continuity of \(F\) is used only for measurability; positivity of \(q\) is needed for the Gaussian majorant to be integrable.

steps.title: The weighted squared-distance moment
steps.body:
Claim. Under the hypotheses of the previous step (\(H\) finite-dimensional, \(q>0\), \(F\) continuous and \(q\)-strongly convex, \(z\) a global minimizer), the function \(x\mapsto\|x-z\|^2e^{-F(x)}\) is Lebesgue integrable on \(H\).

Proof. Multiplying inequality (1) of the previous step by \(\|x-z\|^2\ge0\) preserves it:

\[0\le\|x-z\|^2e^{-F(x)}\le e^{-F(z)}\,\|x-z\|^2e^{-\frac q4\|x-z\|^2}\qquad(x\in H).\]

The function \(y\mapsto\|y\|^2e^{-\frac q4\|y\|^2}\) is integrable by the Gaussian second-moment estimate with \(a=q/4>0\) . By translation invariance of Lebesgue measure its translate \(x\mapsto\|x-z\|^2e^{-\frac q4\|x-z\|^2}\) is integrable, and so is the constant multiple on the right. The left-hand side is continuous (\(F\) is continuous), hence measurable, and the domination principle gives the claim. \(\square\)

steps.title: Contracting coordinates toward the minimizer
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(H\) have finite dimension \(d\), let \(q>0\), let \(F:H\to\mathbb R\) be continuous and \(q\)-strongly convex, let \(z\) be a global minimizer of \(F\), and let \(0<r<1\). Put

\[Z=\int_He^{-F(x)}\,dx,\qquad M=\int_H\|x-z\|^2e^{-F(x)}\,dx,\]

which are finite by the two previous steps. Then

\[Z+\frac q2\,r(1-r)\,M\le r^{-d}Z.\]

Proof. Write \(w(x)=e^{-F(x)}\), \(C=\frac q2r(1-r)\), and let \(D_r(x)=z+r(x-z)=rx+(1-r)z\) be the dilation with centre \(z\) and ratio \(r\).

Pointwise inequality. Fix \(x\in H\). Strong convexity with the points \(z,x\) and the weights \(s=1-r\ge0\), \(t=r\ge0\), \(s+t=1\), gives, since \(st\frac q2=C\) and \(\|z-x\|=\|x-z\|\),

\[F(D_r(x))=F\bigl((1-r)z+rx\bigr)\le(1-r)F(z)+rF(x)-C\|x-z\|^2.\]

Minimality \(F(z)\le F(x)\) multiplied by \(1-r\ge0\) gives \((1-r)F(z)\le(1-r)F(x)\), hence

\[F(D_r(x))\le F(x)-C\|x-z\|^2.\qquad(1)\]

Thus \(-F(x)+C\|x-z\|^2\le-F(D_r(x))\), and since the exponential is increasing, \(w(x)\,e^{C\|x-z\|^2}\le w(D_r(x))\). The inequality \(1+u\le e^u\) with \(u=C\|x-z\|^2\), multiplied by \(w(x)\ge0\), gives \(w(x)(1+C\|x-z\|^2)\le w(x)e^{C\|x-z\|^2}\). Therefore

\[w(x)+C\|x-z\|^2w(x)\le w(D_r(x))\qquad(x\in H).\qquad(2)\]

Change of variables. We show that \(x\mapsto w(D_r(x))\) is integrable and

\[\int_Hw(D_r(x))\,dx=r^{-d}Z.\qquad(3)\]

Write \(w(D_r(x))=v(rx)\) with \(v(y)=w(y+(1-r)z)\). By translation invariance of Lebesgue measure, \(v\) is integrable and \(\int v\,dy=\int w\,dy=Z\). The linear map \(x\mapsto Rx\) with \(R>0\) has determinant \(R^d\) and multiplies the Lebesgue measure of every Borel set by \(R^d\); hence for every integrable \(f\), the function \(x\mapsto f(Rx)\) is integrable and \(\int_Hf(Rx)\,dx=R^{-d}\int_Hf(y)\,dy\) (substitute \(y=Rx\), \(dy=R^d\,dx\)). With \(R=r\) and \(f=v\) this gives (3).

Integration. The left-hand side of (2) is integrable by the two previous steps and the right-hand side by (3). Integrating (2), using linearity and monotonicity of the integral and then (3),

\[Z+CM=\int_H\bigl(w(x)+C\|x-z\|^2w(x)\bigr)\,dx\le\int_Hw(D_r(x))\,dx=r^{-d}Z.\qquad\square\]

Both sides are equal to \(Z\) at \(r=1\). The inequality compares the gain \(\frac q2r(1-r)M\) produced by strong convexity with the loss of volume \(r^{-d}\) produced by the contraction; the next step compares their rates at \(r=1\).

steps.title: A partition comparison for squared distance
steps.body:
Claim. Under the hypotheses of the previous step (\(\dim H=d\), \(q>0\), \(F\) continuous and \(q\)-strongly convex, \(z\) a global minimizer), with \(Z\) and \(M\) as defined there,

\[\int_H\|x-z\|^2e^{-F(x)}\,dx\le\frac{2d}{q}\int_He^{-F(x)}\,dx,\qquad\text{that is,}\qquad M\le\frac{2d}{q}Z.\]

Proof. Let \(C=\frac q2\) and define the polynomial

\[\Phi(r)=r^d\bigl(Z+C\,r(1-r)\,M\bigr)\qquad(r\in\mathbb R).\]

(a) \(\Phi(1)=Z\).

(b) For \(0<r<1\), \(\Phi(r)\le Z\): multiplying the inequality of the previous step by \(r^d>0\) gives \(r^d\bigl(Z+Cr(1-r)M\bigr)\le r^d\,r^{-d}Z=Z\).

(c) By the product rule, \(\Phi'(r)=dr^{d-1}\bigl(Z+Cr(1-r)M\bigr)+r^d\,C(1-2r)M\), where the first term is absent if \(d=0\). At \(r=1\) the factor \(r(1-r)\) vanishes and \(1-2r=-1\), so

\[\Phi'(1)=dZ-CM.\]

(d) Let \(-1<u<0\). Then \(0<1+u<1\), so by (b) and (a), \(\Phi(1+u)-\Phi(1)\le0\). Dividing by \(u<0\) reverses the inequality:

\[\frac{\Phi(1+u)-\Phi(1)}{u}\ge0.\]

As \(u\to0\) with \(u<0\), these difference quotients converge to \(\Phi'(1)\), by the definition of the derivative. A limit of nonnegative numbers is nonnegative, so \(\Phi'(1)\ge0\), that is, \(\frac q2M\le dZ\).

(e) Multiplying by \(2/q>0\) gives \(M\le\frac{2d}{q}Z\). \(\square\)

Only the derivative from the left at \(r=1\) is used, since the dilation inequality is available for \(r<1\) only; the derivative is taken of an explicit polynomial in \(r\), and no derivative of \(F\) appears. For \(d=0\) the claim says \(M\le0\), consistent with \(H=\{0\}\) and \(x=z=0\).

steps.title: Integrability of the squared distance under the Gibbs measure
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(H\) be finite-dimensional, \(q>0\), \(F:H o\mathbb R\) continuous and \(q\)-strongly convex, and \(z\) a global minimizer of \(F\). Then \(x\mapsto\|x-z\|^2\) is integrable with respect to the Gibbs measure \(\pi_F\).

Proof. The argument is the one used for the second moment in the section on Gibbs normalization. Let \( u_F(A)=\int_Ae^{-F(x)}\,dx\), so that \(\pi_F=Z_F^{-1} u_F\).

Positivity of \(Z_F\). By the integrability step, \(e^{-F}\) is integrable and nonnegative, so \(Z_F\) equals the real integral \(\int_He^{-F(x)}\,dx\) (the integral of an integrable nonnegative function is the same whether taken in \([0,\infty]\) or as a real number). This real integral is strictly positive, because its integrand is strictly positive everywhere and \(\lambda(H)>0\): the integral of a nonnegative integrable function is positive exactly when the set where it is nonzero has positive measure. Hence \(Z_F>0\) and \(Z_F^{-1}<\infty\). (The positivity result of the normalization section assumed differentiability; here \(F\) is only continuous, and positivity is obtained from the real integral.)

Integrability. The density \(e^{-F}\) is continuous, hence Borel, and finite. For a measure with a finite Borel density, \(\int|g|\,d u_F=\int|g(x)|e^{-F(x)}\,dx\), so \(g\) is \( u_F\)-integrable if and only if \(ge^{-F}\) is Lebesgue integrable. For \(g(x)=\|x-z\|^2\), the function \(\|x-z\|^2e^{-F(x)}\) is Lebesgue integrable by the weighted moment step. Finally, multiplying the measure \( u_F\) by the finite constant \(Z_F^{-1}\) multiplies \(\int|g|\) by that constant, so \(g\) is \(\pi_F\)-integrable. \(\square\)

steps.title: The Gibbs concentration bound around the minimizer
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(H\) have finite dimension \(d\), let \(q>0\), let \(F:H\to\mathbb R\) be continuous and \(q\)-strongly convex, and let \(z\) be a global minimizer of \(F\). Then

\[\int_H\|x-z\|^2\,\pi_F(dx)\le\frac{2d}{q}.\]

Equivalently, a random vector \(X\) with law \(\pi_F\) satisfies \(\mathbb E\|X-z\|^2\le2d/q\).

Proof. Let \(Z=\int_He^{-F(x)}\,dx\) and \(M=\int_H\|x-z\|^2e^{-F(x)}\,dx\). As in the previous step, \(Z>0\) and the partition function is \(Z_F=Z\). For a nonnegative Borel function \(g\), the integral against \(\pi_F=Z_F^{-1}\nu_F\) is \(Z_F^{-1}\) times the integral against \(\nu_F\), and the integral against the measure \(\nu_F\) with density \(e^{-F}\) is \(\int g(x)e^{-F(x)}\,dx\). With \(g(x)=\|x-z\|^2\) this gives

\[\int_H\|x-z\|^2\,\pi_F(dx)=Z^{-1}\int_H\|x-z\|^2e^{-F(x)}\,dx=Z^{-1}M.\]

By the partition comparison of the fifth step, \(M\le\frac{2d}qZ\). Multiplying by \(Z^{-1}>0\),

\[Z^{-1}M\le Z^{-1}\cdot\frac{2d}{q}Z=\frac{2d}{q}.\qquad\square\]

The bound concerns the distance to the minimizer \(z\), which need not be the mean of \(\pi_F\). The integral is finite by the previous step. For \(d=0\) the bound is \(0\), as it must be.

UnadjustedLangevin/GibbsScore.lean.title: The Gibbs gradient moment from an exponential bound
UnadjustedLangevin/GibbsScore.lean.summary:
This section bounds the gradient \( abla U\) of the potential under the Gibbs measure \(\pi_U(dx)=Z_U^{-1}e^{-U(x)}\,dx\) on a real inner product space \(H\) of finite dimension \(d\) (the notation is that of the section on Gibbs normalization). The assumptions are first-order: \(U\) is differentiable, its gradient is \(L\)-Lipschitz for some \(L\ge0\), that is, \(\| abla U(x)- abla U(y)\|\le L\|x-y\|\) for all \(x,y\), and the partition function \(Z_U\) is finite. The main result is

\[\int_H\| abla U(x)\|^2\,\pi_U(dx)\le Ld.\]

The proof has four steps. The descent inequality \(U(x+v)\le U(x)+\langle abla U(x),v angle+ rac L2\|v\|^2\) and the translation invariance of Lebesgue measure give, for every \(v\in H\),

\[\int_He^{-\langle abla U(x),v angle}\,\pi_U(dx)\le e^{ rac L2\|v\|^2}.\]

Replacing \(v\) by \(-tv\) shows that every directional derivative \(\langle abla U,v angle\) is a sub-Gaussian random variable under \(\pi_U\) with variance proxy \(L\|v\|^2\). A sub-Gaussian random variable with variance proxy \(c\) has second moment at most \(c\), by the inequality \(a^2\le e^a+e^{-a}-2\) and a limit. Summing over an orthonormal basis (Parseval's identity) gives the bound \(Ld\). No second derivative of \(U\) and no integration by parts is used. If \(U\) is \(m\)-strongly convex with \(m>0\), finiteness of \(Z_U\) holds automatically. The bound controls the size of the drift of the stationary Langevin process in the local error analysis of the unadjusted Langevin algorithm.

steps.title: The exponential score comparison
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(L\ge0\) and let \(U:H\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. Then for all \(x,v\in H\),

\[e^{-U(x)}\,e^{-\langle\nabla U(x),v\rangle}\le e^{\frac L2\|v\|^2}\,e^{-U(x+v)}.\]

Proof. A differentiable function with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient satisfies the descent inequality

\[U(y)\le U(x)+\langle\nabla U(x),y-x\rangle+\frac L2\|y-x\|^2\qquad(x,y\in H),\]

obtained by integrating the derivative of \(s\mapsto U(x+s(y-x))\) over \([0,1]\) and bounding the variation of the gradient by its Lipschitz constant. With \(y=x+v\), so that \(y-x=v\), it reads \(U(x+v)\le U(x)+\langle\nabla U(x),v\rangle+\frac L2\|v\|^2\), which rearranges to

\[-U(x)-\langle\nabla U(x),v\rangle\le\frac L2\|v\|^2-U(x+v).\]

The exponential function is increasing, so this inequality persists after exponentiation, and \(e^{a+b}=e^ae^b\) splits both sides into the stated products. \(\square\)

The factor \(e^{-U(x)}\) on the left is the Gibbs weight at \(x\), and \(e^{-U(x+v)}\) on the right is the Gibbs weight at the translated point; this is what makes the inequality integrable against Lebesgue measure in the next step.

steps.title: The directional exponential moment bound
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(L\ge0\), let \(U:H\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, and assume \(Z_U<\infty\). Then for every \(v\in H\),

\[\int_He^{-\langle\nabla U(x),v\rangle}\,\pi_U(dx)\le e^{\frac L2\|v\|^2}.\]

The integral is that of a nonnegative function, taken in \([0,\infty]\); in particular it is finite.

Proof. Let \(w_U=e^{-U}\) and \(g(x)=e^{-\langle\nabla U(x),v\rangle}\). Both are continuous (\(U\) is differentiable, and \(\nabla U\) is Lipschitz, hence continuous), so both are Borel measurable. Recall \(\pi_U=Z_U^{-1}\nu_U\), where \(\nu_U\) has density \(w_U\) with respect to Lebesgue measure. For nonnegative measurable \(g\), the integral against a multiple of a measure is the multiple of the integral, and the integral against a measure with density is the integral of the product with the density. Hence

\[\int g\,d\pi_U=Z_U^{-1}\int_Hw_U(x)\,g(x)\,dx.\]

By the previous step, \(w_U(x)g(x)\le e^{\frac L2\|v\|^2}w_U(x+v)\) for every \(x\). Integrating (monotonicity of the integral) and taking out the constant,

\[\int_Hw_U(x)g(x)\,dx\le e^{\frac L2\|v\|^2}\int_Hw_U(x+v)\,dx=e^{\frac L2\|v\|^2}Z_U,\]

where \(\int_Hw_U(x+v)\,dx=\int_Hw_U(y)\,dy=Z_U\) by translation invariance of Lebesgue measure (substitute \(y=x+v\)). Multiplication by \(Z_U^{-1}\) preserves inequalities in \([0,\infty]\), so

\[\int g\,d\pi_U\le Z_U^{-1}\,e^{\frac L2\|v\|^2}Z_U=e^{\frac L2\|v\|^2}\,\bigl(Z_U^{-1}Z_U\bigr)=e^{\frac L2\|v\|^2},\]

because \(Z_U^{-1}Z_U=1\) when \(0<Z_U<\infty\). Here \(Z_U>0\) holds since \(U\) is differentiable , and \(Z_U<\infty\) is the hypothesis. \(\square\)

steps.title: The sub-Gaussian directional score
steps.body:
Definition. Let \((\Omega,\mu)\) be a measure space and \(c\ge0\). A measurable function \(X:\Omega\to\mathbb R\) has a sub-Gaussian moment generating function with variance proxy \(c\) if for every \(t\in\mathbb R\) the function \(e^{tX}\) is \(\mu\)-integrable and

\[\int_\Omega e^{tX}\,d\mu\le e^{ct^2/2}.\]

Claim. Let \(L\ge0\), let \(U:H\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, assume \(Z_U<\infty\), and let \(v\in H\). Then the function \(X(x)=\langle\nabla U(x),v\rangle\) has a sub-Gaussian moment generating function under \(\pi_U\) with variance proxy \(L\|v\|^2\).

Proof. Fix \(t\in\mathbb R\). Apply the previous step to the vector \(-tv\). Since \(\langle\nabla U(x),-tv\rangle=-tX(x)\) and \(\|-tv\|^2=t^2\|v\|^2\), it gives

\[\int_He^{tX(x)}\,\pi_U(dx)\le e^{\frac L2t^2\|v\|^2}=e^{(L\|v\|^2)t^2/2},\qquad(1)\]

with the left side taken in \([0,\infty]\). The function \(e^{tX}\) is continuous (the gradient is continuous), hence measurable, and nonnegative; by (1) its integral is finite, so \(e^{tX}\) is \(\pi_U\)-integrable. For an integrable nonnegative function the real integral equals the integral taken in \([0,\infty]\), so (1) is the required bound on the real integral. As \(t\) was arbitrary, both conditions of the definition hold. \(\square\)

steps.title: A square bounded by two exponentials
steps.body:
Claim. For every \(a\in\mathbb R\),

\[a^2\le e^a+e^{-a}-2.\]

Proof. The hyperbolic cosine has the everywhere convergent power series

\[\cosh a=\frac{e^a+e^{-a}}2=\sum_{n=0}^\infty\frac{a^{2n}}{(2n)!}.\]

Every term is nonnegative, because \(a^{2n}=(a^2)^n\ge0\) and \((2n)!>0\). For a convergent series with nonnegative terms, every partial sum is at most the sum; keeping the terms \(n=0\) and \(n=1\) gives

\[1+\frac{a^2}2\le\cosh a=\frac{e^a+e^{-a}}2.\]

Multiplying by \(2\) and subtracting \(2\) gives the claim. \(\square\)

The right-hand side is an even function of \(a\) whose Taylor expansion starts with \(a^2\); the inequality says that the remaining terms are nonnegative.

steps.title: A second moment from exponential control
steps.body:
Claim. Let \((\Omega,\mu)\) be a probability space, let \(c\ge0\), and let \(X:\Omega\to\mathbb R\) have a sub-Gaussian moment generating function with variance proxy \(c\). Then \(X^2\) is integrable and

\[\int_\Omega X^2\,d\mu\le c.\]

No assumption \(\int X\,d\mu=0\) is made; the bound is for the uncentred second moment.

Proof. Integrability. By the previous step with \(a=X(\omega)\), \(0\le X^2\le e^{X}+e^{-X}\), and the right side is integrable (take \(t=\pm1\) in the definition); hence \(X^2\) is integrable. (More generally, a random variable with \(\int e^{tX}d\mu<\infty\) for all \(t\) in a neighbourhood of \(0\) has moments of all orders.)

A bound for each \(s>0\). Fix \(s>0\) and put \(t=\sqrt{2s}\), so \(t^2=2s\). The previous step with \(a=tX(\omega)\) gives, for every \(\omega\),

\[2s\,X(\omega)^2=t^2X(\omega)^2\le e^{tX(\omega)}+e^{-tX(\omega)}-2.\]

All terms are integrable, so integrating and using \(\mu(\Omega)=1\) (so that \(\int2\,d\mu=2\)),

\[2s\int X^2\,d\mu\le\int e^{tX}\,d\mu+\int e^{-tX}\,d\mu-2\le2e^{ct^2/2}-2=2e^{cs}-2,\]

where the moment generating function bound is used at \(t\) and at \(-t\), and \((-t)^2=t^2=2s\). Dividing by \(2s>0\),

\[\int X^2\,d\mu\le\frac{e^{cs}-1}{s}\qquad(s>0).\qquad(1)\]

Limit. The function \(s\mapsto e^{cs}\) is differentiable at \(0\) with derivative \(c\), so \(\frac{e^{cs}-1}{s}\to c\) as \(s\to0\) with \(s>0\). The left side of (1) does not depend on \(s\), and non-strict inequalities are preserved under limits; hence \(\int X^2\,d\mu\le c\). \(\square\)

steps.body:
Claim. Let \(H\) have finite dimension \(d\), let \(L\ge0\), let \(U:H\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, and assume \(Z_U<\infty\). Then

\[\int_H\|\nabla U(x)\|^2\,\pi_U(dx)\le Ld.\]

Choose an orthonormal basis \(e_1,\dots,e_d\) of \(H\). For every \(y\in H\), Parseval's identity gives \(\|y\|^2=\sum_{i=1}^d\langle y,e_i\rangle^2\). Put \(X_i(x)=\langle\nabla U(x),e_i\rangle\). By the sub-Gaussian step, \(X_i\) has a sub-Gaussian moment generating function under \(\pi_U\) with variance proxy \(L\|e_i\|^2=L\). By the previous step, applied to the probability space \((H,\pi_U)\), \(X_i^2\) is integrable and \(\int X_i^2\,d\pi_U\le L\). Therefore, by Parseval's identity and linearity of the integral over the finite sum of integrable functions,

\[\int_H\|\nabla U\|^2\,d\pi_U=\int_H\sum_{i=1}^dX_i^2\,d\pi_U=\sum_{i=1}^d\int_HX_i^2\,d\pi_U\le\sum_{i=1}^dL=Ld.\qquad\square\]

For \(d=0\) the bound is \(0\), as \(H=\{0\}\) and \(\nabla U=0\).

steps.title: Square-integrability of the Gibbs gradient
steps.body:
Claim. Under the hypotheses of the previous step (\(L\ge0\), \(U\) differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, \(Z_U<\infty\)), the gradient \( abla U:H o H\) belongs to \(L^2(\pi_U;H)\).

By Parseval's identity \(\| abla U\|^2=\sum_{i=1}^dX_i^2\), a finite sum of integrable functions, which is integrable. A measurable map whose squared norm is integrable belongs to \(L^2\). \(\square\)

Only integrability is needed here, not the quantitative bound \(Ld\) of the previous step.

steps.title: The gradient-energy bound under strong convexity
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(H\) have finite dimension \(d\), let \(m>0\) and \(L\ge0\), and let \(U:H\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable, \(m\)-strongly convex, with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. Then

\[\int_H\|\nabla U(x)\|^2\,\pi_U(dx)\le Ld.\]

Proof. Strong convexity with \(m>0\) and differentiability give \(Z_U<\infty\) . The claim is then the full gradient-energy bound proved above. \(\square\)

The strong convexity constant \(m\) is used only to guarantee a finite partition function; it does not appear in the bound.

UnadjustedLangevin/StationaryMoments.lea.title: Transfer the Gibbs score estimate to an \(L^2\) reference
UnadjustedLangevin/StationaryMoments.lea.summary:
Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\) be a probability space and \(H\) a real inner product space of finite dimension \(d\). We write \(L^2(P;H)\) for the space of (classes up to almost sure equality of) measurable maps \(Y:\Omega o H\) with \(\mathbb E\|Y\|^2=\int_\Omega\|Y\|^2\,dP<\infty\), normed by \(\|Y\|_{L^2}=(\mathbb E\|Y\|^2)^{1/2}\). The law of \(Y\) is the image measure \(P\circ Y^{-1}\), \(A\mapsto P(Y\in A)\). For a potential \(U\) with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient and \(Y\in L^2(P;H)\), the random vector \( abla U(Y):\omega\mapsto abla U(Y(\omega))\) again belongs to \(L^2(P;H)\), because \(\| abla U(y)\|\le\| abla U(0)\|+L\|y\|\).

This section shows that if the law of \(Y\) is the Gibbs measure \(\pi_U\), then

\[\| abla U(Y)\|_{L^2}= igl(\mathbb E\| abla U(Y)\|^2 igr)^{1/2}\le\sqrt{Ld},\]

by transferring the Gibbs gradient-energy bound \(\int\| abla U\|^2\,d\pi_U\le Ld\) through the change of variables formula for image measures. The hypotheses are those of that bound (differentiability, \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient and finite partition function), and the finite partition function is automatic under strong convexity. The Gibbs law of \(Y\) is a hypothesis: no stationarity of any process is proved here. The estimate is applied to the stationary Langevin process, whose law is \(\pi_U\) at every time, to control its drift in the local error analysis of the unadjusted Langevin algorithm.

steps.title: The reference drift norm from its Gibbs law
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(L\ge0\), let \(U:H o\mathbb R\) be differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, and assume \(Z_U<\infty\). Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\) be a probability space and let \(Y\in L^2(P;H)\) have law \(P\circ Y^{-1}=\pi_U\). Then the random vector \( abla U(Y)\in L^2(P;H)\) satisfies

\[\| abla U(Y)\|_{L^2}\le\sqrt{Ld}.\]

Proof. For a measurable map \(Y:\Omega o H\) and a Borel function \(f:H o\mathbb R\), the change of variables formula for the image measure states

\[\int_Hf\,d(P\circ Y^{-1})=\int_\Omega f(Y(\omega))\,P(d\omega),\]

whenever either side is defined (for indicator functions \(f=1_A\) this is the definition \(P\circ Y^{-1}(A)=P(Y^{-1}(A))\); it extends to simple functions by linearity, to nonnegative functions by monotone convergence, and to integrable functions by splitting into positive and negative parts). We apply it to \(f(x)=\| abla U(x)\|^2\), which is continuous since \( abla U\) is Lipschitz, and use \(P\circ Y^{-1}=\pi_U\):

\[\int_\Omega\| abla U(Y(\omega))\|^2\,P(d\omega)=\int_H\| abla U(x)\|^2\,\pi_U(dx)\le Ld,\qquad(1)\]

where the inequality is the Gibbs gradient-energy bound , valid under the present hypotheses. The squared \(L^2\) norm of \( abla U(Y)\) is the left side of (1) , so \(\| abla U(Y)\|_{L^2}^2\le Ld\). Since \(\| abla U(Y)\|_{L^2}\ge0\) and the square root is increasing on \([0,\infty)\), \(\| abla U(Y)\|_{L^2}\le\sqrt{Ld}\). \(\square\)

The bound concerns the \(L^2\) norm of a random vector, not its pointwise values, and it uses only the law of \(Y\): no independence and no information on the joint law of \(Y\) with other random variables is involved.

UnadjustedLangevin/Generator.lean.title: The Gibbs integral of the Langevin generator
UnadjustedLangevin/Generator.lean.summary:
Let \(H\) be a real inner product space of finite dimension \(d\), with Lebesgue measure \(dx\), a fixed orthonormal basis \(e_1,\dots,e_d\), and let \(U:H o\mathbb R\) be differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient for some \(L\ge0\). For a twice continuously differentiable function \(\varphi:H o\mathbb R\) the Langevin generator is

\[\mathcal L\varphi=\Delta\varphi-\langle abla U, abla\varphi angle=\sum_{i=1}^d\Bigl(\partial_{e_i}\partial_{e_i}\varphi-\langle abla U,e_i angle\,\partial_{e_i}\varphi\Bigr),\]

where \(\partial_v\varphi(x)=D\varphi(x)v\) is the derivative in the direction \(v\) and \(\Delta\) is the Laplacian. It is the generator of the overdamped Langevin diffusion \(dY_t=- abla U(Y_t)\,dt+\sqrt2\,dB_t\). The main result of this section is the infinitesimal invariance of the Gibbs measure \(\pi_U(dx)=Z_U^{-1}e^{-U(x)}\,dx\):

\[\int_H\mathcal L\varphi\,d\pi_U=0\qquad ext{for every twice continuously differentiable }\varphi ext{ with compact support}.\]

The proof treats one direction at a time. By the product rule, \(e^{-U} igl(\partial_v\partial_v\varphi-\langle abla U,v angle\partial_v\varphi igr)=\partial_v igl(e^{-U}\partial_v\varphi igr)\), and the integral of the directional derivative of a compactly supported function vanishes (integration by parts). Continuity and compact support make every function involved integrable. Only the first derivative of \(U\) appears. No finiteness of \(Z_U\) is assumed: if \(Z_U=\infty\), then \(\pi_U\) is the zero measure and the identities are trivial. Infinitesimal invariance is a statement about the generator only; that the diffusion started from \(\pi_U\) has law \(\pi_U\) at every time is a different assertion, proved in a later section. The identity is used in the sections on the Dirichlet form and on the Fokker–Planck equation.

steps.title: The generator in one direction
steps.body:
Definition. For a function \(f:H\to\mathbb R\), a point \(x\) and a direction \(v\in H\), write \(\partial_vf(x)=Df(x)v\) for the derivative of \(f\) at \(x\) in the direction \(v\), where \(Df(x)\) is the derivative of \(f\) at \(x\), taken to be \(0\) if \(f\) is not differentiable at \(x\). Let \(U,\varphi:H\to\mathbb R\) and \(v\in H\). The directional Langevin generator in the direction \(v\) is the function

\[\mathcal L_v\varphi(x)=\partial_v\bigl(\partial_v\varphi\bigr)(x)-\langle\nabla U(x),v\rangle\,\partial_v\varphi(x)\qquad(x\in H).\]

The first term differentiates the function \(z\mapsto\partial_v\varphi(z)\) at \(x\) in the direction \(v\). For twice continuously differentiable \(\varphi\) it equals the second derivative \(D^2\varphi(x)[v,v]\), as shown in the step on the Laplacian formula. The convention for non-differentiable points plays no role for the twice continuously differentiable test functions used below. The definition involves only the gradient of \(U\), not its second derivative.

Definition. Let \(e_1,\dots,e_d\) be the fixed orthonormal basis of \(H\). For \(U,\varphi:H o\mathbb R\), the Langevin generator is

\[\mathcal L\varphi(x)=\sum_{i=1}^d\mathcal L_{e_i}\varphi(x)=\sum_{i=1}^d\partial_{e_i} igl(\partial_{e_i}\varphi igr)(x)-\sum_{i=1}^d\langle abla U(x),e_i angle\,\partial_{e_i}\varphi(x).\]

steps.title: The weighted Gibbs integral formula
steps.body:
In this section, as in measure theory generally, the integral of a real function that is not integrable is defined to be \(0\).

Claim. Let \(U:H o\mathbb R\) be differentiable and let \(f:H o\mathbb R\) be any function. Then

\[\int_Hf\,d\pi_U=Z_U^{-1}\int_He^{-U(x)}f(x)\,dx,\]

where \(Z_U^{-1}\) is the real number \(1/Z_U\) if \(Z_U<\infty\) and \(0\) if \(Z_U=\infty\). In particular, if \(Z_U<\infty\) and \(f\) is \(\pi_U\)-integrable, this is the usual formula for integrals against the normalized density.

Proof. Recall \(\pi_U=c\, u_U\), where \(c=Z_U^{-1}\in[0,\infty]\) and \( u_U\) has density \(e^{-U}\) with respect to Lebesgue measure. Since \(U\) is differentiable, \(Z_U>0\) , so \(c<\infty\).

(i) \(\int f\,d(c u_U)=c\int f\,d u_U\). If \(c=0\), then \(c u_U=0\) and both sides vanish. If \(0<c<\infty\), then \(\int|f|\,d(c u_U)=c\int|f|\,d u_U\), so \(f\) is integrable for one measure exactly when it is integrable for the other; for integrable \(f\) the identity holds for simple functions by the definition of \(c u_U\) and extends by dominated convergence along simple approximations, and for non-integrable \(f\) both sides are \(0\).

(ii) \(\int f\,d u_U=\int e^{-U}f\,dx\). The density \(e^{-U}\) is continuous (hence Borel) and finite. As in the section on Gibbs normalization, \(\int|f|\,d u_U=\int e^{-U}|f|\,dx\), so \(f\) is \( u_U\)-integrable exactly when \(e^{-U}f\) is Lebesgue integrable; in that case the identity holds (for indicators by definition of \( u_U\), then for simple functions and by dominated convergence), and otherwise both sides are \(0\).

Combining (i) and (ii) gives the claim. \(\square\)

No finiteness of \(Z_U\) is assumed: if \(Z_U=\infty\) the identity reads \(0=0\).
