steps.title: Integrability of a compactly supported test
steps.body:
A function \(f:H\to\mathbb R\) has compact support if the closure of \(\{f\ne0\}\) is compact.

Claim. Let \(U:H\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and let \(f:H\to\mathbb R\) be continuous with compact support. Then \(f\) is \(\pi_U\)-integrable.

Proof. The product \(e^{-U}f\) is continuous, because \(U\) is continuous, and it vanishes wherever \(f\) does, so it has compact support, contained in a compact set \(K\). A continuous function is bounded on the compact set \(K\), say by \(M\), and Lebesgue measure is finite on compact sets; hence \(\int_H|e^{-U}f|\,dx\le M\lambda(K)<\infty\), and \(e^{-U}f\) is Lebesgue integrable (it is measurable by continuity). By the density criterion recalled in the previous step, \(f\) is \(\nu_U\)-integrable. Finally \(\pi_U=Z_U^{-1}\nu_U\) with \(Z_U^{-1}<\infty\), because \(Z_U>0\) for differentiable \(U\); multiplying a measure by a finite constant preserves integrability. \(\square\)

This guarantees that the integrals in the following steps are integrals of integrable functions, so that linearity of the integral may be used. No finiteness of \(Z_U\) is needed.

steps.title: The derivative of the Gibbs weight
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(U:H\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable. Then for all \(x,v\in H\),

\[\partial_v\bigl(e^{-U}\bigr)(x)=-e^{-U(x)}\langle\nabla U(x),v\rangle.\]

Proof. By the chain rule, \(x\mapsto e^{-U(x)}\) is differentiable with \(D(e^{-U})(x)=e^{-U(x)}\,D(-U)(x)=-e^{-U(x)}DU(x)\), since the exponential is its own derivative. Applying this linear map to \(v\) and using the defining property \(DU(x)v=\langle\nabla U(x),v\rangle\) of the gradient gives the claim. \(\square\)

steps.title: The weighted directional generator integral
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(L\ge0\), let \(U:H\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, let \(\varphi:H\to\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable with compact support, and let \(v\in H\). Then

\[\int_He^{-U(x)}\,\mathcal L_v\varphi(x)\,dx=0.\]

Proof. Put \(w=e^{-U}\) and \(g=\partial_v\varphi\).

Regularity. Since \(\varphi\) is twice continuously differentiable, \(D\varphi\) is continuously differentiable, and so is \(g=D\varphi(\cdot)v\), its composition with the continuous linear evaluation at \(v\). Hence \(\partial_vg\) is continuous. The function \(g\) has compact support: if \(K\) is the closure of \(\{\varphi\ne0\}\), then \(\varphi\) vanishes on the open set \(H\setminus K\), so \(D\varphi=0\) there and \(g\) vanishes outside \(K\); in the same way \(\partial_vg\) vanishes outside \(K\). The weight \(w\) is continuous, and by the previous step \(\partial_vw=-w\langle\nabla U,v\rangle\), which is continuous because the Lipschitz map \(\nabla U\) is continuous.

Integrability. The four functions \((\partial_vw)g\), \(w\,\partial_vg\), \(wg\) and \(w\langle\nabla U,v\rangle g\) are continuous and vanish outside \(K\), hence are Lebesgue integrable (as in the previous step: bounded on \(K\), and \(\lambda(K)<\infty\)).

Integration by parts. For differentiable \(f,h:H\to\mathbb R\) such that \(f\,\partial_vh\), \((\partial_vf)h\) and \(fh\) are integrable,

\[\int_Hf\,\partial_vh\,dx=-\int_H(\partial_vf)\,h\,dx.\qquad(1)\]

In the present situation (\(f=w\), \(h=g\)) this can be checked directly. If \(v=0\) both sides vanish. Otherwise write \(x=y+tv\) with \(t\in\mathbb R\) and \(y\) in the orthogonal complement \(v^\perp\); in orthonormal coordinates adapted to \(v\) this change of variables multiplies Lebesgue measure by the constant \(\|v\|\). For fixed \(y\), the function \(F(t)=w(y+tv)g(y+tv)\) is differentiable with continuous derivative \(F'(t)=\bigl((\partial_vw)g+w\,\partial_vg\bigr)(y+tv)\) and vanishes outside a bounded interval, so \(\int_{\mathbb R}F'(t)\,dt=0\) by the fundamental theorem of calculus. By Fubini's theorem for the integrable function \((\partial_vw)g+w\,\partial_vg\), its integral over \(H\) is \(\|v\|\int_{v^\perp}\int_{\mathbb R}F'(t)\,dt\,dy=0\), which is (1).

By (1) and the previous step,

\[\int_Hw\,\partial_vg\,dx=-\int_H(\partial_vw)\,g\,dx=\int_Hw\,\langle\nabla U,v\rangle\,g\,dx.\qquad(2)\]

Conclusion. By definition \(w\,\mathcal L_v\varphi=w\,\partial_vg-w\langle\nabla U,v\rangle g\), a difference of two integrable functions, so by linearity and (2)

\[\int_Hw\,\mathcal L_v\varphi\,dx=\int_Hw\,\partial_vg\,dx-\int_Hw\langle\nabla U,v\rangle g\,dx=0.\qquad\square\]

Equivalently, \(w\,\mathcal L_v\varphi=\partial_v(w\,\partial_v\varphi)\) is the directional derivative of a compactly supported function. Only the continuity of \(\nabla U\) is used; no second derivative of \(U\) appears.

steps.title: Continuity of the directional generator
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(L\ge0\), let \(U:H o\mathbb R\) have \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, let \(\varphi:H o\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable, and let \(v\in H\). Then \(\mathcal L_v\varphi\) is continuous.

Proof. As in the weighted directional step, \(g=\partial_v\varphi\) is continuously differentiable, so \(x\mapsto\partial_vg(x)=Dg(x)v\) is continuous, being the composition of the continuous map \(Dg\) with evaluation at the fixed vector \(v\). The gradient \( abla U\) is Lipschitz, hence continuous, so \(x\mapsto\langle abla U(x),v angle\) is continuous; \(g\) is continuous. Products and differences of continuous functions are continuous, so \(\mathcal L_v\varphi=\partial_vg-\langle abla U,v angle g\) is continuous. \(\square\)

No differentiability hypothesis on \(U\) beyond the Lipschitz property of its gradient is used, and no support condition on \(\varphi\).

steps.title: Compact support of the directional generator
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(U,\varphi:H o\mathbb R\), where \(\varphi\) has compact support, and let \(v\in H\). Then \(\mathcal L_v\varphi\) has compact support.

Proof. Let \(K\) be the closure of \(\{\varphi e0\}\), a compact set. On the open set \(H\setminus K\) the function \(\varphi\) vanishes identically, so it is differentiable at every point of \(H\setminus K\) with derivative \(0\); hence \(\partial_v\varphi=0\) on \(H\setminus K\). Applying the same argument to \(\partial_v\varphi\), which vanishes on the open set \(H\setminus K\), gives \(\partial_v(\partial_v\varphi)=0\) on \(H\setminus K\). The product \(\langle abla U,v angle\partial_v\varphi\) also vanishes on \(H\setminus K\). Hence \(\mathcal L_v\varphi\) vanishes outside \(K\), so the closure of \(\{\mathcal L_v\varphi e0\}\) is a closed subset of \(K\) and therefore compact. \(\square\)

No regularity of \(U\) or \(\varphi\) is used: derivatives are evaluated only where the function vanishes on a neighbourhood.

steps.title: Integrability of the directional generator
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(L\ge0\), let \(U:H\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, let \(\varphi\) be twice continuously differentiable with compact support, and let \(v\in H\). Then \(\mathcal L_v\varphi\) is \(\pi_U\)-integrable.

Proof. By the two previous steps \(\mathcal L_v\varphi\) is continuous with compact support. The integrability step for compactly supported tests gives the claim. \(\square\)

Continuity alone would not suffice on the unbounded space \(H\); the compact support localizes the integral.

steps.title: Integrability of the full generator
steps.body:
Claim. Under the hypotheses of the previous step, \(\mathcal L\varphi\) is \(\pi_U\)-integrable.

Proof. \(\mathcal L\varphi=\sum_{i=1}^d\mathcal L_{e_i}\varphi\) is a finite sum, each term of which is \(\pi_U\)-integrable by the previous step. A finite sum of integrable functions is integrable. \(\square\)

steps.title: The weighted full generator integral
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(L\ge0\), let \(U:H\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, and let \(\varphi\) be twice continuously differentiable with compact support. Then

\[\int_He^{-U(x)}\,\mathcal L\varphi(x)\,dx=0.\]

Proof. For each \(i\), the function \(e^{-U}\mathcal L_{e_i}\varphi\) is continuous with compact support (by the continuity and compact-support steps, and continuity of \(e^{-U}\)), hence Lebesgue integrable. Distributing the weight over the finite sum and integrating term by term,

\[\int_He^{-U}\mathcal L\varphi\,dx=\int_H\sum_{i=1}^de^{-U}\mathcal L_{e_i}\varphi\,dx=\sum_{i=1}^d\int_He^{-U}\mathcal L_{e_i}\varphi\,dx=\sum_{i=1}^d0=0,\]

where each integral vanishes by the weighted directional step. \(\square\)

steps.title: Infinitesimal Gibbs invariance
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(L\ge0\), let \(U:H\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, and let \(\varphi\) be twice continuously differentiable with compact support. Then

\[\int_H\mathcal L\varphi\,d\pi_U=0.\]

Proof. By the weighted Gibbs integral formula and the previous step, \(\int\mathcal L\varphi\,d\pi_U=Z_U^{-1}\int e^{-U}\mathcal L\varphi\,dx=Z_U^{-1}\cdot0=0\). \(\square\)

Since \(\mathcal L\varphi\) is \(\pi_U\)-integrable (integrability of the full generator), this is a genuine identity between integrals of integrable functions and not an instance of the convention for non-integrable functions.

steps.title: The Laplacian-minus-drift formula
steps.body:
For a twice continuously differentiable \(\varphi\), the Laplacian is \(\Delta\varphi(x)=\sum_{i=1}^dD^2\varphi(x)[e_i,e_i]\), the trace of the second derivative \(D^2\varphi(x)\) (a symmetric bilinear form) with respect to the inner product; the sum is the same for every orthonormal basis.

Claim. Let \(U:H o\mathbb R\) be any function and let \(\varphi:H o\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable. Then for every \(x\in H\),

\[\mathcal L\varphi(x)=\Delta\varphi(x)-\langle abla U(x), abla\varphi(x) angle.\]

Proof. (a) For \(v\in H\), \(\partial_v(\partial_v\varphi)(x)=D^2\varphi(x)[v,v]\). Indeed \(D\varphi\) is differentiable, and \(z\mapsto\partial_v\varphi(z)=D\varphi(z)v\) is its composition with the continuous linear map \(A\mapsto Av\); by the chain rule its derivative at \(x\) in the direction \(v\) is \( igl(D(D\varphi)(x)v igr)v=D^2\varphi(x)[v,v]\).

(b) Summing (a) over \(v=e_1,\dots,e_d\) gives \(\sum_i\partial_{e_i}(\partial_{e_i}\varphi)(x)=\Delta\varphi(x)\).

(c) By the definition of the gradient, \(\partial_{e_i}\varphi(x)=\langle abla\varphi(x),e_i angle\). Expanding \( abla\varphi(x)=\sum_i\langle abla\varphi(x),e_i angle e_i\) in the orthonormal basis,

\[\sum_{i=1}^d\langle abla U(x),e_i angle\,\partial_{e_i}\varphi(x)=\sum_{i=1}^d\langle abla U(x),e_i angle\langle abla\varphi(x),e_i angle=\langle abla U(x), abla\varphi(x) angle.\]

Subtracting (c) from (b) and using the definition of \(\mathcal L\varphi\) as the sum of the directional generators gives the claim. \(\square\)

The identity is pointwise and involves only the gradient of \(U\) (with the convention \( abla U(x)=0\) at points of non-differentiability, it holds for every \(U\)).

steps.title: The stationary identity in conventional notation
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(L\ge0\), let \(U:H\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, and let \(\varphi:H\to\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable with compact support. Then

\[\int_H\Bigl(\Delta\varphi(x)-\langle\nabla U(x),\nabla\varphi(x)\rangle\Bigr)\,\pi_U(dx)=0.\]

Proof. By the previous step the integrand equals \(\mathcal L\varphi(x)\) at every point, and \(\int\mathcal L\varphi\,d\pi_U=0\) by infinitesimal invariance. \(\square\)

UnadjustedLangevin/GeneratorDirichlet.le.title: Generator symmetry and the Dirichlet form
UnadjustedLangevin/GeneratorDirichlet.le.summary:
We keep the setting and notation of the section on the Langevin generator: \(H\) is a real inner product space of finite dimension \(d\) with orthonormal basis \(e_1,\dots,e_d\), \(U:H o\mathbb R\) is differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient (\(L\ge0\)), \(\pi_U(dx)=Z_U^{-1}e^{-U(x)}\,dx\) is the Gibbs measure, \(\partial_v\) denotes the derivative in the direction \(v\), and \(\mathcal L_v\psi=\partial_v\partial_v\psi-\langle abla U,v angle\partial_v\psi\), \(\mathcal L\psi=\sum_i\mathcal L_{e_i}\psi=\Delta\psi-\langle abla U, abla\psi angle\). This section proves the Gibbs integration by parts formula, or Dirichlet identity,

\[\int_H\varphi\,\mathcal L\psi\,d\pi_U=-\int_H\langle abla\varphi, abla\psi angle\,d\pi_U\]

for twice continuously differentiable \(\varphi,\psi\) with compact support. The right-hand side is minus the Dirichlet form \(\mathcal E(\varphi,\psi)=\int\langle abla\varphi, abla\psi angle\,d\pi_U\). Two consequences follow: \(\mathcal L\) is symmetric on this class of functions with respect to \(\pi_U\), \(\int\varphi\,\mathcal L\psi\,d\pi_U=\int\psi\,\mathcal L\varphi\,d\pi_U\), and it is dissipative, \(\int\varphi\,\mathcal L\varphi\,d\pi_U=-\int\| abla\varphi\|^2\,d\pi_U\le0\). As in the previous section the proof is one-dimensional integration by parts in each basis direction, with weight \(e^{-U}\), and only the first derivative of \(U\) enters.

steps.title: The derivative of a weighted test
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(U,\varphi:H\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable. Then for all \(x,v\in H\),

\[\partial_v\bigl(e^{-U}\varphi\bigr)(x)=e^{-U(x)}\Bigl(\partial_v\varphi(x)-\langle\nabla U(x),v\rangle\,\varphi(x)\Bigr).\]

Proof. By the chain rule, \(D(e^{-U})(x)=-e^{-U(x)}DU(x)\). By the product rule,

\[D\bigl(e^{-U}\varphi\bigr)(x)=e^{-U(x)}D\varphi(x)+\varphi(x)\,D(e^{-U})(x)=e^{-U(x)}D\varphi(x)-\varphi(x)e^{-U(x)}DU(x).\]

Applying this linear map to \(v\), using \(DU(x)v=\langle\nabla U(x),v\rangle\) and factoring out \(e^{-U(x)}\) gives the claim. \(\square\)

steps.title: Weighted directional integration by parts
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(L\ge0\), let \(U:H\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, let \(\varphi,\psi:H\to\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable with compact support, and let \(v\in H\). Then

\[\int_He^{-U}\varphi\,\mathcal L_v\psi\,dx=-\int_He^{-U}\,\partial_v\varphi\,\partial_v\psi\,dx.\]

Proof. Put \(a=e^{-U}\varphi\) and \(g=\partial_v\psi\).

Regularity and integrability. As in the section on the generator, \(g\) is continuously differentiable with compact support, \(\partial_vg\) and \(\partial_v\varphi\) are continuous, \(a\) is continuous with compact support, and by the previous step \(\partial_va=e^{-U}(\partial_v\varphi-\langle\nabla U,v\rangle\varphi)\), which is continuous because \(\nabla U\) is continuous. The functions \((\partial_va)g\), \(a\,\partial_vg\), \(ag\), \(e^{-U}\varphi\,\mathcal L_v\psi\) and \(e^{-U}\partial_v\varphi\,\partial_v\psi\) are continuous and vanish outside the support of \(\varphi\) or of \(\psi\), so they are Lebesgue integrable.

Integration by parts. The integration by parts formula along \(v\) (proved in the section on the generator ) gives

\[\int_Ha\,\partial_vg\,dx=-\int_H(\partial_va)\,g\,dx.\qquad(1)\]

Algebra. By the previous step and the definition \(\mathcal L_v\psi=\partial_vg-\langle\nabla U,v\rangle g\),

\[a\,\partial_vg+(\partial_va)\,g=e^{-U}\varphi\,\partial_vg+e^{-U}\bigl(\partial_v\varphi-\langle\nabla U,v\rangle\varphi\bigr)g=e^{-U}\varphi\,\mathcal L_v\psi+e^{-U}\partial_v\varphi\,\partial_v\psi.\]

Integrating, using linearity for the integrable summands and then (1),

\[\int_He^{-U}\varphi\,\mathcal L_v\psi\,dx+\int_He^{-U}\partial_v\varphi\,\partial_v\psi\,dx=\int_Ha\,\partial_vg\,dx+\int_H(\partial_va)\,g\,dx=0,\]

which is the claim. \(\square\)

steps.title: The directional Dirichlet identity under the Gibbs measure
steps.body:
Claim. Under the hypotheses of the previous step,

\[\int_H\varphi\,\mathcal L_v\psi\,d\pi_U=-\int_H\partial_v\varphi\,\partial_v\psi\,d\pi_U.\]

Proof. By the weighted Gibbs integral formula , each side is \(Z_U^{-1}\) times the corresponding Lebesgue integral with weight \(e^{-U}\). By the previous step,

\[\int\varphi\,\mathcal L_v\psi\,d\pi_U=Z_U^{-1}\int e^{-U}\varphi\,\mathcal L_v\psi\,dx=Z_U^{-1}\Bigl(-\int e^{-U}\partial_v\varphi\,\partial_v\psi\,dx\Bigr)=-\int\partial_v\varphi\,\partial_v\psi\,d\pi_U.\qquad\square\]

steps.title: Integrability of the energy density
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(U:H o\mathbb R\) be differentiable, let \(\varphi,\psi:H o\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable, and assume that \(\varphi\) has compact support. Then \(x\mapsto\langle abla\varphi(x), abla\psi(x) angle\) is \(\pi_U\)-integrable.

Proof. Expanding in the orthonormal basis, \(\langle abla\varphi, abla\psi angle=\sum_{i=1}^d\langle abla\varphi,e_i angle\langle abla\psi,e_i angle=\sum_{i=1}^d\partial_{e_i}\varphi\,\partial_{e_i}\psi\). Each term is continuous (the first derivatives of \(\varphi\) and \(\psi\) are continuous) and vanishes outside the support of \(\varphi\), because \(\partial_{e_i}\varphi\) does. By the integrability of continuous compactly supported functions under \(\pi_U\) , each term is \(\pi_U\)-integrable, and so is the finite sum. \(\square\)

Compact support of one of the two functions suffices.

steps.title: Integrability of a test times the generator

Claim. Let \(L\ge0\), let \(U:H\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, let \(\varphi,\psi\) be twice continuously differentiable, and assume that \(\varphi\) has compact support. Then \(\varphi\,\mathcal L\psi\) is \(\pi_U\)-integrable.

Proof. \(\varphi\,\mathcal L\psi=\sum_{i=1}^d\varphi\,\mathcal L_{e_i}\psi\). Each \(\mathcal L_{e_i}\psi\) is continuous (section on the generator), so \(\varphi\,\mathcal L_{e_i}\psi\) is continuous, and it vanishes outside the support of \(\varphi\). Hence each term is \(\pi_U\)-integrable, and so is the finite sum. \(\square\)

steps.title: The Gibbs Dirichlet identity
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(L\ge0\), let \(U:H o\mathbb R\) be differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, and let \(\varphi,\psi:H o\mathbb R\) be twice continuously differentiable with compact support. Then

\[\int_H\varphi\,\mathcal L\psi\,d\pi_U=-\int_H\langle abla\varphi, abla\psi angle\,d\pi_U.\]

Proof. The functions \(\varphi\,\mathcal L_{e_i}\psi\) and \(\partial_{e_i}\varphi\,\partial_{e_i}\psi\) are \(\pi_U\)-integrable (as in the two previous steps). Using linearity of the integral over finite sums of integrable functions, the directional Dirichlet identity, and the basis expansion of the inner product,

\[ egin{aligned}\int\varphi\,\mathcal L\psi\,d\pi_U&=\sum_{i=1}^d\int\varphi\,\mathcal L_{e_i}\psi\,d\pi_U=-\sum_{i=1}^d\int\partial_{e_i}\varphi\,\partial_{e_i}\psi\,d\pi_U\&=-\int\sum_{i=1}^d\partial_{e_i}\varphi\,\partial_{e_i}\psi\,d\pi_U=-\int\langle abla\varphi, abla\psi angle\,d\pi_U.\qquad\square\end{aligned}\]

steps.title: Symmetry of the generator

Claim. Under the hypotheses of the previous step,

\[\int_H\varphi\,\mathcal L\psi\,d\pi_U=\int_H\psi\,\mathcal L\varphi\,d\pi_U.\]

Proof. Apply the Dirichlet identity to \((\varphi,\psi)\) and to \((\psi,\varphi)\): the two sides equal \(-\int\langle abla\varphi, abla\psi angle\,d\pi_U\) and \(-\int\langle abla\psi, abla\varphi angle\,d\pi_U\), which agree because the real inner product is symmetric. \(\square\)

Thus \(\mathcal L\) is a symmetric operator in \(L^2(\pi_U)\) on twice continuously differentiable functions with compact support.

UnadjustedLangevin/LangevinIntegral.lean.title: Existence for the Langevin integral equation
UnadjustedLangevin/LangevinIntegral.lean.summary:
Let the state space be a complete real normed space, let \(g\) be globally \(L\)-Lipschitz, and let \(B\) be continuous with \(B(0)=0\). For a fixed initial state \(x\), consider \(Y(t)-x=-\int_0^tg(Y(s))ds+B(t)\). Setting \(Y=Z+B\) gives an integral equation with time-dependent drift \(f(t,z)=-g(z+B(t))\), continuous in time and \(L\)-Lipschitz in \(z\).

A contraction argument gives a continuous solution on a sufficiently short interval. Restarting with the preceding endpoint and shifted additive input, and concatenating finitely many such solutions, gives existence on every finite nonnegative horizon. Taking the state space to be \(L^2(P;K)\) gives continuity and the integral equation in mean square. This does not assert differentiability or sample-path regularity of the noise.

steps.title: Solving the integral equation on a short interval
steps.body:
Remove the additive input by writing \(Y(t)=Z(t)+B(t)\). The new unknown satisfies \(Z(t)=x+\int_0^t f(s,Z(s))ds\), with \(f(s,z)=-g(z+B(s))\). This time-dependent drift is \(L\)-Lipschitz in \(z\) and continuous in time even though \(B\) need not be differentiable.

Bound \(\|B(t)\|\le C'\) on the compact interval and set \(G=\|g(x)\|+LC'\), radius \(a=2hG\), and drift bound \(M=G+La\). The condition \(Lh\le1/2\) proves \(Mh\le a\), giving the ball-invariance condition in the local contraction theorem for the integral equation. The proof checks these bounds and invokes the contraction fixed-point theorem.

The chosen fixed point gives a continuous \(Z\) with its integral identity. Add back \(B\), use \(B(0)=0\), and rewrite the negative drift integral to obtain \(Y(t)-x=-\int_0^tg(Y(s))ds+B(t)\). The integral identity holds for the resulting continuous real-time function on \([0,h]\).

The shifted unknown has an ordinary time integral even if the additive input has no derivative. The short-time radius and drift bounds ensure that the Picard map preserves its closed ball, while the Lipschitz estimate controls contraction there.

It transforms the unknown by subtracting that forcing, defining f as a time-dependent ordinary differential equation. G, a and M bound its size and the radius of the invariant function ball. The four fields of hpicard verify spatial Lipschitzness, time continuity, the vector-field bound and the radius condition; the last uses hsmall. ODE.FunSpace.exists_isFixedPt_next then gives the integral fixed point. Z and hZeq expose that equation, and adding back B yields the claimed solution with initial value supplied by hB0.

steps.title: Splicing two integral-equation segments
steps.body:
Use \(Y(t)\) up to time \(a\), and \(Z(t-a)\) afterward. The equality \(Z(0)=Y(a)\) makes the pasted path continuous at the join. UnadjustedLangevin/GaussianHilbert.lean.title: An isonormal Gaussian map built from independent Gaussian coordinates
UnadjustedLangevin/GaussianHilbert.lean.summary:
Let \(\iota\) be an arbitrary index set and let \(Q=\bigotimes_{i\in\iota}\mathcal N(0,1)\) be the product of standard Gaussian laws on \(\Omega=\mathbb R^\iota\), the space of all real families \(\omega=(\omega_i)_{i\in\iota}\). Under \(Q\) the coordinates \(\xi_i(\omega)=\omega_i\) are independent standard Gaussian random variables, so their classes \(Z_i\) in the Hilbert space \(L^2(Q)\) form an orthonormal family. Consequently, for every square-summable family of coefficients \(a=(a_i)\in\ell^2(\iota)\) the series \(S(a)=\sum_ia_iZ_i\) converges in \(L^2(Q)\), and \(\|S(a)\|_2^2=\sum_ia_i^2\).

Let \(H\) be a real Hilbert space with a Hilbert basis \((b_i)_{i\in\iota}\). Composing the coordinate map \(x\mapsto(\langle b_i,x\rangle)_{i\in\iota}\) with \(S\) gives a linear isometry \(I_b:H\to L^2(Q)\), \(I_b(x)=\sum_i\langle b_i,x\rangle Z_i\). We prove that every \(I_b(x)\) has mean zero and law \(\mathcal N(0,\|x\|^2)\), and that \(\operatorname{Cov}(I_b(x),I_b(y))=\langle x,y\rangle\) for all \(x,y\in H\); a linear map with these properties is called an isonormal Gaussian map. Finite partial sums of the series are Gaussian because finite sums of independent Gaussian variables are Gaussian; the infinite sums are Gaussian because a centred Gaussian law whose variance is the squared \(L^2\) norm is preserved under limits in \(L^2\), which is proved with characteristic functions.

The construction assumes no previously given Gaussian process. In the following sections the joint Gaussianity of finitely many values of \(I_b\) is deduced from linearity, and \(I_b\) is applied to the indicator functions \(\mathbf 1_{(0,t]}\) in \(L^2\) of Lebesgue measure to obtain a Brownian motion.

steps.title: The product of standard Gaussian laws
steps.body:
Definition. Let \(\iota\) be an arbitrary index set (finite, countable or uncountable) and let \(\Omega=\mathbb R^\iota\) be the set of all families \(\omega=(\omega_i)_{i\in\iota}\) of real numbers. Equip \(\Omega\) with the product \(\sigma\)-algebra \(\mathcal F\), the smallest \(\sigma\)-algebra for which every coordinate map \(\xi_i:\Omega\to\mathbb R\), \(\xi_i(\omega)=\omega_i\), is Borel measurable. Let \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) be the standard Gaussian law on \(\mathbb R\), with density \((2\pi)^{-1/2}e^{-x^2/2}\). The source measure is the product probability measure

\[Q=\bigotimes_{i\in\iota}\mathcal N(0,1)\qquad\text{on }(\Omega,\mathcal F).\]

It is the unique probability measure on \(\mathcal F\) such that, for every finite set \(F\subseteq\iota\) and all Borel sets \(A_i\subseteq\mathbb R\) (\(i\in F\)),

\[Q\bigl(\{\omega\in\Omega:\ \omega_i\in A_i\text{ for all }i\in F\}\bigr)=\prod_{i\in F}\mathcal N(0,1)(A_i).\qquad(1)\]

The existence of such a measure for an arbitrary family of probability measures is the theorem on infinite products of probability measures, a consequence of the Kolmogorov extension theorem. Uniqueness holds because the sets on the left of (1), the measurable cylinders, are closed under finite intersections and generate \(\mathcal F\), so that Dynkin's \(\pi\)-\(\lambda\) theorem applies. The properties of \(Q\) used below (total mass one, the laws of the coordinates and their independence) all follow from (1). No countability of \(\iota\) is assumed anywhere in this section.

Claim. For every \(a\in\ell^2(\iota)\) the family \((a_iZ_i)_{i\in\iota}\) has a sum in \(L^2(Q)\), and the map

\[S:\ell^2(\iota)\to L^2(Q),\qquad S(a)=\sum_{i\in\iota}a_iZ_i,\]

is linear and isometric: \(\|S(a)\|_2=\|a\|_{\ell^2}\) for every \(a\in\ell^2(\iota)\).

Proof. Pythagoras. For every finite set \(F\subseteq\iota\) and all real numbers \(a_i\), expanding the square by bilinearity of the inner product and using the inner products of ,

\[\Bigl\|\sum_{i\in F}a_iZ_i\Bigr\|_2^2=\sum_{i\in F}\sum_{j\in F}a_ia_j\langle Z_i,Z_j\rangle=\sum_{i\in F}a_i^2.\qquad(3)\]

Since \(\|a\|_{\ell^2}^2\) is the supremum of the finite partial sums of \(a_i^2\), for every \(n\ge1\) there is a finite set \(G_n\) with \(\sum_{i\in G_n}a_i^2>\|a\|_{\ell^2}^2-4^{-n}\). Replacing \(G_n\) by \(G_1\cup\dots\cup G_n\), which only increases the partial sum, we may assume \(G_1\subseteq G_2\subseteq\cdots\). Let \(s_n=\sum_{i\in G_n}a_iZ_i\). If \(F\supseteq G_n\) is finite, then \(\sum_{i\in F}a_iZ_i-s_n=\sum_{i\in F\setminus G_n}a_iZ_i\), and by (3)

\[\Bigl\|\sum_{i\in F}a_iZ_i-s_n\Bigr\|_2^2=\sum_{i\in F}a_i^2-\sum_{i\in G_n}a_i^2\le\|a\|_{\ell^2}^2-\sum_{i\in G_n}a_i^2<4^{-n}.\qquad(4)\]

In particular \(\|s_m-s_n\|_2<2^{-n}\) for all \(m\ge n\), so \((s_n)\) is a Cauchy sequence. Since \(L^2(Q)\) is complete, \(s_n\) converges to some element of \(L^2(Q)\), which we call \(S(a)\).

Convergence of all partial sums. For every finite \(F\supseteq G_n\), the triangle inequality and (4) give

\[\Bigl\|\sum_{i\in F}a_iZ_i-S(a)\Bigr\|_2\le2^{-n}+\|s_n-S(a)\|_2,\]

and the right-hand side tends to \(0\) as \(n\to\infty\). Hence \(S(a)\) is the sum of \((a_iZ_i)_{i\in\iota}\).

Linearity. For \(a,c\in\ell^2(\iota)\) and \(\lambda\in\mathbb R\), every partial sum of \(((\lambda a_i+c_i)Z_i)\) is \(\lambda\) times the corresponding partial sum of \((a_iZ_i)\) plus that of \((c_iZ_i)\). By the triangle inequality these partial sums converge to \(\lambda S(a)+S(c)\), and uniqueness of sums gives \(S(\lambda a+c)=\lambda S(a)+S(c)\).

Isometry. By (3), \(\|s_n\|_2^2=\sum_{i\in G_n}a_i^2\), which lies in \((\|a\|_{\ell^2}^2-4^{-n},\|a\|_{\ell^2}^2]\). Since \(|\|s_n\|_2-\|S(a)\|_2|\le\|s_n-S(a)\|_2\to0\), letting \(n\to\infty\) gives \(\|S(a)\|_2^2=\|a\|_{\ell^2}^2\). \(\square\)

steps.body:
Claim. Let \(a=(a_i)_{i\in\iota}\) be any family of real numbers (no summability is assumed) and let \(F\subseteq\iota\) be finite. Then the representatives of the class \(\sum_{i\in F}a_iZ_i\in L^2(Q)\) agree \(Q\)-almost everywhere with the function \(\omega\mapsto\sum_{i\in F}a_i\,\omega_i\).

Consider the four null sets on which, respectively, the representative of this sum differs from the sum of the representatives of \(a_jZ_j\) and of \(\sum_{i\in F'}a_iZ_i\); the representative of \(a_jZ_j\) differs from \(a_j\) times the representative of \(Z_j\); the representative of \(Z_j\) differs from \(\omega_j\) (); and the induction hypothesis fails. Outside their union, which is a null set, the representative of \(\sum_{i\in F}a_iZ_i\) at \(\omega\) equals

\[a_j\,\omega_j+\sum_{i\in F'}a_i\,\omega_i=\sum_{i\in F}a_i\,\omega_i.\]

This is the claim for \(F\), which completes the induction. \(\square\)

steps.title: Finite partial sums have Gaussian laws
steps.body:
For \(m\in\mathbb R\) and \(v\ge0\), let \(\mathcal N(m,v)\) be the Gaussian law with mean \(m\) and variance \(v\): for \(v>0\) it has density \((2\pi v)^{-1/2}e^{-(x-m)^2/(2v)}\), and \(\mathcal N(m,0)\) is the Dirac mass at \(m\). Its characteristic function is \(\int e^{itx}\,\mathcal N(m,v)(dx)=e^{itm-vt^2/2}\) for \(t\in\mathbb R\). A real random variable has a Gaussian law if it is measurable up to a null set and its law is \(\mathcal N(m,v)\) for some \(m\in\mathbb R\) and \(v\ge0\).

Claim. For every family \(a\in\mathbb R^\iota\) and every finite set \(F\subseteq\iota\), the class \(\sum_{i\in F}a_iZ_i\) has a Gaussian law under \(Q\).

Proof. Put \(Y_i=a_i\xi_i\) for \(i\in F\).

Each \(Y_i\) has a Gaussian law. If \(\xi\) has law \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) and \(c\in\mathbb R\), then \(c\,\xi\) has law \(\mathcal N(0,c^2)\): for \(c\ne0\) by the linear change of variables \(y=cx\) in the density, and for \(c=0\) because \(c\,\xi=0\). By this applies to \(\xi_i\) and \(c=a_i\).

The variables \(Y_i\), \(i\in F\), are independent. Let \(m_i(x)=a_ix\). Each \(m_i\) is continuous, so \(m_i^{-1}(A)\) is Borel for every Borel set \(A\). For Borel sets \(A_i\), the independence of the coordinates () gives

\[Q\Bigl(\bigcap_{i\in F}\{Y_i\in A_i\}\Bigr)=Q\Bigl(\bigcap_{i\in F}\{\xi_i\in m_i^{-1}(A_i)\}\Bigr)=\prod_{i\in F}Q(\{\xi_i\in m_i^{-1}(A_i)\})=\prod_{i\in F}Q(\{Y_i\in A_i\}).\]

A finite sum of independent Gaussian variables has a Gaussian law. Let \(Y_i\) have law \(\mathcal N(m_i',v_i)\), and let \(T=\sum_{i\in F}Y_i\). For bounded measurable functions of independent variables the expectation of the product is the product of the expectations; applied to the bounded functions \(y\mapsto e^{ity}\), this gives, for every \(t\in\mathbb R\),

\[\int_\Omega e^{itT}\,dQ=\prod_{i\in F}\int_\Omega e^{itY_i}\,dQ=\prod_{i\in F}e^{itm_i'-v_it^2/2}=\exp\Bigl(it\sum_{i\in F}m_i'-\Bigl(\sum_{i\in F}v_i\Bigr)\frac{t^2}2\Bigr).\]

This is the characteristic function of \(\mathcal N(\sum_im_i',\sum_iv_i)\). By the uniqueness theorem for characteristic functions (two probability measures on \(\mathbb R\) with the same characteristic function are equal), \(T\) has this Gaussian law. In the present case \(T(\omega)=\sum_{i\in F}a_i\omega_i\).

Transfer to the class. By the previous step, the class \(\sum_{i\in F}a_iZ_i\) agrees almost everywhere with \(T\), and functions that agree almost everywhere have the same law. \(\square\)

The computation shows that the law is \(\mathcal N(0,\sum_{i\in F}a_i^2)\). The claim records only that it is Gaussian; its parameters are identified in .

\[|\varphi_X(t)-\varphi_Y(t)|\le\int_\Omega|e^{itX}-e^{itY}|\,dQ\le|t|\int_\Omega|X-Y|\,dQ\le|t|\,\|X-Y\|_2.\qquad(7)\]

Continuity of the Gaussian characteristic function in the norm. The map \(X\mapsto e^{-\|X\|_2^2t^2/2}\) is continuous on \(L^2(Q)\), because \(|\|X\|_2-\|Y\|_2|\le\|X-Y\|_2\) and \(r\mapsto e^{-r^2t^2/2}\) is continuous.

Identification of the characteristic function. Fix \(t\in\mathbb R\) and \(\varepsilon>0\). By (7) and the previous paragraph there is \(\delta>0\) such that \(\|X-S(a)\|_2<\delta\) implies

\[|\varphi_X(t)-\varphi_{S(a)}(t)|<\varepsilon\quad\text{and}\quad\bigl|e^{-\|X\|_2^2t^2/2}-e^{-\|S(a)\|_2^2t^2/2}\bigr|<\varepsilon.\]

By there is a finite set \(F\) with \(\|X_F-S(a)\|_2<\delta\). By the previous step, \(X_F\) has law \(\mathcal N(0,\|X_F\|_2^2)\), so \(\varphi_{X_F}(t)=e^{-\|X_F\|_2^2t^2/2}\). The triangle inequality gives \(|\varphi_{S(a)}(t)-e^{-\|S(a)\|_2^2t^2/2}|<2\varepsilon\). Since \(\varepsilon\) was arbitrary, \(\varphi_{S(a)}(t)=e^{-\|S(a)\|_2^2t^2/2}\) for every \(t\), which is the characteristic function of \(\mathcal N(0,\|S(a)\|_2^2)\).

Conclusion. The representatives of \(S(a)\) are measurable, and by the uniqueness theorem for characteristic functions the law of \(S(a)\) is \(\mathcal N(0,\|S(a)\|_2^2)\). Finally \(\|S(a)\|_2=\|a\|_{\ell^2}\) because \(S\) is an isometry (). \(\square\)

steps.title: The law of an isonormal variable
steps.body:
Claim. For every \(x\in H\), the variable \(I_b(x)\) has law \(\mathcal N(0,\|x\|^2)\) under \(Q\). In particular \(I_b(0)\) has law \(\mathcal N(0,0)\), the Dirac mass at \(0\).

Proof. By definition \(I_b(x)=S(C_b(x))\). The previous step with \(a=C_b(x)\) shows that \(I_b(x)\) has law \(\mathcal N(0,\|C_b(x)\|_{\ell^2}^2)\), and \(\|C_b(x)\|_{\ell^2}=\|x\|\) by Parseval's identity (). \(\square\)

steps.title: Each isonormal variable has a Gaussian law
steps.body:
Claim. For every \(x\in H\), the real random variable \(I_b(x)\) has a Gaussian law under \(Q\).

Proof. By the previous step, its law is \(\mathcal N(0,\|x\|^2)\), which is a Gaussian law with \(m=0\) and \(v=\|x\|^2\ge0\). \(\square\)

The claim concerns one value \(I_b(x)\) at a time. That finite families \((I_b(x_1),\dots,I_b(x_n))\) are jointly Gaussian follows from this claim and the linearity of \(I_b\), and is proved in the next section ().

steps.title: The covariance of two isonormal variables
steps.body:
For real random variables \(X,Y\in L^2(Q)\), the covariance is \(\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\int_\Omega\bigl(X-\int X\,dQ\bigr)\bigl(Y-\int Y\,dQ\bigr)\,dQ\).

Claim. For all \(x,y\in H\), \(\operatorname{Cov}\bigl(I_b(x),I_b(y)\bigr)=\langle x,y\rangle_H\).

Proof. Both means vanish (), so

\[\operatorname{Cov}\bigl(I_b(x),I_b(y)\bigr)=\int_\Omega I_b(x)\,I_b(y)\,dQ=\langle I_b(x),I_b(y)\rangle_{L^2(Q)}.\]

In every real inner product space, expanding \(\|u\pm v\|^2=\|u\|^2\pm2\langle u,v\rangle+\|v\|^2\) gives the polarization identity \(\langle u,v\rangle=\frac14\bigl(\|u+v\|^2-\|u-v\|^2\bigr)\). By linearity, \(I_b(x)\pm I_b(y)=I_b(x\pm y)\), and \(I_b\) preserves norms (). Therefore

\[\langle I_b(x),I_b(y)\rangle=\tfrac14\bigl(\|I_b(x+y)\|_2^2-\|I_b(x-y)\|_2^2\bigr)=\tfrac14\bigl(\|x+y\|^2-\|x-y\|^2\bigr)=\langle x,y\rangle.\]

\(\square\)

For \(y=x\) this gives \(\operatorname{Var}(I_b(x))=\|x\|^2\), the variance found in .

UnadjustedLangevin/GaussianLinearProcess.title: Gaussian linear maps into square-integrable functions give Gaussian processes
UnadjustedLangevin/GaussianLinearProcess.summary:
Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\) be a measure space, let \(H\) be a real vector space and let \(T:H\to L^2(P)\) be a linear map such that every value \(T(x)\) is a real random variable with a Gaussian law. This section proves that finitely many values are then jointly Gaussian: for every finite family \((f_i)_{i\in\iota}\) in \(H\), the random vector \((T(f_i))_{i\in\iota}\) has a Gaussian law on \(\mathbb R^\iota\). The proof uses only linearity. A linear functional of the vector is a finite linear combination \(\sum_ic_iT(f_i)\), which equals the single value \(T(\sum_ic_if_i)\) almost everywhere and is therefore Gaussian by hypothesis.

Consequently, for every index set \(\Theta\) (which may be uncountable) and every family \((f(t))_{t\in\Theta}\) in \(H\), the process \(t\mapsto T(f(t))\) is a Gaussian process: all of its finite-dimensional distributions are Gaussian. No topology on \(H\) is used, and nothing is asserted about the paths \(t\mapsto T(f(t))(\omega)\). The result is applied to the isonormal map of the previous section and the indicators \(f(t)=\mathbf 1_{(0,t]}\) in the construction of Brownian motion.

steps.title: Finitely many values of a Gaussian linear map are jointly Gaussian
steps.body:
Recall that a probability measure on \(\mathbb R\) is Gaussian if it equals \(\mathcal N(m,v)\) for some \(m\in\mathbb R\) and \(v\ge0\), where \(\mathcal N(m,0)\) is the Dirac mass at \(m\). For a finite set \(\iota\), a probability measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathbb R^\iota\) is Gaussian if for every linear functional \(L:\mathbb R^\iota\to\mathbb R\) the image measure \(L_\#\mu\), defined by \(L_\#\mu(A)=\mu(L^{-1}(A))\), is a Gaussian law on \(\mathbb R\). A random vector \(V:\Omega\to\mathbb R^\iota\) has a Gaussian law under \(P\) if it is measurable up to a \(P\)-null set and its law \(V_\#P\) is Gaussian. For \(\iota\) with one element this is the notion for real random variables, since every linear functional on \(\mathbb R\) is \(y\mapsto cy\) and the image of \(\mathcal N(m,v)\) under it is \(\mathcal N(cm,c^2v)\).

Claim. Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\) be a measure space, let \(H\) be a real vector space and let \(T:H\to L^2(P)\) be a linear map such that, for every \(x\in H\), the real random variable \(T(x)\) has a Gaussian law under \(P\). Let \(\iota\) be a finite set and let \((f_i)_{i\in\iota}\) be vectors of \(H\). Then the random vector

\[V:\Omega\to\mathbb R^\iota,\qquad V(\omega)=\bigl(T(f_i)(\omega)\bigr)_{i\in\iota},\]

formed with representatives of the classes \(T(f_i)\), has a Gaussian law under \(P\).

The hypothesis forces \(P\) to be a probability measure, because \(P(\Omega)=T(x)_\#P(\mathbb R)=1\) for any \(x\).

Proof. Measurability. Each coordinate \(\omega\mapsto T(f_i)(\omega)\) is a representative of an element of \(L^2(P)\) and hence measurable. A map into the finite product \(\mathbb R^\iota\) is measurable when all of its coordinates are, so \(V\) is measurable.

Coordinates of a linear functional. Let \(L:\mathbb R^\iota\to\mathbb R\) be linear. Let \(e_i\in\mathbb R^\iota\) be the \(i\)-th unit vector (\(1\) in coordinate \(i\), \(0\) elsewhere) and put \(c_i=L(e_i)\). Every \(y\in\mathbb R^\iota\) equals \(\sum_iy_ie_i\), so by linearity

\[L(y)=\sum_{i\in\iota}c_i\,y_i\qquad\text{for all }y\in\mathbb R^\iota.\qquad(1)\]

Linearity of \(T\). In \(L^2(P)\),

\[T\Bigl(\sum_{i\in\iota}c_if_i\Bigr)=\sum_{i\in\iota}c_i\,T(f_i).\qquad(2)\]

Representatives. If \(u\) and \(w\) represent classes \(U\) and \(W\), then \(u+w\) represents \(U+W\) and \(cu\) represents \(cU\). Hence a representative of \(\sum_ic_iT(f_i)\) agrees with \(\omega\mapsto\sum_ic_i\,T(f_i)(\omega)\) outside a finite union of null sets, which is a null set. By (2) and (1), for \(P\)-almost every \(\omega\),

\[T\Bigl(\sum_{i\in\iota}c_if_i\Bigr)(\omega)=\sum_{i\in\iota}c_i\,T(f_i)(\omega)=L(V(\omega)).\qquad(3)\]

Gaussian law of \(L\circ V\). By hypothesis the variable \(T(\sum_ic_if_i)\) has a Gaussian law. Functions that agree almost everywhere have the same law, so by (3) the variable \(L\circ V\) has a Gaussian law.

Conclusion. For every Borel set \(A\subseteq\mathbb R\), \(L_\#(V_\#P)(A)=P\bigl(V^{-1}(L^{-1}(A))\bigr)=(L\circ V)_\#P(A)\), so \(L_\#(V_\#P)=(L\circ V)_\#P\) is Gaussian. As \(L\) was arbitrary, \(V_\#P\) is a Gaussian measure on \(\mathbb R^\iota\). \(\square\)

steps.title: A Gaussian process from a Gaussian linear map
steps.body:
A family \((X_t)_{t\in\Theta}\) of real random variables, indexed by an arbitrary set \(\Theta\), is a Gaussian process under \(P\) if for every finite set \(J\subseteq\Theta\) the random vector \((X_t)_{t\in J}\) has a Gaussian law on \(\mathbb R^J\).

Claim. Let \(P\), \(H\) and \(T\) be as in the previous step: \(T:H\to L^2(P)\) is linear and every \(T(x)\) has a Gaussian law. Let \(\Theta\) be an arbitrary set and let \(f:\Theta\to H\) be any map. Then the process \(X_t=T(f(t))\), \(t\in\Theta\), formed with representatives of the classes \(T(f(t))\), is a Gaussian process under \(P\).

Proof. Let \(J\subseteq\Theta\) be finite. The previous step, applied with the finite index set \(\iota=J\) and the vectors \(f_t=f(t)\) for \(t\in J\), shows that \((X_t)_{t\in J}=(T(f(t)))_{t\in J}\) has a Gaussian law on \(\mathbb R^J\). \(\square\)

The set \(\Theta\) and the map \(f\) are arbitrary; in particular \(\Theta\) may be uncountable. The claim concerns finite-dimensional distributions only: it asserts no measurability or continuity of the paths \(t\mapsto X_t(\omega)\).

UnadjustedLangevin/CanonicalBrownian.lea.title: Construction of a pre-Brownian motion and of independent Brownian coordinates
UnadjustedLangevin/CanonicalBrownian.lea.summary:
Let \(\lambda\) be Lebesgue measure on \(\mathbb R\) and \(\mathcal H=L^2(\mathbb R,\lambda)\). For \(t\ge0\) let \(e_t\in\mathcal H\) be the class of the indicator \(\mathbf 1_{(0,t]}\). Then \(\langle e_s,e_t\rangle=\lambda((0,\min(s,t)])=\min(s,t)\). Choose a Hilbert basis of \(\mathcal H\), indexed by a set \(W\), and let \(I:\mathcal H\to L^2(Q)\) be the isonormal map of this basis, where \(Q\) is the product of standard Gaussian laws on \(\Omega=\mathbb R^W\) (see ). For each \(t\ge0\) let \(B_t\) be a fixed representative of the class \(I(e_t)\).

We prove that each \(B_t\) is measurable with mean zero, that \(\operatorname{Cov}(B_s,B_t)=\min(s,t)\), that \((B_t)_{t\ge0}\) is a Gaussian process, and that it is a pre-Brownian motion: for every finite set \(F\subseteq[0,\infty)\), the vector \((B_t)_{t\in F}\) has the centred Gaussian law with covariance matrix \((\min(s,t))_{s,t\in F}\). These are the finite-dimensional distributions of Brownian motion; continuity of the paths \(t\mapsto B_t(\omega)\) is not asserted.

For an arbitrary index set \(J\) of spatial coordinates, the product \(Q^{\otimes J}\) on \(\Omega^J\) carries independent copies \(B^{(j)}_t(\underline\omega)=B_t(\omega^{(j)})\), \(j\in J\). Each coordinate process is a pre-Brownian motion, the coordinate paths are independent, and so are their restrictions to every time grid \(\{nh:n\in\mathbb N\}\). The grid restrictions are the form in which the Brownian increments enter the Gaussian innovations of the unadjusted Langevin algorithm in the next section.

steps.title: The Hilbert space of time functions
steps.body:
Definition. Let \(\lambda\) be Lebesgue measure on \(\mathbb R\). The time Hilbert space is \(\mathcal H=L^2(\mathbb R,\lambda)\), the space of classes, modulo equality \(\lambda\)-almost everywhere, of Borel functions \(f:\mathbb R\to\mathbb R\) with \(\int f^2\,d\lambda<\infty\). With the inner product \(\langle f,g\rangle=\int fg\,d\lambda\) it is a real Hilbert space (Riesz–Fischer theorem).

The space \(\mathcal H\) carries no randomness: its elements are deterministic functions of time. It serves as the domain of the isonormal map, and it must not be confused with the space \(L^2(Q)\) of random variables on the Gaussian source.

steps.title: The indicator of a time interval
steps.body:
Definition and claim. For \(t\ge0\), the indicator \(\mathbf 1_{(0,t]}\) of the half-open interval \((0,t]\) is square integrable, and we let \(e_t\in\mathcal H\) be its class.

Proof. The interval \((0,t]\) is a Borel set, so \(\mathbf 1_{(0,t]}\) is Borel measurable, and \(\int\mathbf 1_{(0,t]}^2\,d\lambda=\lambda((0,t])=t<\infty\). \(\square\)

For \(t=0\) the interval is empty and \(e_0=0\). Changing the interval at its endpoints does not change the class, since single points are \(\lambda\)-null; the half-open convention makes the intersection formula of the next step exact.

In particular \(\|e_t\|^2=t\). For \(s\le t\), (1) gives \(\|e_t-e_s\|^2=t-2s+s=t-s\), the length of \((s,t]\).

steps.title: The process
steps.body:
Definition. For each \(t\ge0\), let \(B_t:\Omega\to\mathbb R\) be a fixed representative of the class \(I(e_t)\), chosen to be a strongly measurable function, that is, a pointwise limit of simple functions. The family \((B_t)_{t\ge0}\) is the process studied below.

Different choices of representatives change each \(B_t\) only on a \(Q\)-null set, which may depend on \(t\). Laws, means, covariances and finite-dimensional distributions are not affected by such changes; properties of the paths \(t\mapsto B_t(\omega)\) are, and none is asserted.
steps.lean: process t is valueLp t coerced to a function Sample → ℝ. For an element of Lp this coercion is a strongly measurable representative of the class, fixed once and for all by Mathlib's construction of Lp; this is the representative \(B_t\).

steps.title: Measurability at each time
steps.body:
Claim. For every \(t\ge0\), the function \(B_t:\Omega\to\mathbb R\) is measurable.

Proof. \(B_t\) is strongly measurable, hence a pointwise limit of measurable simple functions, and a pointwise limit of real measurable functions is measurable. \(\square\)
steps.lean: Lp.stronglyMeasurable (valueLp t) states that the representative obtained by the coercion is strongly measurable, and .measurable converts strong measurability into measurability for real-valued functions.

steps.title: The process has mean zero
steps.body:
Claim. For every \(t\ge0\), \(\int_\Omega B_t\,dQ=0\).

Proof. \(B_t\) represents \(I(e_t)\), and every value of the isonormal map has mean zero (). \(\square\)
steps.lean: The proof is the term GaussianHilbert.isonormal_mean basis (timeIndicator t); the integrand process t ω is by definition the representative of GaussianHilbert.isonormal basis (timeIndicator t).

steps.title: The Brownian covariance
steps.body:
Recall that \(\operatorname{Cov}(X,Y)=\int_\Omega(X-\int X\,dQ)(Y-\int Y\,dQ)\,dQ\) for square-integrable \(X,Y\).

Claim. For all \(s,t\ge0\), \(\operatorname{Cov}(B_s,B_t)=\min(s,t)\).

Proof. The covariance of two values of the isonormal map is the inner product of their arguments (), so \(\operatorname{Cov}(B_s,B_t)=\operatorname{Cov}(I(e_s),I(e_t))=\langle e_s,e_t\rangle\), and \(\langle e_s,e_t\rangle=\min(s,t)\) by (1). \(\square\)
steps.lean: The proof is one rewriting chain: process and valueLp are unfolded (each twice) to expose GaussianHilbert.isonormal basis applied to the two indicators; GaussianHilbert.isonormal_covariance turns the covariance into the inner product \(\langle e_s,e_t\rangle\); and timeIndicator_inner is (1).

steps.title: The process is Gaussian
steps.body:
Claim. \((B_t)_{t\ge0}\) is a Gaussian process under \(Q\): for every finite set \(F\subseteq[0,\infty)\), the random vector \((B_t)_{t\in F}\) has a Gaussian law on \(\mathbb R^F\).

Proof. The isonormal map \(I:\mathcal H\to L^2(Q)\) is linear, and each of its values \(I(x)\) has a Gaussian law (). By the theorem that a linear map into \(L^2\) with Gaussian values defines a Gaussian process along every family of vectors (), applied to the family \(t\mapsto e_t\), the process \(t\mapsto I(e_t)\), formed with the representatives \(B_t\), is a Gaussian process. \(\square\)

The proof applies isGaussianProcess_of_linearMap_Lp with the measure probability, the linear map (GaussianHilbert.isonormal basis).toLinearMap (the linear isometry regarded as a linear map), the hypothesis GaussianHilbert.isonormal_hasGaussianLaw basis, and the family timeIndicator. The process produced by that theorem, fun t ω ↦ T (f t) ω, is by definition process.

steps.title: The process is a pre-Brownian motion
steps.body:
For a finite set \(F\subseteq[0,\infty)\), let \(\Gamma_F\) be the centred Gaussian law on \(\mathbb R^F\) with covariance matrix \(C_F=(\min(s,t))_{s,t\in F}\): the probability measure under which every linear functional \(y\mapsto\langle u,y\rangle=\sum_{t\in F}u_ty_t\) has law \(\mathcal N(0,\langle u,C_Fu\rangle)\). The matrix \(C_F\) is positive semidefinite, since \(\langle u,C_Fu\rangle=\|\sum_tu_te_t\|^2\) by (1). A family \((X_t)_{t\ge0}\) of real random variables is a pre-Brownian motion if for every finite \(F\subseteq[0,\infty)\) the vector \((X_t)_{t\in F}\) has law \(\Gamma_F\). These are the finite-dimensional distributions of Brownian motion; no property of the paths is required.

Claim. \((B_t)_{t\ge0}\) is a pre-Brownian motion under \(Q\).

Proof. We use three facts proved above: \((B_t)\) is a Gaussian process, \(\int B_t\,dQ=0\) for every \(t\), and \(\operatorname{Cov}(B_s,B_t)=\min(s,t)\); in particular \(\operatorname{Cov}(B_s,B_t)=s\) whenever \(s\le t\), which together with the symmetry of the covariance determines all covariances.

Fix a finite set \(F\) and let \(\mu\) be the law of \(V=(B_t)_{t\in F}\). Fix \(u\in\mathbb R^F\). Since \(\mu\) is Gaussian, \(\langle u,V\rangle=\sum_tu_tB_t\) has law \(\mathcal N(m,v)\) for some \(m\) and \(v\ge0\), and then \(m\) and \(v\) are its mean and variance. Each \(B_t\) is square integrable, so by linearity of the integral and bilinearity of the covariance,

\[m=\sum_{t\in F}u_t\int_\Omega B_t\,dQ=0,\qquad v=\sum_{s\in F}\sum_{t\in F}u_su_t\operatorname{Cov}(B_s,B_t)=\langle u,C_Fu\rangle.\]

Hence the characteristic function of \(\mu\) at \(u\) is

\[\int_{\mathbb R^F}e^{i\langle u,y\rangle}\,\mu(dy)=\int_\Omega e^{i\langle u,V\rangle}\,dQ=e^{-\langle u,C_Fu\rangle/2},\]

which is also the characteristic function of \(\Gamma_F\) at \(u\). Since probability measures on \(\mathbb R^F\) are determined by their characteristic functions, \(\mu=\Gamma_F\). \(\square\)

From these laws one obtains in particular that \(B_t-B_s\) has law \(\mathcal N(0,t-s)\) for \(s\le t\) and that increments over disjoint intervals are independent; these consequences are used in the next section.

steps.title: The sample space for several coordinates
steps.body:
Definition. Let \(J\) be an arbitrary index set, whose elements label spatial coordinates. The vector sample space is \(\Omega^J\), the set of families \(\underline\omega=(\omega^{(j)})_{j\in J}\) of scalar samples \(\omega^{(j)}\in\Omega\), with the product \(\sigma\)-algebra.

Each coordinate \(j\) receives its own copy of the scalar sample space, so that whole scalar processes, and not only their values at single times, can be made independent across coordinates.
steps.lean: VectorSample I is the abbrev I → Sample; the coordinate index type is called I in the formal statements and \(J\) in the text.

steps.title: The product probability for several coordinates
steps.body:
Definition. On \(\Omega^J\) let \(Q^{\otimes J}=\bigotimes_{j\in J}Q\) be the product of copies of the scalar source probability \(Q\). It is the unique probability measure such that, for every finite set \(K\subseteq J\) and all measurable sets \(A_j\subseteq\Omega\) (\(j\in K\)),

\[Q^{\otimes J}\bigl(\{\underline\omega:\ \omega^{(j)}\in A_j\text{ for all }j\in K\}\bigr)=\prod_{j\in K}Q(A_j).\qquad(2)\]

As for the scalar source, such a product exists for every family of probability measures and every index set \(J\).
steps.lean: vectorProbability I is Measure.infinitePi (fun _ : I ↦ probability), Mathlib's product of an arbitrary family of probability measures, characterised by property (2).

steps.title: The product probability has total mass one
steps.body:
Claim. \(Q^{\otimes J}(\Omega^J)=1\).

Proof. Apply (2) with \(K=\varnothing\): the set on the left is \(\Omega^J\) and the right-hand side is the empty product \(1\). \(\square\)

steps.title: The coordinate processes
steps.body:
Definition. For \(j\in J\), \(t\ge0\) and \(\underline\omega\in\Omega^J\), let

\[B^{(j)}_t(\underline\omega)=B_t\bigl(\omega^{(j)}\bigr).\]

Thus \(B^{(j)}_t=B_t\circ\pi_j\), where \(\pi_j(\underline\omega)=\omega^{(j)}\) is the \(j\)-th projection: the \(j\)-th coordinate process reads the \(j\)-th scalar sample and evaluates the scalar process on it.
steps.lean: coordinate i t ω is defined as process t (ω i), with i : I the coordinate, t : ℝ≥0 the time and ω : VectorSample I the vector sample.

steps.title: Each coordinate process is a pre-Brownian motion
steps.body:
Claim. For every \(j\in J\), the process \((B^{(j)}_t)_{t\ge0}\) is a pre-Brownian motion under \(Q^{\otimes J}\).

Proof. The projection \(\pi_j\) has law \(Q\). It is measurable for the product \(\sigma\)-algebra, and for measurable \(A\subseteq\Omega\), (2) with \(K=\{j\}\) gives \(Q^{\otimes J}(\pi_j^{-1}(A))=Q(A)\).

Composition of laws. Fix a finite set \(F\subseteq[0,\infty)\) and let \(V_F(\omega)=(B_t(\omega))_{t\in F}\), so that \((B^{(j)}_t)_{t\in F}=V_F\circ\pi_j\). For every Borel set \(A\subseteq\mathbb R^F\),

\[Q^{\otimes J}\bigl((V_F\circ\pi_j)^{-1}(A)\bigr)=Q^{\otimes J}\bigl(\pi_j^{-1}(V_F^{-1}(A))\bigr)=Q\bigl(V_F^{-1}(A)\bigr)=\Gamma_F(A),\]

by the law of \(\pi_j\) and by the pre-Brownian property of \((B_t)\) (). Hence \((B^{(j)}_t)_{t\in F}\) has law \(\Gamma_F\). \(\square\)

Mathlib's lemma comp for HasLaw states that if \(Y\) has law \(\nu\) under \(\mu\) and \(X\) has law \(\mu\) under \(P\), then \(Y\circ X\) has law \(\nu\) under \(P\), which is the composition of laws in the proof. The law of the projection is the anonymous constructor with (measurable_pi_apply i).aemeasurable and Measure.infinitePi_map_eval (fun _ : I ↦ probability) i, the marginal identity of the product measure; its type is written out as HasLaw (fun ω : VectorSample I ↦ ω i) probability (vectorProbability I).

steps.title: Independence of the coordinate paths
steps.body:
Let \(\mathbb R^{[0,\infty)}\) be the space of all real functions of time, with the product \(\sigma\)-algebra generated by the evaluations \(p\mapsto p(t)\).

Claim. The path maps \(\underline\omega\mapsto(B^{(j)}_t(\underline\omega))_{t\ge0}\in\mathbb R^{[0,\infty)}\), \(j\in J\), are independent random elements under \(Q^{\otimes J}\).

Proof. Let \(\Phi:\Omega\to\mathbb R^{[0,\infty)}\), \(\Phi(\omega)=(B_t(\omega))_{t\ge0}\). A map into a space with a product \(\sigma\)-algebra is measurable when each of its coordinates is; the coordinates of \(\Phi\) are the measurable functions \(B_t\) (), so \(\Phi\) is measurable. The \(j\)-th path map is \(\Phi\circ\pi_j\). For a finite set \(K\subseteq J\) and measurable sets \(A_j\subseteq\mathbb R^{[0,\infty)}\), the sets \(\Phi^{-1}(A_j)\subseteq\Omega\) are measurable, and (2) gives

\[Q^{\otimes J}\Bigl(\bigcap_{j\in K}\{\Phi\circ\pi_j\in A_j\}\Bigr)=Q^{\otimes J}\bigl(\{\omega^{(j)}\in\Phi^{-1}(A_j)\text{ for all }j\in K\}\bigr)=\prod_{j\in K}Q\bigl(\Phi^{-1}(A_j)\bigr).\]

By (2) with a single index, each factor equals \(Q^{\otimes J}(\{\Phi\circ\pi_j\in A_j\})\), which is the product formula defining independence. \(\square\)

The proof is Mathlib's iIndepFun_infinitePi (on a product measure, measurable functions of distinct coordinates are independent) applied to the map \(\Phi\), whose measurability measurable_pi_iff.mpr process_measurable reduces to the measurability of each \(B_t\).

steps.title: Independence of the coordinate paths on a time grid
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(h\ge0\). The grid paths \(\underline\omega\mapsto(B^{(j)}_{nh}(\underline\omega))_{n\in\mathbb N}\in\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}\), \(j\in J\), are independent under \(Q^{\otimes J}\).

Proof. Let \(R_h:\mathbb R^{[0,\infty)}\to\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}\), \(R_h(p)=(p(nh))_{n\in\mathbb N}\). Each coordinate of \(R_h\) is an evaluation map, so \(R_h\) is measurable. The \(j\)-th grid path is \(R_h\) composed with the \(j\)-th path of the previous step. If \(X_j\), \(j\in J\), are independent random elements and \(R\) is measurable, then the \(R\circ X_j\) are independent, because \(\{R\circ X_j\in A\}=\{X_j\in R^{-1}(A)\}\) with \(R^{-1}(A)\) measurable. \(\square\)

The step size \(h\) may be \(0\), in which case every grid path is constant in \(n\). This is the independence hypothesis on grid paths used to build independent Gaussian innovations in the next section.

Measurability of the restriction is measurable_pi_iff.mpr fun n ↦ measurable_pi_apply _, that is, measurability of each evaluation. The time \(nh\) is formed in ℝ≥0 by the cast (n : ℝ≥0).

UnadjustedLangevin/BrownianInnovations.l.title: Normalized Brownian increments are independent standard Gaussian innovations
UnadjustedLangevin/BrownianInnovations.l.summary:
Let \((B_t)_{t\ge0}\) be a pre-Brownian motion on a measure space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\): for every finite set \(F\subseteq[0,\infty)\) the vector \((B_t)_{t\in F}\) has the centred Gaussian law \(\Gamma_F\) with covariance matrix \((\min(s,t))_{s,t\in F}\) (see ). For a step \(h>0\), the normalized increments over the time grid \(\{nh:n\in\mathbb N\}\) are

\[\xi_n=\frac{B_{(n+1)h}-B_{nh}}{\sqrt h},\qquad n\in\mathbb N.\]

We prove that each \(\xi_n\) has law \(\mathcal N(0,1)\), is square integrable with \(\int\xi_n^2\,dP=1\), and that \((\xi_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\) is an independent family. For a family \((B^{(i)})_{i\in\iota}\) of pre-Brownian motions whose grid paths \((B^{(i)}_{nh})_{n\in\mathbb N}\) are independent over \(i\), the whole array \((\xi^{(i)}_n)_{(i,n)\in\iota\times\mathbb N}\) is independent, and for countable \(\iota\) its joint law is the product measure \(\bigotimes_{(i,n)\in\iota\times\mathbb N}\mathcal N(0,1)\).

The proof of joint independence combines independence across coordinates with independence across time within each coordinate. A general lemma on arrays of random variables, proved here, shows that these two kinds of independence together give independence of the whole array. These results identify the Brownian increments that drive an Euler scheme with the independent standard Gaussian innovations of the unadjusted Langevin algorithm.

steps.title: The normalized grid increment
steps.body:
Definition. Let \((B_t)_{t\ge0}\) be a family of real functions on \(\Omega\), let \(h\ge0\) and \(n\in\mathbb N\). The normalized increment of \(B\) over the \(n\)-th grid interval \([nh,(n+1)h]\) is

\[\xi_n(\omega)=\frac{B_{(n+1)h}(\omega)-B_{nh}(\omega)}{\sqrt h},\qquad\omega\in\Omega,\]

where for \(h=0\) the quotient is given the value \(0\) (with the convention \(x/0=0\)).

For \(h>0\) the increment \(B_{(n+1)h}-B_{nh}\) of a pre-Brownian motion has variance \(h\), so the division by \(\sqrt h\) normalizes the variance to one. The results on the law of \(\xi_n\) below assume \(h>0\); the independence result within one coordinate holds for every \(h\ge0\).
steps.lean: normalizedBrownianIncrement B h n ω is defined for B : ℝ≥0 → Ω → ℝ and h : ℝ≥0. The grid times are formed in ℝ≥0 by the casts ((n + 1 : ℕ) : ℝ≥0) * h and (n : ℝ≥0) * h, and the denominator is Real.sqrt (h : ℝ). Division in \(\mathbb R\) is total with \(x/0=0\), and \(\sqrt0=0\), which gives the convention for \(h=0\).

steps.title: Each normalized increment has the standard Gaussian law
steps.body:
Claim. Let \((B_t)_{t\ge0}\) be a pre-Brownian motion under \(P\), let \(h>0\) and \(n\in\mathbb N\). Then \(\xi_n\) has law \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) under \(P\).

Proof. The law of an increment. For \(s,t\ge0\), the vector \((B_s,B_t)\) has law \(\Gamma_{\{s,t\}}\), under which the linear functional \(y\mapsto y_s-y_t\) has law \(\mathcal N(0,v)\) with

\[v=\min(s,s)-2\min(s,t)+\min(t,t)=s+t-2\min(s,t)=|s-t|\]

(if \(s=t\) the functional is \(0\) and the law is \(\mathcal N(0,0)\), in agreement with \(|s-t|=0\)). Hence \(B_s-B_t\) has law \(\mathcal N(0,|s-t|)\). With \(s=(n+1)h\) and \(t=nh\) we have \(|s-t|=|(n+1)h-nh|=h\), so \(B_{(n+1)h}-B_{nh}\) has law \(\mathcal N(0,h)\).

Scaling. If \(X\) has law \(\mathcal N(m,v)\) and \(c\ne0\), then \(X/c\) has law \(\mathcal N(m/c,v/c^2)\): for \(v>0\) this follows from the substitution \(y=x/c\) in the density, and for \(v=0\) from \(X=m\) almost everywhere. With \(c=\sqrt h\ne0\) (here \(h>0\) is used) and \(m=0\), \(v=h\), the variable \(\xi_n\) has law \(\mathcal N(0,h/(\sqrt h)^2)=\mathcal N(0,1)\), because \((\sqrt h)^2=h\). \(\square\)

steps.title: Square integrability of a normalized increment
steps.body:
Claim. Under the hypotheses of the previous step (\(B\) pre-Brownian, \(h>0\)), \(\xi_n\) is square integrable: \(\int_\Omega\xi_n^2\,dP<\infty\).

Proof. By the previous step and the change-of-variables formula for image measures, \(\int\xi_n^2\,dP=\int x^2\,\mathcal N(0,1)(dx)\), which is finite because the standard Gaussian law has finite moments of all orders. \(\square\)

steps.body:
Claim. Under the same hypotheses, \(\int_\Omega\xi_n^2\,dP=1\).

Proof. By change of variables, \(\int\xi_n^2\,dP=\int x^2\,\mathcal N(0,1)(dx)\), and the second moment of \(\mathcal N(0,v)\) equals its variance \(v\), here \(1\) (see ). \(\square\)

steps.title: Independence of the normalized increments of one process
steps.body:
Claim. Let \((B_t)_{t\ge0}\) be a pre-Brownian motion under \(P\) and let \(h\ge0\). Then \((\xi_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\) is an independent family.

Proof. Independent increments. Let \(0\le t_0\le t_1\le\dots\le t_N\). The vector \(D\) of increments \(D_k=B_{t_{k+1}}-B_{t_k}\), \(0\le k<N\), is a linear image of \((B_{t_0},\dots,B_{t_N})\), whose law is Gaussian; hence \(D\) has a Gaussian law on \(\mathbb R^N\) (a linear functional of \(D\) is a linear functional of the original vector). For \(k<l\) we have \(t_k\le t_{k+1}\le t_l\le t_{l+1}\), and by bilinearity of the covariance and \(\operatorname{Cov}(B_s,B_t)=\min(s,t)\),

\[\operatorname{Cov}(D_k,D_l)=\min(t_{k+1},t_{l+1})-\min(t_{k+1},t_l)-\min(t_k,t_{l+1})+\min(t_k,t_l)=t_{k+1}-t_{k+1}-t_k+t_k=0.\]

So the covariance matrix \(\Sigma\) of \(D\) is diagonal, and the characteristic function of \(D\) at \(u\in\mathbb R^N\) is \(\exp(i\langle u,m\rangle-\frac12\sum_k\Sigma_{kk}u_k^2)\), where \(m\) is the mean vector; this is the product of the characteristic functions of the \(D_k\). By the uniqueness theorem for characteristic functions, the law of \(D\) is the product of the laws of its components, which means that \(D_0,\dots,D_{N-1}\) are independent.

The grid. Since \(h\ge0\), the times \(t_n=nh\) are nondecreasing in \(n\). Independence of an infinite family means independence of each finite subfamily, and every finite set of indices is contained in \(\{0,\dots,N-1\}\) for some \(N\); a subfamily of an independent family is independent. Hence \((B_{(n+1)h}-B_{nh})_{n\in\mathbb N}\) is independent.

Normalization. \(\xi_n=g(B_{(n+1)h}-B_{nh})\) with the measurable map \(g(x)=x/\sqrt h\). If \((X_n)\) is independent and \(g\) is measurable, then \((g(X_n))\) is independent, since \(\{g(X_n)\in A\}=\{X_n\in g^{-1}(A)\}\). \(\square\)

For \(h=0\) every \(\xi_n\) is the constant \(0\), and the claim reduces to the independence of constant functions.

steps.title: Independence of an array from independence of rows and within rows
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(\iota\) be an arbitrary index set and let \(X_{i,n}:\Omega\to\mathbb R\), \(i\in\iota\), \(n\in\mathbb N\), be functions that are measurable up to \(P\)-null sets. Write \(R_i=(X_{i,n})_{n\in\mathbb N}:\Omega\to\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}\) for the \(i\)-th row. Assume:

  1. the rows \(R_i\), \(i\in\iota\), are independent random elements of \(\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}\) (with the product \(\sigma\)-algebra);
  2. for every \(i\in\iota\), the variables \(X_{i,n}\), \(n\in\mathbb N\), are independent.

Then the whole array \((X_{i,n})_{(i,n)\in\iota\times\mathbb N}\) is an independent family.

Proof. Measurable versions. For each \(i\) and \(n\) there is a measurable \(\tilde X_{i,n}\) equal to \(X_{i,n}\) outside a null set \(N_{i,n}\). Since \(\mathbb N\) is countable, \(N_i=\bigcup_nN_{i,n}\) is null, and the row \(G_i=(\tilde X_{i,n})_{n}\) is a measurable map \(\Omega\to\mathbb R^{\mathbb N}\) equal to \(R_i\) outside \(N_i\).

Independence is unchanged by modifications on null sets. If \(Y=\tilde Y\) outside a null set, then for every measurable set \(A\) the events \(\{Y\in A\}\) and \(\{\tilde Y\in A\}\) differ by a subset of a null set and have the same measure; so the product formula defining independence holds for a family if and only if it holds for the modified family. Hence the rows \(G_i\) are independent, and for each \(i\) the coordinates \(\tilde X_{i,n}\) of \(G_i\) are independent.

UnadjustedLangevin/MALACoupling.lean.summary:
For a pair of current states, use one standard Gaussian innovation for both Langevin proposals. The first coordinate always takes its proposal. The second uses the Metropolis acceptance weight and otherwise keeps its current state. Projecting this weighted joint measure gives the ULA transition in the first marginal and the adjusted transition in the second.

In the stated small-step range, the common-noise proposal is nonexpansive. The accepted distance is therefore at most the old distance; the rejected distance is at most the old distance plus the second proposal displacement. If the second marginal is Gibbs, integration bounds the additional mean distance by \(C_{U,L}h\sqrt h\). Starting on the diagonal and iterating gives mean separation at most \(nC_{U,L}h\sqrt h\), while the adjusted marginal remains Gibbs.

UnadjustedLangevin/MALAInvariance.lean.title: Exact Gibbs invariance under the Metropolis-adjusted step
UnadjustedLangevin/MALAInvariance.lean.summary:
The joint law of a Gibbs state and its Langevin proposal has density \(Z^{-1}e^{-U(x)}q_h(x,y)\). Its reverse-to-forward density ratio is \(e^{R_h(x,y)}\), since both state-independent normalizers cancel. The Metropolis acceptance \(\min(1,e^{R_h})\) therefore gives accepted density \(\min\{Z^{-1}e^{-U(x)}q_h(x,y),Z^{-1}e^{-U(y)}q_h(y,x)\}\).

This accepted density is symmetric in the two states. Its first and second marginals agree, and rejected mass remains at the current state. Acceptance and rejection sum to the original input measure, so one adjusted step preserves Gibbs. No invariant-law hypothesis for the transition is used in this proof.

steps.title: The joint starting-proposal law
steps.body:
Push \(\mu\otimes\gamma\) through \((x,\xi)\mapsto(x,T_h(x,\xi))\). Its first coordinate retains the current state, and its second records the Gaussian proposal. This joint measure is the input to the accepted-flow detailed-balance theorem.

The first marginal is the starting law because the Gaussian conditional proposal has mass one. Its second marginal is the unadjusted proposal law. Keeping both coordinates makes forward and reverse density comparisons available on the same product space.

steps.title: The Gibbs-weighted proposal density
steps.body:
Set \(w_h(x,y)=\exp(-U(x)-\|y-x+h\nabla U(x)\|^2/(4h))\). The Gibbs and Gaussian normalization constants are kept in a separate symmetric base measure, so \(w_h\) is strictly positive and the ratio involves only its two exponentials.

With respect to Lebesgue product measure, the pair density is the Gibbs density at \(x\) multiplied by the proposal density from \(x\) to \(y\). Both factors are positive, so reverse/forward ratios can be formed pointwise and canceled without exceptional zero-density cases.

Divide the two positive exponentials and use \(e^a/e^b=e^{a-b}\). Expanding the definition of \(w_h\) shows the exponent difference is exactly the logarithmic Metropolis ratio. Thus \(w_h(y,x)/w_h(x,y)=e^{R_h(x,y)}\).

steps.title: Equality of the innovation and pair-density transitions
steps.body:
Transport acceptance and rejection weights through the measurable pair map using composition of a measurable map with a weighted pushforward. Projecting the accepted pair to its second coordinate gives the proposal; projecting rejected pairs to the first gives the unchanged state. These are precisely the two branches defining one Metropolis-adjusted transition.

UnadjustedLangevin/BrownianLangevin.lean.title: Square-mean Langevin solutions driven by Brownian coordinates
UnadjustedLangevin/BrownianLangevin.lean.summary:
Let \((\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\) be a probability space, let \(\iota\) be a finite set with \(d=|\iota|\) elements, and equip \(\mathbb R^\iota\) with the Euclidean norm \(\|x\|^2=\sum_{i\in\iota}x_i^2\). A real process \((W_t)_{t\ge0}\) is a pre-Brownian motion if for all times \(t_1,\dots,t_k\ge0\) the vector \((W_{t_1},\dots,W_{t_k})\) is centred Gaussian with covariances \(\mathbb E[W_{t_j}W_{t_l}]=\min(t_j,t_l)\); no continuity of sample paths is required. For a family \((W^i)_{i\in\iota}\) of pre-Brownian motions write \(B_t=(W^i_t)_{i\in\iota}\). Different coordinates are not assumed independent anywhere in this section. Let \(L^2=L^2(P;\mathbb R^\iota)\) be the Hilbert space of \(P\)-almost-everywhere classes \([X]\) of random vectors with \(\|X\|_2^2=\mathbb E\|X\|^2<\infty\).

For a starting time \(a\) we define the additive input \(N_a(t)=\sqrt2\,([B_{a+t}]-[B_a])\in L^2\) and prove three properties: \(t\mapsto N_a(t)\) is continuous from \(\mathbb R\) to \(L^2\), \(N_a(0)=0\), and \(\|N_a(t)\|_2=\sqrt{2d}\,\sqrt t\) for \(a,t\ge0\). These are exactly the hypotheses on the additive input in the existence theorems for the integral equation

\[Y(t)-Y(0)=-\int_0^t\mathcal G\bigl(Y(s)\bigr)\,ds+N_a(t),\qquad 0\le t\le h,\]

where \(\mathcal G[X]=[\nabla U\circ X]\) is the gradient of the potential \(U\) acting on square-integrable random vectors and the integral is a Bochner integral in \(L^2\). Applying those theorems gives a continuous curve \(Y:\mathbb R\to L^2\) with prescribed initial value solving this equation, first on a short interval with \(Lh\le\tfrac12\) and then on every finite interval \([0,h]\). The equation holds between elements of \(L^2\); no differentiability of sample paths is involved. These solutions are the Langevin diffusion used as the reference process in the following sections.

steps.title: The Langevin-scaled Brownian input
steps.body:
Definition. For \(s\ge0\) every coordinate \(W^i_s\) has law \(\mathcal N(0,s)\), hence \(\mathbb E\|B_s\|^2=\sum_{i}\mathbb E[(W^i_s)^2]=ds<\infty\) and the class \([B_s]\in L^2\) is defined. For real \(s\) put \(s^+=\max(s,0)\) and

\[\beta(s)=[B_{s^+}]\in L^2,\qquad s\in\mathbb R,\]

so that \(\beta\) is constant on \((-\infty,0]\). For a fixed real number \(a\) (the starting time of the segment) the Langevin input is

\[N_a(t)=\sqrt2\,\bigl(\beta(a+t)-\beta(a)\bigr)\in L^2,\qquad t\in\mathbb R.\]

Claim. If \(a\ge0\) and \(t\ge0\), then \(N_a(t)\) is the class of the random vector \(\sqrt2\,(B_{a+t}-B_a)\), and every coordinate of this vector has law \(\mathcal N(0,2t)\).

Proof. Since \(a\ge0\) and \(a+t\ge0\), we have \(a^+=a\) and \((a+t)^+=a+t\), so \(\beta(a)=[B_a]\) and \(\beta(a+t)=[B_{a+t}]\). Passing to classes is linear: \([X]-[X']=[X-X']\) and \(c[X]=[cX]\). Hence \(N_a(t)=[\sqrt2(B_{a+t}-B_a)]\).

Fix \(i\in\iota\). The pair \((W^i_a,W^i_{a+t})\) is centred Gaussian with covariances \(\min(a,a)=a\), \(\min(a,a+t)=a\) and \(\min(a+t,a+t)=a+t\). A linear function of a centred Gaussian vector is centred Gaussian, and its variance is computed by expanding the square:

\[\mathbb E\bigl[(W^i_{a+t}-W^i_a)^2\bigr]=(a+t)-2a+a=t.\]

So \(W^i_{a+t}-W^i_a\sim\mathcal N(0,t)\), and multiplication by \(\sqrt2\) multiplies the variance by \(2\), which gives \(\mathcal N(0,2t)\). \(\square\)

The subtraction of \(\beta(a)\) makes the input vanish at local time \(0\), whatever the value of the Brownian vector at time \(a\); the factor \(\sqrt2\) is the noise amplitude of the overdamped Langevin equation \(dY=-\nabla U(Y)\,dt+\sqrt2\,dB\).

steps.title: Continuity of the Brownian input in square mean
steps.body:
Claim. Let \((W^i)_{i\in\iota}\) be pre-Brownian motions and \(a\in\mathbb R\). Then the map \(t\mapsto N_a(t)\) is continuous from \(\mathbb R\) to \(L^2\).

Proof. Step 1: \(\beta\) is continuous. Let \(u,v\ge0\). For every \(i\), the difference \(W^i_u-W^i_v\) is centred Gaussian with variance \(u-2\min(u,v)+v=|u-v|\), by the computation of the previous step. Since the squared Euclidean norm is the sum of the squared coordinates, linearity of expectation gives

\[\bigl\|[B_u]-[B_v]\bigr\|_2^2=\sum_{i\in\iota}\mathbb E\bigl[(W^i_u-W^i_v)^2\bigr]=d\,|u-v|.\qquad(1)\]

(This is the exact increment norm ; no independence between coordinates is used, because no products of different coordinates occur.) The positive part is \(1\)-Lipschitz, \(|u^+-v^+|\le|u-v|\) for all real \(u,v\). By (1), for all real \(u,v\),

\[\|\beta(u)-\beta(v)\|_2=\sqrt{d\,|u^+-v^+|}\le\sqrt{d\,|u-v|},\]

and the right-hand side tends to \(0\) as \(u\to v\). Hence \(\beta\) is continuous.

Step 2: composition. The translation \(t\mapsto a+t\) is continuous, so \(t\mapsto\beta(a+t)\) is continuous. Subtracting the fixed element \(\beta(a)\) and multiplying by the fixed scalar \(\sqrt2\) are continuous maps of the normed space \(L^2\), since \(\|(x-c)-(y-c)\|_2=\|x-y\|_2\) and \(\|\sqrt2x-\sqrt2y\|_2=\sqrt2\|x-y\|_2\). The composition \(t\mapsto\sqrt2(\beta(a+t)-\beta(a))=N_a(t)\) is therefore continuous. \(\square\)

Continuity in the norm of \(L^2\) concerns the random vectors as elements of \(L^2\); it says nothing about continuity of the individual sample paths \(t\mapsto B_t(\omega)\). It is the only regularity of the additive input that the existence theorem for the integral equation requires.

steps.title: The Brownian input at zero

steps.title: The exact input norm
steps.body:
Claim. Let \((W^i)_{i\in\iota}\) be pre-Brownian motions, \(d=|\iota|\), and let \(a\ge0\) and \(t\ge0\). Then

\[\|N_a(t)\|_2=\sqrt{2d}\,\sqrt t.\]

\[\mathbb E\|B_{a+t}-B_a\|^2=\sum_{i\in\iota}\mathbb E\bigl[(W^i_{a+t}-W^i_a)^2\bigr]=\sum_{i\in\iota}t=d\,t,\]

so \(\|[B_{a+t}-B_a]\|_2=\sqrt{dt}\). The norm is absolutely homogeneous and \(\sqrt2>0\), hence

\[\|N_a(t)\|_2=\sqrt2\,\sqrt{dt}=\sqrt2\,\sqrt d\,\sqrt t=\sqrt{2d}\,\sqrt t,\]

where \(\sqrt{xy}=\sqrt x\sqrt y\) for \(x,y\ge0\) was used twice. \(\square\)

Both sign conditions are used: \(\sqrt t\) requires \(t\ge0\), and the first step requires \(a\ge0\). If \(a<0\), then \(\beta(a)=\beta(0)\) and \(N_a(t)\) is the increment over \([0,(a+t)^+]\), of norm \(\sqrt{2d\,(a+t)^+}\) instead of \(\sqrt{2dt}\). steps.title: A short-interval square-mean Langevin solution
steps.body:
Let \(U:\mathbb R^\iota\to\mathbb R\) and let \(g=\nabla U\) be its gradient, with the convention \(g(x)=0\) at points where \(U\) is not differentiable. Assume that \(g\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz for some \(L\ge0\): \(\|g(x)-g(y)\|\le L\|x-y\|\). Then \(\|g(x)\|\le\|g(0)\|+L\|x\|\), so for \(X\in L^2\) the random vector \(g\circ X\) is square integrable (here the finiteness of \(P\) is used for the constant \(g(0)\)), its class does not depend on the representative of \(X\), and

\[\mathcal G:L^2\to L^2,\qquad \mathcal G[X]=[g\circ X],\qquad \|\mathcal G[X]-\mathcal G[X']\|_2\le L\|X-X'\|_2 .\]

For a continuous curve \(Y:\mathbb R\to L^2\), the map \(s\mapsto\mathcal G(Y(s))\) is continuous, and \(\int_0^t\mathcal G(Y(s))\,ds\) denotes its Bochner integral in \(L^2\) over \([0,t]\).

Claim. Let \(P\) be a probability measure, \(U\) and \(L\) as above, \(X_0\in L^2\), \((W^i)_{i\in\iota}\) pre-Brownian motions, and \(a,h\in\mathbb R\) with \(a\ge0\), \(h\ge0\) and \(Lh\le\tfrac12\). Then there is a continuous \(Y:\mathbb R\to L^2\) with \(Y(0)=X_0\) such that for every \(t\in[0,h]\)

\[Y(t)-X_0=-\int_0^t\mathcal G\bigl(Y(s)\bigr)\,ds+N_a(t)\qquad\text{and}\qquad\|N_a(t)\|_2=\sqrt{2d}\,\sqrt t.\]

Proof. The short-interval existence theorem for the integral equation with additive input in \(L^2\) states: if \(P\) is a probability measure, \(g=\nabla U\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, \(X_0\in L^2\), the input \(N:\mathbb R\to L^2\) is continuous with \(N(0)=0\), and \(0\le h\), \(Lh\le\frac12\), then there is a continuous \(Y\) with \(Y(0)=X_0\) and \(Y(t)-X_0=-\int_0^t\mathcal G(Y(s))\,ds+N(t)\) for \(t\in[0,h]\). (There the solution is written \(Y=Z+N\); the curve \(Z\) solves \(Z(t)=X_0+\int_0^tf(s,Z(s))\,ds\) with \(f(s,z)=-\mathcal G(z+N(s))\), which is continuous in \(s\) and \(L\)-Lipschitz in \(z\), and the Picard–Lindelöf theorem on \([0,h]\) provides \(Z\); the condition \(Lh\le\frac12\) is the smallness condition of that application.)

We apply it with \(N=N_a\). Continuity of \(N_a\) is the second step and \(N_a(0)=0\) is the third step; the remaining hypotheses are hypotheses of the claim. This gives \(Y\) with the first two properties and the integral equation. For \(t\in[0,h]\) we have \(t\ge0\), and together with \(a\ge0\) the fourth step gives \(\|N_a(t)\|_2=\sqrt{2d}\sqrt t\). \(\square\)

The hypothesis \(a\ge0\) is used only for the norm identity; the equation itself would hold for any real \(a\).

steps.title: A solution on every finite horizon
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(P\) be a probability measure, let \(g=\nabla U\) be \(L\)-Lipschitz (with the convention of the previous step), \(X_0\in L^2\), \((W^i)_{i\in\iota}\) pre-Brownian motions, and \(a\ge0\), \(h\ge0\). \[Y(t)-X_0=-\int_0^t\mathcal G\bigl(Y(s)\bigr)\,ds+N_a(t)\qquad\text{and}\qquad\|N_a(t)\|_2=\sqrt{2d}\,\sqrt t.\]

Its proof fixes \(\delta=1/(2(L+1))\), so that \(L\delta\le\frac12\), and constructs by induction on \(n\) a continuous solution on \([0,n\delta]\): a solution on \([0,n\delta]\) is continued by solving the short-interval problem on an interval of length \(\delta\) with initial value \(Y(n\delta)\) and the shifted input \(s\mapsto N_a(n\delta+s)-N_a(n\delta)\), and the two pieces are joined at \(n\delta\). Choosing \(n\ge h/\delta\) covers \([0,h]\).

This gives \(Y\), its continuity, \(Y(0)=X_0\) and the integral equation on \([0,h]\). For \(t\in[0,h]\), the inequalities \(t\ge0\) and \(a\ge0\) and the fourth step give \(\|N_a(t)\|_2=\sqrt{2d}\sqrt t\). \(\square\)

The norm identity concerns the input, not the unknown \(Y\); it is recorded with the solution because the error estimates for the Euler scheme use the size of the input over each step.
