UnadjustedLangevin/BrownianReference.lea.title: Brownian reference segments for the coupling argument
UnadjustedLangevin/BrownianReference.lea.summary:
We keep the setting of the previous section: \(P\) is a probability measure on \(\Omega\), \(\iota\) is a finite set with \(d=|\iota|\) elements, \((W^i)_{i\in\iota}\) are real pre-Brownian motions with \(B_t=(W^i_t)_{i\in\iota}\), \(L^2=L^2(P;\mathbb R^\iota)\), the gradient \(g=\nabla U\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, \(\mathcal G[X]=[g\circ X]\) is its action on \(L^2\), and \(N_a(t)=\sqrt2([B_{a+t}]-[B_a])\) is the Langevin input started at time \(a\). Fix a step \(h\) and an initial vector \(X_0\in L^2\).

On the \(n\)-th time interval \([nh,(n+1)h]\) we take a solution of the integral equation driven by \(N_{nh}\), started at a knot \(K_n\in L^2\); the knots are defined recursively by \(K_0=X_0\) and \(K_{n+1}\) equal to the endpoint of the \(n\)-th segment. The resulting family of segments \(Y^{(n)}:\mathbb R\to L^2\) represents the Langevin diffusion started at \(X_0\), observed on consecutive intervals of length \(h\), with every segment driven by increments of the same Brownian vector. We also define the normalised endpoint increments \(\xi_n=N_{nh}(h)/\sqrt{2h}\), which serve as the innovations of the Euler scheme, and prove \(N_{nh}(h)=\sqrt{2h}\,\xi_n\) as an identity in \(L^2\).

Finally we verify that the segments, inputs and innovations satisfy all requirements of a stationary reference in the coupling proof of the error bound for the unadjusted Langevin algorithm (continuity, joining, endpoint noise, integral equation, gradient and noise moment bounds), under the explicit hypothesis that every \(Y^{(n)}(t)\), \(t\in[0,h]\), has the Gibbs law \(\pi\). That hypothesis is not proved here; it is established in the section on Gibbs stationarity and discharged in the construction of the canonical reference.

steps.title: A Brownian-driven segment from a given initial class
steps.body:
Definition. Let \(h\ge0\), \(n\in\mathbb N\) and \(X\in L^2\). The start time \(a=nh\) satisfies \(a\ge0\), because \(n\ge0\) and \(h\ge0\). The finite-horizon existence theorem of the previous section, applied with initial value \(X\), start time \(nh\) and horizon \(h\), asserts that the set of curves \(Y:\mathbb R\to L^2\) with

\[\begin{gathered}Y\text{ continuous},\qquad Y(0)=X,\\Y(t)-X=-\int_0^t\mathcal G\bigl(Y(s)\bigr)\,ds+N_{nh}(t)\quad(t\in[0,h]),\\\|N_{nh}(t)\|_2=\sqrt{2d}\sqrt t\quad(t\in[0,h]).\end{gathered}\]

is nonempty. By the axiom of choice we fix one element of this set and denote it by \(S_n(X):\mathbb R\to L^2\). It is the segment started at the class \(X\) and driven by the Brownian increments after time \(nh\).

The choice is made once for every triple \((n,X,h)\); nothing else about \(S_n(X)\) is used than the four listed properties, which are recorded in the next step. (Solutions are in fact unique on \([0,h]\) by a Grönwall argument proved elsewhere, but uniqueness is not needed here.)

Classical.choose takes a proof of an existence statement \(\exists Y,\ \Phi(Y)\) and returns a witness; this is the choice in the definition. The start time is (n : ℝ) * h, the natural number \(n\) coerced to a real number times \(h\), and its nonnegativity is supplied by mul_nonneg (Nat.cast_nonneg n) hh, the product of \(n\ge0\) and hh : 0 ≤ h. The argument initial is the starting class \(X\).

steps.title: The defining properties of the segment
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(h\ge0\), \(n\in\mathbb N\) and \(X\in L^2\). The segment \(S_n(X)\) is continuous, satisfies \(S_n(X)(0)=X\), and for every \(t\in[0,h]\)

\[S_n(X)(t)-X=-\int_0^t\mathcal G\bigl(S_n(X)(s)\bigr)\,ds+N_{nh}(t),\qquad \|N_{nh}(t)\|_2=\sqrt{2d}\,\sqrt t.\]

Proof. By definition \(S_n(X)\) is an element of the set of curves having exactly these four properties. \(\square\)

Each property is used later. Continuity makes the Bochner integral of \(s\mapsto\mathcal G(S_n(X)(s))\) meaningful and is part of the reference requirements; the value at \(0\) is used to join consecutive segments; the integral equation gives the local error of one Euler step after subtraction; the norm identity bounds the size of the input on the segment.

The statement is a conjunction A ∧ B ∧ C ∧ D of continuity, the value … 0 = initial, the integral equation for t ∈ Icc 0 h and the norm identity. Later proofs extract the components with projections: .1 is continuity, .2.1 the initial value and .2.2.1 the integral equation.

steps.title: The successive reference knots
steps.body:
Definition. Let \(h\ge0\) and \(X_0\in L^2\). The knots \(K_n\in L^2\), \(n\in\mathbb N\), are defined by recursion on \(n\):

\[K_0=X_0,\qquad K_{n+1}=S_n(K_n)(h).\]

Each \(K_n\) is an element of \(L^2\): \(K_0\) by assumption, and \(K_{n+1}\) because \(S_n(K_n)\) takes values in \(L^2\). The knot \(K_{n+1}\) is the value at time \((n+1)h\) of the process started at \(X_0\) at time \(0\), obtained by running the integral equation through the intervals \([0,h],[h,2h],\dots,[nh,(n+1)h]\), each time starting from the endpoint of the previous interval.

Lean accepts the recursion because the recursive call is at the smaller index \(n\).

steps.title: The reference segments
steps.body:
Definition. Let \(h\ge0\) and \(X_0\in L^2\). The \(n\)-th reference segment is

\[Y^{(n)}=S_n(K_n):\mathbb R\to L^2,\qquad n\in\mathbb N.\]

Its local time \(t\in[0,h]\) corresponds to the absolute time \(nh+t\). The segment starts from the knot \(K_n\) and is driven by the input \(N_{nh}(t)=\sqrt2([B_{nh+t}]-[B_{nh}])\) for \(nh,t\ge0\), that is, by the increments of the same Brownian vector \(B\) after time \(nh\). In particular its endpoint input \(N_{nh}(h)=\sqrt2([B_{(n+1)h}]-[B_{nh}])\) is the Brownian increment over the \(n\)-th interval, which will also drive the \(n\)-th Euler step.

steps.title: The starting value of each segment
steps.body:
Claim. For \(h\ge0\), \(X_0\in L^2\) and every \(n\in\mathbb N\), \(Y^{(n)}(0)=K_n\).

Proof. By definition \(Y^{(n)}=S_n(K_n)\), and the second property of the segment (with \(X=K_n\)) gives \(S_n(K_n)(0)=K_n\). \(\square\)

Combined with the recursion \(K_{n+1}=S_n(K_n)(h)=Y^{(n)}(h)\), this gives the joining identity \(Y^{(n)}(h)=K_{n+1}=Y^{(n+1)}(0)\) for every \(n\): consecutive segments agree at the common time \((n+1)h\) as elements of \(L^2\), so the concatenated process has no jumps at the knots.

The attribute @[simp] lets the simplifier rewrite \(Y^{(n)}(0)\) to \(K_n\).

steps.title: The initial reference knot
steps.body:
Claim. For \(h\ge0\) and \(X_0\in L^2\), \(Y^{(0)}(0)=X_0\).

Proof. By the previous step with \(n=0\), \(Y^{(0)}(0)=K_0\), and \(K_0=X_0\) by the definition of the knots. \(\square\)

The equality is an identity in \(L^2\), not only of laws: the reference process starts from the given random vector \(X_0\) itself. This matters for the coupling argument, where \(X_0\) is chosen jointly with the initial state of the Euler chain, and the initial error is the \(L^2\) distance between these two specific random vectors.

steps.title: The endpoint Euler innovations
steps.body:
Definition. Let \(h>0\) and \(n\in\mathbb N\). The \(n\)-th Euler innovation is

\[\xi_n=\frac{1}{\sqrt{2h}}\,N_{nh}(h)\in L^2.\]

Since \(nh\ge0\) and \(h\ge0\), the first step of the previous section gives \(N_{nh}(h)=[\sqrt2(B_{(n+1)h}-B_{nh})]\), hence

\[\xi_n=\Bigl[\frac{B_{(n+1)h}-B_{nh}}{\sqrt h}\Bigr],\]

and each coordinate of \(\xi_n\) is \(\mathcal N(0,1)\), because \(W^i_{(n+1)h}-W^i_{nh}\sim\mathcal N(0,h)\) and division by \(\sqrt h\) divides the variance by \(h\). The joint law of the innovations (independence across \(n\) and across coordinates) is not used in this section; it is established for the canonical Brownian source in later sections.

The definition is stated for every real \(h\); for \(h\le0\) one has \(\sqrt{2h}=0\) and Lean's convention \(0^{-1}=0\) makes the value \(0\). All uses below assume 0 < h, where the definition is the displayed quotient. The coordinate laws mentioned after the definition are not part of this declaration.

steps.title: Identification of endpoint noise
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(P\) be any measure on \(\Omega\), \((W^i)_{i\in\iota}\) pre-Brownian motions, \(h>0\) and \(n\in\mathbb N\). Then

\[N_{nh}(h)=\sqrt{2h}\;\xi_n\qquad\text{in }L^2.\]

Proof. Since \(h>0\), \(2h>0\) and therefore \(\sqrt{2h}>0\); in particular \(\sqrt{2h}\neq0\). Using the definition of \(\xi_n\) and the rule \(c(c'x)=(cc')x\) for scalar multiplication,

\[\sqrt{2h}\;\xi_n=\sqrt{2h}\Bigl(\frac1{\sqrt{2h}}N_{nh}(h)\Bigr)=\Bigl(\sqrt{2h}\cdot\frac1{\sqrt{2h}}\Bigr)N_{nh}(h)=1\cdot N_{nh}(h)=N_{nh}(h).\qquad\square\]

This is an identity between elements of \(L^2\), stronger than equality of laws. When the Euler update \(X_{n+1}=X_n-h\,g(X_n)+\sqrt{2h}\,\xi_n\) is compared with the reference endpoint \(Y^{(n)}(h)=Y^{(n)}(0)-\int_0^h\mathcal G(Y^{(n)}(s))\,ds+N_{nh}(h)\), the two noise terms are equal and cancel in the difference. The positivity \(h>0\) is needed to divide by \(\sqrt{2h}\).

steps.title: The stationary Brownian reference
steps.body:
Recall the Gibbs measure of \(U\): with the partition function \(Z=\int_{\mathbb R^\iota}e^{-U(x)}\,dx\in(0,\infty]\),

\[\pi(dx)=Z^{-1}e^{-U(x)}\,dx .\]

If \(U\) is continuous then \(Z>0\), and if moreover \(Z<\infty\) then \(\pi\) is a probability measure. A stationary reference for \(\pi\) with step \(h\) and innovations \((\xi_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\subseteq L^2\) (as defined in the section on Dalalyan's argument) is a pair of families of curves \(Y^{(n)},M^{(n)}:\mathbb R\to L^2\), \(n\in\mathbb N\), such that for all \(n\in\mathbb N\) and all \(t\in[0,h]\):

  1. (R1) \(Y^{(n)}\) is continuous;
  2. (R2) \(Y^{(n)}(h)=Y^{(n+1)}(0)\);
  3. (R3) \(M^{(n)}(h)=\sqrt{2h}\,\xi_n\);
  4. (R4) the law of \(Y^{(n)}(0)\) is \(\pi\);
  5. (R5) \(Y^{(n)}(t)-Y^{(n)}(0)=-\int_0^t\mathcal G(Y^{(n)}(s))\,ds+M^{(n)}(t)\);
  6. (R6) \(\|\mathcal G(Y^{(n)}(t))\|_2\le\sqrt{Ld}\);
  7. (R7) \(\|M^{(n)}(t)\|_2\le\sqrt{2d}\,\sqrt t\).

Claim. Let \(P\) be a probability measure, \(U:\mathbb R^\iota\to\mathbb R\) differentiable with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, \(Z<\infty\), \((W^i)_{i\in\iota}\) pre-Brownian motions, \(h>0\) and \(X_0\in L^2\). Assume

\[\text{the law of }Y^{(n)}(t)\text{ is }\pi\qquad\text{for all }n\in\mathbb N\text{ and }t\in[0,h].\qquad(1)\]

Then \(Y^{(n)}\) (the segments of this section) and \(M^{(n)}=N_{nh}\) form a stationary reference for \(\pi\) with step \(h\) and innovations \(\xi_n=N_{nh}(h)/\sqrt{2h}\).

Proof. We verify (R1)–(R7); \(h\ge0\) is used in the form \(h>0\Rightarrow h\ge0\).

(R1) \(Y^{(n)}=S_n(K_n)\) is continuous by the specification of the segment.

(R2) By the recursion of the knots and the starting value of segment \(n+1\), \(Y^{(n)}(h)=S_n(K_n)(h)=K_{n+1}=S_{n+1}(K_{n+1})(0)=Y^{(n+1)}(0)\).

(R3) This is the endpoint identity \(N_{nh}(h)=\sqrt{2h}\,\xi_n\) of the previous step, which uses \(h>0\).

(R4) Apply (1) at \(t=0\), which lies in \([0,h]\) because \(h\ge0\).

(R5) The specification of \(S_n(K_n)\) gives \(Y^{(n)}(t)-K_n=-\int_0^t\mathcal G(Y^{(n)}(s))\,ds+N_{nh}(t)\) for \(t\in[0,h]\), and \(K_n=Y^{(n)}(0)\).

(R6) Fix \(t\in[0,h]\) and put \(V=Y^{(n)}(t)\), whose law is \(\pi\) by (1). The class \(\mathcal G(V)\) is represented by \(g\circ V\), so by the change-of-variables formula for the image measure,

\[\|\mathcal G(V)\|_2^2=\mathbb E\,\|\nabla U(V)\|^2=\int_{\mathbb R^\iota}\|\nabla U(x)\|^2\,\pi(dx)\le L\,d,\]

where the last inequality is the Gibbs gradient moment bound , valid for differentiable \(U\) with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient and \(Z<\infty\) on a space of dimension \(d\). Taking nonnegative square roots gives (R6); this is the moment transfer .

(R7) Since \(nh\ge0\) and \(t\ge0\), the norm identity of the previous section gives \(\|N_{nh}(t)\|_2=\sqrt{2d}\sqrt t\), in particular \(\le\). \(\square\)

Hypothesis (1) is used only for (R4) and (R6). It is a statement about the constructed process and is not a consequence of the integral equation alone: it requires in addition that \(X_0\) has law \(\pi\) and is independent of the Brownian increments, and its proof (by comparison with Metropolis-adjusted chains) is given in later sections.

steps.title: The reference under strong convexity
steps.body:
Recall that \(U\) is \(m\)-strongly convex on \(\mathbb R^\iota\) if for all \(x,y\) and all \(a,b\ge0\) with \(a+b=1\),

\[U(ax+by)\le aU(x)+bU(y)- rac m2\,ab\,\|x-y\|^2 .\]

Let \(P\) be a probability measure, \(m>0\), \(U:\mathbb R^\iota o\mathbb R\) differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, \((W^i)_{i\in\iota}\) pre-Brownian motions, \(h>0\), \(X_0\in L^2\), and assume the stationarity hypothesis (1) of the previous step. Then the same families \(Y^{(n)}\), \(N_{nh}\), \(\xi_n\) form a stationary reference for \(\pi\).

Proof. The only hypothesis of the previous step that is not assumed here is \(Z<\infty\). It follows from strong convexity : the first-order inequality \(U(x)\ge U(0)+\langle abla U(0),x angle+ rac m2\|x\|^2\), the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and Young's inequality \(\| abla U(0)\|\,\|x\|\le rac m4\|x\|^2+\| abla U(0)\|^2/m\) give the quadratic lower bound \(U(x)\ge U(0)-\| abla U(0)\|^2/m+ rac m4\|x\|^2\) for all \(x\), so \(e^{-U(x)}\le C e^{-m\|x\|^2/4}\) with \(C=e^{-U(0)+\| abla U(0)\|^2/m}\), and the Gaussian function on the right is Lebesgue integrable. Hence \(Z<\infty\), and the previous step applies. \(\square\)

After this step the stationarity hypothesis (1) is the only assumption on the reference that remains to be proved.

UnadjustedLangevin/BrownianSegmentsGloba.title: Reference segments as restrictions of one global solution
UnadjustedLangevin/BrownianSegmentsGloba.summary:
We keep the notation of the two preceding sections: \(L^2=L^2(P;\mathbb R^\iota)\), \(\mathcal G[X]=[\nabla U\circ X]\) for an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, the Brownian input \(N_a(t)=\sqrt2(\beta(a+t)-\beta(a))\), the chosen segments \(S_n(X)\), the knots \(K_n\) and the reference segments \(Y^{(n)}=S_n(K_n)\) for a step \(h\ge0\) and initial vector \(X_0\in L^2\). Let \(T\in\mathbb R\) and let \(Y:\mathbb R\to L^2\) be a continuous curve satisfying the global integral equation

\[Y(t)-X_0=-\int_0^t\mathcal G\bigl(Y(s)\bigr)\,ds+N_0(t),\qquad t\in[0,T].\qquad(\ast)\]

We prove that the segments are pieces of this one curve: \(K_n=Y(nh)\) whenever \(nh\le T\), and \(Y^{(n)}(t)=Y(nh+t)\) for \(t\in[0,h]\) whenever \((n+1)h\le T\). The ingredients are an algebraic identity for the input, \(N_0(a+t)-N_0(a)=N_a(t)\); the observation that the time-shifted curve \(t\mapsto Y(a+t)\) solves the segment equation started at \(Y(a)\) with input \(N_a\); and uniqueness of continuous solutions of the integral equation with given initial value and input. No assertion about laws, stationarity or independence enters. The identification is used later to transfer statements about the law of \(Y(s)\) at fixed times \(s\) to every segment time \(nh+t\).

steps.title: The increment of the Langevin Brownian input
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(P\) be any measure and \((W^i)_{i\in\iota}\) pre-Brownian motions. For all real numbers \(a\) and \(t\),

\[N_0(a+t)-N_0(a)=N_a(t)\qquad\text{in }L^2.\]

Proof. By definition, \(N_0(s)=\sqrt2(\beta(0+s)-\beta(0))=\sqrt2(\beta(s)-\beta(0))\) for every real \(s\). Hence, using linearity of scalar multiplication,

\[N_0(a+t)-N_0(a)=\sqrt2\bigl(\beta(a+t)-\beta(0)\bigr)-\sqrt2\bigl(\beta(a)-\beta(0)\bigr)=\sqrt2\bigl(\beta(a+t)-\beta(a)\bigr)=N_a(t).\qquad\square\]

No sign condition on \(a\) or \(t\) is needed: the identity is linear algebra in \(L^2\). It is the counterpart for the input of the additivity \(\int_0^{a+t}=\int_0^a+\int_a^{a+t}\) of time integrals, and it gives the input of the equation restarted at time \(a\).

The proof unfolds brownianLangevinNoise, simplifies \(0+s\) to \(s\) with simp only [zero_add], and closes the resulting identity between linear combinations of the three classes \(\beta(a+t)\), \(\beta(a)\), \(\beta(0)\) with the tactic module, which normalises both sides as linear combinations with real coefficients and compares them; this is the displayed computation.

steps.title: Shifting the Langevin integral equation
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(P\) be a probability measure, \(\nabla U\) \(L\)-Lipschitz, \(X_0\in L^2\), \((W^i)\) pre-Brownian motions, \(T\in\mathbb R\), and let \(Y:\mathbb R\to L^2\) be continuous and satisfy \((\ast)\) on \([0,T]\). Let \(a\ge0\), \(h\ge0\) with \(a+h\le T\). Then for every \(t\in[0,h]\),

\[Y(a+t)-Y(a)=-\int_0^t\mathcal G\bigl(Y(a+s)\bigr)\,ds+N_a(t).\]

Proof. Fix \(t\in[0,h]\). Then \(a\in[0,T]\), because \(0\le a\le a+h\le T\), and \(a+t\in[0,T]\), because \(0\le a\le a+t\le a+h\le T\).

Increment formula. The map \(s\mapsto\mathcal G(Y(s))\) is continuous, as the composition of the continuous \(Y\) with the Lipschitz map \(\mathcal G\); hence it is Bochner integrable on every bounded interval, and oriented integrals are additive: \(\int_0^{a+t}=\int_0^a+\int_a^{a+t}\). Writing \((\ast)\) at the times \(a+t\) and \(a\) and subtracting, the term \(X_0\) cancels and

\[Y(a+t)-Y(a)=-\int_a^{a+t}\mathcal G\bigl(Y(s)\bigr)\,ds+\bigl(N_0(a+t)-N_0(a)\bigr).\qquad(1)\]

This is the general increment identity for solutions of the integral equation .

Change of variables. Lebesgue measure is invariant under the translation \(r\mapsto a+r\), so

\[\int_a^{a+t}\mathcal G\bigl(Y(s)\bigr)\,ds=\int_0^t\mathcal G\bigl(Y(a+r)\bigr)\,dr.\qquad(2)\]

Conclusion. Substitute (2) and the identity \(N_0(a+t)-N_0(a)=N_a(t)\) of the previous step into (1). \(\square\)

The conclusion says that \(r\mapsto Y(a+r)\) solves, on \([0,h]\), the segment equation with initial value \(Y(a)\) and input \(N_a\). The condition \(a+h\le T\) keeps both times \(a\) and \(a+t\) inside the interval on which \((\ast)\) is assumed.

steps.title: A restarted segment equals the global solution
steps.body:
Claim. Assume the hypotheses of the previous step on \(P,U,L,X_0,(W^i),Y,T\) and \((\ast)\). Let \(h\ge0\), \(n\in\mathbb N\) and \(X\in L^2\) with

\[X=Y(nh)\qquad\text{and}\qquad(n+1)h\le T.\]

Then \(S_n(X)(t)=Y(nh+t)\) for every \(t\in[0,h]\).

Proof. Put \(Z(t)=Y(nh+t)\). This curve is continuous, as the composition of \(Y\) with a translation. Apply the previous step with \(a=nh\ge0\) (since \(n\ge0\) and \(h\ge0\)); its condition \(a+h\le T\) is \(nh+h=(n+1)h\le T\). Using \(X=Y(nh)=Z(0)\), it gives

\[Z(t)-X=-\int_0^t\mathcal G\bigl(Z(s)\bigr)\,ds+N_{nh}(t),\qquad t\in[0,h].\]

By its specification, \(S_n(X)\) is continuous and satisfies the same equation with the same initial value \(X\) and the same input \(N_{nh}\) on \([0,h]\).

Two continuous solutions on \([0,h]\) of the integral equation with the same initial value and the same additive input coincide on \([0,h]\) . We recall the argument. Let \(D(t)=S_n(X)(t)-Z(t)\). Subtracting the two equations, \(X\) and \(N_{nh}(t)\) cancel, so

\[D(t)=-\int_0^t\Bigl(\mathcal G\bigl(S_n(X)(s)\bigr)-\mathcal G\bigl(Z(s)\bigr)\Bigr)\,ds,\qquad t\in[0,h].\]

The integrand is continuous, so by the fundamental theorem of calculus \(D\) is differentiable on \([0,h)\) from the right, with derivative of norm \(\|\mathcal G(S_n(X)(t))-\mathcal G(Z(t))\|_2\le L\|D(t)\|_2\), and \(D(0)=0\). Grönwall's inequality gives \(\|D(t)\|_2\le\|D(0)\|_2e^{Lt}=0\) on \([0,h]\). Hence \(S_n(X)=Z\) on \([0,h]\). \(\square\)

Because the inputs cancel in \(D\), only continuity of the input is required, not differentiability. The statement holds for whichever solution was chosen in the definition of \(S_n(X)\).

Claim. Assume the hypotheses of the second step on \(P,U,L,X_0,(W^i),Y,T\) and \((\ast)\), and in addition \(T\ge0\). Let \(h\ge0\) and \(n\in\mathbb N\) with \(nh\le T\). Then \(K_n=Y(nh)\).

\[K_{n+1}=S_n(K_n)(h)=Y(nh+h)=Y\bigl((n+1)h\bigr).\]

UnadjustedLangevin/ChainLaw.lean.title: The law of a recursion driven by independent noise
UnadjustedLangevin/ChainLaw.lean.summary:
Let \(\mathcal X\) (states) and \(\mathcal Z\) (noise values) be measurable spaces, let \(\mathcal Z^{\mathbb N}\) carry the product \(\sigma\)-algebra generated by the coordinate maps \(w\mapsto w_k\), and let \(F:\mathcal X\times\mathcal Z\to\mathcal X\) be an update rule. The recursion driven by a noise sequence \(w=(w_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}\) is

\[\Phi_0(x,w)=x,\qquad\Phi_{n+1}(x,w)=F\bigl(\Phi_n(x,w),w_n\bigr).\]

For a measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathcal X\) and a measure \(Q\) on \(\mathcal Z^{\mathbb N}\) we define the chain law \(\mathcal L_n(\mu,Q)=(\Phi_n)_\#(\mu\otimes Q)\), the image of the product measure under \(\Phi_n\); here \(f_\#\nu(A)=\nu(f^{-1}(A))\) denotes the image (pushforward) of a measure. We prove that \(\Phi_n\) is measurable when \(F\) is, that \(\mathcal L_0(\mu,Q)=\mu\), and that every realisation of the recursion on a probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\), with an initial state \(X\) independent of the noise sequence \(W\), has law \(\mathcal L_n(P_X,P_W)\), where \(P_X\) is the law of \(X\). If the noise variables \(W_n\) are independent with common law \(\eta\), then \(P_W\) is the infinite product \(\eta^{\otimes\mathbb N}\), so the law of the \(n\)-th iterate depends only on \(F\), \(P_X\) and \(\eta\). Two realisations on different probability spaces with the same input laws therefore have the same output laws.

The main application is the unadjusted Langevin algorithm on \(\mathbb R^d\), with update \(F(x,z)=x-h\nabla U(x)+\sqrt{2h}\,z\), for both the pointwise recursion and its realisation in \(L^2\). Throughout, \(\sqrt{\cdot}\) is the nonnegative square root, with the convention \(\sqrt x=0\) for \(x<0\); the identities of this section hold for every real step \(h\), and the convention only affects \(h<0\), which never occurs in the estimates. Consequently the law of the algorithm does not depend on how the initial state is coupled with other random variables, provided it is independent of the noise; this is what allows the coupling argument to choose the initial coupling freely.

steps.title: The recursion driven by a noise sequence
steps.body:
Definition. For sets \(\mathcal X,\mathcal Z\), a map \(F:\mathcal X\times\mathcal Z\to\mathcal X\), an initial state \(x\in\mathcal X\) and a noise sequence \(w=(w_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}\in\mathcal Z^{\mathbb N}\), define \(\Phi_n(x,w)\in\mathcal X\) by recursion on \(n\):

\[\Phi_0(x,w)=x,\qquad\Phi_{n+1}(x,w)=F\bigl(\Phi_n(x,w),w_n\bigr).\]

By induction, \(\Phi_n(x,w)\) depends only on \(x\) and on \(w_0,\dots,w_{n-1}\): this is clear for \(n=0\), and \(\Phi_{n+1}\) uses \(\Phi_n\) and the single additional coordinate \(w_n\). No measurability or probability enters the definition; laws are assigned to the inputs \((x,w)\) only below.
steps.lean: noiseDrivenChain F initial noise is defined by pattern matching on the index: | 0 => initial and | n + 1 => F (noiseDrivenChain F initial noise n) (noise n). The update has the curried type F : H → Z → H, so F x z is \(F(x,z)\); the noise path is a function noise : ℕ → Z, that is, an element of \(\mathcal Z^{\mathbb N}\). The types H and Z are \(\mathcal X\) and \(\mathcal Z\).

steps.title: The recursion at index zero
steps.body:
Claim. For every update \(F\), initial state \(x\) and noise sequence \(w\), \(\Phi_0(x,w)=x\).

Proof. This is the first clause of the definition. \(\square\)
steps.lean: noiseDrivenChain_zero is proved by rfl: both sides are equal by the defining clause. The attribute @[simp] makes the simplifier use it, which is how it enters the proof of the initial law below.

steps.title: The successor recursion
steps.body:
Claim. For every \(F\), \(x\), \(w\) and \(n\in\mathbb N\), \(\Phi_{n+1}(x,w)=F(\Phi_n(x,w),w_n)\).

Proof. This is the second clause of the definition. \(\square\)

The \((n+1)\)-st state is obtained from the \(n\)-th state with the noise value \(w_n\), and \(\Phi_n(x,w)\) depends only on \(w_0,\dots,w_{n-1}\); the noise used in a step is therefore not yet used by the current state.

steps.title: Measurability of the iterates
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(\mathcal X,\mathcal Z\) be measurable spaces and let \(F:\mathcal X\times\mathcal Z\to\mathcal X\) be measurable for the product \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\mathcal X\times\mathcal Z\). Then for every \(n\in\mathbb N\) the map \((x,w)\mapsto\Phi_n(x,w)\) is measurable from \(\mathcal X\times\mathcal Z^{\mathbb N}\) to \(\mathcal X\).

Proof. Induction on \(n\).

Base case. \(\Phi_0(x,w)=x\) is the first coordinate projection, which is measurable for the product \(\sigma\)-algebra by definition of that \(\sigma\)-algebra.

Inductive step. Assume \(\Phi_n\) is measurable. The map \((x,w)\mapsto w_n\) is the composition of the second projection with the coordinate map \(w\mapsto w_n\), and both are measurable (the latter by definition of the product \(\sigma\)-algebra on \(\mathcal Z^{\mathbb N}\)). A map into a product \(\mathcal X\times\mathcal Z\) is measurable if both of its components are, so \((x,w)\mapsto(\Phi_n(x,w),w_n)\) is measurable. Composing with the measurable \(F\) shows that \(\Phi_{n+1}(x,w)=F(\Phi_n(x,w),w_n)\) is measurable. \(\square\)

Only joint measurability of \(F\) is used, not continuity. Measurability of \(\Phi_n\) is what makes the image measures below well defined.

The conclusion is measurability of fun p : H × (ℕ → Z) ↦ noiseDrivenChain F p.1 p.2 n, where p.1 and p.2 are the two components of the pair. The proof is induction n with: the zero case is measurable_fst; the succ case is hF.comp (ih.prodMk ((measurable_pi_apply n).comp measurable_snd)), in which ih.prodMk pairs the measurable \(\Phi_n\) with the measurable map \((x,w)\mapsto w_n\) (the coordinate evaluation measurable_pi_apply n after the projection measurable_snd), and hF.comp composes with \(F\).

steps.title: The chain law as an image of a product measure
steps.body:
Definition. Let \(\mu\) be a measure on \(\mathcal X\), \(Q\) a measure on \(\mathcal Z^{\mathbb N}\) and \(n\in\mathbb N\). The law of the \(n\)-th iterate with initial law \(\mu\) and noise-path law \(Q\) is the image of the product measure under \(\Phi_n\):

\[\mathcal L_n(\mu,Q)=(\Phi_n)_\#(\mu\otimes Q),\qquad\mathcal L_n(\mu,Q)(A)=(\mu\otimes Q)\bigl(\{(x,w):\Phi_n(x,w)\in A\}\bigr)\]

for measurable \(A\subseteq\mathcal X\) (when \(F\) is measurable, the set on the right is measurable by the previous step). Under \(\mu\otimes Q\) the two coordinates \(x\) and \(w\) are independent with laws \(\mu\) and \(Q\); the coordinates of \(w\) may be dependent under \(Q\). The definition involves only \(F\), \(\mu\) and \(Q\), not a probability space on which the algorithm is run.

Mathlib's Measure.map returns the zero measure when the map is not almost-everywhere measurable; with a measurable update this case does not occur, by noiseDrivenChain_measurable.

steps.title: The initial law
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(\mu\) be a measure on \(\mathcal X\) and \(Q\) a probability measure on \(\mathcal Z^{\mathbb N}\). Then \(\mathcal L_0(\mu,Q)=\mu\).

Proof. Since \(\Phi_0(x,w)=x\), the map \(\Phi_0\) is the first projection. For measurable \(A\subseteq\mathcal X\) the preimage is the rectangle \(A\times\mathcal Z^{\mathbb N}\), and the product measure of a rectangle is the product of the measures of its sides:

\[\mathcal L_0(\mu,Q)(A)=(\mu\otimes Q)\bigl(A\times\mathcal Z^{\mathbb N}\bigr)=\mu(A)\,Q(\mathcal Z^{\mathbb N})=\mu(A)\cdot1=\mu(A).\]

Two measures that agree on all measurable sets are equal. \(\square\)

The hypothesis \(Q(\mathcal Z^{\mathbb N})=1\) is used in the third equality; for a general finite \(Q\) the result would be \(Q(\mathcal Z^{\mathbb N})\,\mu\).

The proof simp [chainLaw] unfolds the definition, rewrites \(\Phi_0(x,w)=x\) with the simp lemma noiseDrivenChain_zero (so the map becomes the first projection), and then uses Mathlib's simp lemmas for the first marginal of a product measure, \((\mu\otimes Q)\circ\mathrm{pr}_1^{-1}=Q(\mathcal Z^{\mathbb N})\,\mu\), and for the total mass \(1\) of a probability measure.

steps.title: The law of an independent realisation
steps.body:
Recall that random variables \(X:\Omega\to\mathcal X\) and \(W:\Omega\to\mathcal Z^{\mathbb N}\) on a probability space \((\Omega,\mathcal F,P)\) are independent if \(P(X\in A,\ W\in B)=P(X\in A)\,P(W\in B)\) for all measurable \(A\), \(B\); equivalently, the joint law of \((X,W)\) is the product of the marginal laws, \(P_{(X,W)}=P_X\otimes P_W\) (two measures on a product space that agree on measurable rectangles agree, by the uniqueness of extension from a \(\pi\)-system).

Claim. Let \(P\) be a probability measure on \(\Omega\), \(F\) measurable, \(X:\Omega\to\mathcal X\) and \(W:\Omega\to\mathcal Z^{\mathbb N}\) almost-everywhere measurable and independent. Then for every \(n\),

\[P_{\Phi_n(X,W)}=\mathcal L_n(P_X,P_W),\]

where \(\Phi_n(X,W)\) is the random variable \(\omega\mapsto\Phi_n(X(\omega),W(\omega))\).

Proof. The random variable \(\Phi_n(X,W)\) is the composition of \(\omega\mapsto(X(\omega),W(\omega))\) with \(\Phi_n\). The image of a measure under a composition is the iterated image, \((\Phi_n\circ(X,W))_\#P=(\Phi_n)_\#\bigl((X,W)_\#P\bigr)\); this holds for the measurable \(\Phi_n\) (previous measurability step) and the almost-everywhere measurable pair \((X,W)\). By independence \((X,W)_\#P=P_X\otimes P_W\). Hence

\[P_{\Phi_n(X,W)}=(\Phi_n)_\#\bigl(P_X\otimes P_W\bigr)=\mathcal L_n(P_X,P_W).\qquad\square\]

Only independence of \(X\) from the whole noise sequence is used; the coordinates of \(W\) may depend on each other.

steps.title: Independent identically distributed innovations
steps.body:
Recall that \(W_0,W_1,\dots\) are (mutually) independent if for all finite sets \(J\subseteq\mathbb N\) and measurable \(B_j\subseteq\mathcal Z\), \(P(W_j\in B_j\ \forall j\in J)=\prod_{j\in J}P(W_j\in B_j)\). For a probability measure \(\eta\) on \(\mathcal Z\), the infinite product \(\eta^{\otimes\mathbb N}\) is the unique probability measure on \(\mathcal Z^{\mathbb N}\) with \(\eta^{\otimes\mathbb N}(\{w:w_j\in B_j\ \forall j\in J\})=\prod_{j\in J}\eta(B_j)\) for all such \(J\) and \(B_j\).

Claim. Let \(P\) be a probability measure, \(F\) measurable, \(X:\Omega\to\mathcal X\) and \(W_k:\Omega\to\mathcal Z\) (\(k\in\mathbb N\)) almost-everywhere measurable, with \(X\) independent of the sequence \(W=(W_k)_{k\in\mathbb N}\), the \(W_k\) mutually independent, and \(P_{W_k}=\eta\) for every \(k\). Then for every \(n\),

\[P_{\Phi_n(X,W)}=\mathcal L_n\bigl(P_X,\eta^{\otimes\mathbb N}\bigr).\]

Proof. Path law. The map \(\omega\mapsto(W_k(\omega))_{k}\) into \(\mathcal Z^{\mathbb N}\) is almost-everywhere measurable, because each coordinate is and the index set \(\mathbb N\) is countable. For finite \(J\) and measurable \(B_j\), independence and \(P_{W_j}=\eta\) give

\[P_W\bigl(\{w:w_j\in B_j\ \forall j\in J\}\bigr)=\prod_{j\in J}P(W_j\in B_j)=\prod_{j\in J}\eta(B_j),\]

so by the uniqueness of the infinite product, \(P_W=\eta^{\otimes\mathbb N}\).

Conclusion. The previous step, applied to \(X\) and the sequence \(W\), gives \(P_{\Phi_n(X,W)}=\mathcal L_n(P_X,P_W)=\mathcal L_n(P_X,\eta^{\otimes\mathbb N})\). \(\square\)

steps.title: Equal input laws give equal output laws
steps.body:
Claim. Let \((\Omega,P)\) and \((\Omega',P')\) be probability spaces and \(F\) measurable. Let \(X,(W_k)\) on \(\Omega\) and \(X',(W'_k)\) on \(\Omega'\) satisfy the hypotheses of the previous step with the same noise law \(\eta\), and assume \(P_X=P'_{X'}\). Then for every \(n\), \(\Phi_n(X,W)\) under \(P\) and \(\Phi_n(X',W')\) under \(P'\) have the same law.

Proof. By the previous step applied on each space,

\[P_{\Phi_n(X,W)}=\mathcal L_n\bigl(P_X,\eta^{\otimes\mathbb N}\bigr)=\mathcal L_n\bigl(P'_{X'},\eta^{\otimes\mathbb N}\bigr)=P'_{\Phi_n(X',W')},\]

where the middle equality substitutes \(P_X=P'_{X'}\). \(\square\)

No relation between the two probability spaces is required. In the coupling argument this is applied to realisations of the algorithm on extensions of a probability space that carry different couplings of the initial state with a stationary reference; all of them produce the same law of the algorithm.

steps.title: Equality with the ULA recursion
steps.body:
For \(d\in\mathbb N\), \(U:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) and \(h\in\mathbb R\), the ULA update is

\[F_h(x,z)=x-h\nabla U(x)+\sqrt{2h}\,z,\qquad x,z\in\mathbb R^d,\]

and the ULA chain with initial state \(x\) and innovations \(w=(w_k)\) is \(X_0=x\), \(X_{k+1}=F_h(X_k,w_k)\), as defined in the section on the noise-driven ULA chain.

steps.title: Measurability of the ULA update
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(d\in\mathbb N\), \(h\in\mathbb R\), \(L\ge0\), and let \(U:\mathbb R^d o\mathbb R\) have an \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. Then \(F_h:\mathbb R^d imes\mathbb R^d o\mathbb R^d\) is measurable for the product of the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebras.

Proof. A Lipschitz map is continuous, and a continuous map between metric spaces is Borel measurable; hence \( abla U\) is measurable. The projections \((x,z)\mapsto x\) and \((x,z)\mapsto z\) are measurable, so \((x,z)\mapsto h abla U(x)\) and \((x,z)\mapsto\sqrt{2h}\,z\) are measurable (compositions and multiplication by constants). On \(\mathbb R^d\), which is second countable, the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra of \(\mathbb R^d imes\mathbb R^d\) is the product of the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebras, so the sum and difference of two measurable \(\mathbb R^d\)-valued maps are measurable. Therefore \(F_h(x,z)=x-h abla U(x)+\sqrt{2h}\,z\) is measurable. \(\square\)

The Lipschitz hypothesis is used only through continuity of \( abla U\); no condition on \(h\) or on convexity is required.

steps.title: The law of the ULA chain
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(P\) be a probability measure, \(d\in\mathbb N\), \(h\in\mathbb R\), \(L\ge0\), \(U:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, and let \(X\) and \(W_k\) (\(k\in\mathbb N\)) be almost-everywhere measurable \(\mathbb R^d\)-valued random variables with \(X\) independent of \((W_k)_k\), the \(W_k\) mutually independent and \(P_{W_k}=\eta\) for all \(k\). Then the \(n\)-th ULA iterate \(X_n\) with initial state \(X\) and innovations \(W_k\) satisfies

\[P_{X_n}=\mathcal L_n\bigl(P_X,\eta^{\otimes\mathbb N}\bigr)\qquad\text{with }F=F_h.\]

Proof. By the previous step \(F_h\) is measurable, so the independent identically distributed case applies to \(F=F_h\) and gives \(P_{\Phi_n(X,W)}=\mathcal L_n(P_X,\eta^{\otimes\mathbb N})\). By the identification step, \(\Phi_n(X(\omega),W(\omega))=X_n(\omega)\) for every \(\omega\). \(\square\)

When \(\eta\) is the standard Gaussian law on \(\mathbb R^d\), \(\mathcal L_n(\mu,\eta^{\otimes\mathbb N})\) is the law of the unadjusted Langevin algorithm after \(n\) steps started from \(\mu\).

steps.title: The square-integrable chain has the same law
steps.body:
Let \(\mathcal G[X]=[\nabla U\circ X]\) be the gradient acting on \(L^2=L^2(P;\mathbb R^d)\). The ULA chain in \(L^2\), with initial class \(X\) and innovation classes \(W_k\), is \(\mathcal X_0=X\), \(\mathcal X_{k+1}=\mathcal X_k-h\,\mathcal G(\mathcal X_k)+\sqrt{2h}\,W_k\). The law of a class is the law of any representative; it does not depend on the representative, because almost-everywhere equal functions have the same image measure.

Claim. Let \(P\) be a probability measure, \(d\), \(h\), \(L\), \(U\) as in the previous step, \(X\in L^2\) and \(W_k\in L^2\) (\(k\in\mathbb N\)), with (representatives satisfying) \(X\) independent of \((W_k)_k\), the \(W_k\) mutually independent and \(P_{W_k}=\eta\). Then for every \(n\), the law of \(\mathcal X_n\) is \(\mathcal L_n(P_X,\eta^{\otimes\mathbb N})\).

Proof. By the corresponding result for the chain in \(L^2\) , any representative of \(\mathcal X_n\) agrees \(P\)-almost everywhere with \(\omega\mapsto X_n(\omega)\), the pointwise ULA iterate started at \(X(\omega)\) with innovations \(W_k(\omega)\). (Induction on \(n\): \(\mathcal G(\mathcal X_n)\) is represented by \(\nabla U\circ\mathcal X_n\), and a countable union of null sets is null.) Almost-everywhere equal maps have equal images of \(P\), since their preimages of every measurable set differ by a null set. Every element of \(L^2\) has an almost-everywhere measurable representative, so the previous step applies to \(X\) and \((W_k)\) and gives \(P_{X_n}=\mathcal L_n(P_X,\eta^{\otimes\mathbb N})\). \(\square\)

UnadjustedLangevin/MarkovLaw.lean.title: Laws of the recursion as iterated Markov transitions
UnadjustedLangevin/MarkovLaw.lean.summary:
We continue with measurable spaces \(\mathcal X\) (states) and \(\mathcal Z\) (noise values), an update \(F:\mathcal X\times\mathcal Z\to\mathcal X\), the recursion \(\Phi_n\) and the chain laws \(\mathcal L_n(\mu,Q)=(\Phi_n)_\#(\mu\otimes Q)\) of the previous section. For a probability measure \(\eta\) on \(\mathcal Z\) we define the one-step transition acting on laws,

\[M_\eta(\mu)=F_\#(\mu\otimes\eta),\]

which is the law of \(F(X,\xi)\) when \(X\sim\mu\) and \(\xi\sim\eta\) are independent, and its iterates \(\mu_0=\mu\), \(\mu_{n+1}=M_\eta(\mu_n)\). The main result is that for measurable \(F\) and probability measures \(\mu\), \(\eta\),

\[\mathcal L_n\bigl(\mu,\eta^{\otimes\mathbb N}\bigr)=\mu_n\qquad\text{for every }n\in\mathbb N:\]

the law of the recursion driven by independent identically distributed noise is the \(n\)-fold iterate of the one-step transition. The key point is that under \(\mu\otimes\eta^{\otimes\mathbb N}\) the current state \(\Phi_n(x,w)\) is independent of the next noise value \(w_n\); this is proved, not assumed, by writing \(\Phi_n(x,w)\) as a measurable function of \(x\) and the finite prefix \((w_0,\dots,w_{n-1})\), which is independent of \(w_n\). We also show that the transition preserves probability measures, and conclude that every realisation of the recursion with an initial state independent of independent identically distributed noise has the iterated transition laws. These laws are the laws of the unadjusted Langevin algorithm used in the final theorems, where the update is the Gaussian Euler step.

steps.title: The state as a function of a finite noise prefix
steps.body:
Definition. For \(n\in\mathbb N\) write \(\mathcal Z^n\) for the set of finite sequences \(v=(v_0,\dots,v_{n-1})\). Define \(\Psi_n:\mathcal X\times\mathcal Z^n\to\mathcal X\) by recursion on \(n\):

\[\Psi_0(x,\varnothing)=x,\qquad\Psi_{n+1}(x,v)=F\bigl(\Psi_n(x,(v_0,\dots,v_{n-1})),\,v_n\bigr)\quad(v\in\mathcal Z^{n+1}).\]

This is the recursion of the previous section evaluated on a finite noise sequence: in the successor clause the first \(n\) coordinates of \(v\) produce the current state, and the last coordinate \(v_n\) is the noise of the next step. Its purpose is to exhibit the \(n\)-th state as a function of finitely many noise coordinates.

The clauses are | 0, _ => x and | n + 1, w => F (finiteNoiseChain F x (fun i : Fin n ↦ w i.castSucc)) (w (Fin.last n)). Here i.castSucc is the index \(i<n\) regarded as an element of \(\{0,\dots,n\}\), so fun i : Fin n ↦ w i.castSucc is the restriction \((v_0,\dots,v_{n-1})\), and Fin.last n is the last index \(n\).

steps.title: Agreement with the full recursion
steps.body:
Let \(\pi_n:\mathcal Z^{\mathbb N}\to\mathcal Z^n\), \(\pi_n(w)=(w_0,\dots,w_{n-1})\), be the prefix map.

Claim. For every \(F\), \(x\in\mathcal X\), \(w\in\mathcal Z^{\mathbb N}\) and \(n\in\mathbb N\), \(\Psi_n(x,\pi_n(w))=\Phi_n(x,w)\).

Proof. Induction on \(n\). For \(n=0\) both sides equal \(x\). Assume the identity for \(n\). The first \(n\) coordinates of \(\pi_{n+1}(w)\) form \(\pi_n(w)\) and its last coordinate is \(w_n\). Hence, by the definition of \(\Psi_{n+1}\), the induction hypothesis and the successor clause of \(\Phi\),

\[\Psi_{n+1}\bigl(x,\pi_{n+1}(w)\bigr)=F\bigl(\Psi_n(x,\pi_n(w)),w_n\bigr)=F\bigl(\Phi_n(x,w),w_n\bigr)=\Phi_{n+1}(x,w).\qquad\square\]

steps.title: Measurability of the finite-prefix state
steps.body:
Claim. If \(F\) is measurable, then for every \(n\) the map \(\Psi_n:\mathcal X\times\mathcal Z^n\to\mathcal X\) is measurable, where \(\mathcal Z^n\) carries the product \(\sigma\)-algebra.

Proof. Induction on \(n\). \(\Psi_0\) is the first projection, which is measurable. Assume \(\Psi_n\) is measurable. The restriction \(v\mapsto(v_0,\dots,v_{n-1})\) from \(\mathcal Z^{n+1}\) to \(\mathcal Z^n\) and the evaluation \(v\mapsto v_n\) are measurable, because each coordinate of a product is measurable and a map into a finite product is measurable when its coordinates are. Hence \((x,v)\mapsto(x,(v_0,\dots,v_{n-1}))\) is measurable, its composition with \(\Psi_n\) is measurable, the pair \((x,v)\mapsto(\Psi_n(x,(v_0,\dots,v_{n-1})),v_n)\) is measurable, and composing with the measurable \(F\) shows that \(\Psi_{n+1}\) is measurable. \(\square\)

steps.title: Independence of the prefix and the fresh innovation
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(\eta\) be a probability measure on \(\mathcal Z\) and \(Q=\eta^{\otimes\mathbb N}\). Then under \(Q\) the prefix \(\pi_n(w)=(w_0,\dots,w_{n-1})\) and the coordinate \(w_n\) are independent random variables on \(\mathcal Z^{\mathbb N}\).

Proof. Step 1. Under \(Q\) the coordinate maps \(w\mapsto w_k\), \(k\in\mathbb N\), are mutually independent. Indeed, for a finite set \(J\) and measurable \(B_j\), the defining property of the infinite product gives \(Q(w_j\in B_j\ \forall j\in J)=\prod_{j\in J}\eta(B_j)\), and \(\eta(B_j)=Q(w_j\in B_j)\) by the same property with a single index.

Step 2 (grouping). If a family of random variables is mutually independent and \(S,T\) are disjoint finite index sets, then the vectors \((w_k)_{k\in S}\) and \((w_k)_{k\in T}\) are independent. (The events determined by the \(S\)-variables of the form \(\bigcap_{k\in S}\{w_k\in B_k\}\) form a \(\pi\)-system generating their \(\sigma\)-algebra, similarly for \(T\); mutual independence gives the product rule on these \(\pi\)-systems, and the \(\pi\)–\(\lambda\) theorem extends it to the generated \(\sigma\)-algebras.) Apply this with \(S=\{0,\dots,n-1\}\) and \(T=\{n\}\), which are disjoint.

Step 3. Measurable functions of independent random variables are independent. The prefix \(\pi_n(w)\) is the vector \((w_k)_{k\in S}\) re-indexed by \(\{0,\dots,n-1\}\), and \(w_n\) is the value at the single index of \(T\); both re-indexings are measurable. \(\square\)

The statement concerns the whole prefix jointly, which is stronger than independence of \(w_n\) from each \(w_k\), \(k<n\), separately; the joint form is required because the current state depends on all earlier noise values together.

steps.title: The transition acting on a law
steps.body:
Definition. For a measure \(\eta\) on \(\mathcal Z\) and a measure \(\mu\) on \(\mathcal X\), the one-step transition is

\[M_\eta(\mu)=F_\#(\mu\otimes\eta),\qquad M_\eta(\mu)(A)=(\mu\otimes\eta)\bigl(\{(x,z):F(x,z)\in A\}\bigr).\]

If \(X\sim\mu\) and \(\xi\sim\eta\) are independent, then \((X,\xi)\sim\mu\otimes\eta\) and therefore \(F(X,\xi)\sim M_\eta(\mu)\). Equivalently, \(M_\eta(\mu)=\int\kappa(x,\cdot)\,\mu(dx)\) for the Markov kernel \(\kappa(x,\cdot)=F(x,\cdot)_\#\eta\), by Fubini–Tonelli; we work with the product form. Independence of the current state and the noise is built into the definition; for the recursion it is proved below.

steps.title: The iterated Markov laws
steps.body:
Definition. For measures \(\mu\) on \(\mathcal X\) and \(\eta\) on \(\mathcal Z\), the iterated transition laws are defined by recursion:

\[\mu_0=\mu,\qquad\mu_{n+1}=M_\eta(\mu_n).\]

This sequence is defined from \(F\), \(\eta\) and \(\mu\) alone, without any random variables.

steps.title: The joint law of a state and the fresh innovation
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(F\) be measurable, and let \(\mu\) on \(\mathcal X\) and \(\eta\) on \(\mathcal Z\) be probability measures; put \(Q=\eta^{\otimes\mathbb N}\). Then for every \(n\), the joint law of the current state and the next noise value under \(\mu\otimes Q\) is a product:

\[\bigl((x,w)\mapsto(\Phi_n(x,w),w_n)\bigr)_\#(\mu\otimes Q)=\mathcal L_n(\mu,Q)\otimes\eta .\]

Proof. Let \(\rho=(\pi_n)_\#Q\) be the law of the prefix, \(\nu=\mu\otimes\rho\), and \(C=\Psi_n:\mathcal X\times\mathcal Z^n\to\mathcal X\). The prefix map \(\pi_n\) is measurable (each coordinate is), \(C\) is measurable by the measurability step, and \(\rho\) is a probability measure, since \(\rho(\mathcal Z^n)=Q(\pi_n^{-1}(\mathcal Z^n))=Q(\mathcal Z^{\mathbb N})=1\). We use repeatedly the rule \((f\times g)_\#(\alpha\otimes\beta)=f_\#\alpha\otimes g_\#\beta\) for measurable \(f,g\) and \(\sigma\)-finite \(\alpha,\beta\) (both sides agree on rectangles: \((\alpha\otimes\beta)(f^{-1}A\times g^{-1}B)=\alpha(f^{-1}A)\beta(g^{-1}B)\)).

(a) Prefix and fresh coordinate. By the independence step and \((w\mapsto w_n)_\#Q=\eta\) (a coordinate of the infinite product has law \(\eta\)),

\[\bigl(w\mapsto(\pi_n(w),w_n)\bigr)_\#Q=\rho\otimes\eta.\qquad(1)\]

(b) Adding the initial state. Applying the rule above with \(f=\mathrm{id}\) and \(g(w)=(\pi_n(w),w_n)\), and then (1),

\[\bigl((x,w)\mapsto(x,(\pi_n(w),w_n))\bigr)_\#(\mu\otimes Q)=\mu\otimes(\rho\otimes\eta).\qquad(2)\]

(c) Regrouping. The bijection \((x,(v,z))\mapsto((x,v),z)\) is measurable in both directions and carries \(\mu\otimes(\rho\otimes\eta)\) to \((\mu\otimes\rho)\otimes\eta\) (associativity of product measures; both agree on boxes \(A\times B\times D\)). Composing with (2),

\[\bigl((x,w)\mapsto((x,\pi_n(w)),w_n)\bigr)_\#(\mu\otimes Q)=\nu\otimes\eta.\qquad(3)\]

(d) Applying the finite recursion. Push (3) forward by \(C\times\mathrm{id}\) and use the rule above:

\[\bigl((x,w)\mapsto(C(x,\pi_n(w)),w_n)\bigr)_\#(\mu\otimes Q)=C_\#\nu\otimes\eta.\qquad(4)\]

(e) Identifying the state marginal. Take the image of both sides of (4) under the first projection. On the right, the first marginal of \(C_\#\nu\otimes\eta\) is \(\eta(\mathcal Z)\,C_\#\nu=C_\#\nu\). On the left we obtain the law of \(C(x,\pi_n(w))\) under \(\mu\otimes Q\), and \(C(x,\pi_n(w))=\Psi_n(x,\pi_n(w))=\Phi_n(x,w)\) by the agreement step; hence the left side is \(\mathcal L_n(\mu,Q)\). So \(C_\#\nu=\mathcal L_n(\mu,Q)\).

(f) Conclusion. Substituting \(C_\#\nu=\mathcal L_n(\mu,Q)\) in (4) and replacing \(C(x,\pi_n(w))\) by \(\Phi_n(x,w)\) on the left gives the claim. \(\square\)

Thus \(\Phi_n(x,w)\) and \(w_n\) are independent under \(\mu\otimes Q\), with laws \(\mathcal L_n(\mu,Q)\) and \(\eta\). The detour through \(\Psi_n\) is what makes the independence of \(w_n\) from the earlier noise usable: \(\Phi_n\) is a function of the whole sequence \(w\), which is not independent of \(w_n\).

steps.title: The successor law is one transition
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(F\) be measurable and \(\mu\), \(\eta\) probability measures, \(Q=\eta^{\otimes\mathbb N}\). Then for every \(n\), \(\mathcal L_{n+1}(\mu,Q)=M_\eta(\mathcal L_n(\mu,Q))\).

By the successor clause, \(\Phi_{n+1}=F\circ m\). The image under a composition is the iterated image, so by the previous step

\[\mathcal L_{n+1}(\mu,Q)=(F\circ m)_\#(\mu\otimes Q)=F_\#\bigl(m_\#(\mu\otimes Q)\bigr)=F_\#\bigl(\mathcal L_n(\mu,Q)\otimes\eta\bigr)=M_\eta\bigl(\mathcal L_n(\mu,Q)\bigr).\qquad\square\]

steps.title: Probability preservation by one transition
steps.body:
Claim. If \(F\) is measurable and \(\mu\), \(\eta\) are probability measures, then \(M_\eta(\mu)\) is a probability measure.

\[M_\eta(\mu)(\mathcal X)=(\mu\otimes\eta)\bigl(F^{-1}(\mathcal X)\bigr)=(\mu\otimes\eta)(\mathcal X\times\mathcal Z)=\mu(\mathcal X)\,\eta(\mathcal Z)=1.\qquad\square\]

steps.title: Probability preservation at every iterate
steps.body:
Claim. If \(F\) is measurable and \(\mu\), \(\eta\) are probability measures, then every \(\mu_n\) is a probability measure.

Proof. Induction on \(n\): \(\mu_0=\mu\) is a probability measure by assumption, and if \(\mu_n\) is one, then \(\mu_{n+1}=M_\eta(\mu_n)\) is one by the previous step. \(\square\)
steps.lean: markovLaws_isProbability is proved by induction n with. The zero case is inferInstanceAs (IsProbabilityMeasure μ), the assumption on \(\mu\). In the succ case, have := ih places the induction hypothesis in the instance context, so that markovStep_isProbability F hF _ η can use it as the probability assumption on \(\mu_n\).

steps.title: Every independent realisation has the iterated law
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(P\) be a probability measure on \(\Omega\), \(F\) measurable, \(\eta\) a probability measure on \(\mathcal Z\), \(X:\Omega\to\mathcal X\) and \(W_k:\Omega\to\mathcal Z\) almost-everywhere measurable, with \(X\) independent of \((W_k)_k\), the \(W_k\) mutually independent and \(P_{W_k}=\eta\) for every \(k\). Then for every \(n\),

\[P_{\Phi_n(X,W)}=\mu_n\qquad\text{with }\mu_0=P_X,\ \mu_{k+1}=M_\eta(\mu_k).\]

Proof. \(P_X\) is a probability measure, since \(P_X(\mathcal X)=P(X^{-1}(\mathcal X))=P(\Omega)=1\). By the independent identically distributed case of the previous section, \(P_{\Phi_n(X,W)}=\mathcal L_n(P_X,\eta^{\otimes\mathbb N})\), and by the agreement step this is \(\mu_n\). \(\square\)

Independence is assumed only between the initial state and the noise, and among the noise variables. The independence of the state at time \(n\) from the next noise value is a consequence, proved above.
steps.lean: In noiseDrivenChain_law_eq_markovLaws, the local instance IsProbabilityMeasure (P.map X) is proved from Measure.map_apply_of_aemeasurable hX MeasurableSet.univ, Set.preimage_univ and measure_univ. The goal is then rewritten with noiseDrivenChain_law_of_iid P F hF X W hX hW hind hiid η hlaw and with chainLaw_eq_markovLaws F hF (P.map X) η n.

UnadjustedLangevin/InitialExtension.lean.title: An independent-noise extension of every initial coupling
UnadjustedLangevin/InitialExtension.lean.summary:
Let \(\mathcal X\) (states) and \(\mathcal S\) (noise source) be measurable spaces, \(\mu\) and \(\pi\) measures on \(\mathcal X\), and \(Q\) a measure on \(\mathcal S\). A coupling of \(\mu\) and \(\pi\) is a measure \(\gamma\) on \(\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\) whose two marginals are \(\mu\) and \(\pi\): \(\gamma(A\times\mathcal X)=\mu(A)\) and \(\gamma(\mathcal X\times A)=\pi(A)\) for measurable \(A\). When \(\mathcal X\) is a normed space, the cost of \(\gamma\) is

\[\mathcal C(\gamma)=\Bigl(\int\|x-y\|^2\,\gamma(dx,dy)\Bigr)^{1/2}\in[0,\infty],\]

and the Wasserstein distance \(W_2(\mu,\pi)\) is the infimum of \(\mathcal C(\gamma)\) over all couplings \(\gamma\) of \(\mu\) and \(\pi\).

For an arbitrary coupling \(\gamma\) we build the probability space \((\mathcal X\times\mathcal X)\times\mathcal S\) with the product measure \(\gamma\otimes Q\), whose points we write \(((x,y),s)\): \(x\) will be the initial state of the algorithm, \(y\) the initial state of the reference process, and \(s\) the noise. We prove that this extension keeps the joint law \(\gamma\) of \((x,y)\), the marginals \(\mu\), \(\pi\) and \(Q\), and the cost \(\mathcal C(\gamma)\); that \((x,y)\) is independent of \(s\); and that \((x,s)\) has law \(\mu\otimes Q\), whatever \(\gamma\) is. Consequently every measurable function of \((x,s)\) — in particular every iterate of a noise-driven algorithm — has a law that does not depend on the chosen coupling. When the noise is an independent identically distributed sequence, its coordinates are independent with the prescribed law and independent of \(x\).

Finally, if \(\mathcal C(\gamma)<\infty\) and \(\pi\) has a finite second moment, then \(x\) and \(y\) are square integrable on the extension, and the corresponding classes \([x],[y]\in L^2(\gamma\otimes Q;\mathcal X)\) have laws \(\mu\) and \(\pi\) and satisfy \(\|[x]-[y]\|_2=\mathcal C(\gamma)\). This is how the transport bound is proved for every coupling and then optimised over couplings.

steps.title: A coupling of probability measures is a probability measure
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(\mu\) be a probability measure on \(\mathcal X\), \(\pi\) a measure on \(\mathcal X\), and \(\gamma\) a coupling of \(\mu\) and \(\pi\). Then \(\gamma\) is a probability measure.

Proof. The first marginal of \(\gamma\) is \(\mu\), so

\[\gamma(\mathcal X\times\mathcal X)=\gamma\bigl(\mathrm{pr}_1^{-1}(\mathcal X)\bigr)=\mu(\mathcal X)=1.\qquad\square\]

Only the first marginal is used; in the applications both \(\mu\) and \(\pi\) are probability measures.
steps.lean: A coupling is the structure Coupling μ π of the section on couplings, with fields joint (the measure \(\gamma\) on H × H), fst : joint.map Prod.fst = μ and snd : joint.map Prod.snd = π. In Coupling.isProbabilityMeasure the auxiliary instance states that the first marginal is a probability measure: rw [c.fst] turns it into the hypothesis on \(\mu\), closed by infer_instance. Mathlib's Measure.isProbabilityMeasure_of_map then transfers this to \(\gamma\): if the image of a measure under an almost-everywhere measurable map (here measurable_fst.aemeasurable) is a probability measure, so is the measure.

steps.title: Adjoining independent noise
steps.body:
Definition. For a coupling \(\gamma\) of \(\mu\) and \(\pi\) and a measure \(Q\) on \(\mathcal S\), the initial extension is the product measure

\[\mathbb P_\gamma=\gamma\otimes Q\qquad\text{on }(\mathcal X\times\mathcal X)\times\mathcal S .\]

A point \(((x,y),s)\) consists of the coupled initial pair and a noise sample. On this space the coordinate maps \(((x,y),s)\mapsto x\), \(\mapsto y\) and \(\mapsto s\) are random variables; their properties are established in the following steps.
steps.lean: initialExtension c Q is defined as c.joint.prod Q, the product measure on (H × H) × S. In Lean the coordinates of a point p are p.1.1 (\(x\)), p.1.2 (\(y\)), p.1 (the pair) and p.2 (\(s\)).

steps.title: Normalization of the product extension
steps.body:
Claim. If \(\mu\) and \(Q\) are probability measures, then \(\mathbb P_\gamma\) is a probability measure.

Proof. By the first step \(\gamma\) is a probability measure, so

\[\mathbb P_\gamma\bigl((\mathcal X\times\mathcal X)\times\mathcal S\bigr)=\gamma(\mathcal X\times\mathcal X)\,Q(\mathcal S)=1\cdot1=1.\qquad\square\]
steps.lean: initialExtension_isProbabilityMeasure first records c.isProbabilityMeasure as a local instance and then obtains the result from Mathlib's instance for products of probability measures, invoked through inferInstanceAs (IsProbabilityMeasure (c.joint.prod Q)).

steps.title: The retained joint initial law
steps.body:
Claim. If \(Q\) is a probability measure, then the law of \((x,y)\) under \(\mathbb P_\gamma\) is \(\gamma\).

Proof. For measurable \(A\subseteq\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\), the preimage of \(A\) under \(((x,y),s)\mapsto(x,y)\) is \(A\times\mathcal S\), and

\[\mathbb P_\gamma(A\times\mathcal S)=\gamma(A)\,Q(\mathcal S)=\gamma(A).\qquad\square\]

The whole joint law of the initial pair is kept, not only its marginals; the dependence between \(x\) and \(y\) chosen in \(\gamma\) is unchanged.
steps.lean: initialExtension_joint states (initialExtension c Q).map Prod.fst = c.joint. The proof simp [initialExtension] unfolds the definition and applies the Mathlib simp lemma for the first marginal of a product measure (the first marginal of \(\gamma\otimes Q\) is \(Q(\mathcal S)\,\gamma\)) together with \(Q(\mathcal S)=1\).

steps.title: The retained initial law of the algorithm
steps.body:
Claim. If \(Q\) is a probability measure, then the law of \(x\) under \(\mathbb P_\gamma\) is \(\mu\).

Proof. The map \(((x,y),s)\mapsto x\) is the composition of \(((x,y),s)\mapsto(x,y)\) with \((x,y)\mapsto x\). The image of a measure under a composition of measurable maps is the iterated image, so by the previous step the law of \(x\) is the first marginal of \(\gamma\), which is \(\mu\). \(\square\)
steps.lean: In initialExtension_initial the map fun p ↦ p.1.1 is rewritten as the composition Prod.fst ∘ Prod.fst (← Function.comp_def), split into two images by ← Measure.map_map measurable_fst measurable_fst, and the inner and outer images are identified by initialExtension_joint and the coupling field c.fst.

steps.title: The retained initial law of the reference
steps.body:
Claim. If \(Q\) is a probability measure, then the law of \(y\) under \(\mathbb P_\gamma\) is \(\pi\).

Proof. As in the previous step, with the second projection \((x,y)\mapsto y\) and the second marginal of \(\gamma\), which is \(\pi\). \(\square\)
steps.lean: initialExtension_reference has the same proof as the previous step, with measurable_snd for the outer projection and the coupling field c.snd.

steps.title: The retained noise law
steps.body:
Claim. If \(\mu\) is a probability measure and \(Q\) is \(\sigma\)-finite (more generally, s-finite, a countable sum of finite measures), then the law of \(s\) under \(\mathbb P_\gamma\) is \(Q\).

Proof. By the first step \(\gamma\) is a probability measure. For measurable \(B\subseteq\mathcal S\),

\[\mathbb P_\gamma\bigl((\mathcal X\times\mathcal X)\times B\bigr)=\gamma(\mathcal X\times\mathcal X)\,Q(B)=Q(B).\qquad\square\]
steps.lean: initialExtension_noise assumes [SFinite Q], Mathlib's class of s-finite measures, under which the product formula for the second marginal is available. It records c.isProbabilityMeasure and closes the goal with simp [initialExtension], which uses the simp lemma for the second marginal of a product measure (\(\gamma(\mathcal X\times\mathcal X)\,Q\)) and \(\gamma(\mathcal X\times\mathcal X)=1\).

steps.title: Independence of the initial pair and the noise
steps.body:
Claim. If \(\mu\) and \(Q\) are probability measures, then the pair \((x,y)\) and the noise \(s\) are independent under \(\mathbb P_\gamma\).

Proof. For measurable \(A\subseteq\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\) and \(B\subseteq\mathcal S\), using the two previous marginal computations,

\[\mathbb P_\gamma\bigl((x,y)\in A,\ s\in B\bigr)=\mathbb P_\gamma(A\times B)=\gamma(A)\,Q(B)=\mathbb P_\gamma\bigl((x,y)\in A\bigr)\,\mathbb P_\gamma(s\in B).\qquad\square\]

Composing with measurable maps, every function of the initial pair is independent of every function of the noise.
steps.lean: initialExtension_independent concludes IndepFun Prod.fst Prod.snd (initialExtension c Q). After recording that \(\gamma\) is a probability measure, it applies Mathlib's indepFun_prod with measurable_id twice: on a product of probability measures, a function of the first coordinate and a function of the second coordinate are independent.

steps.title: The joint law of the initial state and the noise
steps.body:
Claim. If \(\mu\) is a probability measure and \(Q\) is s-finite, then the law of \((x,s)\) under \(\mathbb P_\gamma\) is \(\mu\otimes Q\).

Proof. The map \(((x,y),s)\mapsto(x,s)\) is \(\mathrm{pr}_1\times\mathrm{id}\). For measurable maps \(f,g\) and s-finite measures \(\alpha,\beta\), \((f\times g)_\#(\alpha\otimes\beta)=f_\#\alpha\otimes g_\#\beta\), since both sides agree on rectangles: \((\alpha\otimes\beta)(f^{-1}A\times g^{-1}B)=\alpha(f^{-1}A)\,\beta(g^{-1}B)\). With \(\alpha=\gamma\), \(f=\mathrm{pr}_1\) and \(\beta=Q\), \(g=\mathrm{id}\),

\[\bigl(\mathrm{pr}_1\times\mathrm{id}\bigr)_\#(\gamma\otimes Q)=(\mathrm{pr}_1)_\#\gamma\otimes Q=\mu\otimes Q.\qquad\square\]

The right-hand side does not involve \(\pi\) or \(\gamma\): every coupling produces the same joint law of the algorithm's inputs.
steps.lean: In initialExtension_initial_noise, change rewrites the map as Prod.map Prod.fst id on c.joint.prod Q. The rule \(f_\#\alpha\otimes g_\#\beta=(f\times g)_\#(\alpha\otimes\beta)\) is Mathlib's Measure.map_prod_map c.joint Q measurable_fst measurable_id, used in the reverse direction (.symm), and simpa only [c.fst, Measure.map_id] replaces \((\mathrm{pr}_1)_\#\gamma\) by \(\mu\) and \(\mathrm{id}_\#Q\) by \(Q\).

steps.title: Laws of functions of the initial state and the noise
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(\mu\) be a probability measure, \(Q\) s-finite, \(\mathcal T\) a measurable space and \(f:\mathcal X\times\mathcal S\to\mathcal T\) measurable. Then the law of \(f(x,s)\) under \(\mathbb P_\gamma\) is \(f_\#(\mu\otimes Q)\).

Proof. The random variable \(f(x,s)\) is the composition of \(((x,y),s)\mapsto(x,s)\) with \(f\). Taking images in two stages and using the previous step,

\[\text{law of }f(x,s)=f_\#\bigl(\text{law of }(x,s)\bigr)=f_\#(\mu\otimes Q).\qquad\square\]
steps.lean: In initialExtension_map, the right-hand side is rewritten with ← initialExtension_initial_noise c Q, and the two images are merged by Measure.map_map hf (measurable_fst.fst.prodMk measurable_snd), where the second argument is measurability of \(((x,y),s)\mapsto(x,s)\). The two maps then agree by definition, closed by rfl.

steps.title: The law of the algorithm on the extension
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(\mu\) be a probability measure, \(\mathcal S=\mathcal Z^{\mathbb N}\) with an s-finite measure \(Q\), and \(F:\mathcal X\times\mathcal Z\to\mathcal X\) measurable. Then for every \(n\), the law of \(\Phi_n(x,s)\) under \(\mathbb P_\gamma\) is the chain law \(\mathcal L_n(\mu,Q)=(\Phi_n)_\#(\mu\otimes Q)\).

Proof. Apply the previous step to \(f=\Phi_n\), which is measurable by the measurability of the iterates proved for the noise-driven recursion. \(\square\)

So on every extension, whichever coupling of the initial laws it carries, the \(n\)-th iterate of the algorithm started at \(x\) and driven by \(s\) has the same law \(\mathcal L_n(\mu,Q)\).
steps.lean: initialExtension_chainLaw is the term initialExtension_map c Q _ (noiseDrivenChain_measurable F hF n): the previous step with \(f(x,w)=\Phi_n(x,w)\) and its measurability; the result is the definition of chainLaw F μ Q n.

steps.title: The law of each innovation
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(\mu\) and \(\eta\) be probability measures, on \(\mathcal X\) and \(\mathcal Z\) respectively, and \(Q=\eta^{\otimes\mathbb N}\). Then for every \(n\), the law of the coordinate \(s_n\) under \(\mathbb P_\gamma\) is \(\eta\).

Proof. The map \(((x,y),s)\mapsto s_n\) is the composition of \(((x,y),s)\mapsto s\), whose law is \(Q\) by the noise-marginal step, with the coordinate map \(s\mapsto s_n\), whose image of \(\eta^{\otimes\mathbb N}\) is \(\eta\) by the defining property of the infinite product. \(\square\)
steps.lean: In initialExtension_iid_noiseLaw, change writes the map as (fun w : ℕ → Z ↦ w n) ∘ Prod.snd; the rewrites ← Measure.map_map (measurable_pi_apply n) measurable_snd, initialExtension_noise and Measure.infinitePi_map_eval carry out the two stages.

steps.title: Independence of the innovations
steps.body:
Claim. Under the hypotheses of the previous step, the coordinates \(s_0,s_1,\dots\) are mutually independent under \(\mathbb P_\gamma\).

Proof. A countable family of random variables is mutually independent if and only if the law of the sequence is the infinite product of the individual laws (the infinite product is characterised by its values on cylinder sets, which are exactly the probabilities in the definition of independence). The law of the sequence \((s_n)_n\) is the law of \(s\), which is \(Q=\eta^{\otimes\mathbb N}\) by the noise-marginal step, and each individual law is \(\eta\) by the previous step. Hence the law of the sequence equals \(\bigotimes_n(\text{law of }s_n)\). \(\square\)
steps.lean: initialExtension_iid_independent concludes iIndepFun (fun n (p : (H × H) × (ℕ → Z)) ↦ p.2 n) (initialExtension c …). It first installs the probability instance from initialExtension_isProbabilityMeasure, then applies the reverse direction .mpr of Mathlib's iIndepFun_iff_map_fun_eq_infinitePi_map (independence is equivalent to the joint law being the infinite product of the marginals; the measurability side condition is proved by fun_prop). The resulting equality of measures is closed by simp only [initialExtension_iid_noiseLaw, initialExtension_noise].

steps.title: Independence of the initial state and the noise
steps.body:
Claim. If \(\mu\) and \(Q\) are probability measures, then the initial state \(x\) is independent of the noise \(s\) under \(\mathbb P_\gamma\).

Proof. The pair \((x,y)\) is independent of \(s\), and \(x\) is a measurable function of \((x,y)\); measurable functions of independent random variables are independent. \(\square\)

When \(s\) is a noise sequence, this is independence of \(x\) from the whole sequence, which is the hypothesis used to identify the law of the algorithm.
steps.lean: initialExtension_initial_independent is the term (initialExtension_independent c Q).comp measurable_fst measurable_id: Mathlib's IndepFun.comp applied with the measurable maps \((x,y)\mapsto x\) and the identity.

steps.title: The initial displacement cost
steps.body:
From now on \(\mathcal X\) is a normed additive group with its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra and a second countable topology (for instance \(\mathbb R^d\)), so that \((x,y)\mapsto x-y\) is measurable.

Claim. If \(Q\) is a probability measure, then

\[\Bigl(\int\|x-y\|^2\,d\mathbb P_\gamma\Bigr)^{1/2}=\mathcal C(\gamma)\qquad\text{in }[0,\infty].\]

Proof. The map \(T(((x,y),s))=(x,y)\) is measurable and measure preserving from \(\mathbb P_\gamma\) to \(\gamma\), by the joint-law step (which uses \(Q(\mathcal S)=1\)). The integrand is \(g\circ T\) with \(g(x,y)=\|x-y\|^2\), and for a measure-preserving map the change of variables formula \(\int g\circ T\,d\mathbb P_\gamma=\int g\,d\gamma\) holds for every nonnegative measurable \(g\). Taking square roots gives the claim. \(\square\)
steps.lean: The cost couplingCost c.joint is defined in the section on couplings as eLpNorm (fun p : H × H ↦ p.1 - p.2) 2 c.joint; eLpNorm f 2 ν is Mathlib's \(L^2\) seminorm \((\int\|f\|^2d\nu)^{1/2}\) with values in ℝ≥0∞ (equal to \(\infty\) if \(f\) is not almost-everywhere strongly measurable). initialExtension_cost is the instance of eLpNorm_comp_measurePreserving (the \(L^p\) seminorm of \(g\circ T\) for a measure-preserving \(T\) equals that of \(g\)) with \(g(x,y)=x-y\), whose measurability is proved by fun_prop, and \(T\) the first projection, measure preserving by measurePreserving_fst.

steps.title: Square integrability of the initial difference
steps.body:
Recall that a function \(f\) belongs to \(L^2(\nu)\) (is square integrable) if it is almost-everywhere strongly measurable and \(\int\|f\|^2d\nu<\infty\).

Claim. If \(Q\) is a probability measure and \(\mathcal C(\gamma)<\infty\), then \(((x,y),s)\mapsto x-y\) is square integrable under \(\mathbb P_\gamma\).

Proof. The map is measurable, as the composition of the measurable projection \(((x,y),s)\mapsto(x,y)\) with the subtraction \((x,y)\mapsto x-y\), which is measurable because \(\mathcal X\) is second countable with its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra. By the previous step, \(\int\|x-y\|^2\,d\mathbb P_\gamma=\mathcal C(\gamma)^2<\infty\). \(\square\)
steps.lean: initialExtension_memLp_difference assumes hc : couplingCost c.joint ≠ ⊤. In the Mathlib version used, MemLp f 2 ν is defined as eLpNorm f 2 ν < ∞, and eLpNorm is \(\infty\) for functions that are not almost-everywhere strongly measurable, so this inequality contains the measurability part of the argument. change exposes the inequality; rw [initialExtension_cost] replaces the seminorm by the cost, and lt_top_iff_ne_top.mpr hc concludes.

steps.title: Square integrability of the reference initial state
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(Q\) be a probability measure and assume \(\int\|y\|^2\,\pi(dy)<\infty\), that is, the identity map of \(\mathcal X\) is in \(L^2(\pi)\). Then \(((x,y),s)\mapsto y\) is square integrable under \(\mathbb P_\gamma\).

Proof. The law of \(y\) under \(\mathbb P_\gamma\) is \(\pi\) (reference-marginal step). By the change of variables formula for image measures, \(\int\|y\|^2\,d\mathbb P_\gamma=\int\|z\|^2\,\pi(dz)<\infty\); measurability is transferred in the same way. \(\square\)
steps.lean: initialExtension_memLp_reference is stated with omit [BorelSpace H] [SecondCountableTopology H] in, since it does not need these assumptions. The hypothesis hπ : MemLp (fun x : H ↦ x) 2 π is the finite second moment. hmap rewrites it as a statement about the image measure (initialExtension c Q).map (fun p ↦ p.1.2) using initialExtension_reference, and hmap.comp_of_map (Mathlib's MemLp.comp_of_map: if \(g\in L^p(f_\#\nu)\) then \(g\circ f\in L^p(\nu)\)) gives the result, with the measurability of the projection proved by fun_prop.

steps.title: Square integrability of the initial state of the algorithm
steps.body:
Claim. If \(Q\) is a probability measure, \(\mathcal C(\gamma)<\infty\) and \(\int\|y\|^2\pi(dy)<\infty\), then \(((x,y),s)\mapsto x\) is square integrable under \(\mathbb P_\gamma\).

Proof. Write \(x=(x-y)+y\). Both summands are square integrable, by the two previous steps, and \(L^2\) is closed under addition: \(\|a+b\|^2\le2\|a\|^2+2\|b\|^2\) pointwise, so \(\int\|x\|^2\le2\int\|x-y\|^2+2\int\|y\|^2<\infty\). \(\square\)

No moment assumption on \(\mu\) is made: a finite second moment of \(\mu\) is a consequence of finite cost and a finite second moment of \(\pi\).
steps.lean: initialExtension_memLp_initial is (initialExtension_memLp_difference c Q hc).add (initialExtension_memLp_reference c Q hπ), Mathlib's MemLp.add applied to the two summands; simpa only [Pi.add_def, sub_add_cancel] simplifies \((x-y)+y\) to \(x\).

steps.title: The initial class of the algorithm
steps.body: Definition. Under the hypotheses of the previous step, let \(X_0=[x]\in L^2(\mathbb P_\gamma;\mathcal X)\) be the class of the square-integrable map \(((x,y),s)\mapsto x\). It is the initial state of the algorithm, realised on the extension.
steps.lean: initialExtension_lpInitial c Q hc hπ is defined as (initialExtension_memLp_initial c Q hc hπ).toLp (fun p ↦ p.1.1); MemLp.toLp turns a square-integrable function into its class in Lp H 2 (initialExtension c Q).

steps.title: The initial class of the reference
steps.body: Definition. Under the hypotheses of the reference step (\(Q\) a probability measure, \(\int\|y\|^2\pi(dy)<\infty\)), let \(Y_0=[y]\in L^2(\mathbb P_\gamma;\mathcal X)\) be the class of \(((x,y),s)\mapsto y\). It is the initial state of the reference process, realised on the same space as \(X_0\).
steps.lean: initialExtension_lpReference c Q hπ is (initialExtension_memLp_reference c Q hπ).toLp (fun p ↦ p.1.2); it does not need the finite-cost hypothesis.

steps.title: The law of the initial class of the algorithm
steps.body:
Claim. Under the hypotheses of the definition of \(X_0\), the law of \(X_0\) (of any representative) under \(\mathbb P_\gamma\) is \(\mu\).

Proof. A representative of \(X_0\) agrees \(\mathbb P_\gamma\)-almost everywhere with \(((x,y),s)\mapsto x\). Almost-everywhere equal maps have equal image measures, because the preimages of each measurable set differ by a null set. The law of \(x\) is \(\mu\) by the initial-marginal step. \(\square\)
steps.lean: initialExtension_lpInitial_law unfolds the class, rewrites with Measure.map_congr applied to (initialExtension_memLp_initial c Q hc hπ).coeFn_toLp (the representative of toLp f agrees almost everywhere with f), and concludes with initialExtension_initial c Q.

steps.title: The law of the initial class of the reference
steps.body:
Claim. Under the hypotheses of the definition of \(Y_0\), the law of \(Y_0\) under \(\mathbb P_\gamma\) is \(\pi\).

Proof. As in the previous step, a representative of \(Y_0\) agrees almost everywhere with \(((x,y),s)\mapsto y\), whose law is \(\pi\). \(\square\)
steps.lean: initialExtension_lpReference_law has the same proof as the previous step, with initialExtension_memLp_reference and initialExtension_reference; like the reference square-integrability step it omits the Borel and second-countability assumptions.

steps.title: The distance of the initial classes equals the coupling cost
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(Q\) be a probability measure, \(\mathcal C(\gamma)<\infty\) and \(\int\|y\|^2\pi(dy)<\infty\). Then

\[\|X_0-Y_0\|_{L^2(\mathbb P_\gamma)}=\mathcal C(\gamma),\]

where the right-hand side is the finite real number \(\mathcal C(\gamma)\).

Proof. The norm of a class in \(L^2\) is the \(L^2\) seminorm of any representative. A representative of \(X_0-Y_0\) agrees almost everywhere with the difference of representatives of \(X_0\) and \(Y_0\), and these agree almost everywhere with \(x\) and \(y\); a finite union of null sets is null, so \(X_0-Y_0\) is represented by \(x-y\) almost everywhere. The seminorm is unchanged by almost-everywhere modification, and by the cost step the seminorm of \(x-y\) is \(\mathcal C(\gamma)\). \(\square\)

Thus the initial distance between the algorithm and the reference on the extension is exactly the cost of the chosen coupling. The coupling argument bounds the output distance by a multiple of \(\|X_0-Y_0\|_2\) plus a bias, and then takes the infimum over \(\gamma\).
steps.lean: In initialExtension_lp_cost the right side is (couplingCost c.joint).toReal, the conversion of the finite value in ℝ≥0∞ to a real number. rw [Lp.norm_def] expresses the norm of the class as the real number obtained from the eLpNorm of its representative. hae is the almost-everywhere identity of the representative of \(X_0-Y_0\) with \(x-y\), assembled from Lp.coeFn_sub and the two coeFn_toLp identities by transitivity (.trans) and subtraction (.sub). Finally eLpNorm_congr_ae hae (the seminorm depends only on the almost-everywhere class) and initialExtension_cost finish the computation.

UnadjustedLangevin/GibbsStationarity.lea.title: Gibbs stationarity of the Langevin solution by Metropolis comparison
UnadjustedLangevin/GibbsStationarity.lea.summary:
Let \(U:\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R\) be differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex with \(m>0\), with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, and let \(\pi(dx)=Z^{-1}e^{-U(x)}dx\) be its Gibbs measure. Let \(Y:\mathbb R\to L^2(P;\mathbb R^d)\) be a continuous solution of the Langevin integral equation

\[Y(t)-X_0=-\int_0^t\mathcal G\bigl(Y(s)\bigr)\,ds+N_0(t),\qquad t\in[0,T],\]

driven by a family of pre-Brownian motions through \(N_0(t)=\sqrt2([B_t]-[B_0])\), where \(\mathcal G[X]=[\nabla U\circ X]\). The main theorem states: if \(X_0\) has law \(\pi\), and for every mesh \(h>0\) the normalised Brownian increments \(\xi^{(h)}_{n}=N_{nh}(h)/\sqrt{2h}\) have mutually independent coordinates and are independent of \(X_0\), then \(Y(T)\) has law \(\pi\). This is Gibbs stationarity of the Langevin diffusion, proved without Itô's formula, without the Fokker–Planck equation and without assuming an invariant law.

The proof fixes \(T>0\) and takes meshes \(h_n=T/k_n\) with \(k_n\to\infty\) steps. (i) The Euler scheme with step \(h_n\) driven by the same Brownian increments, \(E_{j+1}=E_j-h_n\mathcal G(E_j)+(N_0((j+1)h_n)-N_0(jh_n))\), converges to \(Y(T)\) in \(L^2\) after \(k_n\) steps (Euler convergence for the integral equation). (ii) These Euler iterates are the unadjusted Langevin algorithm with standard Gaussian innovations, independent of the Gibbs-distributed initial state, so their laws are \(K_{h_n}^{k_n}(\pi)\), where \(K_h(\mu)\) is the law of \(x-h\nabla U(x)+\sqrt{2h}\,\xi\) for \(x\sim\mu\) and an independent \(\xi\sim\mathcal N(0,I_d)\). (iii) The Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm preserves \(\pi\) exactly; coupling it with the unadjusted chain through common Gaussian innovations gives couplings of \(K_{h_n}^{k_n}(\pi)\) and \(\pi\) with expected distance at most \(k_nCh_n\sqrt{h_n}=TC\sqrt{h_n}\to0\). The criterion of the previous section then identifies the law of \(Y(T)\) as \(\pi\). The preparatory results identify the Euler scheme with the unadjusted Langevin algorithm in \(L^2\), compute the law of the latter, and verify that the Brownian innovations are independent standard Gaussian vectors.

steps.title: The representative of the Hilbert-space chain
steps.body:
Let \(H\) be a real inner product space, complete and separable, with its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra (for instance \(\mathbb R^d\)), and \(P\) a probability measure. For \(U:H\to\mathbb R\) with \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient, \(h\in\mathbb R\), an initial class \(X_0\in L^2(P;H)\) and innovation classes \(W_k\in L^2(P;H)\), the ULA chain in \(L^2\) is \(X_0\), \(X_{k+1}=X_k-h\,\mathcal G(X_k)+\sqrt{2h}\,W_k\). The pointwise update is \(F_h(x,z)=x-h\nabla U(x)+\sqrt{2h}\,z\), and \(\Phi_n\) is the noise-driven recursion with update \(F_h\).

Claim. For every \(n\), a representative of \(X_n\) agrees \(P\)-almost everywhere with \(\omega\mapsto\Phi_n\bigl(X_0(\omega),(W_k(\omega))_{k}\bigr)\), computed from representatives of \(X_0\) and \(W_k\).

Proof. Induction on \(n\). For \(n=0\) both are the representative of \(X_0\). Assume the claim for \(n\). The class \(X_n-h\mathcal G(X_n)+\sqrt{2h}W_n\) is represented almost everywhere by \(\omega\mapsto F_h(X_n(\omega),W_n(\omega))\) : the representative of \(\mathcal G(X_n)\) is \(\nabla U\circ X_n\) almost everywhere, and sums and scalar multiples of classes are represented by sums and scalar multiples of representatives. On the intersection of this full-measure set with the one given by the induction hypothesis, which again has full measure, \(X_{n+1}(\omega)=F_h(\Phi_n(X_0(\omega),W(\omega)),W_n(\omega))=\Phi_{n+1}(X_0(\omega),W(\omega))\). \(\square\)

steps.title: The law of the chain follows the Gaussian transition
steps.body:
Let \(\mathcal N(0,I_H)\) denote the standard Gaussian measure on a finite-dimensional \(H\) (the law of \(\sum_jg_je_j\) for an orthonormal basis \((e_j)\) and independent \(g_j\sim\mathcal N(0,1)\)). For a measure \(\mu\) on \(H\), the ULA transition is

\[K_h(\mu)=(F_h)_\#\bigl(\mu\otimes\mathcal N(0,I_H)\bigr),\]

the law of \(x-h\nabla U(x)+\sqrt{2h}\,\xi\) when \(x\sim\mu\) and \(\xi\sim\mathcal N(0,I_H)\) are independent, and \(K_h^n\) is its \(n\)-fold composition.

Claim. Let \(H\) be finite-dimensional, \(P\) a probability measure, \(\nabla U\) \(L\)-Lipschitz, \(h\in\mathbb R\), \(X_0,W_k\in L^2(P;H)\) such that \(X_0\) is independent of the sequence \((W_k)_k\), the \(W_k\) are mutually independent, and every \(W_k\) has law \(\mathcal N(0,I_H)\). Then for every \(n\), the law of \(X_n\) is \(K_h^n(P_{X_0})\).

Proof. By the previous step and the fact that almost-everywhere equal maps have the same image measure, the law of \(X_n\) is the law of \(\Phi_n(X_0,W)\). The update \(F_h\) is measurable, because \(\nabla U\) is continuous. Every element of \(L^2\) has an almost-everywhere measurable representative. The theorem on independent realisations of the recursion with independent identically distributed noise gives that this law is \(\mu_n\), where \(\mu_0=P_{X_0}\) and \(\mu_{k+1}=(F_h)_\#(\mu_k\otimes\mathcal N(0,I_H))=K_h(\mu_k)\). By induction on \(n\), \(\mu_n=K_h^n(P_{X_0})\): for \(n=0\) both sides are \(P_{X_0}\), and \(\mu_{n+1}=K_h(\mu_n)=K_h(K_h^n(P_{X_0}))=K_h^{n+1}(P_{X_0})\). \(\square\)

steps.title: Identification of the Euler scheme with the chain
steps.body:
For a Lipschitz map \(\mathcal G\) on a Banach space, a step \(h\), an initial point \(X_0\) and an input path \(B:\mathbb R\to L^2\), the Euler scheme with exact input increments is

\[E_0=X_0,\qquad E_{k+1}=E_k-h\,\mathcal G(E_k)+\bigl(B((k+1)h)-B(kh)\bigr).\]

Claim. Let \(P\) be a probability measure, \(\nabla U\) \(L\)-Lipschitz, \(h\in\mathbb R\), \(X_0\in L^2\), \(B:\mathbb R\to L^2\) and \(W_k\in L^2\) with

\[B\bigl((k+1)h\bigr)-B(kh)=\sqrt{2h}\,W_k\qquad\text{for every }k\in\mathbb N.\]

Then \(E_n=X_n\) for every \(n\), where \(E\) is the Euler scheme with \(\mathcal G[X]=[\nabla U\circ X]\) and \(X\) is the ULA chain in \(L^2\) with innovations \(W_k\).

\[E_{n+1}=X_n-h\,\mathcal G(X_n)+\sqrt{2h}\,W_n=X_{n+1}.\qquad\square\]
