steps.title: The grid increment of the Brownian input
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(P\) be a probability measure, \(\iota\) a finite set, \((W^i)_{i\in\iota}\) pre-Brownian motions, \(h\in\mathbb R\) and \(k\in\mathbb N\). Then

\[N_0\bigl((k+1)h\bigr)-N_0(kh)=N_{kh}(h).\]

Proof. Since \((k+1)h=kh+h\), this is the increment identity \(N_0(a+t)-N_0(a)=N_a(t)\) with \(a=kh\), \(t=h\): both sides equal \(\sqrt2(\beta(kh+h)-\beta(kh))\) after expanding \(N_0(s)=\sqrt2(\beta(s)-\beta(0))\). \(\square\)

steps.title: The normalised increments are independent standard Gaussian vectors
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(P\) be a probability measure, \((W^i)_{i\in\iota}\) pre-Brownian motions, \(h>0\), and assume that the real random variables \((\xi_n)_i\), \((n,i)\in\mathbb N\times\iota\) (coordinates of representatives of \(\xi_n=N_{nh}(h)/\sqrt{2h}\)), are mutually independent. Then the vectors \(\xi_n\), \(n\in\mathbb N\), are mutually independent and each has the standard Gaussian law \(\mathcal N(0,I_\iota)\) on \(\mathbb R^\iota\).

Proof. Coordinate laws. For each \(n\) and \(i\), \((\xi_n)_i\) agrees almost everywhere with \((W^i_{(n+1)h}-W^i_{nh})/\sqrt h\), which has law \(\mathcal N(0,1)\) because \(W^i_{(n+1)h}-W^i_{nh}\sim\mathcal N(0,h)\) .

Vector laws and independence. A family of mutually independent real random variables indexed by \(\mathbb N\times\iota\), all with law \(\mathcal N(0,1)\), has joint law \(\bigotimes_{(n,i)}\mathcal N(0,1)\). Grouping the coordinates with the same \(n\) into the vector \(\xi_n\) identifies this with \(\bigotimes_n\bigl(\bigotimes_{i\in\iota}\mathcal N(0,1)\bigr)\), and \(\bigotimes_{i\in\iota}\mathcal N(0,1)=\mathcal N(0,I_\iota)\) on \(\mathbb R^\iota\). Hence the sequence \((\xi_n)_n\) has law \(\mathcal N(0,I_\iota)^{\otimes\mathbb N}\), which says exactly that the \(\xi_n\) are independent with law \(\mathcal N(0,I_\iota)\) . \(\square\)

steps.title: The Langevin solution keeps the Gibbs law
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(P\) be a probability measure, \(\iota\) a finite set, \(U:\mathbb R^\iota\to\mathbb R\) differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex with \(m>0\), \(\nabla U\) \(L\)-Lipschitz, and \(\pi\) the Gibbs measure of \(U\). Let \(X_0\in L^2(P;\mathbb R^\iota)\) with law \(\pi\), let \((W^i)_{i\in\iota}\) be pre-Brownian motions, and write \(\xi^{(h)}_n=N_{nh}(h)/\sqrt{2h}\). Assume that for every \(h>0\):

  1. the coordinates \((\xi^{(h)}_n)_i\), \((n,i)\in\mathbb N\times\iota\), are mutually independent;
  2. \(X_0\) is independent of the sequence \((\xi^{(h)}_n)_{n\in\mathbb N}\).

Let \(T\ge0\) and let \(Y:\mathbb R\to L^2\) be continuous with \(Y(t)-X_0=-\int_0^t\mathcal G(Y(s))\,ds+N_0(t)\) for \(t\in[0,T]\). Then \(Y(T)\) has law \(\pi\).

Proof. Case \(T=0\). The equation at \(t=0\) gives \(Y(0)-X_0=0+N_0(0)=0\), so \(Y(0)=X_0\), whose law is \(\pi\).

Case \(T>0\). Choice of meshes. By strong convexity \(\pi\) is a probability measure. Since \(T/(n+1)\to0\) and \(c=\min(1,2/(m+L))>0\) (here \(m+L>0\)), there is \(N\) with \(T/(n+1)<c\) for all \(n\ge N\). Put \(k_n=n+N+1\) and \(h_n=T/k_n\). Then \(h_n>0\), \(h_n\le1\), \(h_n\le2/(m+L)\), \(k_nh_n=T\), and \(h_n\to0\).

Euler approximations. Let \(X^{(n)}\in L^2\) be the ULA chain in \(L^2\) with step \(h_n\), initial class \(X_0\) and innovations \(\xi^{(h_n)}_j\), after \(k_n\) steps. The Euler scheme with exact input increments, step \(T/(j+1)\) and \(j+1\) steps converges to \(Y(T)\) in \(L^2\) as \(j\to\infty\) ; this uses only the integral equation, continuity of \(Y\), \(N_0(0)=0\) and the Lipschitz property of \(\mathcal G\). Along the subsequence \(j=n+N\) it gives the Euler scheme with step \(h_n\) after \(k_n\) steps, which equals \(X^{(n)}\) by the fifth step. Hence \(X^{(n)}\to Y(T)\) in \(L^2\). \(\qquad(1)\)

Laws of the approximations. By the sixth step and hypothesis 1, the innovations \(\xi^{(h_n)}_j\) are independent with law \(\mathcal N(0,I_\iota)\); by hypothesis 2 they are independent of \(X_0\). By the second step, the law of \(X^{(n)}\) is \(K_{h_n}^{k_n}(\pi)\). \(\qquad(2)\)

Metropolis-adjusted comparison chains. One step of the Metropolis-adjusted Langevin algorithm with step \(h\) proposes \(y=x-h\nabla U(x)+\sqrt{2h}\,\xi\) with \(\xi\sim\mathcal N(0,I_\iota)\) and accepts it with probability \(\min\bigl(1,\pi(y)q_h(y,x)/(\pi(x)q_h(x,y))\bigr)\), \(q_h\) being the Gaussian proposal density, and otherwise stays at \(x\). For \(h>0\) it preserves \(\pi\) by detailed balance . Let \(\rho_n\) be the law after \(k_n\) steps of the synchronous coupling started at \((x,x)\), \(x\sim\pi\), in which the unadjusted and the adjusted chain use the same Gaussian vector at every step. Then \(\rho_n\) is a probability measure on \(\mathbb R^\iota\times\mathbb R^\iota\), its first marginal is \(K_{h_n}^{k_n}(\pi)\) and its second marginal is \(\pi\) by invariance . With (2), the first marginal is the law of \(X^{(n)}\). \(\qquad(3)\)

Coupling distance. For \(0<h\le1\) and \(h\le2/(m+L)\), the distance \(\|x-y\|\) is \(\rho_n\)-integrable and \(\int\|x-y\|\,d\rho_n\le k\,C\,h\sqrt h\) after \(k\) steps, where \(C\ge0\) is a constant depending only on \(U\) and \(L\) : the unadjusted proposal map is nonexpansive in this step range, so each step adds at most the expected rejected displacement, which is of order \(h\sqrt h\). With \(k=k_n\) and \(k_nh_n=T\),

\[0\le\int\|x-y\|\,d\rho_n\le k_nCh_n\sqrt{h_n}=TC\sqrt{h_n}\longrightarrow0,\qquad(4)\]

because \(h_n\to0\) and the square root is continuous at \(0\).

Conclusion. By (1), (3) and (4), the criterion of the section on coupling limits applies with \(X_n=X^{(n)}\), \(X=Y(T)\) and the couplings \(\rho_n\), and gives that \(Y(T)\) has law \(\pi\). \(\square\)

The independence hypotheses concern only the Brownian input and its relation to \(X_0\); they hold on the canonical product space constructed in the section on product Brownian motion. No invariance, moment or forward-equation hypothesis on \(Y\) is used: the only information about \(Y\) is the integral equation.

UnadjustedLangevin/CouplingLimit.lean.title: A vanishing coupling distance determines the limiting law
UnadjustedLangevin/CouplingLimit.lean.summary:
Let \(H\) be a real inner product space with its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra. The characteristic function of a finite measure \(\nu\) on \(H\) is

\[\varphi_\nu(t)=\int_He^{i\langle x,t\rangle}\,\nu(dx),\qquad t\in H.\]

If \(H\) is complete and separable (for instance \(H=\mathbb R^d\)), two finite measures with the same characteristic function are equal. This section proves a criterion for identifying the law of a limit. Suppose \(X_n\to X\) in \(L^2(P;H)\), and suppose that for each \(n\) there is a coupling \(\rho_n\) of the law of \(X_n\) with a fixed probability measure \(\pi\) such that the expected distance \(\int\|x-y\|\,\rho_n(dx,dy)\) tends to \(0\). Then the law of \(X\) is \(\pi\).

The proof uses two estimates for the characteristic test \(x\mapsto e^{i\langle x,t\rangle}\), which is bounded by \(1\) and \(\|t\|\)-Lipschitz: the difference of the characteristic functions of the two marginals of a coupling is at most \(\|t\|\) times its expected distance, and \(X\mapsto\varphi_{P_X}(t)\) is continuous on \(L^2\). So \(\varphi_{P_{X_n}}(t)\) converges both to \(\varphi_{P_X}(t)\) and to \(\varphi_\pi(t)\). The criterion is applied in the next section to Euler approximations of the Langevin equation coupled with Metropolis-adjusted chains that preserve the Gibbs measure. Only first moments of the couplings are used, and no optimal coupling is required.

steps.title: A Lipschitz bound for characteristic tests
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(H\) be a real inner product space and \(t,x,y\in H\). Then

\[\bigl|e^{i\langle x,t\rangle}-e^{i\langle y,t\rangle}\bigr|\le\|t\|\,\|x-y\|.\]

Proof. For real numbers \(u,v\), the map \(\theta\mapsto e^{i\theta}\) has derivative \(ie^{i\theta}\) of modulus \(1\), so

\[\bigl|e^{iu}-e^{iv}\bigr|=\Bigl|\int_v^u ie^{i\theta}\,d\theta\Bigr|\le|u-v|:\qquad(1)\]

the unit circle is parametrised by a \(1\)-Lipschitz map. Apply (1) with \(u=\langle x,t\rangle\) and \(v=\langle y,t\rangle\). By linearity of the inner product in its first argument, \(u-v=\langle x-y,t\rangle\), and by the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality \(|\langle x-y,t\rangle|\le\|x-y\|\,\|t\|\). \(\square\)

steps.title: Characteristic differences controlled by the coupling distance
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(H\) be a real inner product space with its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra and a second countable topology, let \(\rho\) be a probability measure on \(H\times H\) with marginals \(\rho_1=(\mathrm{pr}_1)_\#\rho\) and \(\rho_2=(\mathrm{pr}_2)_\#\rho\), and assume \(\int\|x-y\|\,\rho(dx,dy)<\infty\). Then for every \(t\in H\),

\[\bigl|\varphi_{\rho_1}(t)-\varphi_{\rho_2}(t)\bigr|\le\|t\|\int\|x-y\|\,\rho(dx,dy).\]

Proof. By the change of variables formula for image measures,

\[\varphi_{\rho_1}(t)=\int e^{i\langle x,t\rangle}\,\rho(dx,dy),\qquad\varphi_{\rho_2}(t)=\int e^{i\langle y,t\rangle}\,\rho(dx,dy).\]

Both integrands are continuous, hence measurable, and bounded in modulus by \(1\); since \(\rho\) is a probability measure they are integrable. By linearity of the integral, the inequality \(|\int f\,d\rho|\le\int|f|\,d\rho\), the previous step and monotonicity of the integral,

\[\bigl|\varphi_{\rho_1}(t)-\varphi_{\rho_2}(t)\bigr|=\Bigl|\int\bigl(e^{i\langle x,t\rangle}-e^{i\langle y,t\rangle}\bigr)\,d\rho\Bigr|\le\int\bigl|e^{i\langle x,t\rangle}-e^{i\langle y,t\rangle}\bigr|\,d\rho\le\int\|t\|\,\|x-y\|\,d\rho .\]

The last integral is \(\|t\|\int\|x-y\|\,d\rho\), which is finite by the integrability hypothesis. \(\square\)

steps.title: Continuity of the characteristic function in square mean
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(P\) be a probability measure on \(\Omega\), \(H\) a real inner product space with its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra, and \(t\in H\). Then the map \(X\mapsto\varphi_{P_X}(t)=\mathbb E\,e^{i\langle X,t\rangle}\) is continuous on \(L^2(P;H)\).

Proof. Let \(\ell(x)=\langle x,t\rangle\), a continuous linear functional \(H\to\mathbb R\) of norm at most \(\|t\|\). For \(X\in L^2(P;H)\), the real random variable \(\ell\circ X\) satisfies

\[\varphi_{P_X}(t)=\mathbb E\,e^{i\langle X,t\rangle}=\mathbb E\,e^{i\cdot1\cdot\ell(X)}=\varphi_{P_{\ell(X)}}(1),\qquad(2)\]

the characteristic function of the law of \(\ell(X)\) at frequency \(1\); this is the change of variables formula for the two image measures. The map \(X\mapsto\ell\circ X\) is a continuous linear map from \(L^2(P;H)\) to \(L^2(P;\mathbb R)\), since \(\|\ell\circ X\|_2\le\|t\|\,\|X\|_2\) and it does not depend on the representative of \(X\). The map \(Z\mapsto\varphi_{P_Z}(1)\) is continuous on \(L^2(P;\mathbb R)\) ; indeed, by (1), the Cauchy–Schwarz inequality and \(P(\Omega)=1\),

\[\bigl|\mathbb E\,e^{iZ}-\mathbb E\,e^{iZ'}\bigr|\le\mathbb E|Z-Z'|\le\|Z-Z'\|_2 .\]

By (2), \(X\mapsto\varphi_{P_X}(t)\) is the composition of these two continuous maps. \(\square\)

steps.title: Equality of limiting laws from vanishing coupling distance
steps.body:
Limits below are taken along a fixed nontrivial filter on an index set \(I\); the reader may take \(I=\mathbb N\) and limits as \(n\to\infty\), which is the case used later.

Claim. Let \(P\) be a probability measure on \(\Omega\) and \(H\) a real Hilbert space that is separable, with its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra. Let \(X_i,X\in L^2(P;H)\) (\(i\in I\)), let \(\pi\) be a probability measure on \(H\), and let \(\rho_i\) be probability measures on \(H\times H\) such that for every \(i\)

\[(\mathrm{pr}_1)_\#\rho_i=P_{X_i},\qquad(\mathrm{pr}_2)_\#\rho_i=\pi,\qquad\int\|x-y\|\,\rho_i(dx,dy)<\infty,\]

and assume \(X_i\to X\) in \(L^2(P;H)\) and \(\int\|x-y\|\,\rho_i(dx,dy)\to0\). Then \(P_X=\pi\).

Proof. Fix \(t\in H\).

First limit. By the previous step, \(X\mapsto\varphi_{P_X}(t)\) is continuous on \(L^2(P;H)\), so \(X_i\to X\) gives \(\varphi_{P_{X_i}}(t)\to\varphi_{P_X}(t)\).

Second limit. By the second step applied to \(\rho_i\), whose marginals are \(P_{X_i}\) and \(\pi\),

\[0\le\bigl|\varphi_{P_{X_i}}(t)-\varphi_\pi(t)\bigr|\le\|t\|\int\|x-y\|\,\rho_i(dx,dy)\longrightarrow\|t\|\cdot0=0,\]

so, by the squeeze principle, \(\varphi_{P_{X_i}}(t)\to\varphi_\pi(t)\).

Conclusion. Limits in \(\mathbb C\) along a nontrivial filter are unique, so \(\varphi_{P_X}(t)=\varphi_\pi(t)\). As \(t\) was arbitrary, \(P_X\) and \(\pi\) have the same characteristic function. Both are finite measures (\(P_X(H)=P(\Omega)=1\)) on a separable Hilbert space, and such measures are determined by their characteristic functions. Hence \(P_X=\pi\). \(\square\)

The couplings \(\rho_i\) need not be optimal, and only their first moments of \(\|x-y\|\) enter. Nontriviality of the filter excludes the degenerate situation in which every statement holds “eventually” and limits are not unique.

UnadjustedLangevin/ProductReference.lean.title: Dalalyan's bounds from a reference on every coupling extension
UnadjustedLangevin/ProductReference.lean.summary:
Let \(H\) be a separable real Hilbert space with its Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra (in the application \(H=\mathbb R^d\)), \(\mu\) a probability measure on \(H\) (the initial law of the algorithm), \(\pi\) a measure on \(H\) with \(\int\|x\|^2\pi(dx)<\infty\) (the target), \(Q\) a probability measure on a measurable space \(\mathcal S\) (the noise source), and \(W_n:\mathcal S\to H\), \(n\in\mathbb N\), square-integrable noise functions. The unadjusted Langevin update is \(F_h(x,z)=x-h\nabla U(x)+\sqrt{2h}\,z\), and the output law of the algorithm is defined directly on the product space \(H\times\mathcal S\):

\[\nu_n=\Bigl((x,s)\mapsto\Phi_n\bigl(x,(W_k(s))_{k}\bigr)\Bigr)_\#(\mu\otimes Q),\]

where \(\Phi_n\) is the noise-driven recursion with update \(F_h\). For every coupling \(\gamma\) of \(\mu\) and \(\pi\) with finite cost we work on the extension \(\mathbb P_\gamma=\gamma\otimes Q\) of the section on initial extensions, where the algorithm starts at \(X_0=[x]\) and uses the innovations \(\widehat W_n=[W_n(s)]\). We prove that its \(n\)-th iterate has law \(\nu_n\) for every \(\gamma\).

A product reference is a family, indexed by the finite-cost couplings \(\gamma\), of stationary references on \(\mathbb P_\gamma\) (continuous Langevin segments with the Gibbs-type moment bounds, driven by the same innovations \(\widehat W_n\)) that start at \(Y_0=[y]\). Given one, we prove that the output law has finite transport distance to \(\pi\), and we prove Dalalyan's bounds with the true initial Wasserstein distance: for \(0<h\le2/(m+L)\),

\[W_2(\nu_n,\pi)\le(1-mh)^nW_2(\mu,\pi)+\frac{33}{20}\,\frac Lm\sqrt{hd},\]

and for \(2/(m+L)\le h\) with \(Lh<2\), the same with factor \((Lh-1)^n\) and additive term \(\frac{33}{20}\frac{Lh}{2-Lh}\sqrt{hd}\). The proof applies the analytic bound on each extension, where the initial error equals the cost of \(\gamma\), and takes the infimum over \(\gamma\); no optimal coupling is needed. The existence of a product reference is proved in the following sections.

steps.title: The pointwise update
steps.body:
Definition. For \(U:H\to\mathbb R\) and \(h\in\mathbb R\), the unadjusted Langevin update is

\[F_h(x,z)=x-h\nabla U(x)+\sqrt{2h}\,z,\qquad x,z\in H.\]

With \(z\) a standard Gaussian vector it is one step of the unadjusted Langevin algorithm; here \(z\) is arbitrary. As in the section on chain laws, \(\sqrt{2h}\) is read as \(0\) for \(h<0\); only \(h>0\) occurs in the estimates.
steps.lean: pointwiseUpdate U h x z is defined as x - h • gradient U x + Real.sqrt (2 * h) • z, in an arbitrary space H with the section assumptions (InnerProductSpace ℝ H, CompleteSpace H, BorelSpace H, SecondCountableTopology H).

steps.title: Measurability of the update
steps.body:
Claim. If \(\nabla U\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz for some \(L\ge0\), then \((x,z)\mapsto F_h(x,z)\) is measurable on \(H\times H\), for every \(h\in\mathbb R\).

Proof. \(\nabla U\) is Lipschitz, hence continuous, hence Borel measurable. The projections \((x,z)\mapsto x\) and \((x,z)\mapsto z\) are measurable, multiplication by the constants \(h\) and \(\sqrt{2h}\) preserves measurability, and since \(H\) is second countable the Borel \(\sigma\)-algebra of \(H\times H\) is the product \(\sigma\)-algebra, so sums and differences of measurable \(H\)-valued maps are measurable. \(\square\)

steps.title: The extensions are probability spaces
steps.body:
Claim. For every coupling \(\gamma\) of the probability measure \(\mu\) and \(\pi\), the extension \(\mathbb P_\gamma=\gamma\otimes Q\) is a probability measure.

Proof. This is the normalisation of the product extension proved in the section on initial extensions: \(\gamma\) is a probability measure because its first marginal is \(\mu\), and \(Q\) is a probability measure. \(\square\)

steps.title: Square integrability of the lifted noise
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(\gamma\) be a coupling of \(\mu\) and \(\pi\), and let \(W_n\in L^2(Q;H)\) for every \(n\). Then for every \(n\), the map \(((x,y),s)\mapsto W_n(s)\) is square integrable under \(\mathbb P_\gamma\).

Proof. Since \(\gamma\) is a probability measure, the projection \(((x,y),s)\mapsto s\) is measure preserving from \(\mathbb P_\gamma\) to \(Q\): \(\mathbb P_\gamma(\mathcal X\times\mathcal X\times B)=\gamma(H\times H)Q(B)=Q(B)\). For a measure-preserving map \(T\), \(\int\|f\circ T\|^2d\mathbb P_\gamma=\int\|f\|^2dQ\) (change of variables), and \(f\circ T\) is almost-everywhere strongly measurable whenever \(f\) is. With \(f=W_n\) the right side is finite. \(\square\)

steps.body:
Claim. For every \(n\), a representative of \(\widehat W_n\) agrees \(\mathbb P_\gamma\)-almost everywhere with \(((x,y),s)\mapsto W_n(s)\).

Proof. The class of a square-integrable function is represented almost everywhere by that function. \(\square\)

steps.title: The output law of the algorithm
steps.body:
Definition. For \(U\), \(h\), the initial law \(\mu\) and the noise functions \(W_k\), the output law after \(n\) steps is

\[\nu_n=\Bigl((x,s)\mapsto\Phi_n\bigl(x,(W_k(s))_{k\in\mathbb N}\bigr)\Bigr)_\#(\mu\otimes Q),\]

where \(\Phi_n\) is the noise-driven recursion with update \(F_h\). It involves neither \(\pi\) nor a coupling.

steps.title: The chain on the extension is the pointwise recursion
steps.body:
For a coupling \(\gamma\) with \(\mathcal C(\gamma)<\infty\) and \(\int\|y\|^2\pi(dy)<\infty\), let \(X_0=[x]\in L^2(\mathbb P_\gamma;H)\) be the initial class of the section on initial extensions, and let \(X_n\) be the ULA chain in \(L^2(\mathbb P_\gamma;H)\): \(X_{k+1}=X_k-h\,\mathcal G(X_k)+\sqrt{2h}\,\widehat W_k\).

Claim. If \(\nabla U\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, then for every \(n\) a representative of \(X_n\) agrees \(\mathbb P_\gamma\)-almost everywhere with \(((x,y),s)\mapsto\Phi_n(x,(W_k(s))_k)\).

Proof. Induction on \(n\). For \(n=0\), \(X_0\) is represented by \(x\) almost everywhere. Assume the claim for \(n\). The class \(X_n-h\mathcal G(X_n)+\sqrt{2h}\widehat W_n\) is represented almost everywhere by \(F_h(X_n(\cdot),\widehat W_n(\cdot))\), by the representative formula for the \(L^2\) update. On the intersection of the three full-measure sets where this holds, where the induction hypothesis holds, and where \(\widehat W_n=W_n(s)\) (previous step), we get \(X_{n+1}=F_h(\Phi_n(x,(W_k(s))_k),W_n(s))=\Phi_{n+1}(x,(W_k(s))_k)\). \(\square\)

steps.title: The chain on every extension has the output law
steps.body:
Claim. Under the hypotheses of the previous step, the law of \(X_n\) under \(\mathbb P_\gamma\) is \(\nu_n\), for every \(n\) and every finite-cost coupling \(\gamma\).

Proof. By the previous step, the law of \(X_n\) is the law of \(\Psi(((x,y),s))=\Phi_n(x,w(s))\), where \(w(s)=(W_k(s))_k\in H^{\mathbb N}\). The map \(w\) is only almost-everywhere measurable (each \(W_k\) is), so we replace it by a measurable map \(\tilde w:\mathcal S\to H^{\mathbb N}\) with \(w=\tilde w\) \(Q\)-almost everywhere; such a map exists because \(\mathbb N\) is countable and each coordinate is almost-everywhere measurable. Since the projection to \(s\) is measure preserving from \(\mathbb P_\gamma\) to \(Q\), the set of \(((x,y),s)\) with \(w(s)\neq\tilde w(s)\) is \(\mathbb P_\gamma\)-null; similarly it is \((\mu\otimes Q)\)-null in \(H\times\mathcal S\). Hence, using almost-everywhere invariance of image measures twice,

\[\text{law of }X_n=\bigl(((x,y),s)\mapsto\Phi_n(x,\tilde w(s))\bigr)_\#\mathbb P_\gamma,\qquad\nu_n=\bigl((x,s)\mapsto\Phi_n(x,\tilde w(s))\bigr)_\#(\mu\otimes Q).\]

The map \(f(x,s)=\Phi_n(x,\tilde w(s))\) is measurable, as the composition of the measurable \(\Phi_n\) (measurability of the iterates, with the measurable update of the second step) with \((x,s)\mapsto(x,\tilde w(s))\). By the result on laws of functions of the initial state and the noise in the section on initial extensions, \(f(x,s)\) has law \(f_\#(\mu\otimes Q)\) under \(\mathbb P_\gamma\). The two displays are therefore equal. \(\square\)

So the law of the algorithm on the extension does not depend on the coupling \(\gamma\), nor on \(\pi\).

steps.title: A reference on every coupling extension
steps.body:
Recall from the section on Dalalyan's argument that a stationary reference for \(\pi\) with step \(h\), dimension parameter \(d\) and innovations \((\xi_n)\) on a probability space \((\Omega,P)\) consists of curves \(Y^{(n)},M^{(n)}:\mathbb R\to L^2(P;H)\) such that, for all \(n\) and \(t\in[0,h]\): \(Y^{(n)}\) is continuous; \(Y^{(n)}(h)=Y^{(n+1)}(0)\); \(M^{(n)}(h)=\sqrt{2h}\,\xi_n\); \(Y^{(n)}(0)\) has law \(\pi\); \(Y^{(n)}(t)-Y^{(n)}(0)=-\int_0^t\mathcal G(Y^{(n)}(s))\,ds+M^{(n)}(t)\); \(\|\mathcal G(Y^{(n)}(t))\|_2\le\sqrt{Ld}\); and \(\|M^{(n)}(t)\|_2\le\sqrt{2d}\sqrt t\).

Definition. A product reference (for \(d\), \(U\), \(h\), \(L\), \(\mu\), \(\pi\) and the noise functions \(W_n\)) assigns to every coupling \(\gamma\) of \(\mu\) and \(\pi\) with \(\mathcal C(\gamma)<\infty\) a stationary reference for \(\pi\) on \(\mathbb P_\gamma\), with step \(h\), dimension parameter \(d\) and innovations \(\widehat W_n\), whose first segment starts at the reference initial class: \(Y^{(0)}(0)=Y_0=[y]\).

The requirement \(Y^{(0)}(0)=[y]\) ties the reference to the coupling: on \(\mathbb P_\gamma\) the algorithm starts at \([x]\) and the reference at \([y]\), where \((x,y)\sim\gamma\). The definition contains no statement about the law of the algorithm or about convergence; those are proved.

steps.title: Finite output transport distance
steps.body:
Claim. Given a product reference, assume \(W_2(\mu,\pi)<\infty\). Then \(W_2(\nu_n,\pi)<\infty\) for every \(n\).

Proof. Since \(W_2(\mu,\pi)\) is the infimum of \(\mathcal C(\gamma)\) over couplings and is finite, some coupling \(\gamma\) has \(\mathcal C(\gamma)<\infty\). On \(\mathbb P_\gamma\) consider the classes \(X_n\) (the algorithm) and \(Y^{(n)}(0)\) (the reference). The joint law of the pair of representatives is a coupling of their laws with cost \(\|X_n-Y^{(n)}(0)\|_2<\infty\), so

\[W_2\bigl(\text{law of }X_n,\ \text{law of }Y^{(n)}(0)\bigr)\le\|X_n-Y^{(n)}(0)\|_2<\infty .\]

The law of \(X_n\) is \(\nu_n\) by the previous output-law step, and the law of \(Y^{(n)}(0)\) is \(\pi\) by the stationarity property of the reference. \(\square\)

steps.title: The small-step bound with the initial Wasserstein distance
steps.body:
Claim. Let \(d\in\mathbb N\), \(U:H\to\mathbb R\) differentiable and \(m\)-strongly convex with \(\nabla U\) \(L\)-Lipschitz, where \(0<m\le L\), and let \(0<h\le2/(m+L)\). Assume \(\int\|x\|^2\pi(dx)<\infty\), \(W_n\in L^2(Q;H)\), \(W_2(\mu,\pi)<\infty\), and that a product reference is given. Then for every \(n\),

\[W_2(\nu_n,\pi)\le(1-mh)^n\,W_2(\mu,\pi)+\frac{33}{20}\,\frac Lm\,\sqrt{hd}.\]

Proof. Signs. From \(h\le2/(m+L)\) and \(m+L>0\), \(h(m+L)\le2\). Since \(m\le L\) and \(h>0\), \(2mh\le h(m+L)\le2\), so \(mh\le1\) and \(a=(1-mh)^n\ge0\). Also \(b=\frac{33}{20}\frac Lm\sqrt{hd}\ge0\).

Bound for one coupling. Let \(\gamma\) be a coupling with \(\mathcal C(\gamma)<\infty\). On \(\mathbb P_\gamma\), the analytic theorem for a stationary integral reference , applied to the initial class \(X_0\), the innovations \(\widehat W_n\) and the reference supplied for \(\gamma\), gives

\[W_2(\text{law of }X_n,\pi)\le(1-mh)^n\,\|X_0-Y^{(0)}(0)\|_2+b .\]

The law of \(X_n\) is \(\nu_n\) by the output-law step; \(Y^{(0)}(0)=Y_0\) by the definition of a product reference; and \(\|X_0-Y_0\|_2=\mathcal C(\gamma)\) by the cost identity of the section on initial extensions. Hence

\[W_2(\nu_n,\pi)\le a\,\mathcal C(\gamma)+b\qquad\text{for every coupling }\gamma\text{ with }\mathcal C(\gamma)<\infty.\qquad(1)\]

Infimum. The left side of (1) does not depend on \(\gamma\). Because \(W_2(\mu,\pi)<\infty\), the infimum of \(\mathcal C(\gamma)\) over finite-cost couplings equals \(W_2(\mu,\pi)\) (infinite-cost couplings do not lower the infimum), and since \(a\ge0\), \(\inf_\gamma(a\,\mathcal C(\gamma)+b)=a\,W_2(\mu,\pi)+b\). Taking the infimum in (1) gives the claim; both transport distances are finite (the output one by the previous step), so the inequality is between real numbers . \(\square\)

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/ConditionalDrift..title: Conditional expectation of the gradient discrepancy
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/ConditionalDrift..summary: Let \(Y\) be an observed random variable and let \(D\) be a square-integrable random vector. Under the stated measurability assumptions, the conditional expectation given \(\sigma(Y)\) has a measurable representation \(e(Y)\). Conditional Jensen gives \(\int\|e\|^2d(Y_\#P)\le\mathbb E\|D\|^2\). Applied to \(D_t=\nabla U(Y_t)-\nabla U(X)\), this produces the state-dependent discrepancy in the relative-density weak equation and preserves the Gaussian energy bound.

steps.title: A measurable representation of a conditional mean
steps.body:
Assume \(D\in L^2(P)\) and \(Y\) is measurable. The conditional expectation \(\mathbb E[D\mid\sigma(Y)]\) is strongly measurable with respect to \(\sigma(Y)\). Doob–Dynkin factorization, under the stated assumptions on the spaces, gives a strongly measurable field \(e\) such that \(e(Y)=\mathbb E[D\mid\sigma(Y)]\) almost surely. Conditional Jensen and integration give

\[\int\|e(y)\|^2d(Y_\#P)(y)=\mathbb E\|\mathbb E[D\mid\sigma(Y)]\|^2\le\mathbb E\|D\|^2.\]

The conditional expectation is square-integrable, so the integral on the left is finite. The field is determined only up to a null set under the law of \(Y\), which does not affect these integrals.

steps.title: The conditional mean on measurable sets
steps.body:
Suppose \(D\) is integrable and \(e(Y)=\mathbb E[D\mid\sigma(Y)]\) almost surely. For every measurable observation set \(A\), the pushforward integral formula and the defining property of conditional expectation give

\[\int_A e(y)d(Y_\#P)(y)=\int_{Y^{-1}(A)}e(Y)\,dP=\int_{Y^{-1}(A)}D\,dP.\]

The inverse image \(Y^{-1}(A)\) belongs to \(\sigma(Y)\), so the last equality is a valid conditional-expectation identity. All terms are vector-valued integrals under the stated integrability assumptions.

steps.title: Pairing the conditional mean with an observed test
steps.body:
Let \(\varphi\) be strongly measurable, and assume \(\langle D,\varphi(Y)\rangle\) is integrable. The function \(\varphi(Y)\) is measurable with respect to \(\sigma(Y)\). The conditional expectation rule for a continuous bilinear pairing therefore gives

\[\mathbb E[\langle D,\varphi(Y)\rangle\mid\sigma(Y)]=\langle\mathbb E[D\mid\sigma(Y)],\varphi(Y)\rangle.\]

Integrate this equality, replace the conditional mean by \(e(Y)\), and change variables by the law of \(Y\). The result is

\[\int\langle e(y),\varphi(y)\rangle d(Y_\#P)(y)=\mathbb E\langle D,\varphi(Y)\rangle.\]

The integrability hypothesis is required for this test; it is not inferred for arbitrary unbounded functions.

steps.title: The gradient discrepancy before conditioning
steps.body:
On the product space of the initial state and independent Gaussian variable, put \(Y_t(x,z)=x-t abla U(x)+\sqrt{2t}z\) and define

\[D_t(x,z)= abla U\!\left(x-t abla U(x)+\sqrt{2t}z ight)- abla U(x).\]

Thus \(D_t= abla U(Y_t)- abla U(X)\). The order of subtraction fixes its sign in the weak equation: the conditional field is \(e_t(y)= abla U(y)-\mathbb E[ abla U(X)\mid Y_t=y]\). The definition alone asserts no integrability or energy bound.

steps.title: The sigma-algebra of the interpolated state
steps.body: The observation at elapsed time \(t\) is \(Y_t\), and its sigma-algebra is \(\sigma(Y_t)=\{Y_t^{-1}(A):A\text{ measurable}\}\), interpreted as the generated sigma-algebra. A random variable measurable for this sigma-algebra depends only on the value of \(Y_t\). Conditioning the gradient discrepancy on \(\sigma(Y_t)\) therefore yields a field on the state space. If the gradient is Lipschitz, the observation map is measurable and this sigma-algebra is contained in the ambient one.

steps.title: The conditional discrepancy and its second moment
steps.body:
Assume \(\nabla U\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz and \(G_0=\int\|\nabla U\|^2d\mu<\infty\). The Gaussian displacement estimate proves that \(D_t\) is square-integrable and \(\mathbb E\|D_t\|^2\le L^2(t^2G_0+2tn)\), where \(n=\dim E\). Apply the measurable conditional-mean result to obtain a strongly measurable field \(e_t\) satisfying

\[e_t(Y_t)=\mathbb E[D_t\mid\sigma(Y_t)],\qquad \int\|e_t(y)\|^2d\rho_t(y)\le t^2L^2G_0+2tnL^2,\]\[\rho_t=(Y_t)_\#(\mu\otimes\mathcal N(0,I)).\]

The equality identifies the field for the same Gaussian interpolation used in the algorithm. Its square-integrability and energy bound follow from conditional Jensen and the preceding joint Gaussian estimate.

steps.title: The discrepancy energy relative to the Gibbs measure
steps.body:
Suppose a measurable nonnegative density identifies the interpolation law as \( ho_t=r_t u\). The conditional-mean construction gives a square-integrable field under \( ho_t\). Changing measure proves integrability of the weighted square under \( u\), and

\[\int r_t(y)\|e_t(y)\|^2d u(y)=\int\|e_t(y)\|^2d ho_t(y)\le t^2L^2G_0+2tnL^2.\]

The conditional-mean identity is unchanged. This is the form of the energy estimate that appears in entropy production.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/InteriorEntropy.l.title: Entropy comparison using positive-time derivatives
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/InteriorEntropy.l.summary: A continuous function on \([0,T]\) can satisfy an affine comparison using derivative bounds only on \((0,T)\). This applies to Gaussian entropy calculations where derivatives are first proved at positive times. The second result identifies the relative-entropy derivative with the differentiated density integral at an interior time, under the stated local domination assumptions. Control near zero is required separately when passing to the initial law.

steps.title: An affine comparison without endpoint derivatives
steps.body:
Let \(a>0\), assume \(H\) is continuous on \([0,T]\), and suppose \(H'(t)\le-aH(t)+b\) on \((0,T)\). Set \(F(t)=e^{at}(H(t)-b/a)\). Then

\[F'(t)=e^{at}\bigl(a(H(t)-b/a)+H'(t)\bigr)\le0.\]

The mean-value theorem implies that \(F\) is nonincreasing on the closed interval, using continuity at its endpoints and differentiability in its interior. Thus \(F(t)\le F(0)\). Multiplication by \(e^{-at}>0\) and rearrangement give

\[H(t)\le e^{-at}H(0)+\frac ba(1-e^{-at}).\]

The cancellation \(a(b/a)=b\) uses \(a\ne0\). No derivative is required at zero or at \(T\).

steps.title: The entropy derivative at an interior time
steps.body:
Fix \(0<t<T\). Suppose the relative densities are positive, \(C^1\), normalized and locally dominated for entropy differentiation at every time in \((0,T)\). Dominated differentiation gives the derivative of \(\int r_u\log r_u\,d u\) at \(t\). A sufficiently small neighborhood of \(t\) lies in \((0,T)\); on this neighborhood the finite-density entropy formula identifies that integral with relative entropy. Equality of the functions near \(t\) therefore yields

\[ rac d{dt}\operatorname{KL}(r_t u\mid u)=\int\dot r_t(x)(\log r_t(x)+1)\,d u(x).\]

The assumptions concern interior times only. Continuity or a one-sided bound at zero must still be proved before applying an estimate that involves the initial entropy.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/GradientMoment.le.title: A gradient moment bound from a coupling
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/GradientMoment.le.summary: Let \((X,Y)\) couple \(\mu\) and \( u\), with finite squared distance, and suppose the gradient is \(L\)-Lipschitz. The inequality \(\| abla U(X)\|\le L\|X-Y\|+\| abla U(Y)\|\) gives a second-moment bound under \(\mu\) when that moment is finite under \( u\). For a normalized Gibbs target, the latter is at most \(nL\). An explicitly assumed entropy bound on the coupling cost then gives the stated entropy-dependent gradient estimate. The final ULA entropy theorem instead obtains its gradient moment directly from exponential integrability of the Gibbs score.

steps.title: Integrability and the coupling estimate
steps.body:
Let \(c\) have marginals \(\mu, u\), and assume \(\int\|x-y\|^2dc<\infty\) and \(\int\| abla U\|^2d u<\infty\). Lipschitzness and \((a+b)^2\le2a^2+2b^2\) give the pointwise inequality

\[\| abla U(x)\|^2\le2L^2\|x-y\|^2+2\| abla U(y)\|^2.\]

The right-hand side is integrable under \(c\). Measurability and domination imply integrability of the first-coordinate gradient square, hence of \(\| abla U\|^2\) under \(\mu\). Integration and the marginal identities give

\[\int\| abla U\|^2d\mu\le2L^2\int\|x-y\|^2dc(x,y)+2\int\| abla U\|^2d u.\]

steps.title: The estimate for a Gibbs target
steps.body:
Let \( u=Z^{-1}e^{-U}dx\) be a Gibbs probability measure, with differentiable \(U\) and \(L\)-Lipschitz gradient. Probability normalization supplies a finite positive partition function. The Gibbs score estimate proves square-integrability and \(\int\| abla U\|^2d u\le nL\), without strong convexity. Substituting these facts in the coupling estimate gives

\[\int\| abla U\|^2d\mu\le2L^2\int\|x-y\|^2dc+2nL.\]

The same argument proves gradient square-integrability under \(\mu\); it is not assumed before this conclusion.

steps.title: Substitution of an entropy bound on the coupling cost
steps.body:
Suppose the given finite-cost coupling also satisfies

\[\int\|x-y\|^2dc(x,y)\le rac2\alpha\operatorname{KL}(\mu\mid u),\qquad \alpha>0,\quad \operatorname{KL}(\mu\mid u)<\infty.\]

Multiply this inequality by \(2L^2\ge0\) and substitute it in the preceding gradient estimate. Since \(2L^2(2/\alpha)=4L^2/\alpha\),

\[\int\| abla U\|^2d\mu\le rac{4L^2}{\alpha}\operatorname{KL}(\mu\mid u)+2nL.\]

The cost-to-entropy estimate is an explicit hypothesis for the supplied coupling. This result does not prove a transport inequality from LSI.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/InterpolationDens.title: Construct the positive Gaussian mixture and Gibbs-relative density
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/InterpolationDens.summary:
Let \(\mu\) be the initial probability, \(t>0\), and \(c_t(x)=x-t abla U(x)\). The update \(c_t(X)+\sqrt{2t}Z\), with \(Z\) an independent standard Gaussian vector, has density \(q_t(y)=\int K_t(x,y)d\mu(x)\), where \(K_t(x,y)=(4\pi t)^{-d/2}\exp(-\|y-c_t(x)\|^2/(4t))\). This follows by conditioning on \(X\) and applying Tonelli. No initial Lebesgue density is needed.

Each Gaussian component is positive and bounded by \((4\pi t)^{-d/2}\). The mixture is consequently positive and finite at every observation. Dominated convergence gives spatial continuity, and parameter integration gives measurability. If the Gibbs probability has density \(J(y)=Z^{-1}e^{-U(y)}\), the positive continuous function \(r_t=q_t/J=Ze^Uq_t\) satisfies \(r_t u=q_tdy\) and \(\int r_td u=1\). Its differentiability, entropy, and Fisher information require the subsequent estimates.

steps.title: The nonnegative Gaussian mixture integral
steps.body:
For \(t>0\), put \(c_t(x)=x-t\nabla U(x)\) and \(C_t=(4\pi t)^{-d/2}\). Define

\[K_t(x,y)=C_t\exp\!\left(-\frac{\|y-c_t(x)\|^2}{4t}\right),\qquad q_t^{\mathrm{ext}}(y)=\int K_t(x,y)d\mu(x).\]

For fixed \(x\), this is the Gaussian density with mean \(c_t(x)\) and covariance \(2tI_d\). The mixture is initially defined by a nonnegative integral, which may take the value infinity. Tonelli is therefore available before a pointwise finiteness assertion has been proved.

The subsequent peak bound will show that this same integral is finite at every \(y\), even for an initial law with no density or moments. The positive-time assumption is used in the Gaussian normalization and denominator.

A Lipschitz gradient is continuous and measurable, so \(c_t\) is measurable in the starting point. The map \((x,y)\mapsto y-c_t(x)\) is jointly measurable. Squared norm, multiplication by the fixed scalar, and exponential preserve measurability, so \(K_t\) is a jointly measurable nonnegative kernel.

Integration in \(x\) against \(\mu\) yields a measurable function of \(y\). The mixing measure is finite and hence sigma-finite, as required for measurable parameter integration. This measurability assertion concerns the defining formula and does not use a positive-time finiteness estimate.

steps.title: The update law has the Gaussian mixture density
steps.body:
Let \(X\sim\mu\), let \(Z\sim\mathcal N(0,I_d)\) be independent, and write \(Y_t=c_t(X)+\sqrt{2t}Z\). For a measurable set \(A\), independence and the pushforward formula give

\[\mathbb P(Y_t\in A)=\int\mathbb P\bigl(c_t(x)+\sqrt{2t}Z\in A\bigr)d\mu(x).\]

The inner probability is \(\int_AK_t(x,y)dy\), by the fixed-state affine Gaussian density. Joint measurability permits Tonelli under \(\mu\) and Lebesgue measure restricted to \(A\). Consequently

\[\mathbb P(Y_t\in A)=\int_A\left(\int K_t(x,y)d\mu(x)\right)dy=\int_Aq_t^{\mathrm{ext}}(y)dy.\]

Thus the mixture is the density of the update law. Equivalently, the same computation applies to every nonnegative measurable test function. It does not assume that \(\mu\) itself has a density.

steps.title: Use positivity of every Gaussian component
steps.body:
At positive time the normalizer \(C_t\) is strictly positive, and the exponential is strictly positive at every finite argument. Hence \(K_t(x,y)>0\) for every pair \(x,y\).

Fix \(y\). The nonnegative measurable function \(x\mapsto K_t(x,y)\) is positive on the whole state space, which has \(\mu\)-mass one. A nonnegative integral can vanish only when its integrand is zero almost everywhere. Therefore \(q_t^{\mathrm{ext}}(y)>0\). This proves positivity at every observation, before any assertion about its finiteness.

steps.title: Bound every mixture value by the common Gaussian peak
steps.body:
For \(t>0\), the Gaussian exponent is nonpositive, hence

\[0\le K_t(x,y)\le C_t,\qquad q_t^{\mathrm{ext}}(y)\le C_t.\]

The proof establishes the exponential bound with the fact that an exponential with nonpositive exponent is at most one: the numerator \(-\|y-c_t(x)\|^2\) is nonpositive and the denominator \(4t\) is positive. Multiplication by the nonnegative normalizer preserves the inequality, and the same inequality holds for nonnegative extended values.

Monotonicity of the nonnegative integral integrates this pointwise bound. The integral of the constant \(C_t\) equals \(C_t\mu(E)=C_t\) because \(\mu\) is a probability measure. This theorem requires no regularity of the gradient: its bound concerns the nonnegative integrand at every point, and the upper nonnegative integral remains monotone even before measurability is established.

The exponential factor is at most one, independently of the Gaussian center. Hence averaging over any starting probability retains the same peak bound, without requiring an initial moment.

steps.title: Strict positivity of the relative density
steps.body:
Assume the Gibbs target is a probability and \(t>0\). The partition positivity result and target normalization give \(0<Z<\infty\). The Gaussian peak and positivity results give \(0<q_t(y)<\infty\) at every observation. The ordinary exponential \(e^{U(y)}\) is also finite and strictly positive.

Every factor in \(r_t(y)=Ze^{U(y)}q_t(y)\) is therefore a positive finite real number, proving \(r_t(y)>0\). Both positivity and finiteness are needed: neither an infinite mixture value nor a zero partition could be used as an ordinary positive relative density.

steps.title: The relative density represents the update law
steps.body:
Fix \(t>0\) and assume the Gibbs partition satisfies \(0<Z<\infty\), as proved under the target normalization hypotheses. Let

\[J(y)=Z^{-1}e^{-U(y)},\qquad r_t(y)=Ze^{U(y)}q_t(y).\]

The mixture \(q_t\) is finite and measurable, and the Gibbs density is strictly positive. Pointwise multiplication therefore gives the ordinary identity

\[r_t(y)J(y)=\bigl(Ze^{U(y)}q_t(y)\bigr)\bigl(Z^{-1}e^{-U(y)}\bigr)=q_t(y).\]

Integrating over any measurable set identifies the measures:

\[r_t\nu=q_tdy=\rho_t.\]

The last equality is the Gaussian-mixture law identity already proved. Hence this relative density represents the specified interpolation law. Positivity, spatial regularity, time differentiation, and finite entropy remain separate properties established in the subsequent analysis.

steps.title: Normalization of the relative density
steps.body:
The measure induced by the constructed relative density is a probability measure:

\[\int r_t\,d u=1\qquad(t>0).\]

Integrating the identity \(r_t u= ho_t\) over the entire state space gives \(\int r_t\,d u=1\), because the Gaussian update is a probability law. Thus the explicitly constructed density is normalized; no separate assumption about its mass is required.

Positivity, continuity, and normalization all concern this same density. Normalization alone does not imply finite entropy or Fisher information; these properties will follow from the positive-time moment and derivative bounds.

Integrating the law identity on the whole space gives \(\int r_t\,d u=1\). Normalization is therefore inherited from the Gaussian transition rather than proved by a separate algebraic manipulation of a possibly infinite density.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/BoundedLog.lean.title: Bounded logarithmic tests and their entropy primitives
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/BoundedLog.lean.summary:
For \(M=m+1\), define \(\chi_m(z)=M\arctan(z/M)\) and \(w_m(z)=(1+(z/M)^2)^{-1}\). Then \(\chi_m\) is smooth and bounded, \(\chi_m^{\prime}=w_m\), \(0\le w_m\le1\), and \(|\chi_m(z)|\le|z|\). For each fixed \(z\), the test and its derivative converge to \(z\) and 1 respectively.

For a positive density value \(r\), the primitive \(\Phi_m(r)=\int_1^r\chi_m(\log u)du\) has derivative \(\chi_m(\log r)\), is nonnegative, and is bounded by \(r\log r-r+1\). Its pointwise limit is this entropy integrand. These estimates justify bounded tests in the weak equation, their time chain rules, and dominated convergence to the entropy identity under finite relative entropy.

steps.title: Choose the bounded test and its weight
steps.body:
For a natural number \(m\), write \(c=m+1>0\). Define

\[\chi_m(z)=c\arctan(z/c),\qquad w_m(z)=\frac1{1+(z/c)^2},\qquad\Phi_m(r)=\int_1^r\chi_m(\log u)du.\]

The positive offset in \(c\) prevents division by zero even for \(m=0\). The interval integral is oriented: when \(r<1\), its sign reverses. The formulas define these expressions for every real argument; the entropy claims below explicitly require \(r>0\).

The scale \(M=m+1\) is strictly positive for every allowed index, avoiding a zero denominator. The arctangent bounds the test uniformly in its argument, while the derivative weight remains between zero and one.

steps.title: Differentiate and bound the test
steps.body:
The arctangent chain rule gives \(\chi_m(0)=0\) and \(\chi_m^{\prime}(z)=w_m(z)\). The denominator is at least one, so \(0\le w_m\le1\). The derivative bound implies that \(\chi_m\) is 1-Lipschitz, hence \(|\chi_m(z)|\le|z|\). Independently, \(|\arctan u|<\pi/2\) gives \(|\chi_m(z)|\le c\pi/2\). This last bound controls the time derivative integrand without any log-integrability requirement. Since arctangent has the sign of its argument, \(\chi_m\) does too.

The test is smooth of all orders because arctangent is smooth and \(c>0\). In its first derivative, the factor \(1/c\) from the inner argument cancels the outer factor \(c\), leaving exactly the stated weight.

Differentiating arctangent gives the rational weight \(1/(1+(z/M)^2)\). Its denominator is at least one, proving nonnegativity and the upper bound used to dominate every truncated score energy.

steps.title: Dominate the entropy endpoints
steps.body:
We have \(\Phi_m(1)=0\). For \(r\ge1\), both \(\log u\) and its test are nonnegative on \([1,r]\), giving \(\Phi_m(r)\ge0\). For \(0<r\le1\), the test is nonpositive on \([r,1]\), and reversing the interval again gives nonnegativity.

On the positive side, \(0\le\chi_m(\log u)\le\log u\). On the negative side, \(\log u\le\chi_m(\log u)\le0\); reversing the interval preserves the corresponding upper bound for the primitive. In both cases,

\[0\le\Phi_m(r)\le\int_1^r\log u\,du=r\log r-r+1.\]

Pointwise convergence of the test and domination by \(|\log u|\), integrable on the finite interval between 1 and \(r\), prove \(\Phi_m(r)\to r\log r-r+1\). These are exactly the hypotheses for dominated convergence against the finite-KL relative density later.

The entropy integrand \(r\log r-r+1\) is nonnegative and dominates the bounded primitives. For a probability density its integral equals KL, so finite relative entropy supplies the endpoint majorant for dominated convergence.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/GaussianMeasurabi.title: Jointly measurable density and relative score

At positive time the density is everywhere positive. Dividing its gradient by the density and adding \(\nabla U\) yields one jointly measurable relative score field, equal pointwise to \(\nabla\log r_t\). At the lower endpoint use an explicit upper bound \(H(s)\le M(s)\), where \(M\) is continuous at zero. steps.title: Integrate the affine differential inequality
steps.body:
Suppose \(H\) is absolutely continuous on \([s,t]\) and \(H^{\prime}\le-aH+b\) almost everywhere, with \(a>0\). Set \(F(u)=e^{au}(H(u)-b/a)\). Products of absolutely continuous functions on a compact interval are absolutely continuous. The product rule holds almost everywhere and gives \(F^{\prime}(u)=e^{au}(a(H(u)-b/a)+H^{\prime}(u))\le0\).

The fundamental theorem of calculus for absolutely continuous functions gives \(F(t)-F(s)=\int_s^tF^{\prime}\le0\). Multiply by \(e^{-at}>0\), cancel the exponentials, and rearrange:

\[H(t)\le e^{-a(t-s)}H(s)+\frac ba(1-e^{-a(t-s)}).\]

The proof removes no exceptional set by assuming a derivative there; both differentiability and the inequality are used only almost everywhere.

Local absolute continuity gives an integrable derivative and the fundamental theorem on each positive compact interval. Multiplying by the smooth integrating factor preserves absolute continuity, so integrating its almost-everywhere derivative bound is legitimate.

UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/Compatibility.lea.title: Why the LSI constant cannot exceed smoothness
UnadjustedLangevin/LSI/Compatibility.lea.summary:
Let \( u(dx)=Z^{-1}e^{-U(x)}dx\) on a nontrivial finite-dimensional real Hilbert space. Suppose \(U\) is differentiable, \( abla U\) is \(L\)-Lipschitz, and the target satisfies the stated positive \(C^1\)-density log-Sobolev inequality with constant \(\alpha\). Then \(\alpha\le L\). No position moment, Hessian, or strong convexity is assumed.

For bounded \(C^1\) tests with \(\| abla f\|\le D\), apply the inequality to normalized exponential tilts. The small-tilt limit gives \(\alpha\operatorname{Var}_ u(f)\le D^2\). For a unit vector \(v\), Gibbs integration by parts applied to \(\sin(t\langle v,x angle)\), together with the directional score second-moment bound \(L\), gives \(\alpha(\int\cos(t\langle v,x angle)d u)^2\le L\). Bounded convergence as \(t\downarrow0\) proves the conclusion without integrability of \(x\).

steps.title: Integrability of bounded exponential tests
steps.body:
If \(|f|\le B\), then \(tf\le |t|B\), so \(0<e^{tf}\le e^{|t|B}\). The right side is an integrable constant under every finite measure. Measurability follows from that of \(f\); integrable domination then proves integrability of the exponential. Assume \(\int e^f d u\le e^c\). First derive \(f\in L^1(\mu)\) with the preceding theorem. Apply the Young inequality to \(a=d\mu/d u\) and \(f-c\), and integrate: \(\int(f-c)d\mu\le\int\Phi(a)d u+\int e^{f-c}d u-1\).

Probability normalization identifies \(\int\Phi(a)d u\) with the finite relative entropy and \(\int(f-c)d\mu=\int f d\mu-c\). The MGF hypothesis makes \(\int e^{f-c}d u\le1\), canceling the final two terms. Thus \(\int f d\mu\le H(\mu\mid u)+c\), together with the integrability witness used in its derivation. The proof explicitly justifies each weighted integral and subtraction.

Subtract a scalar normalization from the observable before applying the inequality. Choosing that normalization as the logarithm of its exponential moment produces the variational entropy bound with the sharp log-moment term.

steps.body:
For \(b>0\), the real radial Gaussian \(e^{-b\|v\|^2}\) is integrable on every finite-dimensional real Hilbert space. This also follows from the complex Gaussian integrability formula at real positive precision: taking its norm gives exactly the displayed real exponential. This supplies the finite integral needed in the Gaussian linearization argument.

A positive Gaussian precision gives integrable radial decay in finite dimension. This supplies the auxiliary Gaussian averaging measure used to turn directional score estimates into a squared-score estimate.

steps.title: The nonnegative radial Gaussian integral
steps.body:
Let \(b>0\) and let \(d\) be finite. The radial Gaussian \(v\mapsto e^{-b\|v\|^2}\) is nonnegative and integrable. Its nonnegative extended integral therefore equals its ordinary integral, and Gaussian integration gives

\[\int_{\mathbb R^d}e^{-b\|v\|^2}dv =\left(\frac\pi b\right)^{d/2}<\infty.\]

The expression on the right is strictly positive because \(b>0\). It supplies the finite nonzero normalizing constant for the auxiliary Gaussian average. In dimension zero the empty product is one, so the same formula remains valid. Nonnegativity also permits Tonelli to exchange this Gaussian averaging with the target integral before their final numerical bound is evaluated.

The identity is proved for nonnegative integrals before any integrability of a random score is assumed.

Completing the square in the auxiliary variable evaluates its exponentially tilted Gaussian integral. The remaining factor is an exponential of the squared norm of the vector paired with it.

The proof uses the standard conditional-product KL identity with the constant Markov kernel \(x\mapsto\eta\); its conditional products are exactly the ordinary product measures. This equality supplies the independent-noise step in data processing.

On this full-measure set the density ratios are ordinary positive finite values, so the logarithm product rule applies. This proves \(\log(d\mu/d u)=\log(d\mu/d ho)+\log(d ho/d u)\), as an almost-everywhere identity under \(\mu\). The positivity and finiteness checks prevent using logarithm algebra at a zero or infinite density.

Suppose truncated identities have the form \(B_n-A_n=\int q_n d u\). Assume the two endpoint sequences converge to their intended values, \(q_n o q\) almost everywhere, and \(|q_n|\le g\) with \(g\in L^1( u)\). Dominated convergence gives convergence of the right-hand integrals, while the endpoint limits give convergence of the left-hand differences. Their equality for every \(n\) and uniqueness of limits prove \(B-A=\int qd u\).

In the entropy application, the endpoints are truncated entropy integrals and \(q_n\) are bounded-test fluxes on a fixed time interval. Spatial energy estimates supply the pointwise flux limit and a time-integrable dominating bound. This lemma passes the integrated identities to the limit without assuming in advance that the full entropy has already been differentiated.

Pass the approximating integrated identities to the limit in both endpoints and flux. Endpoint domination and spacetime flux domination are checked separately because they use different reference measures and majorants.

steps.title: Regularity supplied by the limiting integral identity
steps.body:
Assume only \(q\in L^1(a,b)\) and the exact identity \(H(t)=H(a)+\int_a^t q(u)du\) throughout \([a,b]\). The primitive of \(q\) is absolutely continuous; adding \(H(a)\) and using the identity proves that \(H\) is absolutely continuous.

Lebesgue differentiation gives derivative \(q(t)\) for the primitive at almost every interior time. The identity holds in an interior neighborhood of each such time, so the derivative transfers to \(H\). This gives precisely the final entropy comparison inputs: local absolute continuity and the flux as derivative almost everywhere.

The limiting identity expresses the function as a constant plus an integral of an \(L^1\) flux. It therefore supplies both local absolute continuity and its almost-everywhere derivative, providing the regularity needed for entropy comparison.

Let \(\pi=Z^{-1}e^{-U}dy\), let \(Y_t=X-t abla U(X)+\sqrt{2t}Z_0\) with independent standard Gaussian \(Z_0\), and write \( ho_t=\mathcal L(Y_t)\), \(r_t=d ho_t/d\pi\), and \(S_t= abla\log r_t\). Under the stated potential, log-Sobolev, and finite initial gradient-energy hypotheses, positive-time entropy is finite. Its time regularity is proved by integrating bounded approximations.

For the bounded tests \(\chi_m(\log r_t)\), the Gaussian weak equation and the time chain rule give exact integrated identities on \([a,b]\subset(0,\infty)\). The entropy integrand dominates their endpoints. Half the sum of the frozen-velocity and relative-score energies dominates their fluxes independently of \(m\) and is integrable in time. Dominated convergence therefore yields \(H( ho_b\mid\pi)-H( ho_a\mid\pi)=\int_a^bq(t)dt\). This proves local absolute continuity and derivative \(q\) almost everywhere. The score-pairing identity subsequently writes that derivative as \(-I_t+\mathbb E\langle abla U(Y_t)- abla U(X),S_t(Y_t) angle\).

steps.title: Removing bounded log weights by dominated convergence
steps.body:
Let \(w_m(z)=[1+(z/(m+1))^2]^{-1}\). For a measurable scalar field \(z\) and an integrable field \(f\),

\[\int w_m(z(x))f(x)\,d\nu(x)\longrightarrow\int f(x)\,d\nu(x).\]

The pointwise limit is \(w_m(z(x))\to1\), proved in the pointwise convergence of bounded-log derivative weights to one. Each weighted integrand is measurable, because the weight is obtained by division, squaring and inversion of measurable real functions. Furthermore \(0\le w_m\le1\), so \(|w_m(z)f|\le|f|\). The proof invokes dominated convergence with the integrable majorant \(|f|\). This lemma later removes the truncation from the Gaussian flux, whose two factors are square integrable.

The derivative weights converge pointwise to one and stay between zero and one. Multiplying by the already integrable unweighted pairing gives a common absolute majorant, so dominated convergence removes the weight without changing the reference measure.

steps.title: Why the square-integrable flux pairing is integrable
steps.body:
If \(v,s\in L^2(\nu;E)\), then

\[|\langle v,s\rangle|\le\|v\|\|s\|,\qquad \|v\|\|s\|\in L^1(\nu).\]

Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the integral of the product of the two norms by their finite square norms. The absolute inner product is bounded by this norm product, proving absolute integrability of the pairing. This remains true on the stated measure space without assuming its total mass is finite.

For square-integrable fields \(a,b\), use \(|\langle a,b\rangle|\le(\|a\|^2+\|b\|^2)/2\). The right side has finite integral, proving absolute flux integrability before signed Fubini or limiting arguments.

steps.title: The real Gibbs density and its normalization
steps.body:
Write \(Z=\int e^{-U(x)}\,dx\), and let \(\pi\) be the normalized Gibbs law. Define

\[J(y)=Z^{-1}e^{-U(y)}.\]

The existing probability-mass argument proves \(0<Z<\infty\); differentiability makes \(U\) measurable and gives strict positivity of the partition function. Consequently \(J(y)>0\) at every point. The measure identity is

\[\pi(dy)=J(y)\,dy.\]

The density identity follows from multiplying the unnormalized Gibbs weight by the finite scalar \(Z^{-1}\). Since \(0<Z<\infty\), the resulting measurable function \(J\) is positive and has integral one. The same expression therefore represents the target in ordinary Lebesgue integration; strong convexity is not needed for this change-of-density step.

The Gibbs density is positive and finite pointwise, and its integral is one. Thus \(J\Phi_m(r_t)\) may be read as a Lebesgue representation of the same bounded relative-entropy primitive integrated against Gibbs.

steps.title: The time derivative of the weighted entropy primitive
steps.body:
Let \(p_t\) be the Lebesgue density of the frozen Gaussian update, and let \(r_t=p_t/J\) be its relative density. For the bounded entropy primitive \(\Phi_m\), one has \(\Phi_m'(r)=\chi_m(\log r)\) for \(r>0\). At every positive time, the kernel differentiation result gives \(\partial_t p_t=\dot p_t\), hence

\[\partial_t r_t=Ze^{U}\dot p_t,\qquad \partial_t[J\Phi_m(r_t)]=\chi_m(\log r_t)\dot p_t.\]

The proof applies the time chain rule first to the constant multiple defining \(r_t\), then to the derivative formula for the bounded entropy primitive, then to multiplication by \(J\). The remaining coefficient cancels because \(J(y)Ze^{U(y)}=1\), using the inverse of the strictly positive real partition function and \(e^{-U}e^U=1\). This cancellation is what permits the spacetime estimate to use the Lebesgue \(L^1\) bound on \(\dot p_t\).

Because \(J\) is time independent and \(Jr_t=p_t\), differentiating \(J\Phi_m(r_t)\) gives \(\chi_m(\log r_t)\dot p_t\). This cancellation avoids differentiating the Gibbs density in time.

steps.title: Identifying finite entropy through the chosen density
steps.body:
Let \( u\) be the reference probability and suppose \(\mu=r u\) is a probability measure, \(r\ge0\) is measurable, and \(H(\mu\mid u)<\infty\). Then

\[\mathrm{kl}(r)=r\log r+1-r\in L^1( u),\qquad \int\mathrm{kl}(r)\,d u=H(\mu\mid u).\]

The Radon–Nikodym derivative of \(r u\) relative to \( u\) is \(r\) almost everywhere. Finite KL gives integrability of its logarithm under \(r u\); changing measure makes \(r\log r\) integrable under \( u\). Since \(r\) and the constant one both have finite integral, so does \(r\log r-r+1\). Their probability masses agree, so integrating the last two terms cancels them and gives the stated entropy identity.

The relative entropy is finite at positive time by LSI and the Fisher bound. The density formula therefore identifies it with the ordinary integral of \(r_t\log r_t-r_t+1\), whose mass corrections cancel by normalization.

\[0\le\Phi_m(r_t(y))\le\mathrm{kl}(r_t(y)).\]

The left-hand side is measurable: continuity of \(r_t\) and the derivative of \(\Phi_m\) at positive arguments give continuity of their composition. Integrable domination therefore proves integrability for each truncation from this finite entropy majorant. Initial density differentiability, initial Fisher information and a second moment of the state are not required.

For every fixed positive time,

The density identity \(r_t\pi=\rho_t\), with \(r_t=Ze^Up_t\), identifies the integral of \(r_t\log r_t-r_t+1\) with \(H(\rho_t\mid\pi)\). The limit is therefore the relative entropy of the specified Gaussian interpolation law.

Pointwise convergence of the primitive to \(r\log r-r+1\), together with the finite entropy majorant, gives convergence of both positive-time endpoint entropies. This limit is independent of any time-flux limit.

The test-gradient norm is at most the relative-score norm, whose square is integrable. Continuity of the test derivative supplies measurability. Thus the bounded logarithmic test is \(C^1\) and has finite gradient energy, exactly the conditions required by the Gaussian weak equation.

Applying the same identity on every subinterval expresses \(H_m\) as a constant plus the primitive of the integrable flux \(q_m\). Thus \(H_m\) is absolutely continuous, and Lebesgue differentiation gives \(H_m'(t)=q_m(t)\) almost everywhere. Boundedness of the test and space-time integrability of the density derivative suffice; no common spatial bound for every time derivative is assumed.

steps.title: Square-integrability of the Gaussian flux factors

The initial gradient belongs to \(L^2(\mu)\), and the standard Gaussian noise belongs to \(L^2\). Pulling both to the independent product space and taking their scalar combination proves \(V_t\in L^2(\mu\otimes\gamma)\). The relative score belongs to \(L^2(\rho_t)\). Since \(\rho_t\) is the pushforward of \(\mu\otimes\gamma\) by \(Y_t\), the measurable-map characterization of \(L^2\) gives

\[\widehat S_t=S_t\circ Y_t\in L^2(\mu\otimes\gamma).\]

The initial-gradient and Gaussian moment bounds justify the linear combination defining \(V_t\) in the product \(L^2\) space. The explicit score equals \(\nabla\log r_t\) at positive time, so pushforward change of variables preserves its square energy under composition with \(Y_t\). Cauchy–Schwarz then proves integrability of the inner product of these two fields.

The relative score has finite square energy by the Fisher estimate. The frozen velocity has finite square energy by its Gaussian component and initial gradient, so their flux pairing is absolutely integrable by Cauchy–Schwarz.

The relative density is \(r_t(y)=Z e^{U(y)}p_t(y)\). The partition factor \(Z\) is constant in space, \(e^U\) is \(C^1\) because \(U\) is \(C^1\), and the Gaussian mixture \(p_t\) is \(C^1\). Therefore \(r_t\) is \(C^1\) at every positive time.

The ordinary product rule combines the constant partition, the continuously differentiable exponential of the potential, and the continuously differentiable Gaussian mixture. The resulting relative density is positive and normalized by the established law identity, so it belongs to the target LSI test class.

The relative density is the product of the mixture density with the positive reciprocal Gibbs density. The product rule gives \(C^1\) regularity, while pointwise positivity and normalization are inherited from the interpolation law.

steps.title: The log-Sobolev inequality for the interpolation law
steps.body:
The log-Sobolev hypothesis states that the normalized Gibbs target is a probability and that its inequality holds for every positive normalized \(C^1\) relative density. The constructed \(r_t\) satisfies each of these test conditions: positivity and normalization follow from the mixture law identity, and \(C^1\) regularity follows from the preceding derivative calculation.

Applying the inequality and then using \(r_t u= ho_t\) gives

\[2\alpha\,H( ho_t\mid u)\le I( ho_t\mid u).\]

Here the entropy and Fisher information are initially nonnegative extended values. This application assumes neither is finite. Their finiteness is established below from the gradient moment and Gaussian score estimate. Thus the original positive-density formulation of the log-Sobolev inequality suffices.

steps.title: Record the square-norm Jensen inequality for probability measures
steps.body:
For a square-integrable random vector \(F\) under a probability measure, convexity of squared norm gives

\[\left\|\int F\,d\mu\right\|^2\le\int\|F\|^2\,d\mu.\]

The norm is convex and nonnegative, and squaring is convex and increasing on nonnegative numbers. Their composition is therefore convex. Square integrability supplies integrability both of \(F\) and of \(\|F\|^2\), so Jensen applies to this convex function on the whole vector space. This general lemma is used under the normalized Gaussian posterior at each proposed state.

For a probability measure, expand \(\int\|v-\int v\|^2\ge0\). This gives \(\|\int v\|^2\le\int\|v\|^2\), the vector Jensen inequality used for the posterior mean score.

steps.title: The conditional distribution of the initial mixture component

\[\lambda_y(dx)=\frac{K_a(c(x),y)}{p(y)}\,\mu(dx).\]

Weight the initial probability by \(K_a(c(x),y)/p(y)\). Positive precision makes the kernel positive and finite, so its mixture denominator is positive. The next calculation shows that this weight integrates to one, establishing the posterior probability before Jensen is applied.

At observation \(y\), weight the initial law by \(K_t(x,y)/p_t(y)\). The denominator is the mixture value, making this a probability describing which initial component contributed to that observation.

The last expression defines this flux. Its divergence equals the density's time derivative, while the weak equation consequently carries a minus sign after integration by parts. Domination therefore proves absolute integrability of the coordinate derivative, as required before Fubini and integration by parts.

steps.title: Apply global integration by parts after proving all three product integrabilities
steps.body:
For one unit coordinate \(v\), global integration by parts gives

\[\int D_v\langle F_{t,x}(y),v\rangle\,\psi(y)\,d\mu(x)\,dy=-\int\langle F_{t,x}(y),v\rangle D_v\psi(y)\,d\mu(x)\,dy.\]

The coordinate derivative times the bounded test is integrable by derivative domination. The flux times the directional test derivative is integrable by the finite-gradient-energy pairing estimate, and the flux times the test is integrable by boundedness. Fubini provides these three section conditions for almost every initial state. At such a state both functions are differentiable, so global directional integration by parts applies. Integrating its section identity over the initial law gives the displayed equality. The required condition at infinity is integrability of these products; no additional pointwise test decay is assumed.

The product, its directional derivative, and the flux-gradient pairing are all integrable. These checks make global integration by parts applicable without assuming compact support of the bounded test.

steps.title: The weak equation for bounded continuously differentiable tests
steps.body:
Sum the coordinate identities over an orthonormal basis. The divergence identity turns the sum on the left into \(\dot K_t\), while completeness of the basis turns the sum on the right into \(\langle F_{t,x},\nabla\psi\rangle\). Fubini then yields

\[\int\dot p_t(y)\psi(y)\,dy=-\int\langle F_{t,x}(y),\nabla\psi(y)\rangle\,d\mu(x)\,dy.\]

Each coordinate integrand is integrable by the preceding estimates, so finite sums commute with their integrals. The time derivative of the kernel is integrable, and multiplication by the bounded test preserves that property. Fubini consequently exchanges the starting-state and observation integrals and identifies their mixture with \(\dot p_t\). All integrability conditions follow from the Gaussian law, initial gradient energy, boundedness of the test, and finite test-gradient energy.

Sum the coordinate identities and use divergence equal to the kernel time derivative. Fubini identifies the mixture derivative on the left, producing the weak equation for every admitted bounded finite-energy test.

All pairings are integrable by the square-energy estimates on the independent initial/noise space. Young's inequality bounds the error pairing by \(I_t/4\) plus its squared-gradient discrepancy. steps.title: The positive-time entropy derivative inequality almost everywhere
steps.body:
The relative entropy is absolutely continuous on every compact interval inside \((0,\infty)\), and its derivative equals the raw flux almost everywhere there. To use this fact on an entire finite range \((0,T)\), choose the countable intervals

\[\left(\frac1{n+1},T+1\right),\qquad n=0,1,2,\ldots.\]

Intersect their full-measure derivative sets. Every \(t\in(0,T)\) belongs to at least one such interval because \(1/(n+1)\to0\). At that time the derivative equals the raw flux, so the pointwise flux bound gives

\[H'_t\le-\frac34 I_t+t^2L^2G_0+2tdL^2\quad\text{for almost every }t\in(0,T).\]

Each interval has a full-measure set of times where the local entropy derivative equals the flux. Their countable intersection still has full measure. For any positive time outside this null set, choose \(n\) with \(1/(n+1)<t\); the local chain rule then applies at that time. Inserting the pointwise flux estimate proves the derivative inequality. The argument makes no assertion about a derivative at zero, where the initial law need not have a smooth density.

The local entropy identity supplies its derivative almost everywhere, and the pointwise flux bound holds at every positive time with finite energies. Intersecting these full-measure time conditions yields one almost-everywhere derivative inequality suitable for integration.
